summary: A list of ward meeting places in the Sun of November 29, 1898 has, for the Eleventh Ward, 'Mechanics' Hall, York road, opposite Merryman's lane'. An earlier version of this entry took the hall for the building on this corner. It was across York Road: Polk's directories of 1901 and 1903 list 'Mechanics' Hall, 1045 York rd', an odd, east-side number, which was also the address of the Waverly Bottling Works and of Waverly Lodge No. 42. 'Opposite Merryman's lane' therefore means facing the mouth of the lane from the east side. The hall at the corner itself in these years was Sinclair's Hall. Which present-day lot 1045 York road is has not been settled on a map, so the entry remains here for now.

summary: The Sun of April 19, 1900, under 'Died On The York Road. James H. Barrett Stricken With Apoplexy': 'James H. Barrett, of 1609 Aisquith street, suffered an attack of apoplexy yesterday morning, about 9.30 o'clock, and fell in front of Riley's saloon on the York road, near Merryman's lane. He was carried into the tinshop of James Sinclair, at York road and Merryman's lane, by Officer James Boone, of the Northern district, and two citizens, but died before a physician could be summoned.' 'Riley's saloon' is William H. Reilley's, on the license list at 1102 York road that March; this corner's part is the pavement in front of it. The tinshop was a separate building: Polk's 1901 directory lists Wallace W. Sinclair, stoves, at 1042 York road, south of the lane. The same article is filed on 3224 Greenmount.

summary: Real-estate notice in the Sun of October 1, 1910: 'Five two-story brick houses, Nos. 1100, 1102, 1104, 1112 and 1114 York road, near Merryman's Lane, have been transferred by the Auxiliary Realty Company to the Cityco Realty Company, in fee.' The Evening Sun of the same day has the same transfer ('Five neat two-story brick dwellings'). 1100 and 1102 are this corner (today's 3200-3202) and 1104 is 3204; 1112 was James E. Sinclair's house in the directories of 1887-1901, about today's 3220. Thompson's 1889 plat letters both the apex lot and the lots at 1112-1114 'J. E. Sinclair', so the five were at least in part the old Sinclair holdings. On November 10, 1910 Cityco sold 1100 and 1102 back to Auxiliary, and in June 1911 the corner went to Frederick H. Samstag and wife. Update Oct. 17, 2026 (S.C.L. 2610/401 read): the transfer is read (752:mdlr-scl2610-402-auxiliary-cityco-five-lots-1910): Auxiliary's deed of Sept. 30, 1910 to Cityco, S.C.L. 2610/402, in fee, for $5 and other considerations, with a $9,000 purchase-money mortgage back (2610/403); the five houses are 1100, 1102, 1104, 1112 and 1114 York Road, the west-side frontage from Merryman's Lane north about 181 ft.

summary: The Sun's list of transfers, June 9, 1911, prints two consecutive lines for this corner: 'Auxiliary Realty Company to Elizabeth Pangiris, n.w.c. York road and Merrymans lane, 36.10 1/4 x 55', and 'Real Estate Pooling Company to Frederick H. Samstag and wife, 1100 and 1102 York road; 36.10 1/4 x 55, g.r. $120'. The two lines give the same dimensions, 36 feet 10 1/4 inches by 55 feet. How title passed from Pangiris to the Real Estate Pooling Company is not shown, and the deeds have not been read; Elizabeth Pangiris also took three lots from trustees in 1905, and her role is not established. The Samstags took the corner subject to a ground rent of $120 a year. The lot was already about its present width (the deeds since 1976 say 36 feet 1/2 inch); Thompson's 1889 plat had given the apex lot 28.8 feet. An earlier version of this entry named Auxiliary Realty as the Samstags' grantor.

summary: ★ FATAL ACCIDENT: John L. Schlick, 55, construction foreman, killed in a 20-foot fall from a ladder while building the Provident branch at 3111 Greenmount
data: {"url":"https://www.newspapers.com/image/369692065","page":"17","evidence":"The Evening Sun, 9 September 1936, p.17 (image 369692065), read in full from the page scan 2026-08-11. Headline 'FOREMAN, 55, DIES IN FALL OFF LADDER / John L. Schlick Fractures His Skull In 20-Foot Drop To Sidewalk'. Verbatim: 'John L. Schlick, construction foreman, was killed today in a fall from a ladder at a building project at 3111 Greenmount avenue. What caused him to fall was not known. Other workers said he was ascending the ladder, braced against the front wall of the new building, and at the top lost his balance and dropped backward. He struck his head on the sidewalk twenty feet below.' Pronounced dead on arrival at Mercy Hospital, skull fractured. 'The building on which he was employed is being erected for use as a branch of the Provident Savings Bank.' Aged 55, of 26 Mallow Avenue, Catonsville. summary: Eliza and Mary Moses and their brother James Moses sued Charles C. Fulton, proprietor of the Baltimore American, in the Court of Common Pleas for $10,000 in libel damages. The claim was over an article of the 17th inst. (Jan 17, 1881) calling their house at the corner of Huntington avenue and Bartlett street, near Waverly, haunted. The article also said their father was a gypsy (he was an Englishman) and that their brother hanged himself (he did not). The plaintiffs live in the adjoining house, and the 'haunted' one has been rented to a family for over ten months. Their counsel, Mr. Salmon, suspects the rumors were started by someone who wants to force a sale and profit from the planned opening of Bartlett street through the property.

summary: Silas Peirce, born in Baltimore County and now of Oregon, Holt County, Missouri, recalls the York turnpike from Towsontown to Baltimore about sixty years earlier (c. 1826). Heading south he names Bowen & Sons' smithy, Govanstown near the 4-mile stone, Loudenslager's and Synard's taverns and Gill's saddlery. Next came the 'two-mile gate', kept by a man named Mumma, probably David, with several public houses near it: John Given's tavern north of the gate on the east side and Bowers's grocery on the west side. A short distance below the gate stood a large two-story building kept as a public house by Walker, popular with soldiers from Baltimore and Fort McHenry. Farther south were a large brick mansion on the west side, Starr's tavern on the east side, Jenkins's stone tanyard at the first mile stone, a stone wall with six old cannon on the east side, and the Hay Scale Tavern (Jacob Brookhardt; earlier Father Shealey). He also recalls an 1828 political meeting at or near the two-mile gate with Gen. Stansbury, James M. Buchanan and Philpot, and a gathering at Slade's tavern. The editor adds that the two-mile gate is the same toll-gate now in Waverly, a town of several thousand. The cannon wall is now the Greenmount Cemetery wall, and nearly five miles of the road are built up, with a horse railway.

summary: William Hoffman, 85, the city's last old-time lamplighter, died Nov. 14, 1969 at the Bolton Hill Nursing Home. summary: Deed made Feb. 19, 1992 and recorded March 18, 1992 (Liber S.E.B. 3136, folios 493 to 496; read on the scan): American Pants Company of Baltimore, Inc., a Maryland corporation, 'formerly Sample Stores of Baltimore, Inc.', by its vice-president, conveys to Jong Sul Kang in fee simple, for $220,000, 'the same lots of ground which by Deed dated June 10, 1974 and recorded ... in Liber RHB No. 3139, folio 15 was granted and conveyed by Jack O. Chertkof, Trustee, unto Sample Stores of Baltimore, Inc.', adding that Sample Stores of Baltimore 'is now known as American Pants Company of Baltimore, Inc. pursuant to Articles of Amendment'. The seller certifies that the sale is not of all or substantially all of its assets. Exhibit A, a survey description by NTT Associates, Inc., makes the two 1974 lots one parcel: beginning on the east side of Greenmount Avenue at the end of the first line of the lot M. Estelle Bateman deeded to the Provident Savings Bank on March 18, 1904 (R.O. 2062/398), at the north wall of the building, 218.29 ft south of the southeast corner of Greenmount Avenue and Thirty-Second Street; south 46.98 ft to the center of a thirteen-inch party wall; east 101.67 ft to the west side of Old York Road 'as established by Baltimore City in June 1967'; north 51.06 ft; and west 114.60 ft along the north face of the building, 'containing 5,220.6 square feet, more or less, the improvement thereon being know as 3107 Greenmount Avenue'. The exhibit abbreviates the 1974 parties as 'Jack O'Chertkof surviving Trustee' and 'Sample Stores, Inc.' American Pants was a clothing retailer, the Sample Store, not a garment maker.

summary: 1972-10-18: On the death of Evelyn D. Vinson, personal representatives (Richard V. & Robert D. Blackwell, Nancy C. McClain) conveyed 2601 Greenmount Ave (Block 4070) to Robert D. Blackwell and Nancy C. McClain (DEED, Book 2957 pp.742-744). READ IN FULL (RHB 2957/742-744, made 10/4/1972, rec. 10/18/1972): Richard V. Blackwell, Robert David Blackwell and Nancy C. McClain, personal representatives of the Estate of Evelyn D. Vinson (d. 2/15/1972 testate; Estate No. 15167, Orphans Court of Anne Arundel County) convey to Robert David Blackwell and Nancy C. McClain as tenants in common, $5, no title examination. Lot: E side Greenmount ('formerly called York Road'), beginning 400 ft south of the SE corner of 27th St ('formerly called Oxford Street'), 25 x 200 ft; improvements known as No. 2601 Greenmount Ave; RESERVING a 20-ft strip off the rear for the 40-ft street 'now known as BOONE STREET.' ★ RECITAL: the same lot which by deed of May 15, 1961, Liber J.F.C. 1070/378, was conveyed by EDGAR D. PHOEBUS and FLORENCE L. PHOEBUS, his wife, to Robert L. Vinson and Evelyn D. Vinson; Robert L. Vinson died 11/20/1970. THE PHOEBUS FAMILY held 2601 until 1961 — and the kinship to 2701's 'Omar E. Phoebus & Sons' is PROVEN: Omar Ellwood Phoebus was Edgar D. and Florence's son (1939-40 court dockets naming 'his parents'; Edgar's 1961 and Omar's 1965 obituaries). One family, two corners. Attorneys Goodman, Meagher & Enoch; notarized Harford County. [CONFIRMED BY DEED, 2026-07-15: JFC 1070/378 pulled and read — Phoebus to Vinson, May 15, 1961, exactly as recited; Edgar signed by mark.]

summary: James E. Sinclair conveyed a lot on the York Turnpike at the corner of Merryman's Lane to Robert Riddell Brown, then leased it back. Baltimore County real estate transfers of June 17, 1887, as printed in the Sun of June 20: 'James E. Sinclair and wife to Robert Riddell Brown, lot on York turnpike, corner of Merryman's lane, $1,200. Robert Riddell Brown to James E. Sinclair, lease of last-mentioned lot, rent $60.' A sale and lease-back of this kind created a ground rent of $60 a year on the lot. Which corner is not stated, and Sinclair had ground on both sides of the lane: the apex lot north of it (this parcel) and a corner lot south of it, which an 1885 sale notice describes as conveyed to him by Austin Dall, trustee. The apex carried a ground rent of $120, not $60, when the Samstags took it in 1911. The entry stays here as possible until the two county instruments are read. The same clipping is filed on 3224 Greenmount. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Sinclair held the fork north of Merryman's Lane from 1872 (Huff's 'Huntington' leasehold, 10 perches on the road, 752:mdlr-eha74-321-huff-sinclair-huntington-1872) and the Wilson lot next north from 1872 to 1873 (768:mdlr-jb84-387-wilson-trustees-sinclair-reversion-1873), so the 1887 'corner of Merryman's lane' is more likely this corner (still an inference). Update Oct. 16, 2026 (J.W.S. 162 read): both County instruments are read. Sinclair and wife to Robert Riddell Brown, June 13, 1887, $1,200, in fee (J.W.S. 162/70, 752:mdlr-jws162-70-sinclair-brown-apex-fee-1200-1887), and Brown's lease back of June 14 at $60 (J.W.S. 162/71): the lot is the apex at the corner of the York Turnpike and Merryman's Lane, 36 ft 1/2 in to a division wall, 42 ft back and 55 ft on the lane, so the corner here is this apex, no longer an inference.

summary: Classifieds in the Sun of April 22 and 23, 1929, three months after Frederick H. Samstag's death, read: '3200 GREENMOUNT AVE. Cor. Merryman Lane. Apply H. M. Moser, 801-803 Fidelity Bldg.' The heading above the notice is cut off in the clippings; it stands among real-estate listings and was evidently an offer to rent, since that June the widow leased the building to Benjamin A. Kriger. The notice names no owner. An earlier version of this entry attributed it to the Waverly Corporation's broker; the Waverly Corporation was the owner of 3236 Greenmount, which Kriger leased in December 1935, and has no known tie to this corner. Nor is this the first use of the address: the directories print 3200 Greenmount from 1913 and the license lists from 1916.

summary: Sale notices offered the fee-simple two-story brick corner restaurant building 'known as 3200 Greenmount Ave. (corner 32nd Street)': first a trustee's sale on the premises for February 17, 1983 (Sun, February 13), then an assignee's sale for March 31, 1983 (Sun, March 13 and 27), signed Vicki B. Finkelstein, Assignee, with A. J. Billig & Co. as auctioneers. The notices describe a restaurant kitchen and food-preparation room on the first floor and rest rooms and storage on the second, rented, 'from information received', at $550 a month, on a lot fronting 36 feet on Greenmount Avenue and 55 feet on Merryman's Lane. The assignment of the defaulted 1976 mortgage to Finkelstein is dated March 3, 1983 (S.E.B. 23/855). Whether either sale was held is not shown by anything read. The owner, The Hotspot Family Restaurant, Inc., was in the United States Bankruptcy Court under case 83-B-0571, and it was the corporation itself, as debtor in possession, that deeded the corner to Young H. Kim in April 1985 (S.E.B. 537/359).

summary: The block sits in the old village of Huntingdon on the York Turnpike (York Rd = later Greenmount Ave). Baltimore City annexed Waverly in 1888 and converted its lanes to the numbered street grid — so by the 1901 city directory these buildings are already '443/445/447 E 25th St,' NOT 'Huntingdon Ave.' A SEPARATE Huntingdon Avenue survived on the west/Hampden side of the city (house numbers in the 800s–900s, meeting 25th at 221 W 25th) and still exists today.

summary: 'Treutlein, Edward L., 2452 Greenmount Ave ... 12' appears in a Baltimore civic name-list printed in the German-language Der Deutsche Correspondent (published July 2, 3 & 5, 1909): ~27 residents from across the city, each with an address, a ward number (Treutlein = Ward 12, Waverly), and some marked '(verheiratet)' married or '(Wittwe)' widow. Because the list includes WOMEN, it is NOT a 1909 jury venire; the format (names + address + marital status + ward, run three days) fits a naturalization or court/legal notice, though the column heading isn't legible in the scan and the LoC full-text blocked automated retrieval. NOTE: the 1909 Polk directory lists the Amos/Ward household at 2452, so Treutlein's exact tie to this house is unconfirmed (a short-term resident, or a contact address) — the value here is placing him, a German-American, at the address in the German community's paper.

summary: The building at 2602–2608 Greenmount (Block 3836A, a ~9,400 sq ft brick warehouse built 1910) was the home of GREENMOUNT MOVING & STORAGE CO., founded 1915 by George Roscoe Conklin (1887–1966) and run by the Conklin family for ~75 years, to 1990. George married Bertha Florence Callender in 1908; their sons worked the business — Herbert E. Conklin's 1940 WWII draft card names his employer as 'George R. Conklin / Green Mount Storage, 2608 Greenmount Ave' — and the 1950 U.S. Census lists George R. Conklin (62) at the address, occupation 'furniture moving.' The company's original hand-painted truck signage still survives. (The 1922–23 city directory also shows a small 'soft drinks' parlor in a corner bay of the complex, and the 2600 corner earlier held a veterinary surgeon then a blacksmith/auto shop.)

summary: The '2643 ball player' (Polk lists him as Robert W. MacLeary, occupation 'ballplayer,' 1915-17) is identified as minor-league pitcher 'CHALKY' McCLEARY (b. Jan 19, 1892; 'MacLeary'/'McCleary' spelling variant). His pro career ran 1913-1922: the Waterbury Contenders (Eastern Assn), the Portsmouth Truckers (Virginia League), and the Blue Ridge League - chiefly the HAGERSTOWN TERRIERS. His standout year was 1916 with Hagerstown: 18-8, 2.57 ERA over 235 innings - 3rd in the Blue Ridge League in wins and the best win-loss pct among the top starters, in the same Class-D league as future St. Louis Cardinals star Bill Sherdel. He played Class C/D ball out of town but kept his Baltimore home at 2643 Greenmount with his widowed mother Jessie (which is why the off-season Polk directory lists him here). His Waverly neighbor and 1915-16 Portsmouth/Hagerstown TEAMMATE was catcher Krozer 'Doc' Milliman (b. Feb 13, 1886, Baltimore; 2449 Greenmount; a 10-season minor-leaguer, 1906-16, who caught for the 1912 Anderson Electricians in the Carolina Association of Charlotte-Hornets-game-fixing infamy) - the two of them part of a documented cluster of men who listed 'ballplayer' as their occupation along Greenmount within a few blocks of Oriole Park, 1915-17 (2643, 2449, and 2825 Greenmount) - a grouping I've informally called 'ballplayers' row' (a descriptor, not a period name).

summary: The twin storefront at 2637-2639 Greenmount was HARVEY'S ORIOLE TAVERN (Harvey's Oriole Tavern Inc, by 1972). The 'Oriole' name comes from the neighborhood ballpark: Terrapin Park / 'Old' Oriole Park stood two blocks north (29th-30th & Greenmount), built 1914 for the Federal League Terrapins, renamed Oriole Park by Jack Dunn in 1916 (the International League club — Lefty Grove pitched at this park in the 1920s; Babe Ruth's 1914 Orioles stint was at the adjacent, earlier Oriole Park across 29th St, a common conflation), and burned July 3-4, 1944. From 1977-1985 the tavern's real estate and license were held by the SAPPERSTEIN family — Gilbert Sapperstein (1932-2016), Baltimore's best-known liquor-license broker (secured creditor to failing bars via his Star Coin Machine Co. and Allstate Boiler Service; later tangled in gambling charges and a 2005 city-schools bribery case; father of developer Mark Sapperstein of Silo Point/McHenry Row), his wife Sondra, and his brother Jerome 'Jerry' Sapperstein (1938-2023) and Rita. Later McKinley H. Waites (1985) -> Bessey Ikem & Odile Koudou (2004) -> Caring Hands Health Solutions (2016). ('Harvey' himself — the pre-1972 namesake — is not yet identified.)

summary: George Roscoe Conklin, founder of the Greenmount storage business, was born in 1887 in Sunnybrook (rural Baltimore County near Phoenix), attended Sunnybrook School and Baltimore Polytechnic Institute, and worked as a contractor and builder before entering the warehouse business ~1910. Per his Evening Sun obituary, 'both of his warehouses at 2604 Greenmount avenue were built by his construction firm' - he literally built the buildings his moving-and-storage company ran from. A member of Chestnut Grove Presbyterian Church (Sunnybrook) and the Junior Order of United American Mechanics, he died of a heart attack at his home on Merrymans Mill Road on Feb. 7, 1966, and is buried in Chestnut Grove Presbyterian Church Cemetery, Phoenix, alongside his parents Walter H. Conklin (1853-1936) and Barbara Brown Conklin (1852-1892). Wife: Bertha Florence Callender (1883-1967).

summary: 3130 Greenmount Avenue was the general offices of THE HOOPER FOOD CO., Inc., a Baltimore seafood-restaurant chain. It began with G. Carroll Hooper, a stockbroker ruined by the 1929 crash, who in December 1932 opened a seafood restaurant in a converted one-car garage at 511 Gorsuch Ave in Waverly. 'Hooper's' grew into a small chain: restaurants at 511 Gorsuch Ave, 415 E 32nd St, and 3 W Chesapeake Ave (Towson), plus seafood stores at 3200 Old York Rd and the North Avenue Market - a food business strung right along the York Road/Greenmount spine. Its menus survive in the Enoch Pratt Free Library's 'Maryland Menus' collection (Digital Maryland). Its flagship 511 Gorsuch Ave location later became Eddie & Brooks Robinson's Gorsuch House restaurant (near Memorial Stadium) - so one corner carried a Depression-era seafood chain and, later, an Orioles Hall of Famer's restaurant.

summary: An Evening Sun 'Mr. Peep's Diary' column (Aug 24, 1966) caught Charles R. 'Bull' Robinson between his day job and his mat career: the boys at the John Eager Howard Recreation Center (Linden Ave & Konig St), where he was director, were startled to learn their director was a pro-wrestling 'baby face' (hero). The piece confirms he was an all-American guard at Morgan State (1947-51) and a pro lineman for the Green Bay Packers (1951) and Baltimore Colts (1954), and adds color: he learned that a lineman could 'pick up some nice change' wrestling from his Packers teammate 'Dick the Bruiser' (Dick Debruser), trained with wrestler Frank Veney at the YMCA, went on the road as a 'clean' grappler in 1955, and won some 70 matches from 'villains' before his first loss - beating the 234-pound Angelo Savoldi at the Baltimore Civic Center. He'd been a Bureau of Recreation athletic teacher ~9 years (earlier at the Lafayette Rec Center) and, at 225 lbs, still taught wrestling to teenaged boys 'only for body building and muscle coordination, never for competition.' In 1966 he lived at 2313 N. Monroe St.

summary: 2736 Greenmount Ave (the SE corner of Greenmount & 28th) was BULL ROBINSON'S LIQUORS, opened in the late 1960s and run for about 20 years by Charles Rogers 'Bull' Robinson until he sold it in 1989. Robinson (May 30, 1925 - Feb. 3, 2007) was a Lester Manor, Virginia native and a Morgan State College star - a physical-education graduate who captained both the football and boxing teams (two unbeaten football squads, 1949-50; All-CIAA; heavyweight boxing champion; Morgan State Athletic Hall of Fame, 1974). Drafted by the Green Bay Packers in 1951 as an offensive tackle (on the Packers' integrated roster), he played defensive middle guard for the BALTIMORE COLTS in 1953-54 - scoring his only NFL touchdown on Oct. 10, 1954, recovering a fumble in the end zone against the Chicago Bears. He then wrestled professionally in the 1960s (some 70 wins, debuting at the Baltimore Civic Center) and worked for the Baltimore Department of Recreation and Parks, directing the John Eager Howard Recreation Center in Reservoir Hill and coaching semipro football and basketball while steering his athletes to college scholarships. His wife of 23 years, Mazie Price, died in 1973; he died of cancer at 81 in Towson in 2007.

summary: Dr. Bertha E. Tapman kept her physician's home office at 2733 Greenmount (1915-23). A Baltimore native, she graduated the Woman's Medical College of Baltimore in 1906, worked at Johns Hopkins' Harriet Lane Clinic and as physical examiner at the Baltimore City Juvenile Court (1907-12), then ran a general practice specializing in obstetrics & gynecology — 'delivered babies at home and in Baltimore hospitals' — keeping the Greenmount office plus a second on W. North Ave. She married Dr. Maurice E. Shamer; their daughter Miriam Shamer Daly also became a physician, and living descendants still hold Dr. Tapman's diploma. She was socially close to the art-collecting Cone sisters.

summary: The physician who kept a home office at 2733 Greenmount (listed 1915-1923) was Dr. Bertha Tapman Shamer, one of Baltimore's longtime woman gynecologist-obstetricians. She graduated cum laude from the Women's Medical College of Baltimore in 1907 at just 20 - too young to be licensed in Maryland, so she worked a year in the Johns Hopkins pharmacy until old enough. She was associated with Johns Hopkins Hospital 1909-14 and served as an examiner for the Juvenile Court 1915-22 (overlapping her 2733 practice), then spent most of her life in private practice, delivering babies in homes and hospitals and seeing patients into her 80s. She married Dr. Maurice E. Shamer, a fellow obstetrician-gynecologist (they met at Church Home & Hospital); their children Dr. Miriam S. Daly, Margaret S. Petersen, and Dr. David H. Shamer largely followed into medicine. A charter member of the Maryland branch of the Women's American Medical Association. She moved to Albion, Michigan in 1974 and died there May 15, 1978, aged 91.

summary: The 2800 block is the ballpark block. The 1915 Sanborn shows the WEST (even) side of Greenmount between 28th and 29th as 'Oriole Park - International League Base Ball Park' (grandstand, bleachers, office), with 'Terrapin Park - Federal League Base Ball Grounds' (the 1914-15 Baltimore Terrapins) on the next block up (29th-30th) - both 'Closed at Time of Survey.' The even-side rowhouses (2800, 2802, 2810...) were built only after the old park was cleared (~1920). The odd (east) side was a brick 3-story residential row - including 2825, home of the Russell ballplayers, directly across from the park.

summary: 2825 Greenmount was the 1910s home of the Russell baseball family: father Charles A. Russell (carpenter), mother Mary K., five sons and three daughters (per SABR). Three sons pitched professionally - Clarence 'Lefty' Russell, Allan E. 'Rubberarm' Russell (1924 World Series champ; see other entries), and Frank Russell (Roanoke, Virginia League, 1911). The 1914 Polk lists Allen and Frank as 'ballplayer' at 2825 with their carpenter father. The family MOVED NORTH within the corridor to reach this block: the 1901 Polk lists Charles Russell at '2650 York Rd' = '2650 Greenmount' - the SAME house under both the old road-name and the new grid number (in the lower corridor the York Rd and Greenmount numbers coincided, unlike the 3200s where York Rd kept its own 1000s numbering) - and by 1914 they had moved about two blocks north to 2825 Greenmount, at 28th St directly across from Oriole Park.

summary: 2841 Greenmount (pre-1919 '2833'; earlier '2829 York Rd') was the Coggins home, near neighbors of the ballplaying Russells at 2825. Father Edward R. Coggins ran an express/transfer business; sons were Edward R. Coggins Jr. (clerk), Howard R. (lineman/foreman), David (a Baltimore Sun paper carrier), and daughter Grace (stenographer). The family held 2841 Greenmount into the 1940s (all the parents and Edward Jr. died there - an earlier note that they 'left ~1922-23' was WRONG). The baseball tie is DOCUMENTED and now corroborated by age: SABR says Hagerstown 'sent their second baseman, Eddie Coggins, a neighbor of Russell's,' to sign 18-year-old Lefty in 1908, and the Baltimore Sun box score of Sept 5 1908 shows 'Coggins, 2b ... Russell, p' together. Edward R. Coggins Jr. died Dec 30 1946 AGED 63 - i.e. born ~1883 - exactly the right age for the ~25-year-old Hagerstown second baseman of 1908, confirming he is the 'Eddie Coggins' who signed his neighbor Lefty.

summary: Clarence 'Lefty' Russell (b.1890-d.1962) came up on corridor sandlots: the Frisby Stars and the 25th Street Christian Church Sunday-school nine, which he led to consecutive league titles in 1906-07 (the church stood on the north side of E 25th St between Calvert and Guilford Ave). Baltimore church baseball was a thriving world then - a Catholic League (St. Andrew's, Holy Cross, St. Gerard's, St. John's, St. Clement's, St. Michael's), an Episcopal 'Church League' (Church of the Messiah, St. Paul's), and the Sunday-school circuit Russell's team won. In June 1908, at 18, he signed with Hagerstown (Sunset League); the man the club sent to sign him was its second baseman EDDIE COGGINS - his own Greenmount neighbor from up the block (2833/2841) - and the two then played together (Baltimore Sun box score, Sept 5 1908: 'Coggins, 2b ... Russell, p'). Two years later his 24-14, 219-K season for the IL Orioles - at the park across from 2825 - made him Connie Mack's record $12,000 purchase.

summary: The west (even) side of the 2900 block, between E 29th and E 30th, WAS the ballpark. The 1915 Sanborn (sheet 710, Block 3) labels it 'TERRAPIN PARK - FEDERAL LEAGUE BASEBALL GROUNDS - CLOSED AT TIME OF SURVEY' - an all-FRAME (wood) grandstand ~22 ft high with a main Grand Stand and Pavilions A & B, and a run of OPEN BLEACHERS fronting directly on Greenmount across the mid-block (roughly 2906-2928, where the Polk shows no houses). Built for the Federal League Baltimore Terrapins (1914-15); the Polk lists it as 'Balto Baseball Co / Federal League Baseball Co, Greenmount av c 29th' (1914-15). After the Federal League folded, Jack Dunn's International League Orioles moved in and it became 'Oriole Baseball Park' (Polk, 1918) - the park where the IL Orioles won seven straight pennants (1919-25) and the Negro-NL Elite Giants played (1938-42), until it burned July 3-4, 1944. This parcel (2920) sits on the old bleacher frontage.

summary: A full-page Baltimore Sun Sunday feature (Feb 26 1911, by C. Starr Matthews) profiled the corridor's Lefty Russell as a clean-living local boy - 'a star athlete who leads simple life,' with 'no bad habit,' a 'model man for a team,' who as a boy 'did not care much about attending school' and instead 'regularly went frog shooting… on the banks of the brickyard pond' with a little rifle ('Lefty was a crack shot'), a hobby the paper credits for his batting eye ('a good batter, a clever pool player and a splendid bowler'). It fixes his boyhood haunts on the corridor: he swam 'on the banks of Herring Run, near the famous old race course,' and 'hooked school regularly to go swimming.' It notes he toughened up 'in the winter of 1909 in a lumber camp,' then 'made good in the Eastern League and… was bought by Connie Mack,' with a debut for the Athletics against the Boston Red Sox in which he 'twice fanned Tris Speaker' and 'became a hero.' The piece gives his real name as Clarence Dixon Russell (this paper's spelling; SABR has 'Dickson') and notes he would turn 21 on July 8, 1911.

summary: The feature traces Lefty's climb. Hagerstown's Eddie Coggins - a York Road neighbor - saw 'the making of a great twirler' and tipped his manager to sign the boy in 1908: 'that is the way those York road boys take care of each other.' Lefty in turn got his Sunday-school catcher Will Callahan signed. Oriole VP Moses N. Frank re-signed Lefty for Baltimore by meeting him on the street and beating Savannah's offer by $50/month to keep him home; Lefty picked up his 'spitter' at Wilkes-Barre under Mal Kittridge (1909). To toughen up for 1910 he and three companions - Tommy Bell, CHALKY McCLEARY (a fellow corridor ballplayer, 2643 Greenmount up the block), and his own brother Howard Russell - spent the winter of 1909 chopping wood at a lumber camp just north of Towson (up York Road); the shy Lefty's only recorded dinner-table words were 'I think I will, please' to an offer of lemon pie. His Athletics debut against Boston, twice fanning Tris Speaker, made him a hero - though, not knowing Speaker, he told Eddie Collins 'they all look alike to me.'

summary: The 1911 Sun feature explains how the Russell boys became ballplayers: 'they learned to play the game with the balls that were hit over the fences of Oriole Park, for they have lived near the ballpark for years,' and were on the professional diamond 'before they had cast aside short trousers.' All THREE brothers pitched for the same 25th Street Christian Sunday-school team - Lefty, Allen ('mastered the art of twirling with both hands' - AMBIDEXTROUS), and Frank (a right-hander bound for Roanoke) - 'two more prospects for $12,000 beauties in the Russell family.' Lefty's first team was the Frisby Stars, a Frisby-street sandlot nine (ages 10-13) that played 'on grounds back of Oriole Park' (a May 11 1906 Sun notice names its manager as George Annan of Mount St, Waverly). Its neighborhood rivals were the Boone Rippers and the Oxford Sluggers, the Russell and Bonthron families fighting 'running down the York road.'

summary: The Frisby-street sandlot world that produced Lefty Russell had a documented cast. The Frisby Stars' rivals were the BOONE RIPPERS - a real Waverly youth nine advertising for games as early as 1903 (Baltimore Sun, Aug 6 1903, contacts Norfleet Mercer & C.E. Harris) - and the OXFORD SLUGGERS, named for Oxford Avenue (the Waverly street that became modern E 27th St). The 'other' ballplaying family the 1911 feature paired with the Russells, the BONTHRONS, were real ballplayers: Harry L. Bonthron is listed by occupation as 'ballplyr' in the 1909 Polk directory (400 Lorraine Ave, off the 2600 block of York Rd/Greenmount) and starred that same August for the Westminster semipro club - 'BONTHRON'S FINE WORK: He Makes Homers And Figures In Fast Double Plays' (Baltimore Sun, Aug 11 1909, p.9). The Scottish-descended Bonthron clan (stonecutters, machinists, printers) clustered just east of Greenmount (David C. at 412 Oxford Ave = ~411 E 27th St; Henry at 55 Gutman Ave). So the corridor's sandlot war centered on TWO ballplaying families a few blocks apart - Russells and Bonthrons. (Not related to the 1930s Princeton runner Bill Bonthron, a separate Detroit family.)

summary: The 'famous old race course' near Herring Run where the boy Lefty swam (per the 1911 Sun feature) is the documented HERRING RUN RACE COURSE - a 19th-century Baltimore track along Herring Run in NE Baltimore (named in the Baltimore Sun as early as Oct 8 1855, 'strayed or stolen from Herring Run race course,' and still a live reference in an 1889 classified). It sat in what is now the Herring Run Park / Clifton Park - Lake Montebello area, about 1.5-2 miles ENE of the Greenmount corridor; omnibuses carried gamblers out to it. It is a DIFFERENT track from the Govane's Town (York Road) course up in Govans (an earlier note that guessed 'Govans' is corrected here). Lefty's boyhood haunts thus reached NE toward Herring Run. [Map check, 2026-07-11: the 1877 Hopkins Waverly plate and the early-1900s Baltimore City Archives ownership plat (both now in the Data Room) were examined; both cover the York Road village core and stop short of Herring Run, so neither pins the course. Its precise footprint remains documented by name only — NE Baltimore, Herring Run corridor.]

summary: Harry L. Bonthron (b. ~1883, Baltimore) - the ballplaying son of the Bonthron family in the Frisby-street sandlot world - was a genuine minor-league professional, and a decade older than Lefty Russell. His Baseball-Reference register shows FIVE pro seasons, 1901-1905: Harrisburg and Reading of the Pennsylvania State League (Class D, 1901-02); Fargo of the Northern League (Class D, 1903 - 84 games, .200); Coatesville of the Pennsylvania League (independent, 1904); and the Norwich Reds of the Connecticut State League (Class B, 1905, his highest level). By 1909 he was back home, listed by occupation as 'ballplyr' (400 Lorraine Ave, off the 2600 block) and starring for the Westminster semipro club - 'Bonthron's Fine Work: He Makes Homers And Figures In Fast Double Plays' (Baltimore Sun, Aug 11 1909). So the corridor's 'other' ballplaying family, the Bonthrons, produced a real Class-B professional - a generation ahead of the Russell boys next door.

summary: The Russell parents were Charles A. Russell (carpenter) and Mary K. Russell, nee MILLS. Per SABR the 1900 census put nine children at 1906 York Road - SIX sons and three daughters (beyond Lefty, Allen, Frank, and Howard, two more sons remain unidentified). Charles A. Russell died suddenly Nov 4 1928, aged 76 (b. ~1852), and was buried at Loudon Park Cemetery; his wife Mary K. (nee Mills) had already predeceased him. His funeral was held from the home of his daughter, Mrs. James H. Strain, at 610 East 31st Street - the only one of the three Russell daughters yet identified (by married name). Allan 'Rubberarm' Russell died Oct 20 1972 (of 21 N Wickham Rd; Loudon Park, Spruce 46; survived by daughter Janette Russell); Lefty had died Jan 22 1962 (Dulaney Valley). The three sisters' given names still require the 1900/1910 census (login-gated).

summary: The Coggins were a serious ballplaying family a full decade before Eddie signed Lefty. In 1897 'Edward Coggins, c.' and 'Lawrence Coggins, c.f.' played for the youth nine the 'Lilies of the Valley' (ages 11-14; Baltimore Sun 'New Organizations' amateur-club directory, May 11 1897) - Edward at ~14 fits his ~1883 birth. By 1903 THREE Coggins brothers - William Coggins (1b), Edward Coggins (ss), and Lawrence (lf) - played for the Maryland Athletic Club, a nine the Amateur Athletic Union's Thomas K. Barrett declared PROFESSIONAL (because ex-pro Frank Bevans played on it); the M.A.C. played its games at ORIOLE PARK, the corridor ballpark blocks from the Coggins home (Baltimore Sun, 'Shock to M.A.C. Players,' May 30 1903). So Edward R. Coggins Jr.'s arc runs 1897 sandlot -> 1903 semipro at Oriole Park -> 1908 Hagerstown pro (where he signed his neighbor Lefty Russell).

summary: An Oct 1906 court docket (Court of Common Pleas) lists 'Daniel Coggins vs. United Railways and Electric Company' and 'Edward Coggins vs. same' - two Coggins family members with pending suits against Baltimore's streetcar monopoly (typical streetcar-accident/damage actions of the era), adding a Daniel Coggins to the family roster. CAUTION - two same-surname items are NOT this corridor family: (1) Hannah Henton Coggins, a Philadelphia artist who died in New York in 1902 (father Edward H. Coggins killed at Antietam) is a separate Philadelphia family; (2) an 1867 Baltimore County divorce, Mary Amanda Coggins vs. Edward Coggins (he abandoned her in 1862 and left Maryland), is an earlier Baltimore Coggins of unconfirmed relation. Do not conflate either with the 2841 Greenmount Cogginses.

summary: Polk lists 'Sinclair Jas M, tinner, 1001 York rd' from 1907 to 1913, 'plumber, 3011 Greenmt av' from 1915 to 1921, and 'metalwkr, 3011 Greenmt av' in 1923. The 1914 volume misprints the number as 3101 in the alphabetical entry and 3001 in the business list; the 1922 alphabetical entry reads 'Jas M (Ena) sheet metal wks 3013 Greenmt av' while that year's business list keeps 3011. The shop was not his home: he lived at 410 Waverly Avenue (410 East 31st Street) in 1903-08 and at 2116, later 2118, Oak Avenue from 1909. The 1915 Sanborn plate letters the two-story brick building 'Plumbing & Tin Shop', the 1928 plate '3011 / 1003 TIN SHOP'. He and his wife bought the 3011 lot from J. Holliday Reipe on March 1, 1927 (S.C.L. 4707/12, known from recitals), and the National Register inventory says the building 'was used for many years as James M. Sinclair's sheet metal workshop', citing the directories of 1928 and 1937. He died Jan. 6, 1948 (Baltimore City estate OLD48532). He came from the Sinclair family of the 3200 block: Polk 1901, read on the page, has 'Sinclair Jas M, tinner, 1112 York rd' beside 'Sinclair Jas E, clk, 1112 York rd', and Wallace W. Sinclair was a tinner at 1102 York road in 1888-89. The same couple held the 3111 Greenmount ground until 1934, and in 1940 the Evening Sun quoted James M. Sinclair's memory of the York turnpike tollgate. An earlier note of a 'John G. Sinclair' at 3011, and of the shop as home and business, is not borne out by the directories.

summary: Polk lists four building and loan associations at 3015 Greenmount in the early 1920s: the Echodale Bldg & Loan Assn (842 N. Eutaw St. in 1920; 3015 in 1921, 1922 and 1923), the Republic Bldg & Loan Assn (1921, 1922), the Civic Bldg Assn or Bldg & Loan Assn (1922, 1923) and the Waverly-Guilford Bldg Assn (1922, 1923). There is no separate 'Guilford' association: the name is the Waverly-Guilford's. The Civic was incorporated in May 1921 with $1,300,000 authorised capital by Rodney J. Brooks, John J. Kernan and Edward B. Smith, and the Waverly-Guilford in February 1921 with $20,000 by Harry B. Onion, Arthur B. Thompson and Gordon Gambrill (Manufacturers Record). The Rainy Day association, at 3015 in 1917-20, had moved to 501 E. 20th St. Next door, Polk 1923 lists the York Road Bldg Assn at 3017, which it had owned since 1921. One small brick office carried four associations at once, a pattern also seen at 3001 Greenmount in 1922.

The Leight family's later title is recited from 1931: 3010 by assignment from Lula Smith to Charles T. and Ella B. Leight, 1931 (S.C.L. 5263/428), with deeds from William H. Wolfe of 1948 and 1950; 3020 from William H. Flayhart Jr., the Leights' son-in-law, and his wife, 1932 (S.C.L. 5328/111); a Vineyard Lane lot from Wolfe, 1953. 1953-03-02: Charles T. summary: 3036 was the south part of the 3036-3038 lot until 2021. Its chain up to 2013 is on 3038: the Ruppersbergers to Irvin A. Forrest in 1975; Forrest's 1985 ground lease to the Carters; Brown, Jones and Pettiford in 1993; Peter S. Lee Realty from about 1994; S & B Developers 2 LLC in 2013, financed by PeoplesBank (released April 2022, MB 24514/199). The state's records put the combined lot's 1994 sale ($25,500) and 2013 sale ($118,000) on this account. In March 2021 S & B assigned 3036 for $66,150 to Equity Trust Company as custodian for Rhonda Johnson's IRA (MB 23168/383), but used the whole lot's description; a deed of correction in 2022 (MB 24850/446) cut it back to 3036 alone, clearing the way for the 3038 sale. The March 2022 survey shows the lot as 10 feet wide and 1,562 square feet under a two-story frame house. The $120 ground rent under it was the Nochumowitzes' from 1999 and bail-bond collateral from 2008 to 2019 (release MB 21139/99).

summary: Ruppersberger family: Gusta Ruppersberger sold John Schuman a slice on January 13, 1873 (Baltimore County EHA 79/37), which the later deeds except; that slice is probably 3034. The Ruppersberger and Magers trustees sold the rest to Irvin A. Forrest in July 1975 (RHB 3265/573), bought with a same-day Patapsco Federal loan (3265/576) that was released in 1984. On March 11, 1985 Forrest sold the buildings as a leasehold to Darrell K. Carter, Lee Carter and Daniel Allen and kept a $240 ground rent (SEB 465/473); they borrowed from Golden Prague (465/476). June 12, 1990: Lee and Daniel assign to their brother Darrell (SEB 2508/532), who pledges it with three other houses to Regal Savings in 1991 (SEB 2749/467). May 20, 1993: Darrell sells to Brown, Jones and Pettiford, Inc. of 3042 Greenmount for $42,000 (SEB 3688/480). About October 1994: Peter S. Lee Realty, Inc. buys, probably for $25,500 (deed SEB 4534/419, not pulled), and borrows from Westview Federal in 1996 (SEB 5700/312); the Lees owned 3040-3044 next door from 1992 to 1998. April 17, 2013: Peter and Grace Lee, as surviving shareholders and trustees of the company, sell to S & B Developers 2 LLC for $118,000 (FMC 15154/58). S & B splits it. 3036 goes to Equity Trust Company as custodian for Rhonda Johnson's IRA in May 2021 for $66,150 (MB 23168/383). 3038 goes to Naoui LLC on April 5, 2022 for $106,000 (MB 24850/453), to Yeza LLC on August 17, 2023 for $127,200 (XAC 26243/88), and to Acorn Developers Ventures LLC on March 18, 2025 for $184,440 (XAC 27809/97). The ground: Forrest's $240 rent became two $120 rents, one per house, held by Paul and Amy Nochumowitz under a 1999 deed (8354/146) and pledged to a bail-bond company from 2008 to 2019. Open: the 1985 lease price, the 1994 and 2013 deeds, and who holds the ground rent now.

summary: 1937: Ruppersberger family to George E. Zepp (Liber SCL 5767/252). 1944: George and his wife Matilda take title jointly (M.L.P. 6612/428, via Helen M. Bordley). 1949: George dies about August 2 and Matilda holds it alone. 1976: Matilda sells to Morris, Leo and Herman Bloom, trading as Bloom Realty (R.H.B. 3339/45), and carries a $30,000 mortgage paid off in October 1983. Bloom Realty used 3042 as its address. 1992: Howard Alan Bloom sells to Peter and Grace Lee (3366/367). 1998: the Lees sell to Monica Ann Brown for $148,000 (FMC 7977/302), with First Union and seller financing. In 2003 she refinanced with Wachovia, and by 2006 she lived in Florida. March 2013: it leaves her name for $110,320, coded by the state as not arm's length (a foreclosure, gift or auction). That buyer's deed is 15075/383 and the buyer is not yet named. About July 2013: 3040 Greenmount LLC buys it for $190,000 (15473/448). The LLC refinances in 2014, pays off in June 2024, and sells to O & O Realty Inc. for $700,000 in October 2024. Each state sales row names the seller's own deed, not the new one. Open: the 1937, 1944 and 1992 deeds themselves; how Bloom Realty passed to Howard Alan Bloom; the March 2013 buyer.

summary: The Waverly Building Association of Baltimore County leased the lot from James M. Biggs on October 10, 1910 for 99 years at $72 (SCL 2613/232) and had its office here by 1920. It gave part to The Lakeshire Company in 1931 (SCL 5252/353) and bought the ground from Amelia E. Joesting in January 1947 (MLP 7079/61). Renamed Waverly Savings and Loan and merged into Metropolis Building Association in 1975, it sold the building to Irvin A. Forrest on August 23, 1977 for about $14,000 (RHB 3529/425), bought with a $9,800 Patapsco Federal loan (3529/428). On December 1, 1984 Forrest, by then in Florida, created a $120 ground rent (SEB 387/462) and sold the leasehold through Cherlan Realty to Stanford H. Cohan, Albert B. Cowing and Daniel E. Cohan for $37,500 (387/466), lending them $22,500 (387/469, released 2005). June 22, 2005: the partners sell to Louis Ostraw for $115,000 (FMC 6603/818), still the owner of record. The ground rent went to Paul and Amy Nochumowitz in 1999 (8354/146), was pledged to Lexington National Bail Services from 2008 to 2019, and moved to their company A&P, LLC on November 13, 2017 (MB 19711/506). Open: the 1931 Lakeshire deed, how the ground rent passed from Forrest to the Nochumowitzes, and whether A&P still holds it.

summary: July 31, 1961: Straw Man, Inc. to Samuel and Hilda Rashbaum (JFC 1116/187); Hilda died 1969. July 21, 1976: Samuel, by then in Florida, sets up a revocable trust with Gerald M. Rashbaum and Frances Kessler as trustees (RHB 3661/738), and deeds this lot and the 3100-3104 corner across 31st Street into it on August 7, 1978 (3661/745). In 1979 the city dealt with the trust through the Kessler household at 3427 Birch Hollow Road. The trust was re-recorded in 1987 (SEB 1211/555). May 18, 1993: the trust ends and Gerald and Frances, as beneficiaries, deed both corners to Arkay Properties, Inc. for no money (SEB 3755/235); the $235,140 in the state's data is the tax base. Arkay stopped paying taxes: tax sale May 2007, Property Homes, LLC foreclosed against Arkay and took a tax deed for $75,000 in 2009 (FMC 11912/13), then sold to R H Family, LLC of 3106 Greenmount for $170,000 in March 2010 (FMC 12501/498).

summary: Root of title, per the 1870 instruments that put Huntingdon Land Company of Waverly here (EHA 65/405-411, pulled live 9/25): Jacob Aull held two pieces here, one from a 99-year lease James Wilson and wife gave him May 28, 1846 (AWB 367/140, not yet pulled), the other from ground leases going back to John Wakeman in 1839 and William R. Jones/Richard H. Townsend in 1842 (PK 92/84 and PK 320/150, not yet pulled). Trustees David S., Thomas J. and Henry R. Wilson also deeded an adjoining toll-gate lot to the turnpike company on February 3, 1870, which the company then bonded onward to Huntingdon Land Co. -- and that bond states a public hall was already being built there, so construction started by early 1870, not "1872-73" as this row previously said. (The same three first names and initials show up as trustees spelled "Wilms" selling a lot a few blocks south in 1871-73, property 729 -- probably the same people, not confirmed.) March 1 and 8, 1870: Aull assigns and leases his pieces to the Huntingdon Land Company of Waverly (EHA 65/408, /409). By 1875 the company also picked up JB 94/312 (not yet pulled). In 1943 The Lakeshire Company held the Hall and took a right of way and party-wall rights from Jacob and Anna Becker next door (MLP 6544/392). July 31, 1961: Straw Man, Inc. to Samuel and Hilda Rashbaum (JFC 1116/187). 1976-78: Samuel puts it and 3048 across 31st into a family trust (RHB 3661/738, /745), trustees Gerald M. Rashbaum and Frances Kessler; re-recorded 1987 (SEB 1211/555). May 18, 1993: the heirs deed both corners to Arkay Properties, Inc. for no money (SEB 3755/235). October 30, 1997: Arkay, by Gerald M. Rashbaum as its president, sells to Williams Realty, LLC for $170,000 (PMB 7723/329), financed by a $120,000 NationsBank loan (PMB 7723/335, released 2001). By February 2005 Williams Realty gives PM & BK, LLC an option to 2006 that lapses (FMC 6368/1334). January 9, 2009: Williams Realty to WABKF, LLC (Domingo Kim), seller-financed, recorded 2011, $400,000 (FMC 13399/61). November 13, 2018: WABKF to Baltimore Community 4, LLC for $414,000 (MB 20672/331). January 2021: Baltimore Community 4 to Waverly Arts LLC (Jacob Wittenberg, Edgemont Builders) for $75,000, with a perpetual ban on liquor, adult and smoke or vape stores (MB 23061/1). Waverly Arts backed a $1.5 million Reinvestment Fund loan to its sister company Waverly Arts II in March 2021; a year later, March 2022, it refinanced with its own $2,000,000 loan from Standard Insurance Company (MB 24862/392), which Standard partly syndicated to Lincoln National (12.65%) and PL Mortgage Fund (14.15%) in 2023.

summary: Before 1974 the title is known only in pieces. The ground was probably part of the 204-ft tract assigned to George C. H. Coffield in 1865 (lot arithmetic). J. S. Bateman owned 69 ft here on the 1889 plat; M. Estelle Bateman conveyed the bank lot on the north to the Provident Savings Bank on March 18, 1904 (R.O. 2062/398, recited) and still owned the remaining 44.8 ft about 1913; she died on Feb. 15, 1920. Who held the lot from 1920 is not known; the Franklin Realty & Finance Company was lessor of the store at 3105-7 in 1929. From 1974 the chain is on record: Jack O. Chertkof, Trustee, to Sample Stores of Baltimore, Inc., June 10, 1974 (R.H.B. 3139/15, recited; the later deeds say June 12); Sample Stores of Baltimore renamed American Pants Company of Baltimore, Inc. on April 2, 1987; American Pants Company of Baltimore to Jong Sul Kang, Feb. 19, 1992, $220,000 (S.E.B. 3136/493); Jong Sul Kang to Joon Sun Kang for life with powers of disposition, Sept. 23, 1993 (S.E.B. 3969/335); Joon Sun Kang to Jong Sul Kang and Joon Sun Kang on the same terms, June 27, 2007 (F.M.C. 9677/661); and Jong Sul Kang and Joon Sun Kang to 3107 Greenmount Avenue, LLC, May 11, 2016, $320,000 (L.G.A. 18114/101). American Pants Company of Baltimore was a clothing retailer, the Sample Store, not a garment maker, and the building was a store, not a factory. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1974 Chertkof deed is read (737:mdlr-rhb3139-15-chertkof-trustee-sample-stores-1974-read), and so are the 1902 and 1904 Bateman deeds (738:mdlr-ro1984-398-dawkins-clara-bateman-estate-m-estelle-bateman-1902, 738:mdlr-ro2062-398-bateman-provident-bank-lot-1904-read): the Bateman ground was 70 ft 6 in of the Coffield tract held through William Hammel (1869) at one cent, with the Methodist trustees' 1872 sub-lease on the south.

summary: The SE corner of Greenmount & E 32nd St, at the 'Old York Road wedge' where the two roads fork, opened as an independent corner grocery run by the Keyes family. William F. Keyes Jr. was the grocer, living over the store in 1915; his father William F. Keyes ('clk' 1915) took over the grocery by 1920, by which time the family had moved to 2952 Greenmount and the son had become a florist (1520 E Chase). It was a heavily-advertising corner store (~800 Baltimore-newspaper mentions from 1914). The Keyes left the corner by 1922.

summary: After the bakery era, 3213-3215 (Block 4076, Lot 7) was owned by Kang Jung Yi and Kyung Cha Yi, Korean-American merchants who ran Dandy Men's Store (its storefront listed at 3219 Greenmount). A Sept 23 1985 $60,000 purchase-money deed of trust to First National Bank of Maryland (SEB 658/574) also encumbered 902 Sibley Road in the county; a Nov 14 1985 confirmatory agreement (SEB 707/336) corrected the owners' names after their naturalization — Kang Jung Yi became Dandy Kangjung Lee and Kyung Cha Yi became June Kyungcha Lee (the husband adopting the store's own name, 'Dandy'). A 1997 intra-spousal deed put title in June Kyung Cha Lee alone (Liber 658/570), secured by a Korea Exchange Bank indemnity mortgage (Book 6291/113, satisfied 2001, FMC 1889/357). By 2001 she had moved to Allentown, PA; on Dec 30 2003 she and So Cheung Lee refinanced with a $202,500 Wachovia Bank deed of trust (FMC 4871/350), paying off a prior $128,671 balance. The lender succession — First National → Korea Exchange → Wachovia — tracks the corridor's Korean-immigrant merchant thread.

summary: 3221 was an investment parcel of Alan Wurtzburger (Apr 22 1900 – Feb 20 1963), a Baltimore commercial real-estate investor who was also one of the museum world's great collectors (BMA Trustee 1955-62). That dual identity resolves why a celebrated art collector held a modest Greenmount storefront: 3221 — and its corner neighbor 3223, which Alan bought out of an estate in 1934 (Emanuel E. Ottenheimer, Executor → Alan Wurtzburger) — were income/rental parcels in his real-estate portfolio, not a shop the family ran. Alan deeded 3221 to his wife Janet E. Cohn Wurtzburger (Jan 29 1908, Cleveland – Dec 24 1973) on June 1 1945 — confirming the 'C.' in the land record's 'Janet E. C. Wurtzburger' is COHN (a German-Jewish surname), not 'Cahn.' On Janet's death the 1976 estate split 3221 between their children Jon Alan Wurtzburger (b.1934; stockbroker, a retired Governor of the New York Stock Exchange, aviator and philanthropist) and Margot 'Peggy' Wurtzburger Milch, who sold it to the Lim family in 1979. (Emanuel E. Ottenheimer was of the Baltimore German-Jewish Ottenheimer publishing family; no Wurtzburger–Ottenheimer kinship is documented — the 1934 deed was a real-estate transaction.)

summary: Alan and Janet Wurtzburger were among the Baltimore Museum of Art's greatest benefactors. In two phases they gave the museum its foundational non-Western holdings — 400+ African, Oceanic, and Pre-Columbian sculptures (major African gift 1954-55; Pre-Columbian core 1958), establishing the Wurtzburger Gallery of the Primitive Arts (1958; catalogued by Paul S. Wingert, 'The Alan Wurtzburger Collection of African Sculpture,' BMA 1958) — and they assembled a landmark modern-sculpture collection: a Rodin (a 'Balzac'), Bourdelle, Maillol, Henry Moore, Jacob Epstein, Marino Marini, Jacques Lipchitz, Ossip Zadkine, Alexander Calder, Isamu Noguchi, and José de Rivera. The sculpture was first displayed on the grounds of their Stevenson (Baltimore County) estate 'Timberlane' (landscaped by James Rose and Thomas Church); the 1.1-acre Alan and Janet Wurtzburger Sculpture Garden opened at the BMA in 1980 (landscape architect George Patton). The Wurtzburgers belong to the same German-Jewish art-collecting-and-philanthropy tradition as Baltimore's Cone sisters.

summary: Sanborn's 1928 atlas, Vol. 7, sheet 735 (the east side of the 3000 and 3100 blocks of Greenmount Avenue), letters the shop at the tip of the wedge '3011 / 1003' and 'TIN SHOP': a two-story brick building with 8-inch walls and one height figure (22 ft), a one-story frame strip on the north half of the front and a one-story frame wing behind. North of it 3013 is a one-story frame store ('S'), deeper than in 1915, and the lot beyond it (3015) is brick. The plate prints the Greenmount number over the old York road number, which ties 1003 York road to 3011 directly. In 1915 the same shop was drawn as two brick blocks with separate heights (20 ft and 30 ft); whether the single figure of 1928 reflects a rebuilding about 1920, the year the assessment record gives, cannot be told from the plates. The printing of this sheet corrected to May 1950 still shows 3011 as the tin shop and 3013 as a one-story frame store, beside a paste-over that redraws 3015 as a brick 'PET HOSPITAL'.

summary: On the 1928 Sanborn atlas (Baltimore Vol. 7, sheet 735) the same one-story brick footprint stands at 3015, now labelled 'S' (store) with a 10-foot rear annex, and the same two-story frame building at 3017 is now labelled 'office'; 3013 is still a one-story frame store, and 3019 and 3021 are both stores. The labels have swapped since 1915, when 3015 was the 'Office' and 3017 the store. The swap fits the occupants: the Rahe shoe store had left 3017 by 1923, the York Road Building Association bought 3017 in 1921 and met there in 1925 and 1926, and in 1928 the 3015 store was offered for rent as new (February) and held a barber shop (September 1928 to April 1929). A June 1928 advertisement places the 'York Rd. Building & Loan Assn.' at 3117 Greenmount, so the 1928 'office' at 3017 is not proven to be the association's. Neither building gained a story between 1915 and 1928, so the National Register description of 3015 as originally two-story fits neither plate.

summary: Sanborn Fire Insurance Map, Baltimore Vol. 7 (1915), sheet 717 (Library of Congress sanborn03573_014), which carries the 3000 to 3200 blocks of Greenmount Avenue with brick and frame footprints, uses and street numbers. 3026 is the southernmost of four contiguous 2-story brick dwellings ('D 2') numbered 3026, 3028, 3030 and 3032, at the corner of Vineyard Lane, with a 1-story frame porch across the front and a small 1-story frame addition at the rear; the plate prints only the Greenmount number, with no York Road number beside it. Behind the row, across the alley, on the north side of Vineyard Lane: a 1-story frame blacksmith shop ('Bl. Sm.') with sheds, a 1 1/2-story frame stable, and a 2-story frame dwelling numbered 10. Polk's directories of 1913 to 1915 put Charles H. Clark, odorless excavator, at 10 Vineyard Lane with his business at number 8, and the horseshoer Dennis Driscoll at 8 Vineyard Lane in 1914 and 'Vineyard la nr Greenmt' in 1915, so the shop was probably Driscoll's and the house Clark's (the directory lines were read mostly in the text of the volumes). That ground is a separate lot, today's 3020 Vineyard Lane.

summary: Sanborn Fire Insurance Map, Baltimore Vol. 7 (1915), sheet 717 (Library of Congress sanborn03573_014; the index prints 'Greenmount Ave. 3000-3238 *717'). On the west side north of Vineyard Lane stand four contiguous two-story brick dwellings ('D 2'), each about 14 to 15 ft wide, each with a one-story frame porch across the front and a one-story frame kitchen at the rear, numbered 3026, 3028, 3030 and 3032 from south to north, with no York Road number on any of them. A narrow passage opens into the rear yards between 3028 and 3030. North of them stand the frame stores 3034, 3036 and 3038 (also printed with their York Road numbers 1002, 1004 and 1006), then the Zepp garage and the group numbered 3042, 3044 (Photo Supplies), 3046 (Office) and 3048, each also printed with its superseded number (3028, 3030, 3032, 3034). A 'T.H.' label stands in Vineyard Lane in front of 3026. The toll house is gone; its lot holds the four dwellings.

summary: Sheet 735 of the 1928 volume shows three one-story brick stores ('S', 12 ft high) numbered 3105, 3107 and 3109 at the street line of this lot, each about 16 ft wide by the sheet's scale. They stand across what was the open front yard of 1915 and butt the same two-story frame dwelling ('D'), whose front bays now meet their rear walls. North of 3109, past a narrow passage, is a one-story brick 'Bank' (3111) with a two-story frame 'Storage' building numbered 3111 1/2 behind it; south of 3105 the two-story building on the old church site is numbered 3103, with 'Awning Mfg 2nd' and a candy maker's kettles at the rear. So the stores were built between the 1915 sheet, which shows only the house, and 1928; Polk's 1922 directory already lists shops at all three numbers. Read on the sheet; widths are scaled, not printed.

summary: Prod's prior citation for this row (Vol.7 sheet 739) was wrong: that sheet's actual content is Old York Road/Ready Ave/Gorsuch Ave/Belle Terre Ave/the Waverly Theatre -- a real but entirely different part of the city, not the 3300 block of Greenmount. The correct sheet, found via Vol.6's own printed index ('Greenmount Ave...3300-3440=*656'), is Vol.6 sheet 656 (LOC item sanborn03573_017). Read directly: 3322 is a single pink (brick), 2-story, 22-foot-wide 'S' (store) building. It is the corner building immediately south of the Venable Ave/Greenmount intersection, with nothing -- no building, no lot -- between it and that crossing (the gap on the sheet contains a water-main and test-hole marker for the Venable Ave crossing itself, not vacant ground bordering 3326/3328, which sits across that intersection on a different block face entirely). No structure or address labeled '3324' appears anywhere on this sheet. Combined with the 1915 Sanborn's 'vacant land, 3324-3340' finding and the modern SDAT record's single account, this establishes that 3324 was never a physically separate building -- the 1922-23 Polk appearance of '3324' was a secondary address for part of this same building, not an absorbed neighbor.

summary: Sanborn Fire Insurance Map, Baltimore Vol. 7 (1915), sheet 716, Library of Congress sanborn03573_014, west frontage between Henderson Av (modern Venable Ave) and Calvin Ave, read at native resolution. 3342 over 1202 and 3344 over 1204: one 2-story brick building, 'S' (store) on both units, the figure 22' printed on each unit (a height, not a frontage), with 1-story strips (yellow, frame) across the front and rear; the use label on the 3344 unit carries an overprinted mark that can be read 'Sal.' (saloon). North of it is a gap of about 19 to 20 ft with no building and no number (modern 3330). Then '3348 P.': a 2-story brick 'S' with a 1-story rear (modern 3332); the figure 24' printed on it is a height, and the plate draws the store about 19 ft wide. North of 3348 P., on the ground of modern 3334-3338, the plate shows two frame buildings set back from the street: a 1 1/2-story building on a lot numbered '1206', marked 'VACANT (OLD)', and a one-story 'BICYCLE REPAIR SHOP' on a lot numbered '3350 A.'. The plate itself prints the old York Road numbers: 3326 = 1202 and 3328 = 1204. The 1-story frame strips front and rear are already on this plate, so the '1-story addition ca. 1925' of B-5229 is not evident as a later structure.

summary: Sanborn Fire Insurance Map, Baltimore Vol. 7 (1915), sheet 716, Library of Congress sanborn03573_014, west side of Greenmount between Henderson Av (today's Venable Avenue) and Calvin Avenue, read at native resolution. From the corner: the 2-story brick double store 3342 / 1202 and 3344 / 1204 (today's 3326 and 3328); a gap with no building and no number (later 3330); the 2-story brick store '3348 P.' with a one-story rear (today's 3332, on tax lot 001); then the ground that is this lot today. First a lot printed '1206' alone, about 30 ft wide, with a 1 1/2-story frame building marked 'VACANT (OLD)' and a one-story frame rear section. Then a lot printed '3350' with an 'A.' beside it, about 22 ft wide, with a one-story frame 'BICYCLE REPAIR SHOP'. Both buildings stand a few feet back from the street line. North of them come '1208' and '1210' (one-story brick stores, both 'VACANT' and lettered 'IN POOR REPAIR'), '3346 / 1212' (2 stories, vacant) and '3348A / 1214' (today's 3354 to 3360). So the frontage of today's 3334-3338 was not open ground in 1915: it held an old frame building and a small bicycle shop where the concrete-block row now stands. The '1206' and '3350 A.' lots together correspond to tax lot 002; the widths are scaled from the plate, not surveyed.

summary: Sanborn Fire Insurance Map, Baltimore Vol. 6 (1928), sheet 656, the sheet for the west side of the 3300 block (Vol. 7 sheet 739, cited here earlier, covers only the east side). MOTOR', also set back; then '3354 / 1208', 'AUTO REPAIR'. No building on the sheet is numbered 3334, 3336, 3338 or 3340: the concrete-block row had not been built. The '3352 / 3350' lot is about 25 ft wide on the plate, the width of the fee lot of the 1910 deed.

summary: The 1915 Sanborn sheet (Vol.7, sheet 716) shows the stretch corresponding to old-numbers 1208 through 1214 (roughly 3352-3358) as three separate lots marked 'VACANT... IN POOR REPAIR,' plus one 22-by-88-foot 2-story store at the north end (old-1214). This directly conflicts with Polk's 1914 listing of John P. Lacey's feed store at 3354 (old-1208). Not resolved either direction: possible explanations include a Sanborn field survey that predates Lacey's occupancy becoming visible, a marginal/seasonal feed operation the surveyor didn't count as 'occupied,' or a stale directory listing. The 1915 sheet's own numbers pair old-1212/1214 with modern-3346/3348 (not 3354/3356), but the 1928 sheet (Vol.6 sheet 656) shows the SAME old numbers, 1208 and 1210, paired with the modern numbers 3354 and 3356 -- meaning Greenmount's modern numbering on this frontage was itself revised between 1915 and 1928, and old-1208 is confirmed via the later sheet's relabeling to be the same lot that becomes 3354. Recorded as a genuine, documented tension between two primary sources rather than silently picking one.

summary: Prod's prior citation (784:sanborn-vol7-1928-sheet739) cites Vol.7 sheet 739 as covering '3300 block Greenmount Ave.' That sheet's actual content is Venable Ave/Old York Rd/Ready Ave/the Waverly Theatre/Gorsuch Ave/Belle Terre Ave -- a real but entirely different location, not Greenmount's 3300 block at all (the same bug class independently found and fixed on pid 778). The correct sheet for this parcel's 1928 coverage is Vol.6, even/west side, sheet 656. B-5229 files three overlapping paragraphs under Block 3884 Lot 003 (one tax lot, per the city's own live parcel record PIN 3884003): 3358 alone and '3354-3356' both cite Murphy's Food Market (1928); 3354 alone cites Stadium Garage (1928). Reading sheet 656 directly resolves the apparent contradiction: the lot held (at least) three separate storefronts -- 'AUTO REPAIR' at 3354 and 'BATTERY SERVICE STATION' at 3356 (matching 'Stadium Garage'), immediately next to a separate pink 'S' (generic store) building at 3358/3360 (matching 'Murphy's Food Market'). One lot, multiple tenants, not a contradiction. Not fully verified only because the Sanborn label is the generic 'S' rather than naming Murphy's specifically -- kept at probable.

summary: The plate prints '3348A' over '1214' on a 2-story brick store ('S'), 22 ft wide, with 8-inch walls, a 1-story frame strip at the street (about 7 ft deep by scale) and an open 10-ft passage on its north side (the 10-ft alley of the deeds). To the south, '3346 / 1212' (modern 3358) is a 2-story brick building marked 'VACANT ... IN POOR REPAIR' (Frank A. McLaughlin's saloon at 1212 York rd is in Polk 1901-09). The plate's 22 ft differs from the 17-ft lot of the deeds and SDAT. The plate does not name the occupant. The pairing '3348A / 1214', repeated as '3360 / 3348A' on the 1928 plate, is the decisive evidence that the old York Road number of 3360 is 1214.

summary: Read on the MDLandRec page images. This row once recorded that the corner had no digital ownership deed; the chain below refutes that. Fee: the trustees of James Wilson to John Bolgiano, Lots 16 and 17 of the Wilson plat (200 x 100 ft at the northwest corner of the York Turnpike and Wilson Street, now Venable Avenue), Jan. 14, 1871, $1,870 (Baltimore County E.H.A. 70/115). Ground rent and leasehold: Bolgiano and wife lease the two lots to Bernard Bertling for 99 years renewable at $200 a year, Sept. 21, 1876 (Baltimore County J.B. 97, folio 57[?], recited); Bertling to George Miller, Oct. 1, 1880, $900 (Baltimore County W.M.I. 119/71); Miller's executrix Elizabeth Mueller to herself, Aug. 31, 1888 (J.B. 1206/357); Elizabeth Muller, widow, to John P. and Mary E. Lacey, July 1, 1904, $3,525 (R.O. 2083/495). The 25-ft lot to the north: James D. Lacey to John P. and Mary E. Lacey in fee, Nov. 15, 1910 (S.C.L. 2620/254, recited). Mary E. Lacey's executor to The Miller Realty Corporation at auction, June 17, 1969, $78,000 (R.H.B. 2529/79), with a $55,000 Maryland National Bank purchase-money mortgage (R.H.B. 2529/81; released 1979, R.H.B. 3793/536, index). The Miller Realty Corporation to Max Properties, Inc., articles of transfer, Jan. 27, 1989 (S.E.B. 2174/344). A confirmatory quitclaim by Miller Realty's directors-trustees of March 2015 (L.G.A. 17028/076) concerns only the 25 x 60 ft Brentwood Avenue lot, Block 3884 lot 036, which SDAT had left in Miller Realty's name. Max Properties, Inc. to 3326 Greenmount Avenue, LLC, Nov. 7, 2016, recorded Nov. 14, $750,000 (MB 18621/389). Still open: who held the $200 rent after Bolgiano and when it was merged (the 1969 deed does not say; the 1989 papers mention a 1972 Mercantile-Safe Deposit reversion), and the 1876 lease itself. Update Oct. 12, 2026: the Bolgiano deed (E.H.A. 70/115-118) is now on file as a scan on this property (see mdlandrec-eha70-115). It closes its recital 'For title see Liber W.G. 71 folio 582, W.G. 114 folio 437 and W.G. 114 folio 439' (James Wilson's own deeds of 1802 and 1811, filed as 776:mdlr-wg71-582-edwards-vanbibber-wilson-1802 and 752:mdlr-wg114-437-whitely-wilson-fee-1811) but names no tract and does not say which of them covers Lots 16 and 17. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1972 deed of reversion is read (776:mdlr-rhb2876-259-mercantile-hazen-weiss-miller-realty-reversion-merged-1972): the $200 rent was merged and extinguished; the reversion had passed from Joseph A. Bolgiano's will (Safe Deposit and Trust Co., substituted trustee) to Mary Mildred Hazen and Jane Collison Weiss on Dec. 27, 1935 (S.C.L. 5589/225); the 1876 lease is cited at folio 584 of J.B. 97, not 57 (776:negative-jb97-57-not-bolgiano-bertling-lease). Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1876 lease is read at J.B. 97/584 (776:mdlr-jb97-584-bolgiano-bertling-lease-200-rent-1876: redeemable only to 1881) and the 1935 deeds (776:mdlr-scl5589-225-bolgiano-trust-flora-joyce-hazen-weiss-1935: Joseph A. Bolgiano's trust for his daughter Flora B. Joyce, to her daughters Hazen and Weiss).

summary: The chain, from the deeds read on the page images or scans (1871, 1880, 1888, 1904, 1969, 1989, 2016) and, where marked, from recitals. Tax lot 3884/002 is the north 30 ft of Lots 16 and 17 of the Wilson plat plus a separate 25-ft lot north of them. Lots 16 and 17 (100 ft on the turnpike from Wilson Street, now Venable Avenue): James Wilson's trustees to John Bolgiano, Jan. 14, 1871, $1,870 (Baltimore County E.H.A. 70/115); Bolgiano's 99-year renewable lease of both lots to Bernard Bertling at $200 a year, Sept. 21, 1876 (recited); Bertling to George Miller, Oct. 1, 1880, $900 (Baltimore County W.M.I. 119/71); Elizabeth Mueller, executrix of John George Mueller, to herself, Aug. 31, 1888 (J.B. 1206/357); Elizabeth Muller, widow, to John P. and Mary E. Lacey, July 1, 1904, $3,525 (R.O. 2083/495). The 25-ft lot (100 to 125 ft from Wilson Street, 120 ft deep): William Gutman's lot with a one-story brick store on the 1889 ward plat; James D. Lacey, unmarried, to John P. and Mary E. Lacey in fee, Nov. 15, 1910 (S.C.L. 2620/254, recited; how he came by it is not known). Mary E. Lacey held both until her death on May 28, 1968; her executor sold the whole 125-ft assemblage, 'Nos. 3326-28-30-32-34-36-38 Greenmount Avenue and 412-414 Venable Avenue', at auction to The Miller Realty Corporation for $78,000, deed June 17, 1969 (R.H.B. 2529/79), with a $55,000 purchase-money mortgage to Maryland National Bank the same day (R.H.B. 2529/81; released 1979, R.H.B. 3793/536, index). A deed of reversion of Jan. 17, 1972 from Mercantile-Safe Deposit and Trust Company, trustee under the Hazen and Weiss deeds of trust, to Miller Realty (R.H.B. 2876/259, recited) was evidently the purchase of the $200 ground rent, which would have merged rent and leasehold. The Miller Realty Corporation to Max Properties, Inc., articles of transfer of Jan. 27, 1989, with 19 other parcels (S.E.B. 2174/344), and a confirmatory deed of Jan. 26, 1989 (S.E.B. 2000/313). Max Properties, Inc. to 3326 Greenmount Avenue, LLC, Nov. 7, 2016, recorded Nov. 14, one deed for tax lots 001, 002, 034, 035 and 036 at $750,000 (MB 18621/389). The deeds describe the ground as 100 ft plus 25 ft throughout; the City re-drew the two tax lots in 1949 (lot 1 from 100 to 70 ft, lot 2 from 25 to 55 ft), which is when 3334-3338 became a tax lot of its own. Update Oct. 12, 2026: the Bolgiano deed (E.H.A. 70/115-118) is now on file as a scan on this property (see mdlandrec-eha70-115). It closes its recital 'For title see Liber W.G. 71 folio 582, W.G. 114 folio 437 and W.G. 114 folio 439' (James Wilson's own deeds of 1802 and 1811, filed as 776:mdlr-wg71-582-edwards-vanbibber-wilson-1802 and 752:mdlr-wg114-437-whitely-wilson-fee-1811) but names no tract and does not say which of them covers Lots 16 and 17. summary: A full deed read (RHB 2992/491-493, see 783:BC-RHB2992-491) and the MDLandRec address index resolve this placeholder chain in full. Goldie Pollack (nee Sibelman, presumed) died intestate in Baltimore County in 1971, owning an undivided one-third interest; her brothers Paul and Morris Sibelman, who owned the remaining two-thirds, bought out her estate's share for $36,000 and on 1973-02-14 resold the whole property to two Papadopoulos couples (Evdokimos & Stella; John & Eva) as tenants by the entireties. The Papadopoulos family sold to RAYMOND R. ELLISON and SONDRA E. ELLISON on 1976-10-29 (Deed Book 3408, pp.538-540). The Ellisons sold to JERRY FRIEDENBERG AND PAUL FRIEDENBERG on 1987-12-23 (Deed Book 1556, pp.181-184; a co-mortgagor, Sheila Friedenberg, is a third family member). Jerry and Paul Friedenberg sold to Oh Yung O & Oh Kyung T on 2006-09-22 (Deed Book 8369, pp.270-276), confirming this parcel's existing 2023 sale citation. This corrects the placeholder's unlabeled pre-1972 leg and its missing owner first names, and supersedes an earlier, unconfirmed Register-of-Wills-based guess at the 1976-87 owner's identity that this session's own sleuthing had floated before the primary deed was read. Simon Sibelman (d.1943-04-29, the only Sibelman estate in Baltimore City, see 783:sibelman-simon-estate-1943) may still be the parent of Paul, Morris and Goldie -- plausible but not proven by this deed.

summary: The Bateman clippings filed on 3107 belong to the family of James S. Bateman, grocer, who lived in the frame house numbered 1021 York road and later 3109 Greenmount, on this lot, from the 1870s or 1880s; his daughter M. Estelle Bateman owned the lot until her death in 1920. Their grocery stand was next door at 1023 York road (3111). Polk lists the family at 1023 in 1887 and at 1021 from 1889, the 1889 plat letters the lot 'J. S. Bateman', and the 1915 Sanborn sheet prints 1021 and 3109 on the house. The 1887 guardianship order, the 1887 death notice of Mary A. Bateman, the 1880 Normal School list (Mary E. Bateman, probably M. Estelle) and the 1899 advertisement are this family. The 1839 list of appointments, the 1870 Charles County sheriff's sale, the 1884 grocers' list and the two temperance-union reports have no tie to this lot beyond the surname and may concern other Batemans; the 1873 legal notice and the 1897 Rider-to-Bateman transfer have not been re-read against the lot.

summary: The National Register nomination for the Waverly Main Street Historic District (B-5229, listed 2013) lists 3010-3020 Greenmount as a contributing one-story tan-brick commercial building, 'built ca. 1960', with a historic use of 'residence of Charles T. The Leight residence of the 1928 directory is the frame house of about 1845 at 3020 (old 922 York road), which the row replaced.

summary: In Sept 1927 federal 'dry agents' raided a saloon in the 2500 block of Greenmount Avenue and arrested eight men ('Dry Agents Raid Saloon And Arrest Eight Men'); no liquor was found. Among those arrested was EDWARD R. COGGINS (then of the 2300 block Greenmount) — the corridor Coggins family later at 2841 who signed pitcher 'Lefty' Russell — alongside John F. Emerick and saloon figure Louis A. Saylor of the 2500 block. Days later U.S. Commissioner J. Frank Supplee condemned the wholesale arrests (attorney R. Palmer Ingram); Saylor was released on $100 bail. In March 1928 William Brown of the 2500 block drew sixty days on a sale-and-possession charge.

summary: Samuel H. Tagart (the deed's own spelling; 'Taggert' in the 1988 deeds is a misreading), acting as court-appointed trustee, assigned to George C. H. Coffield a lot of 103 perches on the east side of the York Turnpike for the rest of a 99-year renewable term at a yearly rent of one cent. The deed, read in full on the scan (Baltimore County Liber J.H.L. 43, folios 548-550; see 742:mdlr-jhl43-548-tagart-coffield-1865), is the earliest documented root of title for the 3117 Greenmount parcel; later deeds describe the lot relative to the northwest corner of the Coffield tract. It passed a leasehold, not the fee; the original lessor and lease are not recited. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1868 instrument is read (742:mdlr-eha59-86-coffield-smith-sublease-1868) and it is a SUB-lease of Coffield's own term less one year, at $150, renewable by sub-leases reserving one day, with a one-time buyout at $2,500 in March 1878. The $150 rent was therefore a sub-rent beneath Coffield's one-cent ground lease. Update Oct. 14, 2026: folios 549 to 550 read (742:research-jhl43-549-550-coffield-tract-description-no-tract-name): 103 perches, one cent, no tract name.

summary: Trustees James L. Hennegan and George L. Lochboehler assigned 3117 Greenmount Avenue to Eyring Realty Corporation, an affiliate of E. Eyring & Sons Co., the contractor that built the showroom in 1928, by a deed of assignment dated February 22, 1933 (S.C.L. 5349/727 per the 1988 Crittenton deed; folio 127 and February 23 in the 1988 Hong deed and later copies) for about $19,000, subject to the annual sub ground rent of $1,200 (the Miller Brothers sub-lease of 1928). What Eyring bought was the leasehold and the building, not the fee: the 1988 Crittenton deed (S.E.B. 1815/128, scan read) calls it the 'leasehold title for 3117 Greenmount Avenue', and the Hong deed's 'fee simple title' wording is title-company shorthand. The superior interest stayed with the reversioner under Coffield's 1868 sub-lease ($150 a year). Coffield himself held a renewable 99-year leasehold at one cent a year (the 1865 assignment, J.H.L. 43/548), so what the later deeds call the fee is that superior leasehold unless the true fee was acquired separately. The Safe Deposit and Trust Company of Baltimore, trustee u/w Ellen M. Schaeffer, sold it to Florence Crittenton Mission on October 28, 1936 (S.C.L. 5669/442, recited only), and Crittenton sold it to Eyring Realty Enterprises, Inc. on July 18, 1988 (S.E.B. 1815/128). Reported publicly two weeks after the assignment (Sun, March 8, 1933). Update Oct. 14, 2026: the deed is read (742:mdlr-scl5349-127-trustees-eyring-realty-1933): a LEASEHOLD, $19,000, dated Feb. 23, 1933, recorded Mar. 7, at S.C.L. 5349/127 (not 727), under a decree of Oct. 21, 1932 in Erhard Eyring et al. v. The Miller Brothers Furniture Co. et al. (Docket 72-C/663), subject to the $1,200 sub-rent.
