summary: Dorothy Dietrich, Wilhelmina Dietrich, and Helen Dietrich Butler, heirs of the Dietrich family that held the leasehold of the lot and had sub-leased it to Miller Brothers in 1928, conveyed the $1,200 sub-ground rent and sub-reversion to Eyring Realty Corporation by the 'Sub Lease Merger Deed' of December 30, 1936 (S.C.L. 5686/215) for merging and extinguishment. This was not a conveyance of fee title: the sub-rent merged into Eyring's sub-leasehold, leaving one leasehold, still 'subject to the payment of the annual rent of $150.00 ... as created in the indenture' of March 2, 1868 (Coffield to George Vandyke Smith, Baltimore County E.H.A. 59/86). The reversion and the $150 rent (what the later deeds call the fee; Coffield himself held a renewable 99-year leasehold at one cent a year, J.H.L. 43/548) stayed with the reversioner, which had passed them to Florence Crittenton Mission on October 28, 1936 (S.C.L. 5669/442, recited only); Crittenton conveyed them to Eyring Realty Enterprises, Inc. on July 18, 1988 (S.E.B. 1815/128), whose merger clause as to 3117 finally united leasehold and fee. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the deed is read (742:mdlr-scl5686-215-dietrich-eyring-subrent-merger-1936): it conveys the $1,200 sub-rent to merge it (not the fee); the 1928 sub-lease is S.C.L. 4854/321, Mar. 3, 1928, by Lula S. Dietrich, widow; the grantors held by an administratrix's deed from Wilhelmina Dietrich of Apr. 27, 1931 (S.C.L. 5213/440); $15,000 mortgage the same day to Erhard Eyring's surviving trustees.

summary: 2711 Greenmount was VINCENT'S 2711 MEAT MARKET — an "American and Italian Grocery" (as the storefront signage reads) — run by the Sicilian-immigrant Bongiorno family from Calascibetta, Enna: Vincent (Vincenzo) Bongiorno and his wife Pietrina (Scavuzzo). Family photographs show the store interior (walls of canned goods, the counter scale, the fresh-meats case, produce bins, the family working the counter) and a son in WWII uniform in the doorway beneath the 'Vincent's 2711 Meat Market' sign. Established after the Colgan/Weidner era (exact founding year undocumented; the family was in Baltimore by 1940) and run into the 1960s; Vincent died 1963, Pietrina 1968.

summary: The grocery was held up at gunpoint on the night of August 6, 1961. A young gunman, about 19, walked into the store in the 2700 block of Greenmount, produced a pistol and took $10 from the cash register. When the robber reached for the wallet of grocer Vincent Bongiorno (given as age 65), Bongiorno swung at him but missed; the bandit backed off but fled with the register cash.

summary: 2709 Greenmount was a family bakery and confectionery run by the Weidners — a long-settled German-American Roman Catholic family (St. Ann's parish, New Cathedral Cemetery). It was a father-and-son operation: Edward Paul Weidner Sr. (b. 1873, Baltimore) the candymaker/confectioner, and his son Leo Edward Weidner (b. 1891) the baker, both living over the store, with kin John (carpenter) and Paul A. (ironworker) in the household. The bakery opened around 1916 and is documented in the 1917 and 1918–19 Polk directories, including the classified 'Retail Bakers' trade section — whose OCR garbled the surname to 'Weldinger,' the source of the long-standing 'Weidinger' misreading. Leo, a WWI veteran, never married and died in 1949 (buried at Baltimore National Cemetery); Edward Sr. died in 1929 (New Cathedral Cemetery).

summary: After the Weidners, 2709 turned into a high-turnover rental. For a single directory year — 1922 — it was the home of May Tillet, widow of Robert Tillet, who kept the household, with Charles Currie, an awning erector, boarding there. Both are near-ghosts: neither appears at 2709 (or traceably anywhere in Baltimore) in any other year. Robert Tillet was already dead and never shows up alive in a city directory, so May likely arrived on Greenmount already widowed. Currie's trade ties him to the corridor's small awning industry — most plausibly the Jefferson awning works six blocks up at 3332–3337 Greenmount — though no employment record confirms it.

summary: Weeks after her husband Vincent died (Feb 10, 1963), the widow Pietrina Bongiorno acquired the leasehold to 2709 Greenmount — the parcel next door to the family store at 2711 — on March 27, 1963 (JFC 1461/477). When Pietrina died in 1968 the leasehold vested in Frances Thalwitzer.

summary: The 2700 Greenmount block sits in Harwood, which was originally the pre-1888 Baltimore County hamlet of 'OXFORD' — a country village annexed to Baltimore City in 1888 alongside Waverly, Peabody Heights, Homestead and Friendship along the York Road/Greenmount spine. E 27th St at this corner was 'OXFORD AVENUE' until the 1908 Brune street-renaming (primary source: Report of Commissioner William H. Brune, Apr 30 1908 — Oxford Ave → E 27th St; Huntingdon Ave → 25th; Barnum/Brady Ave → 28th; Waverly Ave → 31st). The nearby Oxford Club (2837) and 'Oxford Sluggers' ballclub took their name from this Oxford Avenue. The rowhouses (built c.1910-13) stand on the 1688 Huntington/Stansbury land patent, a few blocks from the original Oriole Park (25th & Greenmount, 1882-89) that gave the Orioles their name; rowhouse developer James Keelty began his career building at 25th & Greenmount c.1904. 'Harwood' is a 20th-c. community name (Harwood Improvement Association organized 1972) of undocumented origin — no Harwood estate is documented.

summary: Louis Rabai ran his Greenmount Avenue bakery until he sold it in 1952, after roughly two decades of ownership.

summary: After Louis Rabai sold the Greenmount shop (1952), it is reported operating by the mid-1950s as 'Burri's French Bakery' — 'Burri' almost certainly the Brusini family name (the co-founding branch, related to the Rabais by the Vicarini-sisters marriages) continuing the bakery before its later Butter Crisp era.
data: {"evidence":"Jeff Jetton's 3213-3215 Greenmount monograph (city-directory citation); the Brusini/Rabai family link (1918 Brusini-Vicarini marriage; Mary Rabai's sister Rose Brusini).","headline":"Continues as Burri's (Brusini) French Bakery (~1956)","image_id":"wp-1956-burris","relevance":"Ties the mid-century bakery succession back to the founding Brusini family.","confidence":"verify","source_document":"Jeff Jetton monograph; Brusini-Vicarini-Rabai family records"}

summary: Michael Gotti incorporated Butter Crisp Bakery, Inc. at 3215 Greenmount Ave on March 21, 1977 (MD entity D00740985; Articles of Incorporation Film F2378/Folio 461), taking over the former Rabai's/Burri's storefront and continuing the parcel's ~50 years of bakery use. Gotti (an Italian surname; home at 5900 Benton Heights Rd, NE Baltimore) was the resident agent/proprietor. The bakery hired an 'all-around baker, morning shift' in 1978 and advertised through the 1980s. (Michael Gotti the baker is thinly documented — no obituary or grave found online, and he is NOT the New York crime-family John Gotti.)

summary: Louis Rabai, 'long the proprietor of a bakery [on] Greenmount avenue' and 'a leader in the Italo-American community,' died at 54 after a long illness. He came from Italy in 1923 to join his brother John B. Rabai in baking, went into business for himself ~1933, and sold his shop in 1952. He served ten years (three terms) on the Baltimore City Jail Board and was for a time chairman of Italy's own Boys Town in Rome.

summary: Mary Vicarini Rabai, who with her husband John B. Rabai ran a series of businesses called Rabai's French Bakery (downtown stores supplying French bread and hard dinner rolls to restaurants), died at 93. Born in Paris in 1896 to Italian parents, she came to Baltimore's Little Italy at age 8 and married John B. Rabai in 1914. Their children included Ermine (DePasquale) — pictured working at the Greenmount store in 1938 — Edith Segraves, and Cmdr. John F. Rabai. (The Rabai's French Bakery was the family's downtown/wholesale line, distinct from Louis Rabai's Greenmount retail shop.)

summary: The bakery family had TWO men named Louis, often conflated: (1) Louis RABAI (b.1902 Italy, immigrated 1923 to join his brother John, ran the Greenmount store, City Jail Board, d. Mar 14 1957) — buried New Cathedral Cemetery Plot VV-714, beside brother John B. Rabai (1896-1961) at VV-704; and (2) Louis BRUSINI, who married Rosa Vicarini (sister of John's wife Mary), making him John's brother-in-law and bakery co-founder. John B. Rabai m. Mary Vicarini (b. Paris 1896, d.1990) in 1914; their children were Ermine (DePasquale), Edith (Segraves), and John Frank Rabai (1921-2013, ran the bakery after WWII). Living descendants include grandson Peter DePasquale (Ermine's son) and Amy Brusini. A charming coda: the widowed Mary Rabai sailed on the RMS Caronia's Mediterranean cruise from New York on May 6, 1965.

summary: Rabai's Bakery was founded in the 1920s by Louis (Luigi) Brusini and his brother-in-law John B. Rabai — the two men had married the Vicarini sisters (John m. Mary Vicarini 1914; Louis Brusini m. Rosa Vicarini 1918). The original location was on Edmondson Avenue in West Baltimore; the business grew to multiple stores, including the Greenmount Avenue retail bakery (run by John's brother Louis Rabai) and a Park Heights Ave branch.

summary: In Waverly memory Rabai's was a beloved fixture a couple of doors from the Waverly Theater (near Zales): people stopped after church or after a movie. Remembered for yeast doughnuts, sticky pecan buns, crumb cake, milk bread, coconut sticks, meringue pies, and a peach cake called 'the unofficial taste of Baltimore summers.' A neighborhood boy traded his Morning Sun paper for a bun at the back door; delivery driver Jim Frizzera brought fresh rolls to the neighbors. 'Some of the nicest people in the world.'

summary: After the Rabai's/Burri's bakery era, the same storefront at 3215 Greenmount Avenue carried on as the Butter Crisp Bakery (incorporated 1977 under Michael Gotti). A July 3, 1978 Evening Sun help-wanted ad — 'BAKER. All around, morning shift, apply in person only. Butter Crisp Bakery, 3215 Greenmount Ave.' — confirms it operated at Rabai's exact address and was actively hiring its own bakers. Butter Crisp has a substantial newspaper footprint (~39 Baltimore Sun/Evening Sun matches), running from 1978 through a cluster of mentions in September 1987 (its apparent closing, amid the wave of 1980s Avenue store closings that alarmed the community) and a final trace into July 1988 — roughly a decade at the corner before the storefront's later conversion (today Raven Grocery & Dollar Mart, the Art Deco front lost).

summary: A late-1930s streetscape photograph of the Greenmount & E 32nd St node (the Old York Rd wedge) captures the commercial cluster 3201's corner store anchored. Legible businesses include a White Coffee Pot restaurant, the Family Finance Corporation, Brandau's / 'Marlboro' Clothes, and a W.L. Douglas 'Cinderella Shoe Shop' selling Weather Bird Shoes, with a large HEINZ OVEN-BAKED BEANS billboard mounted atop the corner building. On the sidewalk at the corner stands an open-air fruit-and-flower stand — crates of produce and potted flowers — the kind of outdoor display the 3201 corner grocery ran. A 1960s color view of the same stretch shows the block's later tenants (Nifty Cleaners, Roberts Jewelers) with the Waverly Theatre marquee and a streetcar beyond.

summary: The mid-to-late-20th-century owner of 3201 Greenmount was Matthew Swerdloff, a colorful Baltimore figure. Reared in Forest Park, he graduated City College (1944, lacrosse attackman), took a B.A. (1952) and law degree (1955) at the University of Baltimore, played lacrosse there (1952 North-South Game at NY's Polo Grounds, All-American honorable mention). In 1958-59 he was GENERAL MANAGER of the (Eastern Basketball League) Baltimore Bullets — a struggling minor-league pro basketball team he kept afloat by scrounging backers, doing front-office work unpaid while practicing law (the club ran ~$15,000 in the red, drew 500-600 fans a game, sat 6th at 7-11). He was also head coach of the Maryland Lacrosse Club and became a legendary lacrosse referee ('the Charley Eckman of lacrosse') — refereeing 1953-73 and 1986-95, president of the Southern Lacrosse Officials Assn, co-founder of the National Intercollegiate Lacrosse Officials Assn, teacher of youth lacrosse at the JCC (1960), and founder of the Heroes summer lacrosse leagues (1965) that gave players scholarships. He later worked in real estate (owning this Greenmount corner). A Mount Washington resident, he died Feb 25, 1995 (age 64) of a heart attack while refereeing a scrimmage at Anne Arundel Community College; his estate sold 3201 in July 1996.

summary: The Waverly Theatre at 3211 Greenmount Ave opened in 1909 as a neighborhood movie house, designed by architect Alfred 'A.' Lowther Forrest in partnership with Oliver Birkhead Wight. Its façade was a classical temple-style front with a large arched window and a decorative 'W' monogram — a scaled-down echo of the Beaux-Arts elegance the pair brought to Baltimore's downtown picture palaces. The Waverly is the project that ties Forrest and Wight together; its success led to Wight's involvement in their subsequent commissions. The building survives today as a retail store, still recognizable by its original theatre front.

summary: Alfred Lowther Forrest was born 1862 in Notting Hill, London, trained in architecture in London from age 19, and emigrated to the U.S. in 1898 (Boston/New York) before settling in Baltimore by 1907 — a city rebuilding after the 1904 Great Fire. He briefly worked for Baldwin & Pennington (B&O Railroad architects) before opening his own North Charles St office. A prolific theatre architect — 'he designed more than a dozen theaters, most of them in Baltimore' (Headley) — his works include the Victoria/Embassy Theatre (1908), the New Theatre (1910, co-designed with Wight), the Second-Empire Macht Building (1908, an early post-fire landmark), and Roland Avenue M.E. Church (1912). He left Baltimore for Rochester, NY ca.1928 and died in 1951, age 89.

summary: Oliver Birkhead Wight was a Baltimore-born architect (b. ca.1876–1880) who became one of the city's principal theatre designers of the 1910s–1930s. His early collaboration with Forrest on the Waverly (1909) and the New Theatre (1910) gave him his start in cinema architecture; by 1915 he was a registered AIA architect. His masterpiece was the Parkway Theatre (1915), modeled on London's West End and now restored as the SNF Parkway Film Center in Station North. He also remodeled the Howard Theatre (1920), designed the Arcade (1928) and Avon (1933) in Hamilton, the Irvington (1925), and the Carroll Theatre in Westminster (now the Carroll Arts Center) — collectively shaping Baltimore's neighborhood-cinema landscape.

summary: By the 1980s the Waverly had closed as a theatre and its front converted to retail — a 'SHOE CITY / The Family Shoe Store' occupied the storefront. Per a kilduffs.com account, the decorative 'W' was still visible atop the building into the 1980s before a new coat of siding hid it; the building's front remained 'easy to spot,' and the old sloped theatre floor survived in the stockroom. A new food store was later built in the rear of the old theatre. The Waverly was remembered as the neighborhood's favorite movie house, one block south of the more upscale Boulevard Theatre.

summary: The original 1909 iron-front picture-show-and-billiards was extensively renovated in 1919 and reopened in 1921 under the name 'the New Waverly Theatre.' The rebuilt brick-and-concrete house seated more than 1,300 people and featured a gold fiber screen and a five-piece orchestra to accompany the pictures — a major upgrade from the storefront nickelodeon. The reopening coincided with the 1919 opening of the Olmsted-designed 33rd Street boulevard and the 1921 debut of the rival, larger Boulevard Theatre three blocks north; the Waverly remained the smaller neighborhood 'community theatre' while the Boulevard drew the Guilford/Peabody Heights crowd.

summary: In the decades before air conditioning, theatres commonly closed in the summer heat. Waverly manager Harry Kahn worked around this by creating an open-air theatre in the open lot behind the building — a bed-sheet screen, wooden folding chairs, and a piano player — so the Waverly could keep showing pictures through the summer. A small, human detail of how a neighborhood movie house survived the season.

summary: Like the other movie theatres on Greenmount Avenue, the Waverly operated under racial segregation for much of its life. The National Register nomination notes the pointed contrast that while the Avenue's movie theatres were segregated, its 'refined stores' were open to everyone and employed Black workers — a marker of the everyday geography of Jim Crow in a mixed commercial district. Part of the corridor's civil-rights-era social record.

summary: The Waverly Theatre — the first theatre in Waverly village, running from silent films through talkies — closed in 1969 after sixty continuous years (1909–1969). The building was converted to commercial retail ca.1970 and given a sheet-metal facade ca.1990; the decorative 'W' that long survived on the parapet was covered over. Part of the building had also housed the Knockblock (Knowblock) Brothers' grocery store (1937), and the storefront later became Shoe City, with today's Raven Grocery & Dollar Mart occupying the space. The terrazzo paving of the former ticket booth still survives at street level (at the 3203 entrance bay).

This fixes the exact reopening date of the rebuilt house (the NPS-cited '1921' reopening = Feb 21, 1921).

summary: By 1963 the Crown five-and-dime had wound down here: a Circuit Court trustee's sale in the matter of the Trust Estate of Crown 5c & 10c to $1.00 Stores, Inc. auctioned the property Monday, September 23, 1963. The Greenmount piece was described as '3203-3205-3207-3209 Greenmount Ave.' — a 2-story brick business property with 3 stores and separate-entrance offices above, fronting ~70 feet on Greenmount with an average depth of 175 feet and 'running from Greenmount Avenue to Old York Road' (a through-lot spanning the wedge between the two streets), zoned 1st commercial. Stores at 3203 and 3207-9 were rented ($10,200/yr gross); 3205 and the upstairs offices were vacant. The SAME trust estate also owned a separate property five miles north — 507-509-511 York Road in Towson (Baltimore County), leased to a well-known tenant — sold at the same auction. (The two 'York Road/Greenmount' addresses are the same historic road by lineage but different places: Greenmount Ave is the straightened city segment of the old York Turnpike, with 'Old York Road' surviving as the fork behind the 3200 block; the Towson store is a wholly separate location.) The Greenmount frontage later passed to Eli & Yetta Miller / The Miller Realty Corporation and the 1981 Princess Shops rehab.

summary: The Greenmount storefront was not just a Crown branch — it was the CHAIN'S ORIGIN. A full-page Aug 27, 1936 Evening Sun ad narrating 'THE STORY OF CROWN STORES' opens with 'CHAPTER ONE — The First Crown Store — 3207-09 Greenmount Ave.,' followed by Chapter Two (735-37 Washington Blvd), Chapter Three (517-19 York Rd, Towson — the 1932 'Store No. 3'), and Chapter Four, the newest unit being opened that night at 5118-20 Park Heights Ave ('The Ten-Cent Store Beautiful'). Crown billed itself as 'Maryland's Own Chain — Owned and Operated by Marylanders.' So the corridor birthed a homegrown Baltimore five-and-dime chain: from this 3207-09 Greenmount flagship (c.1930, predating the 1932 Towson store) the chain grew to four stores by 1936 and at least six by 1950. Crown's trust ultimately owned the entire 3203-3209 frontage before auctioning it in 1963.

summary: As the chain's founding store, 3207 Greenmount doubled as Crown's hiring office and headquarters. A long run of Baltimore Sun / Evening Sun help-wanted ads placed from '3207 Greenmount Ave.' (phone UNiversity 6880) recruited for the whole chain — an Aug 27 1941 ad sought 'young ladies… selling positions open in our various stores… Apply Miss Stricker' (naming the store's hiring manager); others sought receiving/stockroom young men (1941), a store manager and stock man (1943), 'girls 16 or over' to 'earn Xmas money… in your own neighborhood' (1943), window trimmers (1944), and sign-holders (1948). A Sept 1943 ad's segregated 'Porters — Colored. Steady work' reflects the era's Jim Crow hiring language. By Oct 1958 the firm advertised as the incorporated 'Crown 5c & 10c to $1 Stores, Inc.' of 'Baltimore 18, Maryland,' a self-described 'rapidly expanding chain' hiring assistant managers — 3207 Greenmount still its address.

summary: On the night of Nov 25, 1951, burglars used a 4-pound maul to batter open the large second-floor office safe at Rabai's Bakery, 3215 Greenmount Avenue, and escaped with $3,320 in cash — the noise drowned out by the dough-mixing machinery running in the basement as the bakers worked below. Owner Louis Rabai told police the thieves also took a solid gold cigarette lighter ($240) and a $300 pocket watch, and drank a bottle of the bakery's brandy (kept for use in the recipes). The robbers had scaled a light pole in the side alley, forced the second-floor window of chiropodist Dr. Jacob Ostroff, and crossed into the Rabai office; the break-in was discovered the next morning by attorney J. Philip Knapp, whose office was nearby. Sgt. Allen Berman of the Northeastern district investigated. A press photo shows 'Louis Rabai inspects battered safe in his bakery.'

summary: The proprietor of Rabai's Bakery was a fixture of Baltimore's Italian-American civic and political world. Louis Rabai chaired the arrangements committee of the Italian-American Civic Club of Maryland — organizing its Columbus Day banquet in Oct 1945 (with Anselm Sodaro as club president) and standing among the Little Italy families who feted Mayor Tommy D'Alesandro at the club's 1947 testimonial dinner. In July 1947 Mayor D'Alesandro appointed Rabai to the Baltimore City Jail Board (term to July 1, 1951), on which he served, through reappointment in 1955, until his death — a tenure that included the board's March 1957 vote to desegregate the jail's visiting system (removing the Jim Crow sign). He was also the 'third man' in the uncropped photograph State's Attorney Anselm Sodaro used to defend himself in the bitter 1954 primary. Rabai's Bakery itself made a wartime Red Cross War Fund honor roll of organizations that exceeded their campaign goals.

summary: The Waverly Tower Shopping Center opened October 30, 1957, dedicated by Mayor D'Alesandro as 'the city's first redevelopment project' completed — and, per the Urban Renewal agency, the second finished redevelopment area in the nation (the Waverly project was conceived 1950 and officially launched 1953). Its owner-developer was Community Research and Development, Inc., whose president was JAMES W. ROUSE (chairman Jack Meyerhoff) — the same James Rouse who would go on to build the Harundale Mall (one of the country's first enclosed malls, then CRD's 'third project'), the new town of Columbia, Maryland, and Baltimore's own Harborplace. The Waverly Tower thus stands at the very start of Rouse's shopping-center career, just after CRD's first center in Easton. Designed by Cochran, Stephenson and Wing and named for the WWIN radio tower rising from its parking lot (300-350 cars), the center had 17 stores and a ~77,000 sq ft shopping component with a 400-foot frontage on Greenmount; alongside it Harry Bart built 28 apartment buildings (320-321 units). Some 250 aging structures were razed across ~19 acres between Greenmount Ave and Mathews St and the extensions of E 28th and E 29th Streets — the west-side 2800-block frontage, the rowhouses that had risen after the old Oriole Park ballpark cleared.

summary: A July 1957 pre-opening feature by Sun business editor Carroll E. Williams detailed the Waverly Tower's 17 outlets and ~65,000 sq ft of store/storage space. The anchor was a Food Fair supermarket (22,000 sq ft); the next largest were Eagle's Store (9,000 sq ft — the first Baltimore outlet of the Charlotte, N.C. chain) and Sunray Drugs (7,000 sq ft). Other tenants, 'all of this city,' included National Shores, David's Credit Jewelers, Rabai's Bakery, and Adolph's Beauty Salon, with a White Tower Restaurant on the north side of the 29th St extension just east of Greenmount, plus Moore's Toy Stores, One-Hour Valet and Terry Shops. Community Research & Development had been formed in January 1957 to build shopping centers 'in scattered parts of the nation'; its first was in Easton, this its second, and its third — the regional Harundale center off Ritchie Highway near Glen Burnie — was about to break ground. The Baltimore Gas & Electric survey of the moment counted 30 completed shopping centers in the area with 495 outlets, of which 'Waverly, 13' was one — the corridor entering the postwar shopping-center age.

summary: East 33rd Street is one of Baltimore's Olmsted-designed parkways, the 'green ribbon' connecting the city's major parks. The 1903 Municipal Art Society call for new parks led the city to commission the Olmsted Brothers (OBLA), whose 1904 'Report Upon the Development of Public Grounds for Greater Baltimore' proposed the parkway system. In 1907 Baltimore spent $70,000 of a $1-million park-bond issue assembling a 60-acre parcel along the newly-authorized 33rd Street boulevard. Construction of 33rd Street and the Alameda — linking Wyman Park, Venable Park, Lake Montebello and Clifton Park — began in 1911; the roads were paved and opened to traffic in 1914, and the tree-and-shrub 'parking' of the median was completed in 1916. As originally designed the parkways were to be 120-foot curvaceous boulevards (a central drive, two ancillary drives, a bike path, a promenade, and planted medians); financial and land constraints yielded the straighter four-lane road with the wide grassy, tree-lined median that still defines 33rd Street at Greenmount.

summary: On August 31, 1972, about 100 Waverly residents took their battle against the paving-over of part of the grassy 33rd Street median to the city director of public works. The flashpoint was a proposed left-turn-lane at Greenmount & 33rd; residents charged it was part of a larger plan to divert heavy traffic out of the wealthier, less-populated Guilford section — 'the matter of the median strip had become somewhat of a class issue for the Waverly residents.' A vivid instance of the Greenmount/Waverly-vs-Guilford fault line playing out at this exact corner.

summary: One of 33rd Street's most storied living landmarks stands west of Greenmount at Union Memorial Hospital. In November 1939, after his release from Alcatraz (where he had served time for tax evasion), Al Capone came to Baltimore's Union Memorial Hospital to be treated for syphilis (paresis). In gratitude he gave the hospital two Japanese weeping cherry trees; one was later lost to a hospital-wing expansion, but the other still blooms each spring and is celebrated as a Baltimore landmark. A vivid piece of the 33rd Street boulevard's lore, on the same Olmsted parkway that runs through the Greenmount corridor's north edge. (Note: Union Memorial fronts 33rd St near Calvert/University Parkway, roughly a mile west of the Greenmount & 33rd corner; recorded here as 33rd-Street-corridor context. The popular retelling that Capone 'took over the entire 5th floor' is folklore-grade.)

summary: East 33rd Street hardened into a social boundary. It became the dividing line between Waverly (north) and Better Waverly (south) and between their two neighborhood associations — the Waverly Improvement Association (WIA) took the north side of 33rd as its southern border, and the Better Waverly Community Organization (BWCO) took the south side as its northern border. The 1940 Federal Home Loan Bank Board study 'Waverly: A Study in Neighborhood Conservation' selected the area north of 33rd for conservation while describing the area to its south as a 'slum district' — helping cement 33rd Street as a border. The line had a racial dimension too: the corridor's segregated schooling put the white school at Greenmount & Gorsuch (later up on 34th) and the 'colored' school near Brentwood, Barclay and Merryman (its site now the 32nd Street/Waverly Farmers' Market parking lot). The 1972 fight over paving the median for a left-turn lane at Greenmount & 33rd (Waverly vs 'wealthier Guilford') was the same fault line at the same corner.

summary: The most famous landmark on the 33rd Street boulevard east of Greenmount was the stadium at Venable Park. A predecessor 'new stadium' was erected in 1922 in the portion of Venable Park north of the 33rd Street boulevard (Baltimore/Municipal Stadium), later rebuilt as Memorial Stadium — home of the Baltimore Colts and Orioles, 'the old gray lady of 33rd Street.' The Colts left for Indianapolis in 1984 and the Orioles left for Camden Yards in 1992; the site was later redeveloped (with the old Eastern High School property) into Stadium Place and a community playground. Hundreds of thousands of fans passed through the Waverly/Greenmount commercial corridor to reach games here — the north-end counterpart to the corridor's earlier Oriole/Terrapin ballparks at 29th-30th.

summary: The hub of the old village was the York Turnpike toll gate, which stood at York Road and Gilmore Lane. Established with the turnpike (laid out 1741; toll road financed from ~1810), the Waverly toll gate and house served as a center of commerce and communication until the toll gates along the road were removed in 1894. Its recorded gate keepers were David Mumma, William Eaton, T. S. Bonsal, and T. Schoofield — the men who took the tolls from travelers, farmers driving livestock to market, and stagecoaches on Baltimore's main overland road to the north.

summary: The Aull family were among the founders of Waverly village. Jacob Aull kept a shoemaker's shop in the 1830s hamlet of Huntingdon (the pre-Waverly settlement), and his residence — a snow-capped gambrel-roofed frame cottage dated 1836 — stood on the west side of York Road near 31st Street. The Aulls put down deep roots along the road: a later Jacob H. Aull built the 'Eagle Nest' mansion (1884) on the west side of York Road near 25th Street, and the 'old Aull residence' at Brentwood and East 31st survives today as the Thir-Tea-First Street Café & Tea. The family name threads through a century of village life.

summary: Louis J. Aull, a builder of the next Aull generation, put up his own Victorian frame residence in 1888 at 414 Waverly Avenue, running his shop at 3101 Talbot Street. The house — photographed with a mounted policeman and the family on the porch — later had a commercial storefront added; from 1988 to 2001 it housed the 'Old Waverly History Exchange & Tea Room,' owned by Donna Beth Joy Shapiro and Fred Shoken, who restored parts of it (and used this very image on their sign) while wishing they could have removed the storefront and restored the original front porch. A neat closing of the loop: a founding builder's house became a shop celebrating the village's history.

summary: Bavarian immigrant Jacob Aull (1804-1876) purchased a gravel pit on the west side of the York Turnpike in the 1830s, built a house and opened a cobbler shop — considered the FIRST non-agricultural enterprise in the area (alongside a corn husk depot, a blacksmith, and three small stone houses). Old Land Marks item 2: 'Residence, Late Jacob Aull, 1836; West side York Road, near 31st Street.' NPS B-5229 p51: 'Around the time Waverly became an official community in 1830 a few stores in the hamlet included a blacksmith and a shoemaker's shop owned by Bavarian immigrant Jacob Aull... his sons would go on to build houses during the first construction boom in Waverly.' Wife: Christiana Gusema (1812-1880); five children incl. Louisa Frederika, Margaret Eva, Louis J., Jacob Henry.

summary: A first-person village census in prose. Verbatim highlights: OXFORD: 'numerous neat and cosy houses. Several of them are owned by Mr. John Knobloch. There is also a fine brick store... of which Mr. Theodore A. Bokel is proprietor... contains many fine and convenient residences. Several of these are owned by Mr. A. D. Clemens, the owner of most of the land.' TOLLGATE: 'Before reaching Waverly, a point commonly known as the "first tollgate," is the finely-situated place of Mr. Samuel Brady.' RAILROAD & BAPTIST CHURCH: 'The Peabody Heights and Waverley railroad, extending from the present Charles street terminus at Northern Boundary avenue to Waverley, will be completed... about the first of August... The route of this road will cause the tearing down of the old Baptist church, situated near the tollgate. Another site has been selected, and a new church will be erected at a cost of from $10,000 to $15,000. The pastor, Rev. John Berg, has already about $5,000... to be built of brick, and is to seat about 500 persons.' ESTATES: 'On the road running from the right of the tollgate... are the fine places of Messrs. Henry Taylor, A. Hoen, M. P. Smith, George Saunders, W. S. Thompson'; 'the fine Wilson estate, embracing several acres... adjoining which on the north is the magnificent McDonald estate, which binds both on the York road and Charles street avenue... The McDonald mansion is a model for convenience and comfort'; 'the elegant place of the late Mrs. Gen. McDonald... the elegant country residence of Mr. Charles Taylor, and the fine cottages of Dr. R. Sappington, Mr. Atkinson, Mr. Milholland, Mr. Savin... and the fine place of Mr. I. N. Steele.' HALL: 'Among the numerous attract[ions is] a fine public hall, erected re[cently at] $12,000' — the hall standing by JULY 1871. Explains booklet items 15/16 (the railroad forced the Baptist church move; the 1873 'new church' at Barclay & 31st is Rev. Berg's brick church).

summary: 'A requiem mass for Joseph Varsalona, a shoe repairman in Baltimore for 54 years, will be offered at 10 A.M. Friday at St. Ann's Church, Greenmount avenue and 22d streets. Mr. Varsalona died unexpectedly Monday at his summer home in Bowley's Quarters. He was 84. Born in Sicily, he came to Baltimore in 1919 and shortly afterwards opened Joe's Shoe Repair Shop at 2703 Greenmount avenue, which he operated until the time of his death. He was known to his customers and friends as Mr. Joe. He was a member of the Moose and the Sons of Italy. Survived by his wife, the former Josephine Domina; a daughter, Mrs. Concetta Carmen Meyls; three grandchildren and three great-grandchildren.' A 52-year single-proprietor storefront — one of the longest business tenures documented anywhere on the corridor. SSDI VERIFIED (2026-07-15): Joseph Varsalona b. Burial not yet located — Most Holy Redeemer Cemetery (Belair Rd) is the lead for the Sicilian-Baltimore family.

summary: 'A requiem mass for John T. Hayes, a retired city worker and decorated Army veteran of World War II... Mr. Hayes, who was born in Baltimore, died unexpectedly Tuesday at his home, 2701 Greenmount avenue. He was 63.' Drafted June 1942; served in the African, Middle Eastern and European theaters with the 315th Infantry Regiment. Under barrage, he crawled to the crest of a hill, found a German tank, moved to within 50 yards and hit it with two phosphorous rifle grenades; returned through 'a gantlet of small arms and artillery fire,' located a bazooka, and — 'firing one well-aimed rocket,' per his Distinguished Service Cross citation — destroyed it. After discharge (Dec. 1945, Technical Sergeant, DSC + Purple Heart): shipyard worker at Sparrows Point, then ~15 years a city sanitation worker until 1970. Survived by sisters Mary Ellen O'Keefe (Edison, N.J.), Helen Dambrogi and Beatrice Hayden (Baltimore) and brother Martin R. Hayes. The corner's second front-line war story, thirty years after the Meyls valentine at 2703. THE AWARD RECORD FOUND (agent research 2026-07-15, homeofheroes.com valor database): Private John T. Hayes, Jr., U.S. Army — Distinguished Service Cross for action 24 OCTOBER 1944, awarded by Headquarters, Seventh U.S. Army, GENERAL ORDERS NO. 63 (1945). The date lands precisely on the 315th Infantry's celebrated fight east of EMBERMENIL, Lorraine (Foret de Parroy sector): Companies A and F of the 315th earned Presidential Unit Citations for repelling German armor there 20-24 October 1944 — a private killing a tank with a bazooka fits that action exactly (rank at action Private; the obit's Technical Sergeant = later rank). Identity match held PROBABLE: the online record carries no unit/hometown, and the 79th Division's 1946 history's awards appendix is ambiguous on OCR — full citation text lives in Seventh Army GO 63 (NARA RG 407/338 or Fold3), queued.

summary: READ IN FULL from the MSA image — and the 'Marguerite E. Wolf' mystery dissolves: she was a STRAW. The deed's own caption reads 'Marguerite E. Wolf, of Baltimore City... (straw-party).' September 28, 1973 (recorded October 31): Wolf conveys BOTH lots — 2701 (northeast corner of Twenty-seventh Street, formerly Oxford Avenue, and Greenmount Avenue, formerly the York Turnpike Road, 15 x 90 ft) and 2703 — for $1.00 to 'Josephine Varsalona, Concetta Meyls and Rosemarie M. Meyls, as joint tenants and not as tenants in common, the survivor of them.' The companion instrument, RHB 3074/881-883, recorded the same minute-stamp run (receipts 287468/287469), is the OUT leg: Josephine Varsalona to Wolf, same day, same notary (George Sempeles). Purpose: after Joseph Varsalona's death 'on or about May 31, 1971' vested the corner in Josephine alone, the widow used the straw round-trip to re-title into a JOINT TENANCY with her daughters, putting survivorship in place — estate planning by deed, the parcel's THIRD straw conveyance (Neuman 1916, Coughlin/Lovitt 1923, Varsalona/Wolf 1973). The out-leg recites the whole chain: 2701 from Catherine T. Kelly by deed of May 31, 1930 (SCL 5124/305); 'NO TITLE EXAMINATION MADE.' RECITAL-ERROR FINDING: the 1985 deed (SEB 487/238) cites this instrument as 'Liber 3072 folio 884' — WRONG; RHB 3072/884 is an unrelated Hamilton deed for a 409 E. North Avenue leasehold. The real liber is 3074, found by name-searching Varsalona: lesson — recitals can miscite; verify by party search.

summary: THE DEED READ IN FULL (SCL 3799/101, pulled 2026-07-15): dated November 14, 1921 — AARON AND IDA NEUMAN convey 2701 Greenmount IN FEE SIMPLE to THOMAS J. COUGHLIN AND CATHERINE KELLY, unmarried, AS JOINT TENANTS — roughly $12,000 per the Sun's transfer column. THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERS: the newspaper compressed the grantees to 'Thomas J. Coughlin, etc.,' but the deed shows CATHERINE KELLY — identified as Coughlin's NIECE — was a CO-PURCHASER FROM DAY ONE, not merely the executrix-legatee she appears as in 1929-30. The 1923 Lovitt straw round-trip consolidated title in Coughlin alone; his will (ERD 164/299) then devised the corner back to her, and she sold to the Varsalonas in 1930. Recital: the Neumans held under the 1916 Williams straw pair (SCL 3047/411-412), Aaron having merged the fee in 1915 (Mutual Life, SCL 2979/316) onto the leasehold he took from Jacob Klein in 1903. Signatures witnessed/notarized by Jeannette S. Fleischer — the same notary as the 1923 straw legs. The 19-year Neuman era ends; two weeks later Neuman bought 2705-2707 from Max Cohen.

summary: The vacant corner store at 2601 Greenmount played the EXTERIOR of Freddy's BBQ Joint — the hole-in-the-wall where Kevin Spacey's Frank Underwood eats ribs alone, run by his confidant Freddy Hayes (Reg E. Cathey, who won the 2015 Primetime Emmy for Outstanding Guest Actor in a Drama for the role). In the pilot Underwood dines on the side patio — the 26th St corner exposure; the production dressed the already-weathered storefront and removed the signage when filming wrapped (interior accounts conflict: re-dressed in place vs. a set at the Joppa, Md. soundstage — both claims recorded). In-universe the joint sits in a rough quarter of Washington; in fact it was Better Waverly, a storefront Google Street View shows vacant since at least 2007, earlier a fried-chicken restaurant, a bookstore and a community center (per iamnotastalker's location work). The location stayed a fan mystery until the owner's 2014 sale listing outed it. The corridor's biggest latent-IP fact: a flagship-series canon location, deed-anchored to this ground. A production still (supplied 2026-07-15) shows the dressed corner: hanging 'Freddy's BBQ JOINT' blade sign, painted sign over the corner door, the one-story wood-boarded storefront tight against the three-story row — with a laundromat sign visible up the block toward 2603. The dressed building is unmistakably the one-story corner standing today.

summary: A Superintendent of Transportation Office photograph (shared by Marvin Welch, Baltimore Past and Present Photos, 10/13/2021): the vast low tabernacle built for evangelist BILLY SUNDAY's 1916 Baltimore campaign, at York Road and 29th Street — 'in the left center background is a sign that reads ORIOLE PARK circa 1915.' Streetcar No. 790 passes on York Road; crowds mill; a horse cart stands at the curb; new rowhouses rise behind. The block's sacred-and-profane double bill: the Federal League ballpark and the sawdust trail side by side. RENUMBERING EVIDENCE in the caption: 'it was situated in 1916 at York Road and 10TH STREET. Only later were these streets renamed Greenmount Avenue and 29th Street' (the cross-streets north of North Ave carried numbers from 9th upward before the 1919-era renumbering; Sun columnist Jacques Kelly, in the thread, disputes how current '10th street' ever was). GEOGRAPHY RESOLVED (agent research: SABR/Wikipedia): the tabernacle stood ACROSS 29th Street from this parcel — on the SOUTHWEST corner block (28th-29th/Greenmount/Barclay), the abandoned AMERICAN LEAGUE PARK site, Waverly's old 'York Road grounds' where professional baseball ran 1889-1914 (Oriole Park II of 1889; the 1901-02 American League Orioles; the International League Orioles through Babe Ruth's 1914 rookie season). The photo thus captures BOTH ballpark blocks at once: the revival shed on the dead park, the 'Oriole Park' sign on the living one (Terrapin, this parcel's block). THE CAMPAIGN (Sun retrospective 7/2/2005 + campaign histories): February 2 - April 23, 1916; the 15,000-seat 'Salvation Shed'; over a million hearers; 23,027 'trail hitters'; ~96,000 through the doors on the final day, when 'Home Run' Baker and four other Yankees hit the sawdust trail. Sunday was himself a former big-league ballplayer — the evangelist-outfielder preaching on a dead ballpark beside a live one.

summary: A color slide (Baltimore Memories collection; shared by baltimore.history, captioned 'The Boulevard Theatre located 3302 Greenmount Avenue. (1963)'): the Boulevard's marquee reads 'LEE RE[MICK] — THE RUNNING MAN — TECHNICOLOR' (Carol Reed's film, released October 1963); a yellow PCC streetcar No. 7105 loads passengers mid-avenue; 'NO LEFT TURN 6AM-9PM' on the mast arm. Across Greenmount, the east side's full midcentury lineup: the grand brick hall with green arched windows lettered BOULEVARD BOWLING LANES, KUSEN'S RESTAURANT — BAR, a Remington cards-and-gifts shop, MAB PAINTS, and the Save-A-Dollar market up the block. The 3300 block as complete entertainment district: movies, bowling, bar-restaurant, all trading at once in the streetcar system's final years. THE HOUSE (agent research, Cinema Treasures/Kilduffs/Sun): opened October 8, 1921 — 1,625 seats, architect Ewald J. Blanke, a Durkee house (sister to the Senator) with a Skinner organ; twinned 1984; closed 1989; gutted for retail with the auditorium ceiling still intact above the drop ceilings; the 1948 marquee came down in fall 2022; bought ~2016 for $1.2M by the CENTRAL BALTIMORE FUTURE FUND (the same fund that later helped Red Emma's land at 3128) with a 2020 reuse RFP pending. AND THE BOWLING HALL ACROSS THE STREET: the upstairs duckpin lanes ('the Boulevard,' 25 cents a game) sat one flight above HARRY W. SCHWAAB'S soda fountain and confectionery — homemade pistachio and coffee ice cream, wedding cakes — and F. SCOTT FITZGERALD kept Schwaab's number in his personal address book during his 1930s Baltimore years (Sun 7/1/1992; Sun 2/8/1998).

summary: A 7-inch 45: 'SWEENEY'S TWIST (Billy Martin) — BILLY MARTIN and his Corvairs — MONITOR RECORDS #1402-A, 45 R.P.M., Jalo Music, Inc. - BMI,' b/w 'I Found My Baby' (1962). Per collector documentation (Discogs r4207180; popsike auction notes), the record is a tribute to Sweeney's Lounge on Greenmount Avenue — the bar is named in the lyrics — produced by Baltimore DJ Jack Gale on the local Monitor label. A Greenmount corner bar with its own twist record at the height of the dance craze: place-made IP, pressed in vinyl, still trading among collectors sixty years on (Jeff holds a copy). The through-line from the 1942 amateur nights to the 1962 record is the venue's own: the stage that paid cash prizes eventually paid in canon. PRODUCER IDENTIFIED (agent research 2026-07-15): Jack Gale (1925-2018), Baltimore-born WITH-AM 1230 morning host 1957-63 and later Billboard DJ of the Year (1970), was recording local acts (Ronnie Dove, the Kings, the Combonaires) at Biddle Street Studios in exactly this period; 'JALO' = JAck + LOvey Gale (his wife's public records list The Jalo Corporation and Lovey Music Inc.), and Jalo Records 1406 (Ronnie Dove, June 1962) shares Monitor 1402's numbering series — Monitor was almost certainly a Gale imprint. 'Billy Martin' himself remains unidentified (a Montreal-trumpeter attribution on citizenfreak looks like name-collision; no Baltimore Jam band listing) — possibly a pickup band for the one-off. The side was later anthologized on the 'Buzzsaw Joint Cut 7' compilation LP.

summary: 'THE SUBURBAN LEAGUE — Waverly, Govans And Towson All Win From Opponents. ROLAND PARK GETS BUMPED... Waverly, 4; Roland Park, 2. Amid the cheers of 500 persons the Waverly White Sox of the Suburban League won their thirteenth straight victory by defeating the Roland Park Club... A. Bonthron started to pitch for Waverly and for four innings pitched great ball, but owing to a sore arm gave way to Green... a neat squeeze play pulled off by Kuzm and Sommer tied the score.' League standing: Waverly 13-0, 1.000. Five hundred fans for a Waverly nine in 1908 — the sandlot tradition that runs through the Loyalty Club (1923, from 2705) and the Rosebud A.C. (1930, from 2703), six years before the Terrapins built their park at 29th. HOME GROUNDS (probable, agent research): Waverly's diamond was the 'YORK ROAD GROUNDS' — the block at 28th-29th/Greenmount/Barclay, per SABR 'at the corner of York Road and Tenth Street (now 29th Street and Greenmount Avenue),' pro baseball's home 1889-1914 and the amateur showcase ground when the Orioles were away (Interclub championships drew 4,600 there). Deeper still: the WAVERLY BASE BALL CLUB of 1860, formed by lawyer William Clapham Pennington, merged into the Pastimes when its players left for the Civil War — Waverly's sandlot lineage runs 1860 -> White Sox 1908 -> Loyalty Club 1923 -> Rosebud A.C. 1930.

summary: The Waverly Park and Shop directory (Evening Sun, June 11, 1958, p. 49) lists 'VINSON'S ANIMAL HOSPITAL, 3015 Greenmount Avenue' among the association's 35 members. The hospital was the practice of two brothers from Loachapoka, Alabama: Dr. Fletcher L. Vinson (1897-1955), in Baltimore by 1929, and Dr. Bryant C. Vinson (1909-1982). It opened as 'a new Modern Small Animal Hospital' next door at 3013 Greenmount in March 1931, was still at 3013 in 1934, and is listed at 3015 from September 1935, a year after Fletcher bought the lot (September 18, 1934, S.C.L. 5481/414). By 1958 Bryant ran it; he retired in 1975. The practice's own history gives 1930 as its founding year and Kummer (1941) gives 1927. No kinship with the Vinsons of 2601 Greenmount is shown.

summary: Michael A. Fletcher, Evening Sun: 'For 16 years, Tom Fannin drew customers to Early Attic, his Waverly antiques shop, by displaying a few pieces of fine wood furniture on the sidewalk out front... at 415 E. 32nd St.' A city inspector's violation notice (March) revealed that sidewalk-display permits were BANNED in the Waverly commercial district under the 'hard-fought urban renewal plan for the area in 1979' — city housing official Roseann Walsh: 'We have a history of people displaying used washing machines and dryers on the sidewalk.' The Board of Estimates split 2-2 (City Solicitor Neal M. Janey + Comptroller Hyman A. Pressman FOR — 'I think what is being asked for here is reasonable'; Council President Mary Pat Clarke + DPW Director George Balog AGAINST — 'The minute we [approve this] we might as well build shelves on 32nd Street'), Mayor Kurt L. Schmoke abroad and unable to break the tie. Dating ~1989-91 from the officeholders; Early Attic thus open since ~1974 — the building's second act after the Hooper's Restaurants general offices. Its painted EARLY ATTIC letters still clung to the facade in 2020 Street View (Dixon-for-Mayor banner era), letters falling, before Red Emma's took the building. OWNERSHIP CONFIRMED (2026-07-15): Thomas R. Fannin owned the building, selling it 7/1/2016 for $240,000 to 415 East 32nd Street, LLC — the assembler that sold the pair to Red Emma's in 2022.

summary: Christina Tkacik, Sun, 5/5/2021: 'Red Emma's is on the move. Baltimore's cooperatively-run, radical bookstore and cafe is moving for the fourth time, this time to what owners call their forever home in Waverly... You may have heard a rumor that Red Emma's is buying a building. That rumor is FALSE. We're actually buying TWO buildings!' — 415 E. 32nd Street and the storefront at 3128 Greenmount Avenue. Co-founder Kate Khatib; the co-op (ex-30 W. North Ave, then Mid-Town Belvedere ~2018) 'can now own part of the business and have a say in how its run' for every worker; North Avenue pizzeria Joe Squared moved in as announced; purchase supported by the state housing department's Neighborhood Business Initiative capital grants, the Central Baltimore Partnership, Central Baltimore Future Fund and WAVERLY MAIN STREET. The Hooper's-offices/Early Attic building becomes home to a worker-owned bookstore-cafe — and its twin at 3128 is Sweeney's old cafe. THE TRANSACTION (agent research, SDAT open data + liquor board, 2026-07-15): the deal closed January 12, 2022 — $800,000 for BOTH parcels in one arms-length multi-parcel transfer from 415 EAST 32ND STREET, LLC (deeds Liber 18420/348 for 3128 Greenmount; Liber 18262/191 for 415 E 32nd). The seller LLC had assembled the pair in 2016: 3128 bought 8/31/2016 for $376,500 from J.T.M. Greenmount, LLC, and 415 E 32nd bought 7/1/2016 for $240,000 from THOMAS R. FANNIN — Early Attic's proprietor owned his building. Financing: Seed Commons committed a $1 million non-extractive renovation line/mortgage (mortgage payment ~half the co-op's prior rent). The entity: RED EMMA'S COOPERATIVE CORPORATION (Baltimore liquor board, July 2022 — a Class B license requesting LIVE ENTERTAINMENT, principals Mary Al-Khatib and Andrew Scotti). Soft opening at 3128: late October 2022. The live-entertainment license makes the venue lineage official.

summary: SCL 5124/305, read line-by-line. 'THIS DEED made this 31st day of May... 1930... between Catherine T Kelly unmarried of Baltimore City... and Joseph Varsalona and Josephine Varsalona his wife... as tenants by the entireties' — consideration a nominal $5.00 (the real price rode the same-day purchase-money mortgage: at least $6,500). The recitals close two loops in one paragraph: 2701 came to Kelly 'by the last will and testament of Thomas J Coughlin recorded... in Liber E R D #164 folio 299... devised to the said Catherine T Kelly in fee simple,' and to Coughlin 'by deed dated December fifth 1923... Liber SCL No 4114 folio 511... conveyed by William Lovitt' — the return leg of the 1923 straw round-trip, now precisely cited. Witness/notary: Lennox B. Clemens, the Waverly Building Association's own attorney. Recorded May 31, 1930 at 11:11 A.M. — deed, mortgage and settlement all inside one Saturday morning. The Varsalonas, nine years at 2703 (Joe's Shoe Repair), now owned the corner next door; the family would hold both until April 1985. Coughlin bought for ~$12,000 in 1921; his estate let the corner go in the first Depression spring at roughly its $7,000 inventory value.

summary: Same page-run as the Kelly deed (SCL 5124/305-307), recorded minutes behind it: Joseph and Josephine Varsalona mortgage to the WAVERLY BUILDING ASSOCIATION OF BALTIMORE COUNTY, which had 'received therefrom an advance of Six Thousand and five Hundred ($6,500.00) Dollars on fifty (50) shares of stock standing in their names... Said sum so loaned being paid as part of the purchase money' for 2701. Security: THREE parcels — Block 4071's 2701 (the deed of even date) and 2703 (the 1921 Stoler assignment, ground rent $90), plus Block 3837's 319 EAST TWENTY-SEVENTH STREET, a third Varsalona holding acquired by assignment from Edgar N. Dinsmore, November 17, 1925 (SCL 4491/99), subject to $60 ground rent — the family compound wrapped around the corner. Terms are pure building-association mechanics: weekly dues of 25 cents per share plus 15 cents weekly interest per $130 share advanced, interest stepping down 15 cents with each $130 of principal retired; attorney Lennox B. Clemens. An immigrant shoemaker buying his corner with neighborhood mutual-society money — the Waverly Building Association underwrote the block it was named for.

summary: Recited in full in MLP 6320/478: 'by lease dated the twenty fourth day of May 1898 and recorded... in Liber RO No 1734 folio 497 etc was demised and leased by Charles C McColgan unto William L Dail for the term of ninety nine years renewable forever at and for the annual rent of ninety dollars ($90.00) payable in equal half yearly installments on the first days of June and December.' The creation of 2703's ground rent — the classic Baltimore two-estate split at the moment the east side of the York Turnpike Road was being cut into 15-foot storefront lots, when the cross street was still Oxford Avenue. Every subsequent leasehold paper on 2703 (Samuels 1915, Stoler 1915-21, Varsalona 1921-42) paid this $90 until the Varsalonas extinguished it in 1942.

summary: SCL 3762/310-312, read line-by-line: THREE instruments recorded back-to-back on the same afternoon (2:51, 2:53 o'clock stamps). (1) ASSIGNMENT: 'Max Stoler and Sophie Stoler his wife... and Joseph Varsalona and Josephine Varsalona his wife' — the leasehold at 'Number 2703 York Turnpike Road or Greenmount Avenue' (east side, 15 ft north of the NE corner of the Turnpike and Oxford Avenue, 15 x 90 to the ten-foot alley), subject to the $90 annual ground rent; recites the Stolers took it by assignment from LOUIS SAMUELS, December 20, 1915 (SCL 3019/136). Notary: Rudolph M. Winterling. This is the deed behind the family legend: Joseph Varsalona, arrived from Sicily in 1919, opens Joe's Shoe Repair — and the Sun's shoemaker-wanted ad runs from 2703 exactly three weeks later (August 17, 1921). He would work this room 50 years, to the week of his death. The Jewish shoe-store family hands the shop to the Sicilian shoemaker — the corridor's succession pattern in a single page.

summary: Second instrument in the run (SCL 3762/310-312): 'Joseph Varsalona and Josephine Varsalona... justly indebted unto the said Giovannai [sic] Geppi in the full sum of thirty hundred ($3000.00) dollars... at the expiration of two years... with interest... at the rate of six per cent per annum payable half yearly... Said principal sum being part of the purchase money.' Named attorney: VINCENT J. DEMARCO. Geppi's oath that the consideration was bona fide came 'at the same time' — and both his oath and his 1924 release are signed 'Giovanni x his mark Geppi': the lender could not write, but he could fund a storefront. Release witnessed by Vincent J. Demarco and JOSEPH J. CULOTTA, recorded January 17, 1924 — paid off in two and a half years. Italian-community private credit doing what banks wouldn't for a 1919 arrival: with the Stolers' $1,500 take-back (next instrument), the whole ~$4,500 acquisition was financed within the community. (Same-surname note: the Geppi name later becomes Baltimore-famous via Diamond Comic Distributors' Steve Geppi — kinship unresearched.)

summary: Third instrument in the run (SCL 3762/312): 'Joseph Varsalona and Josephine Varsalona his wife... justly indebted unto the said Max Stoler and Sophie Stoler his wife in the full sum of fifteen hundred dollars ($1500.00) which sum they gave promised to repay at the expiration of three years.' summary: MLP 6320/477-478, read line-by-line: 'THIS DEED Made this 29th day of May... 1942... by Monumental Life Insurance Company formerly called Mutual Life Insurance Company... unto Joseph Varsalona and Josephine Varsalona his wife... in consideration of the sum of fifteen hundred dollars and accrued ground rent... the aforesaid rent payable out of said lot and the reversion thereto... with the intent that the aforesaid annual rent may be forever merged and extinguished.' Signed by Howard M. Emmons, Vice President; witness Harry C. Roth, Controller; notary Emily C. Linke; recorded June 2, 1942. The recitals carry the lot's full pedigree back to birth (the 1898 McColgan-Dail lease and the 1898 sale of the reversion to Mutual Life). Wartime thrift note: the family that lost an engagement ring at Rocky Point that same summer of 1942 was simultaneously retiring the ground under its shop. Financing echo of 1930: a same-week $1,500 purchase-money share loan from TITLE PERMANENT BUILDING & LOAN (next instrument).

summary: MLP 6320/478-479: 'Joseph Varsalona and Josephine Varsalona his wife... members of said body corporate have received therefrom an advance of fifteen hundred dollars ($1500.00) being part of the purchase money for the hereinafter described property on fifteen (15) shares of its stock, the due execution of this mortgage having been a condition precedent.' Weekly dues of $3.75 plus interest-and-premium of $1.80 per week stepping down 12 cents per $100 retired — the identical share-loan machinery the Waverly Building Association ran for the family's 1930 purchase of 2701. summary: Deed dated May 15, 1961, recorded May 17 at 12:15 P.M. (Liber JFC 1070, folio 378): Edgar D. Phoebus and Florence L. Phoebus, his wife, convey 2601 Greenmount Avenue to Robert L. Vinson and Evelyn D. Vinson, his wife. THE SIGNATURE IS THE STORY: Edgar executed by mark — 'Edgar D. (X, his mark) Phoebus' — the man who had owned the corner since 1947 could not (or could no longer) sign his name; he was dead by October 8. The lot runs 25 x 200, spanning 375-400 feet south of 27th Street, with a 20-foot reservation for BOONE STREET at the rear — the paper ghost of a street the plat promised. Recital: the Phoebuses took title from Levi A. Barnett et al. and George D. Burdette et al. by deed of January 27, 1947 (MLP 7080/179). Witnesses David Kimmelman and Richard H. Lerch; notary Ursula F. McCormick (her certificate misrenders him 'EDGAR L. PHOEBUS'). A later hand noted in the margin: 'ORDER FILED 1-11-71' — some 1971 proceeding touched this title, an open thread. Financed the same run by a $7,500 Yolanda Building Association purchase-money mortgage.

summary: Same run as the deed (Liber JFC 1070, folio 380, recording stamp JUL 20 1961): Robert L. and Evelyn D. Vinson give the YOLANDA BUILDING ASSOCIATION a $7,500 purchase-money mortgage on 2601 Greenmount, secured by 75 shares of the association's stock. The corner's fourth building-association purchase in the corridor pattern — Waverly Building Assn financed the Varsalonas' 2701 in 1930, Title Permanent their 2703 fee in 1942, Augusta the Phoebuses' own purchase of 2601 in 1947, and now Yolanda finances the Phoebuses' buyers. The share-accumulation loan (borrow the price, buy shares weekly until they retire the debt) was the immigrant and working-class mortgage machine of rowhouse Baltimore for a century, and 2601's title chain samples four different associations doing it.

Burdette, his wife, convey 2601 Greenmount to Edgar D. Phoebus and Florence L. Phoebus. Documentary stamps — $13.20 U.S. and $12.00 Maryland — price the sale at roughly $12,000. The Phoebuses financed with an $8,060 Augusta Building & Loan mortgage, and held the corner fourteen years.

summary: Deed dated June 25, 1962, recorded June 26 at 10 A.M. (Liber JFC 1302, folio 548): Mark Levy, widower, grants the 2705 Greenmount leasehold to PAUL VERNON MEYLS AND CONCETTA MEYLS, his wife, as tenants by the entireties — $5 'and other good and valuable considerations,' with U.S. documentary stamps of $4.40 implying an actual price near $4,000. The lot: east side of 'York turnpike road,' 30 feet north of the northeast corner at 27th Street ('formerly called Oxford Avenue'), 15 x 90 to a 10-foot alley — subject to the $90 annual ground rent payable May 17 and November 17, with benefit of renewal forever (recital: Nathan and Daisy Platt's lease to Levy, May 17, 1962, JFC 1281/7). THE CONVERGENCE: Concetta Meyls was Concetta Carmen Meyls née VARSALONA — daughter of Joseph and Josephine Varsalona of 2701-2703. Eighteen days after the on-premises auction (June 7), the family that had held the corner pair since 1921-30 took the third house in the row through the daughter's marriage. Eleven years later the 1973 Wolf straw deed would put Concetta on 2701-2703's title too; in 1985 the Meylses sold all three to Strucko as a single group. Witness and notary Mary Margaret Sloman; grantee-index stamp July 24, 1962, assignment code 52543.

summary: Deed dated August 1, 1892, recorded the same day at 2:20 P.M. (Liber JB 1404, folio 446): ENOCH PRATT and Maria Louisa Pratt, his wife, convey to Charles C. McColgan, for $45,000, roughly twenty-seven numbered lots 'lately a part of Baltimore County' — the ground on BOTH sides of Oxford Street (now 27th) at the York Turnpike, plus Barclay Street frontage. The lots are numbered on 'the plat of Oxford,' filed in the case of PARKHURST vs. FRISBY in the Circuit Court for Baltimore County — the plat that still governed deed descriptions here in 2001. Lots 72-74 with 114-115 run north from Oxford Street 150 feet along the east side of the Turnpike, 400 feet deep to FRISBY STREET: the ground under 2701-2719 Greenmount, which McColgan would lease to builder William L. Dail in 1898. Lots 75-82 (part) with 107-113 run 375 feet SOUTH from Oxford 'to the lot conveyed by said Enoch Pratt and wife to EDWARD J. COLL' — with 'the use benefit and advantage of a reservation of TWENTY FEET of the Easternmost portion of the lot conveyed as aforesaid to Coll to be used for the purpose of a Street to be opened fifty feet wide.' That clause is the birth certificate of BOONE STREET, the paper street that haunts 2601's deeds into the 1960s. Recital: Pratt himself took the tract from Horatio L. Whitridge and Robert Dobbin, Trustees, December 18, 1868 — the philanthropist held this edge of Waverly for 24 years. Test Jno. T. Maddox, J.P.; per Jas Bond, Clerk.

summary: Lease dated and recorded May 24, 1898, 1:15 P.M. (Liber RO 1734, folio 497): Charles C. McColgan leases to WILLIAM L. DAIL ten lots — the entire future row 2701-2719 Greenmount, each 15 x 90 feet on the east side of the York Turnpike Road running north from the northeast corner of Oxford Avenue — for 99 years renewable forever at NINETY DOLLARS a year ground rent on each lot severally, with a 6% capitalization clause. This is the row's birth instrument: Dail was the BUILDER (his same-run indemnity mortgage pledges the corner lot against $1,200 owed Jacob Klein for building materials), and the ten $90 ground rents created here are the ones traced through the row's deeds for the next century. Recitals: Enoch Pratt and wife to McColgan, August 1, 1892 (JB 1404/446); James T. Lowe to McColgan, surrender, August 17, 1894 (JB 1526/714). Test George McCaffray; Robt Ogle, Clerk.

The mortgage proves Dail built the row himself on Klein credit, and it explains what the chain shows five years later: by October 17, 1903 Jacob Klein held 2701's leasehold outright (Klein to Aaron Neuman assignment, RO 2309/553 — the page missing from the digitized volume), the materialman having taken the corner store. The corner's first financing, before any bank or building association touched it.

summary: Deed dated and recorded December 2, 1898, 4:20 P.M. (Liber RO 1764, folio 209) — ten days after leasing the row to builder Dail, McColgan sells the REVERSIONS and $90 ground rents on the FIRST FOUR lots (2701, 2703, 2705, 2707) to the MUTUAL LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY OF BALTIMORE for $6,545.45 — exactly four times $1,636.36, a $90 rent capitalized at 5.5%. The insurer (later Monumental Life) would collect the corner's ground rents for decades: it sold 2701's fee to Aaron Neuman in 1915, 2703's to the Varsalonas in 1942 ('forever merged and extinguished'), and 2705's to the Levys by deed of redemption in 1945. Witness/notary Jno. Spring Jr.; Robt Ogle, Clerk. Recites the Dail lease (RO 1734/497).

summary: Deed dated May 28, 1915 (Liber SCL 2979, folios 316-317): the Mutual Life Insurance Company of Baltimore conveys the FEE — the reversion and $90 ground rent it had bought from McColgan in 1898 — to AARON NEUMAN, who had held 2701's leasehold since taking it from Jacob Klein in 1903. Leasehold and reversion merge; the tailor now owns his corner outright. Seventeen years an insurer collected the corner's rent; the merchant on the premises finally bought it out. (2703's fee would not merge until 1942, 2705's until 1945.)

summary: Two deeds recorded back-to-back May 13, 1916, 12:21 P.M. (Liber SCL 3047, folios 411-412): Aaron Neuman conveys 2701 to John Williams, who immediately reconveys to AARON AND IDA NEUMAN AS TENANTS BY THE ENTIRETIES. A classic Baltimore straw round-trip — the corner's second (after the Stolers' 1915 trip next door at 2703) — done for no other purpose than converting Aaron's sole ownership into a marital tenancy a year after he bought the fee. The row's running straw-party count reaches FIVE by 1973: Stoler/Samuels 1915 (2703), Neuman/Williams 1916 (2701), Coughlin/Lovitt 1923 (2701), Levy/Bach 1947 (2705), Varsalona/Wolf 1973 (2701+2703) — every one an intra-family tenancy rearrangement.

summary: Deed dated August 1, 1892, recorded the same day at 2:20 P.M. (Liber JB 1404, folio 446): ENOCH PRATT and Maria Louisa Pratt, his wife, convey to Charles C. McColgan, for $45,000, roughly twenty-seven numbered lots 'lately a part of Baltimore County' — the ground on BOTH sides of Oxford Street (now 27th) at the York Turnpike, plus Barclay Street frontage. The lots are numbered on 'the plat of Oxford,' filed in the case of PARKHURST vs. FRISBY in the Circuit Court for Baltimore County — the plat that still governed deed descriptions here in 2001. Lots 72-74 with 114-115 run north from Oxford Street 150 feet along the east side of the Turnpike, 400 feet deep to FRISBY STREET: the ground under 2701-2719 Greenmount, which McColgan would lease to builder William L. Dail in 1898. Lots 75-82 (part) with 107-113 run 375 feet SOUTH from Oxford 'to the lot conveyed by said Enoch Pratt and wife to EDWARD J. COLL' — with 'the use benefit and advantage of a reservation of TWENTY FEET of the Easternmost portion of the lot conveyed as aforesaid to Coll to be used for the purpose of a Street to be opened fifty feet wide.' That clause is the birth certificate of BOONE STREET, the paper street that haunts 2601's deeds into the 1960s. Recital: Pratt himself took the tract from Horatio L. Whitridge and Robert Dobbin, Trustees, December 18, 1868 — the philanthropist held this edge of Waverly for 24 years. Test Jno. T. Maddox, J.P.; per Jas Bond, Clerk.

summary: Two assignments recorded back-to-back December 20, 1915 (Liber SCL 3019, folios 135-136): Max Stoler assigns the 2703 leasehold (east side of the York Turnpike Road, 15 feet north of the Oxford Avenue intersection, 15 x 90) to Louis Samuels, who immediately reassigns to MAX AND SOPHIA STOLER AS JOINT TENANTS. The 'Samuels' name that surfaced in the 1921 Varsalona deed's recital was never an owner at all — he was the straw man in the shoe-store family's tenancy rearrangement, five months after little Marian Stoler was struck by the streetcar out front. RECITAL, one link deeper: Aaron Neuman granted 2703 to Max Stoler by deed of December 23, 1908 (liber handwritten and ambiguous, '2?17' folio 433 — probes of SCL 2417 and 2517 both missed; unresolved). So 2703's chain runs Neuman -> Max Stoler 1908 -> straw 1915 -> Varsalonas 1921.

summary: From the recital in the 1915 straw pair (SCL 3019/136): Aaron Neuman granted and conveyed 2703 Greenmount to MAX STOLER by deed dated December 23, 1908, recorded in a liber whose handwritten citation reads '2?17,' folio 433. Direct probes of SCL 2417/433 (April 1908 — a Wells & McComas building-association release) and SCL 2517/433 (August 1909 — an Ogle trustee deed) both missed, so the exact liber remains unresolved (candidates 2317/2617, or the grantor index at the Maryland State Archives). The DATE is documentary; the instrument itself is still unread. It marks the arrival of the Stoler shoe family — 2703's occupants and owners until the Varsalonas bought in 1921 — and shows Neuman, the 2701 tailor, dealing lots to his own block's merchants.

summary: Assignment dated April 12, 1923, recorded April 17 at 12:16 P.M. (Liber SCL 3996, folio 308): AARON AND IDA NEUMAN assign the 2705 Greenmount leasehold ($90 ground rent, June/December; '27th Street, formerly called Oxford Avenue') to MARK LEVY AND BESSIE LEVY, his wife, as tenants by the entireties. Nominal $5 consideration, but $9.50 in cancelled U.S. documentary stamps prices the sale near $8,600. RECITAL: the Neumans had held 2705 only sixteen months — they took it by assignment of December 2, 1921 (SCL 3805/141) from MAX COHEN, two weeks after selling 2701 to Coughlin and Kelly. The same run carries the Washington & Lafayette Building Association's release of the Neumans' 1921 purchase mortgage (SCL 3813/170) to clear title. Test/notary Lennox B. Clemens; Stephen C. Little, Clerk. The tailor's family exits the block's ownership; the Levy era (1923-1962) begins.

summary: Two purchase-money mortgages in the same April 12, 1923 run: (1) folios 309-311 — Mark and Bessie Levy to the WAVERLY BUILDING ASSOCIATION OF BALTIMORE COUNTY, $5,070 advanced on 39 shares of stock (George E. Leight, President; attorney Lennox B. Clemens; released February 28, 1929, liber 4977/436); (2) folios 311-312 — a $1,730 second mortgage back to AARON NEUMAN himself, a five-year note with ten $51.90 semiannual interest coupons (6%), expressly subordinate to the Waverly mortgage (released early, October 28, 1926, liber 4653/421). Purchase structure on ~$8,600: $5,070 association money, $1,730 seller paper, roughly $1,800 cash. The Waverly Building Association's THIRD appearance in this one chain family — it financed the Levys' 2705 in 1923, the Varsalonas' 319 E. 27th in 1925, and the Varsalonas' 2701 in 1930, Leight signing and Clemens notarizing each time.

summary: From the recital in the Levys' 1947 straw deed (MLP 7179/375): by Deed of Redemption dated January 17, 1945 (Liber MLP 6695, folio 255), the MONUMENTAL LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY OF BALTIMORE — successor to the Mutual Life Insurance Company that bought the corner four's reversions from McColgan in 1898 — conveyed 2705's reversionary estate to Mark and Bessie Levy, 'whereby the leasehold and reversionary estates... were merged... thereby vesting in them the entire fee simple estate.' The third of the 1898 reversions to come home (2701 in 1915, 2703 in 1942, 2705 in 1945): forty-seven years of an insurer collecting $90 a year, ended for a redemption price. Instrument itself not yet pulled.

summary: Three deeds executed July 12, 1947, all notarized by HERBERT H. MILLER, recorded together July 18 at 1:50-1:51 P.M. (Liber MLP 7179, folios 374-378): (1) Mark and Bessie Levy convey 2705 Greenmount in fee to FRANCES BACH, unmarried — a straw. Its recitals give 2705's true chain: leasehold from Aaron Neuman by assignment of April 12, 1923 (SCL 3996/308); reversion from Monumental Life by Deed of Redemption, January 17, 1945 (MLP 6695/255), merging the fee. (2) Bach reconveys 2705 to MARK AND BESSIE FOR LIFE, tenants by the entireties, with full powers of sale, lease and mortgage — remainders: one half to ALFRED LEVY absolutely, the other half to LOUIS LEVY for life, then to Alfred. (3) Bach conveys a half-interest in 3910 FERNHILL AVENUE — the family HOME, furniture and furnishings included, 'excluding any and all cash and/or securities' — to Mark and Bessie for life, remainder to NATHAN AND DAISY PLATT. The plan in one sentence: the store to the sons, the house to the daughter. Fifteen years later the widowed Mark would use those reserved powers to redirect 2705's fee to Daisy instead (JFC 1281/5) — and in 1987 her children's gift of the ground rent to Alfred Levy quietly RESTORED the 1947 intent. A margin note on all three deeds — 'order filed 8/21/58' — marks some 1958 proceeding, an open thread. Miller notarized the family's paper in 1947, 1962 and 1987: forty years the Levys' lawyer.

summary: Fee-simple deed dated May 17, 1962, recorded May 18 at 12:45 P.M. (Liber JFC 1281, folio 5, 'PREPARED WITHOUT TITLE EXAMINATION — NO STAMPS'): MARK LEVY, widower, conveys 2705 Greenmount to NATHAN PLATT AND DAISY PLATT, his wife — identified in the deed itself as 'the son-in-law and daughter of the said Mark Levy' — for $5 'and of the natural love and affection which the party of the first part has for the parties of the second part,' exercising the powers reserved in the 1947 Bach deed. RECITALS: Frances Bach's deed of July 12, 1947 (MLP 7179/376) gave Mark and Bessie a life estate with full powers of sale; 'the said Bessie Levy having since departed this life on APRIL 27, 1961,' Mark conveys 'the entire fee simple interest, both life estate and remainders.' One minute later (12:46 P.M., folio 7) the Platts leased the lot back to him for 99 years at $90 — so the daughter got the fee and the rent, and the old man kept a leasehold he auctioned that June to the Meyls family. Test/notary Herbert H. Miller; James F. Carney, Clerk.

summary: The August 1, 1892 Pratt-to-McColgan deed (JB 1404/446) reveals 2601's pre-history: Pratt's lots south of Oxford Street run 375 feet down the east side of the York Turnpike 'to the lot conveyed by said Enoch Pratt and wife to EDWARD J. COLL' — the big unsubdivided corner tract, which the 1940 City plat shows as 375 feet along York Road by 90 feet deep. So 2601 (and 2565 and 2567 beside it) sit in Coll's parcel, bought from Enoch Pratt before August 1892. The deed carries 'the use benefit and advantage of a reservation of TWENTY FEET of the Easternmost portion of the lot conveyed as aforesaid to Coll to be used for the purpose of a Street to be opened fifty feet wide should such a street be hereafter opened to Oxford Street' — the origin of the 20-foot BOONE STREET reservation that rides every 2601 deed through 1946 and 1961. A street promised in 1892, never opened, formalized as a utility corridor by Coll's heirs in 1940, and still a paper ghost when Edgar Phoebus signed by mark in 1961.

summary: Agreement dated May 21, 1940, recorded June 7 at 9 A.M. (Liber MLP 6043, folio 136, plat at 136a): JULIA A. COLL AND ELLA C. COLL, joint tenants — heirs of the Edward J. Coll who bought the corner tract from Enoch Pratt before 1892 — grant the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, for ONE DOLLAR, the right to lay 'sewers drains water pipes and other municipal utilities' through the family land, per Department of Public Works plat R.W. 20-32930 (drawn May 14, 1940, W.O. 1949). The recorded plat maps the tract: YORK ROAD frontage of 375 feet from 27th ('OXFORD') Street, 90 feet deep to a 10-foot alley, with a 10-foot right-of-way running through the back land — the utility corridor that tracks the never-opened BOONE STREET reservation of the 1892 Pratt deed. No buildings may ever be erected over it. Test/notary Leo C. McDonagh; approved George Cobb, Chief Engineer, and City Solicitor Charles C. G. Evans; M. Luther Pittman, Clerk. Two single women signing away a strip of an 1892 family purchase so the pipes could go in — the Colls still owned the 2601 tract in 1940, six years before the Russells sold it out of the family orbit.

summary: Purchase-money mortgage dated November 6, 1946, recorded November 8 at 2:32 P.M. (Liber MLP 7032, folios 202-204): LEVI A. BARNETT AND HELEN A. BARNETT and GEORGE D. BURDETTE AND ETTA S. BURDETTE — the four names the 1947 deed's recital compressed to 'et al.' — mortgage 2601 Greenmount to the AURORA FEDERAL SAVINGS & LOAN ASSOCIATION for $5,500 of purchase-money balance at 4.5%, $57.05 a month (John L. Fisher, President; notary Katherine E. Wich; M. Luther Pittman, Clerk; margin cross-reference '1/30/47 LIBER 7080 FOL 179' — the release recorded with their exit sale). Recites their same-day purchase from ARTHUR J. RUSSELL AND LELIA M. summary: In November 1843 the Rev. W. A. Hewitt was sent to the village of Huntingdon by the Rt. Rev. William Rollinson Whittingham, Bishop of Maryland, at the request of Mr. THOMAS HART, who wished to have his grandchildren baptized without the journey to the mother parish, St. Paul's, downtown. The congregation was born with those baptisms and the ideals of the OXFORD (Tractarian) MOVEMENT that Bishop Whittingham was planting in Maryland. Huntingdon was then a village of some seventeen great estates (Montebello, Clover Hill, Homewood, Guilford, Greenmount, Homestead); it was annexed to Baltimore City in 1888 and renamed Waverly after Scott's novels. On 24 November 1843 Bishop Whittingham himself preached in the congregation's temporary chapel. St. John's is the anchor of a three-parcel campus that survives today: the church and its 1.83-acre churchyard (3009½ Greenmount), the rectory (3001 Old York Road), and this 1914 parish hall (3009 Greenmount).

summary: The cornerstone of the first church was laid 22 April 1846; it was consecrated by Bishop Whittingham on 11 November 1847, and it was resolved that St. John's would be a 'FREE' CHURCH — NO PEW RENTS, ever, an egalitarian stance for the era. For two years the rector returned his stipend toward the building and installed the furnace at his own expense. The 1847 building (which stood on the church parcel, 3009½ Greenmount) is attributed by the CHAP Landmark Report to ROBERT CARY LONG JR. (1810-1849), Baltimore's leading Gothic Revival architect — an attribution absent from the parish's own history and from the 1975 National Register form (which assigns no architect and names Abraham Bucher as 'in charge of building').
