The Baltimore Housing Authority sponsored it; the U.S. Housing Authority and HOLC supplied technical services.

summary: The FHLBB published *Waverly: A Study in Neighborhood Conservation* (1940), prepared by economist Arthur Goodwillie under HOLC Deputy General Manager Donald H. McNeal, making the Waverly neighborhood the federal government's national demonstration project for 'neighborhood conservation' — the preventive alternative to slum demolition and a direct ancestor of postwar urban renewal. The 107-page book was offered 'for the inspiration and guidance of other urban communities... throughout the United States.' Waverly was chosen as the 'almost ideal' setting for 'an experimental study in scientific neighborhood conservation.'

summary: The 1940 study defined 'Waverly' as the white residential area north of 33rd Street; it described the district to its south — which includes the Oriole Park (V) ground at 29th–30th & Greenmount — as 'a fully developed... slum district' where 'occupancy is being gradually relinquished to an economically needy and racially mixed residential type,' and which was 'definitely threatening the Area — by its contiguity and by actual infiltration.' The two were separated only by 'a wedge-shaped tract, improved with modern homes... narrow at the west and continuously widening toward the east,' and 'the slum's pressure to cross this sharply defined barrier... [had] been successfully resisted hitherto only by means of the high neighborhood standards.'

summary: The report's summary Table No. 24, 'Dominant Factors in Waverly,' listed under Social conditions the very first factor — 'Race' — with the Favorable entry 'All white.' summary: The study documented the federal mortgage apparatus at work in Waverly: the Federal Housing Administration had graded the neighborhood from 58 ('eligible but poor') to 84 ('good') for mortgage-insurance eligibility, refusing Title II insurance anywhere rated below 50; and the Home Owners' Loan Corporation held 122 mortgages and owned 20 properties in the Area — 'the largest single property holder in the Area.'

summary: To make the conservation program permanent, the study established the Waverly Conservation League, incorporated June 13, 1940, with organizing personnel supplied by HOLC: an Advisory Committee of 25 (including the executive heads of the four local improvement associations), an Operating Committee with a chairman from each of the Area's six districts, and 'block captains' for each block. It prescribed 'beneficial restrictions' — deed covenants limiting land to single-family residential use, which it framed as 'effective protection against undesirable infiltration' — and proposed a municipal Department of Conservation to run 'clean-up, paint-up, fix-up' campaigns and enforce restrictions.

summary: The study's Appendix C proposed model legislation drawn from the Waverly experiment — a 'Neighborhood Improvement Act' and an 'Urban Redevelopment Corporations Act' — as templates for other jurisdictions, and the FHLBB explicitly offered the whole formula for 'the treatment of similarly threatened small-home neighborhoods everywhere... increasingly great urban districts throughout the United States.' The Waverly Test thus fed the legal and administrative machinery that became postwar urban renewal.

summary: When Terrapin Park opened, the city met it with force: 75 officers under Capt. Moxley at the park, 50 more at Oriole Park across the corner, a uniformed man 'at practically every corner' out the York Road, and a mounted squad. From day one the wedge was a place the police surrounded, choreographed, and controlled.

summary: Before the pennant and the fire, a vast wooden revival tabernacle for evangelist Billy Sunday stood at the wedge — York Road & 29th, the exact corner — drawing crowds past the streetcar barns, an 'Oriole Park' sign already visible in the background. summary: For 1937 booking agent Douglass O. Smith secured Oriole Park for the Elite Giants' night games, opening a park 'shut to colored teams for years.' Then it closed again: owner Tom Wilson wanted the park but balked at Smith's fee, and white residents complained to park officials about 'the noise and fanfare' of the night games. For 1938 the Elites were pushed to Bugle Field. The line was undone not by a rule but by a fee and a neighborhood's noise complaint — the same pretext used to evict the Elites for good in 1942.

summary: The 1939 Elite Giants — with championship-series games played on this ground during the season — clinched the Negro National League title over the Homestead Grays. In the deciding game at Yankee Stadium, Sept 24, 1939, Jonas 'Lefty' Gaines shut out the Grays for seven innings and Baltimore won 2–0, taking the NNL championship and the Ruppert Cup — the best season in the franchise's Baltimore run, by a club shut out of the white ballpark's gate.

summary: When Black world featherweight champion Chalky Wright defended his title at the park (stopping Baltimore's Harry Jeffra by TKO, Jun 19, 1942, before ~6,000), he carried a lineage: his grandfather, Caleb Baines Martin, was a runaway from a Natchez plantation who became a Buffalo Soldier and the first African-American ranch owner in southwest Arizona. The site's clearest world-championship night ran a bloodline from bondage to a title belt onto this ground.

summary: Eighty-six years before the ballpark burned, another fire took the same corner. St. John's Episcopal — standing 'at the first toll-gate on the York road,' the exact spot where home plate would sit — was deliberately torched at 2 a.m.; the sacramental vessels stolen, the building gone before the companies arrived. 'The walls are of stone, and they are still good' — and the stone church survives today. Two fires, 86 years apart, on one tollgate corner (1858 arson; the July 4, 1944 ballpark blaze).

summary: At Shiloh AME on E. 28th St., Richard L. Steiner of the Baltimore Redevelopment Commission told ~100 families they'd get 'a good price' for homes the city had claimed. The Waverly site — 17 acres bounded by Greenmount Ave., Reese St., 27th and 30th (taking in the ballpark parcel's own blocks) — was one of Baltimore's first two blighted-area clearance projects. Residents formed the interracial Waverly Area Association to protect themselves. The graded corridor 'cleared' acre by acre — the through-line from the 1937 map to the bulldozer.

summary: Miller E. and Doris Morton execute a deed of trust to Jay Fred Cohen and Carlton P. Bennett, trustees for Landbank Equity Corporation, securing a $50,000 note against two properties: 501 East 22nd Street and 2616 Greenmount Avenue. No standalone release of this specific instrument was found among the supplied later releases (which instead cover different, similarly-dated Landbank deeds of trust on other Morton properties). Maryland Tax-Property §14-844(b) provides that a valid tax-sale judgment vests title free and clear of prior encumbrances, subject to statutory exceptions — so this lien is understood to have been extinguished by the 2026 foreclosure judgment even without a recorded release, though this should be confirmed by title underwriting.

Ausby grants alternative service nunc pro tunc and enters judgment foreclosing the right of redemption, vesting Vertex TL LLC with absolute and indefeasible fee-simple title to 2616 Greenmount. summary:
The full published obituary (supplied by Jeff, 2026-08-05) confirms and greatly expands the Find A Grave excerpt. Doris Cynthia Morton was born Nov 3, 1927 in Live Oak, Florida; as a teenager in Daytona Beach she attended Campbell Street High School and was crowned "Miss Campbell Street." She later lived in New York City, fellowshipping at Faith Temple under Bishop Dr. Alvin A. Childs Sr., before relocating to Baltimore in the early 1970s, where she married Bishop Miller Elbin Morton, founder of Eden Light Baptist Church, and became its Head Deaconess. She served as a long-time Board Member of the Eastside Democratic Organization (EDO), focused on minority representation and Black political empowerment in Baltimore City.

CRITICAL CROSS-LINK: the obituary states Doris and Miller "owned and operated two tire businesses, one on Huntington Avenue and the other on Harford Road," later combined into one Harford Road location, "Glide N Ride" (now "Quick Tire Ride") — run by the couple for nearly 40 years. This independently confirms and explains the 1983-84 white-paper finding that the Mortons' 2616 Greenmount mortgages tied the property to "Dot Tire Company" and to holdings on Huntingdon Avenue and Harford Road: Dot Tire Company was the Mortons' own tire business, the direct predecessor of Glide N Ride / Quick Tire Ride. After Miller's death in 2012, Doris ran the tire shop alone for another decade, working daily until age 94 and earning the nickname "The Tire Lady"; in her final years her son-in-law Harry M. Smith assisted.

She was predeceased by her parents, Lorenzo Washington and Stella McCray, and her youngest daughter Linda D. Cruse. She is survived by daughters Fleeter M. Reed and Deborah C. Cruse (m. Harry); sons Claude "Champ" Reed and Everett "Chubby" Cruse; step-son Romeko Morton; grandson Maurice (Belinda) Smith; granddaughter Unissa Cruse-Ferguson; great-grandson Kyle Smith; nephew Corey White; niece "Rosemary"; and several godchildren.

The 1953 Sanborn sheet (LOC item sanborn03573_044, sheet 732 -- a republication of the 1928 base plate with paste-on corrections, not an independent resurvey) depicts 2616 Greenmount as a pink-shaded (brick), 2-story ("2B") dwelling ("D"), one of a uniform unbroken row from 2614-2654 on the south side of Greenmount Ave between Boone St and the block interior -- no occupant name or commercial signage. The 1928 edition (item sanborn03573_018, same sheet 732) shows the identical footprint and story count. This is in tension with a real-estate ad (Evening Sun, Oct. 13 1922) and repeated 1978-82 tax notices describing the house as "three-story, eight-room." Possible explanations include a Sanborn surveyor undercount, a rear addition not reflected in the story label, or a genuine discrepancy between the fire-insurance survey and the real-estate description -- left as an open question rather than resolved.

summary: MD Business Express confirms LANDBANK EQUITY CORPORATION OF MARYLAND, INC. (Dept. ID D01560093) is status Forfeited, and Garrison Holding Corp. (D00462200) is also Forfeited (note: two similarly-named active MD entities, "Garrison Holding, LLC" and "Garrison Holdings, LLC," are NOT related to the 1983 mortgagee). Research into the Virginia Beach parent, Landbank Equity Corporation, found that it collapsed into Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September 1985 -- roughly 18 months after issuing the $50,000 deed of trust against 2616 Greenmount and 501 E 22nd St -- converting to Chapter 7 liquidation (In re Landbank Equity Corp., 83 B.R. 362 and 77 B.R. 44, E.D. Va. 1987, trustee Laurence H. Levy). Owners William R. Runnells Jr. and Marika Runnells ran a mortgage-fraud scheme -- falsifying loan documents, placing loans in employees'/relatives' names, and selling them to FNMA and savings & loans as bona fide -- and were later criminally convicted and sentenced to 30+ years combined plus $500,000 fines each (Washington Post, Jan. 29 1991, "Landbank Equity Owners Sentenced to Prison Terms"). This almost certainly explains why the white paper's supplied record set found no conventional release of the SEB 202/367-370 deed of trust: the lender ceased to exist as a going concern within about 18 months of making the loan, and any release would have had to come through a bankruptcy trustee rather than the original company -- not a data omission, but a real historical dead end in the lien's paper trail. This directly addresses the white paper's own "Medium-High" risk flag on the missing Landbank release.

summary: Every Polk directory from 1914 through 1923 lists 3315 and 3317 Greenmount Avenue as DWELLINGS occupied by skilled tradesmen and city workers — not as shops. 3315: Robt F Crafton, bricklayer (1914, 1915, 1921); Oliver Inderrieden, bricklayer (1915); Jas O Inderrieden, bricklayer (1918); Wm B Inderrieden, plumber (1921); Wm Brew, plumber, wife Charlotta (1923). 3317: Wm H Bull, motorman (1915); Otto Gliewe, streetcar conductor (1918); Bernard A Murphy, policeman, wife Sadie (1920, 1921, 1922); Geo L, machinist (1923). No commercial listing appears at these numbers in any year. This establishes the parcel's pre-commercial condition and reframes the 1922–23 assemblage: George Esselman did not build on vacant ground — he bought and cleared an occupied residential row of bricklayers, streetcar men and a policeman to put up his garage.

summary: The buyer of the 1922 assemblage was not an abstract investor. The 1923 Polk directory lists 'Esselman Motor Co, Geo Esselman pres, Frank T Richards v-pres-sec, GREENMT AV COR 33D N' — that is this parcel, the northeast corner of Greenmount and 33rd. The 1922 directory adds 'Esselman Geo Co (Geo Esselman) LUMBER, 3225 Greenmt av', a second Esselman business four blocks south on the same avenue, and lists him personally as 'Esselman Geo (Margt V; Esselman Motor Co) h 3007 n Calvert' (in 1923, wife Virginia). Earlier books show him purely as a lumber dealer ('Esselmann Geo E lumber 208 e 31st n', 1918; 'Esselman Geo lumber 3007 n Calvert', 1921). So the man who bought 3313–3327 in June 1922 and applied to build a two-story brick garage there in October 1923 was a Greenmount Avenue lumberman moving into the automobile trade, and the garage he built was his OWN dealership. Deed-owner and operator are the same person. Update Oct. 14, 2026: George Esselman died intestate about Dec. 28, 1923, leaving his widow Virginia (d. about July 4, 1924; will E.R.D. 149/438 to her daughter Lillian K. Winbigler) and his daughter Maude E. Shorey, who sold to Schwaab in 1925 (773:mdlr-scl4507-266-esselman-heirs-schwaab-1925).

summary: The Sun's restaurant column announces the end of the Greenmount Uncle Lee's: the owners are retiring, their children will not take the business, and the restaurant is for sale. It also fixes the restaurant's historical claim — that Uncle Lee's introduced Baltimore to Szechuan cooking about two decades earlier, i.e. c. 1977–79 — and separates the Greenmount house from the Inner Harbor one at 44 South Street, which it says had different owners and would not be affected by the sale. This is the closing bracket on the parcel's restaurant era, and it lands one year before Sunho Corp's charter was allowed to forfeit (6 Oct 1998).

summary: A two-photograph Sun news feature, shot by Duy Do, showing the mural on this building being painted in the July heat. It names the artist: veteran Baltimore cartoonist TOM CHALKLEY, who designed the mural and called it 'the Great Wall of Waverly', with BECCA MATHIAS and ALIYAH SAUNDERS working alongside him on the scaffolding. The mural occupies the side wall of 3313 Greenmount at the Greenmount/E 33rd Street crossing and depicts neighborhood life — faces, street signs, the playground, the farmers market. It is the parcel's single most visible piece of authored, attributable creative work.

summary: Maryland SDAT's charter record for the corporation that held this building for 38 years. Principal office: 3313-19 GREENMOUNT AVE. Resident agent: AN PAN LEE, 44 SOUTH STREET, Baltimore 21202 — the address of the second Uncle Lee's Szechuan at the Inner Harbor, which the Sun in 1997 described as having different owners; the shared agent address makes a family connection likely but not proven. Charter lifecycle: incorporated 9 July 1979 (film F2449 folio 859, 6pp) — three months after Henry Y.C. Lee bought the property on 18 April 1979 and four months before he deeded it into the corporation on 26 November 1979; FORFEITED 7 October 1987; revived 30 March 1993 (film F3500 folio 310); FORFEITED AGAIN 6 October 1998 — one year after the restaurant went up for sale; then dormant for eighteen years until ARTICLES OF REVIVAL (STOCK) were filed 3 January 2017, five months before the 29 June 2017 sale, evidently to make the corporation capable of signing the deed; ARTICLES OF DISSOLUTION filed 21 August 2019, winding it up two years after the sale. The corporate registry independently corroborates the restaurant's rise, its 1998 collapse and the 2017 exit.

summary: On 30 April 2012 Councilwoman Mary Pat Clarke introduced legislation for Baltimore City to condemn, purchase and then resell 3313 Greenmount Avenue, the vacant former Uncle Lee's. Her stated reason was that the owner had no interest in improving the building's deteriorated state — and, pointedly, that the decay was threatening the Great Wall of Waverly mural on its flank. Clarke: 'When you start messing with murals on Greenmount Avenue you've gone too far.' The city never acquired the building; it stayed in Sunho Corp's hands another five years. This is the moment the parcel's public value was argued in the Council chamber on the strength of the artwork attached to it rather than the building itself.

summary: A local history feature assembling the parcel's late-20th-century story. It dates Uncle Lee's opening to 1979 and describes what it replaced: a deteriorating grocery store — matching the July 1977 liquidation auction of Eddie's Supermarket's fixtures. It records that the operation opened as HALF RESTAURANT, HALF CHINESE MARKET, selling jasmine teas and gyoza wrappers, so the building's supermarket back-of-house was carried straight over into an immigrant food-retail use. On the Memorial Stadium trade it quotes assistant manager PO CHANG from a 1993 Baltimore Sun piece: 'The stadium used to bring a lot of people, mostly tourists, from different areas like D.C., Virginia and Pennsylvania.' On the mural it credits TOM CHALKLEY and GREG GANNON, completed August 2010 at Greenmount and E 33rd, depicting neighborhood faces, street signs, the playground and the farmers market — and notes that water damage from the Uncle Lee's building was already threatening it, three months before Clarke's condemnation bill.

summary: A Baltimore Sun article dated 1999-07-30 ('From NationsBank to Bank of America; New name being put on buildings, ATMs, stationery, cards') confirms the branch-level rebrand already logged in prod as a corporate name change following NationsBank's October 1998 merger with BankAmerica Corp. (a $38 billion deal creating the first coast-to-coast bank). The Maryland conversion, budgeted at $9 million for the mid-Atlantic region and targeted for completion by August 30, 1999, touched 205 branches and 516 ATMs statewide (111 branches and 318 ATMs in the Baltimore area alone) -- 3339 Greenmount's own sign change was one of hundreds happening simultaneously, not a distinct local event. Local president William Couper: 'It doesn't change their account numbers, their checks or their plastic cards' -- i.e. no ownership or account change for customers, purely branding.

summary: The Baltimore City Council adopted the Waverly Business Area Urban Renewal Plan as Ordinance 79-1029 (1979), the statutory instrument governing the Greenmount Avenue commercial corridor's 1976-1983 revitalization program. The URP, not a merchant-taxing district, was Baltimore's late-1970s corridor tool: it carried acquisition authority and binding design standards for storefront appearance. The ordinance remains recited in later amending legislation (Ord. 11-470; Ord. 12-71). Waverly was never designated a Retail Business District under the 1982 RBD ordinance, and was not among the 1977 Shopsteading areas (Jonestown, Union Square, Washington Hill) -- the three DHCD programs are distinct and are frequently conflated.

summary: The 1977 'Waverly Design Standards' folder of the Department of Housing and Community Development shows the district's design rules from first draft to ordinance text. A two-page handwritten 'Waverly Business Area, Summary of Design Standards' sets the visual floor for every storefront: show windows not filled, boarded or covered by signs and kept within 13 feet of grade; no broken or painted glass; frames, trim and walls repaired and painted; security grilles inconspicuous and removable during business hours; only soft, retractable awnings; and no new Formstone, aluminum siding, wood shakes or pebble-faced plywood, with margin revisions showing the siding rule being renegotiated. Its sign page limits flat signs to 12 inches of projection below 13 feet, allows freestanding signs only at gas stations (past or present) up to 24 feet, caps projecting signs at 5 feet out and 10 to 15 feet up, bans rooftop signs and billboards, and allows marquees only on operating theatres. An earlier three-page draft would have required applied facings such as Formstone and aluminum siding to be removed within 24 months, nonconforming signs within two years and billboards within five, with all plans reviewed by HCD. The typed rehabilitation standards of the Waverly Business Area Urban Renewal Plan follow, including a rule that every store display its street number together with the Waverly logo, and that parking lots be paved, lit and screened by walls or planting at least 48 inches high. An April 28, 1977 working note lists open issues: Peddler's Village, volunteers, projecting signs on side streets only, a bus shelter, Burger King's compliance ('style of Annapolis store'), trash, security grilles, the logo, building numbers and historic preservation. City Archives BRG48-43-10-5, 40 scans.

The sheets set a 9 square foot maximum sign face, 4 feet 0 inches maximum projection, 10 feet 0 inches minimum clearance and 15 feet 0 inches maximum height, below the parapet and second-floor sills, and one sheet compares Greenmount Avenue with the side streets. summary: The Waverly Logo folder preserves dozens of hand-drawn studies for a WAVERLY district wordmark: pencil perspective constructions, marker color comps, tracing-paper overlays, photocopied stencils, and a resolved horizontal master with registration ticks. Deputy City Archivist Jeni Spamer, examining the originals on 13 Aug 2026, confirmed that the terminal Y was modeled on Memorial Stadium. Read west to east, the most developed studies appear to encode the district's geography in order: a domed tower in the W (Johns Hopkins' Gilman Hall), an arched form over the centre letters (the Boulevard Theatre's 1948 marquee at 3302 Greenmount, at the 33rd Street crossing), the stadium as the Y, a row of street trees for the 33rd Street promenade, and Greenmount Avenue cutting through on the diagonal. Attribution of the design remains unresolved. An earlier proposal dated July 21, 1977 set a street number inside a block 'W' instead (BRG48-43-10-16). Three earlier 'Waverly' identification signs, designed by DHCD staff, were ordered in August 1976 and stored at the Sisson Street Yard by November 1976 (BRG48-43-10-19). Box 10B, folder 38.

summary: Freestanding 'WAVERLY PARKING' pylon studies on tracing-paper overlays, taped over a lined-pad layout, with human figures for scale and reviewer markup recorded in situ (one variant marked 'NOT OK'; another initialled and dated '5/8'). The pylons would have carried the district wordmark at architectural scale, functioning simultaneously as parking identification, wayfinding, district gateway, and branding (Box 10, folders 19 and 26). A pylon was built. The designs.s steel sign details specify a triangular sign about 3'-6" on a side around a round reinforced concrete column, and on April 17, 1979 DHCD sent drawings of 'a proposed concrete pylon to be constructed on East 32nd St. near Greenmount Ave.' for utility clearance; the lot's landscaping estimate budgets one 'I.D. Pylon' at $3,000. A concrete sign pylon on 32nd Street, almost certainly this one, was then built under Contract 2572, the Greenmount sidewalk contract, by Mahoney Brothers and its subcontractor David Green and Associates. The city specified a 20-inch concrete column in September 1979. By November 7, 1979 the minutes record that 'the pylon for the sign on 32nd Street has not been constructed in the specified location by about 2 ft'; it was moved, and HCD inspected it. Sign drawings sent November 1979 (the minutes do not quote the sign.s wording) set the sign colors in Tnemec paint and the direction of the sign, and replaced text on the concrete column with blue coloring and an anti-graffiti coating. The December 22, 1980 punch list includes 'Sign Pylon - paint with anti-graffiti paint.' The files do not say how long it stood; it is absent from the 2013 National Register description of the district, and no photograph of it has been found. City Archives BRG48-43-10-7, -14, -20.

summary: The July 1978 Waverly Merchants Association newsletter, signed by president George Bluso and carrying the new WAVERLY wordmark as its masthead, announced the Commercial Revitalization Project as a merchant-city partnership and published the capital schedule: fall 1978 curb and sidewalk replacement on Greenmount from 29th to 35th; brick sidewalk paving, benches and landscaping at the 33rd Street median between Barclay and Old York Road; spring 1979 reconstruction and widening of sidewalks on 31st and 32nd from Brentwood to Greenmount with brick paving, benches, tree plantings and special lighting; and resurfacing, striping, landscaping and lighting of the Waverly Shop & Park Lot. It explained the loan programs (the city's REAL rehabilitation loans at 7% over 20 years and three SBA programs), said the urban renewal plan and its design standards would go to City Council that fall with two years to comply, and credited the logo to the Commercial Revitalization staff. It reported that Seven-Eleven had contracted for the old Gulf station at 33rd Street and Merryman Lane, introduced new staffer Harvey Schwartz and the Waverly Development Committee, carried a sanitation column by Bob Moore Jr. of the Gorsuch House, and called the committee's July 27, 1978 meeting at Moore's Gorsuch House, with a community wall mural and a merchant insignia on the agenda. A fall art show and sidewalk sale was to be chaired by Marie Halka of the Oakenshaw Improvement Association and Alan Orman of Harry's Liquors. The issue included a map of the project area. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, pages 2-5.

summary: The city did not expect merchants to rescue the corridor alone. The DHCD folder sequence tracks a capital program from concept to execution: Public Improvement Miscellaneous (1977), Public Improvement (1978-79), Public Improvements with the consulting firm Hurst-Roche (1978-79), Drawing and Specification Information (1979), Parking Lot Construction (1980-81), Parking Lot Expenditures (1980), 33rd Street median (1977-80), and Tree Grates (1983). The 'Tree Grates 1983' folder turns out to be about failing Neenah cast-iron grates across the city's revitalized streets, not a new Waverly installation (BRG48-43-10-17). Work on the 33rd Street median began earlier than the folder list suggests, with city crews in fall 1976 (BRG48-43-10-19). The Greenmount sidewalk work was Contract 2572, built by Mahoney Brothers in 1979-80 for $676,653 (BRG48-43-10-20). Interventions comprised curb replacement, sidewalk and brick paving, landscaping, benches, tree planting and special lighting. The theory of change was physical and economic: improve the pedestrian environment, create a coherent identity, make parking legible, strengthen individual storefronts, organise merchants, and thereby make the district competitive.

summary: A 1978-1979 folder titled 'Waverly Public Improvements (Hurst-Roche)' records the engagement of Hurst-Rosche Engineers, Inc. on the corridor's streetscape work, alongside a separate Consultants-Waverly folder (1978-79). Hurst-Rosche was an Illinois firm (founded 1937, Hillsboro) that opened a Baltimore-area office by January 1970 at 5202 Baltimore National Pike, Catonsville, later Timonium (1983) and Cockeysville (1995), operating in Maryland into the early 2000s. Its entire documented Maryland portfolio is state-highway and traffic engineering; this DHCD folder is the only known trace of any Baltimore City work by the firm, and no published record connects it to graphic or urban design. Whether the firm or a subconsultant produced the district identity is unresolved.

summary: On 19 August 1983, Herman Katkow, Director of the Mayor's Advisory Committee on Small Business, wrote to 'Dear Waverly Merchant' on City of Baltimore letterhead. The letter opens with men's-room graffiti he had seen -- 'APATHY REIGNS!' answered by 'SO WHO CARES?' -- and argues that apathy reigns in Waverly, that no insurer will write a policy against declining sales, that districts which promote collectively provide their own sales insurance, and that the city 'can't afford wheel spinning with unorganized and uninterested areas.' A reply form was attached; the letter closes 'IT'S UP TO YOU!' The attached reply form, addressed to Margaret Williams of the Commercial Revitalization Division, offered two answers: 'I am interested in helping my own business and am willing to participate in the reorganization of the Waverly Merchants Association', or 'Go away -- don't bother me!' (BRG48-43-10-18, pages 2-3). More than seventy merchants were trading in Waverly that year, so the failing asset was not the merchant base but the organisation. Katkow was himself a Pennsylvania Avenue merchant (the Beverly Shop, 1721-23 Penn Ave, destroyed c.1977 by a gas fire during Metro construction), founder of PALMA in 1953, and small-business director under seven mayors. Filed under 'Waverly / 29th and Greenmount.'

summary: The Waverly Merchants Association, the business body that signed the 1978 revitalization newsletter, appears in no IRS exempt-organization record: it was an unincorporated voluntary association with no charter, no standing, and no assets to outlive its volunteers, and it is functionally absent from the record after 1983. Its residents' counterpart, the Waverly Improvement Association, was IRS-recognised in April 1978 (EIN 52-1099887) and survives. The merchants' functional successor, Waverly Main Street, was not founded until 2000, leaving a seventeen-year gap in which the corridor held a residents' association and a capital program's worth of physical improvements but no merchant institution to steward them. Stanley Adler, of Adler's House of Fashion at 3220/3240 Greenmount, had served as association president in May 1974.

summary: The Baltimore Afro-American devoted its editorial page of 16 February 1946 to two integrated gatherings held in segregated Baltimore theatres. During Boy Scout Week, a thousand scouts attended a jamboree sponsored by a downtown store at the Boulevard Theatre, and 'here again members of both races were admitted without discrimination.' The paper paired this with a Jehovah's Witnesses convention at the Lyric, whose 300-odd Black members 'were seated indiscriminately throughout the Lyric, which, in the past, has discouraged interracial gatherings or refused to admit colored citizens.' It then recorded the managements' response and its own verdict: 'While the management of both the Lyric and Boulevard Theatres were quick to point out that there has been no change in their policy, these two incidents are proof enough for us that their jim-crow practices are silly.' The Boulevard, at 3302 Greenmount, therefore excluded Black patrons as stated policy in 1946, admitting them only when a scout jamboree made the rule inconvenient.

summary: The Boulevard Theatre opened 8 October 1921 at 3302 Greenmount Avenue, at the 33rd Street crossing, designed by E. G. Blanke of the firm Blanke & Zink and operated as a Durkee first-run house. Its signature street presence during the revitalization years was the projecting semicircular marquee added in 1948, which is the plausible referent for the arched element at the centre of the WAVERLY wordmark; no facade arch is documented. The house was twinned in the early 1980s and closed in 1989. It should not be confused with the earlier Waverly Theatre at 3211 Greenmount (1909-1969), one block south.

summary: A proposed sign for the Golden Star, a Cantonese restaurant at 3326-3330 Greenmount Avenue, survives in the DHCD 'Waverly Harry's Facade + Logo' folder: Claude Neon Signs Sketch No. 8277 of February 18, 1982, a 33-foot illuminated 'SZECHUAN GOLDEN STAR RESTAURANT CANTONESE' sign with a pagoda crest and star, the existing 'Golden Star' character-panel sign to remain. Claude Neon's letter of February 19 shows the city's Marsha Rozansky reviewing it and having the sign cut down in height; the drawing is the sign company's, reviewed by the program, not drawn by it. The Golden Star was a Lin-family late-night house open by about 1970 (twenty-one years in business as of January 1991) and familiar enough locally to appear on screen in John Waters's Polyester in 1981. Its closing date is unresolved between 1991 and the arrival of a successor buffet. The drawing is evidence that the revitalization program's technical assistance reached immigrant-owned businesses on the corridor, not only long-established ones.

summary: The DHCD folder 'Waverly Harry's Facade + Logo' holds the program's most thorough work for a single merchant: about two dozen facade studies for Harry's Liquors at 3113 Greenmount Avenue, in pencil, ink and color, and about forty studies for a bottle-silhouette logo. The facade studies try a horizontal 'HARRY'S LIQUORS' sign band, an awning, a new storefront and brick, pebble or tile in place of the aluminum siding ('alum siding, would you like something better?' reads one note); staff planned color xeroxes with interchangeable parts so the owner could compare them. A page from a wine book showing bottle shapes was clipped in as reference for the logo. The owner was Alan (Allan) Orman, who sat on the 1976 merchants' steering committee and chaired the 1978 fall art show. A phone slip records his call asking for a list of contractors, a cost estimate from Bob Quilter and help with the storefront, and a note in the file carries figures of $8,500 and $6,000. Architect Steve Broache wrote to him enclosing a sheet on the city's REAL rehabilitation loan program and asking him to call Bob Klepper, who ran it. Design, contractor lists, cost estimates and loan referral were one service. The Harry's pages are undated; Broache's letter is on the 1976-77 All-America City letterhead and the related notes date from 1977, so the work was probably done in 1977-79. The one 1982 document in the folder, a sign proposal, belongs to the Golden Star Restaurant. A Harry's Liquors trades at the address today on an active licence, in a building whose retail lineage runs from Knoblock Brothers' grocery in the 1920s through leather goods by 1937 to liquor thereafter. The file documents the Harry.s Liquors name and its owner in the late 1970s, filling part of the gap before the continuous record that begins in 2013; the original Harry is still unidentified. City Archives BRG48-43-10-16, 85 scans.

summary: The revitalization program resurfaced, striped, landscaped and lit the Waverly Shop & Park Lot at 3201 Barclay Street (Block 3881A, Lot 001), with design work in 1979-80 and construction in 1980-81, plus a dedicated expenditures file in 1980. The lot has a merchants' prehistory: a June 1958 'Park Free While You Shop' co-operative announcement listed some thirty-five participating stores and a new 32nd Street parking lot. The ground itself carries a buried history, having been the site of segregated Public School No. 115, in operation from 1889 until the 1950s and demolished in 1960. A deed recorded 30 November 1979 (WA 3844/396) falls inside the rebuild window and may record a city acquisition rather than an internal transfer. The lot remains city-owned and is operated today as the 'Waverly Lot.' Box 10 folders 24-26, 36; Box 10B folder 41. The 'Waverly Parking Lot' folder (BRG48-43-10-12) confirms the rebuild: Hurst-Rosche designed it in 1979, R. Marcantoni & Sons built it under Bureau of Highways Contract 2611 from June 19 to November 22, 1980, and the city accepted it on March 3, 1981.

summary: The 32nd Street Farmers Market opened on 30 May 1980, conceived the previous year by a city housing employee who walked past the Waverly Shop & Park Lot while the revitalization program was rebuilding it. The market has operated continuously ever since, outlasting the Waverly Merchants Association, the urban renewal plan that authorised the lot's reconstruction, and every other institution involved in the 1976-1983 program. It is the most durable thing the Waverly System produced, and it was not in the plan.

summary: The Department of Housing and Community Development's 1979 file 'Subway Shop, Greenmount & Calvin' is about the Subway Sandwich Shops store at 3400 Greenmount Avenue, the corner of Calvin Avenue. The tenant was Subway Sandwich Shops, whose contact Jim Smith worked from Lexington and Liberty Streets downtown; the owner was Robert Hogan of R. J. Hogan Contractors, across the street at 3411 Greenmount. The file does not say whether this was the national Subway chain or a local business of the same name. DHCD architect Steve Broache drew a series of site plans for the store's parking lot from June 26, 1979, and sent Hogan a layout on July 17. Broache's notes record Hogan calling on July 5 and promising a decision by July 9, and three options: accept the city's drawing, take his own site plan to the Site Plan Review Committee with the city work omitted, or do nothing, with the curb cuts deleted at his expense. On July 30 Broache resent the drawing to Smith, noting uncertainty about what site plan would be acceptable for 'the Subway Store at Greenmount and Calvin'. On August 24, 1979, with notice to proceed already issued for the district's sidewalks, trees and benches, Commercial Revitalization Coordinator Patricia Massey told Hogan the committee had approved Broache's plan. It called for angle parking with one-way circulation, a 17-foot and a 20-foot curb cut on Greenmount (Smith had wanted more room to get in), and 10 feet of new sidewalk on Calvin. The city would pay for sidewalks, curb cuts, trees and brick trim; Hogan would build the screening planters under a building permit, 'to avoid problems which have occurred in the past'. The plan would go to the contractor unless Hogan offered an alternative by September 5. The folder also holds a 1953 Sanborn map sheet of the block and city street-improvement sheets for Greenmount at Calvin. The corner had been a Shell service station on five former Calvin Avenue lots; Shell Oil assigned its interest to Hogan and Joseph M. Ziegler Jr. on August 2, 1978, so the Subway store was the first use of the converted station lot under its new owners, who held it until 1987. City Archives BRG48-43-10-10, 30 scans.

summary: The Department of Housing and Community Development's 1979 file 'A+P Gorsuch Avenue' documents A&P's plan to remodel its Waverly supermarket, store #815 at 609 Gorsuch Avenue. A&P's own site plan (S.P. #815, dated August 9, 1978) shows a 23,612 sq ft store on the block bounded by Gorsuch Avenue, Old York Road, East 32nd Street and Tinges Lane, with parking lots north of Gorsuch and east of Tinges and a new enclosed loading dock on 32nd. That block now lies inside the Giant site at 601 E 33rd St. On January 16, 1979, A&P Senior Area Manager James P. Wiley wrote to Patricia Massey of DHCD that, after his December 14 letter and a call from David Hunter, the city had still not set a meeting with interested parties on the remodeling. A note on the letter records a January 25 Waverly Improvement Association meeting at Waverly Presbyterian Church, 3401 York Road. The program answered with its own facade studies: an elevation titled 'Gorsuch Avenue A&P' and color renderings with a glass arched canopy, a red sign band with the A&P roundel and a painted fruit mural in the corner windows, plus a 'Proposed Alterations' scheme with a seamed-metal entrance pavilion. A twenty-frame photo survey (negative sleeve 'WAVERLY A+P', no. 1763, with its contact sheet) circles the streamline building, its parking frontage and a delivery at the rounded corner. Site plan review in November 1979 asked A&P to close two unused curb cuts; permit no. 974 was filed November 6 and a revised plan resubmitted, with a second A&P application (no. 993) for York Road two days later. The store anchored the district for six decades: opened in the late 1930s as half A&P and half Acme with Stadium Bowling Lanes upstairs, doubled when A&P absorbed the Acme half around 1959, and closed as a Super Fresh on 30 January 1999. The shell stood until spring 2003 and the Waverly Crossroads Giant opened on the 4.46-acre assembly in July 2004. City Archives BRG48-43-10-4, 41 scans.

summary: George J. Bluso (1920-2009, buried Dulaney Valley Memorial Gardens, Timonium; wife Angelina 1924-2004) purchased 3223 Greenmount Avenue on 16 March 1977 and signed the July 1978 Waverly Merchants Association newsletter as president sixteen months later, announcing the city's commercial revitalization program and its capital schedule. He held the property into the 1990s. Newspaper research records a George J. Bluso of the same city with a 1953 gambling conviction (given as age 34, of the 5600 block Purdue Avenue), a September 1960 federal arrest for bookmaking without a federal gambling stamp, a May 1961 appearance in reporting on a case connected to an East Baltimore Street club (given as age 42, same Purdue Avenue address), a Baltimore Sun description in 1970 as 'a major gambling figure in the area' who served a year in 1964, and a reported federal decision vacating a wagering-tax conviction (Bluso v. United States, 375 F. Supp. 1085, D. Md. 1974). CAUTION: the two newspaper ages agree with each other at a birth of about 1918-19, while the memorial gives 1920; year-only memorial dates are frequently approximate, but the identification is NOT yet confirmed. The decisive test is the grantee clause of the 16 March 1977 deed (RHB 3457/824-830): if it names a grantee residing in the 5600 block of Purdue Avenue, the merchants' president and the gambling defendant are the same man.

summary: Preservation documentation was not performed decades after the revitalization program as an unrelated exercise; it was intertwined with it. The Commission for Historical and Architectural Preservation's City of Baltimore Neighborhood Survey covered Waverly in 1977, surveyed by Michelle Belco, generating Maryland Inventory of Historic Properties forms in a wave running roughly B-2776 to B-2817, with the Greenmount corridor's forms at B-2785 through B-2791. The DHCD program kept its own 'Waverly Historic Survey 1977-1978' folder holding Maryland Historical Trust inventory forms for 3021-3031 Greenmount, the Waverly Town Hall (then the Northside Bar), the row from Harry's Liquors at 3113 to the firehouse, the 1902 Waverly firehouse, the Waverly Theatre (then a Goodwill store), the Boulevard Theatre, and a house in the 600 block of Homestead Street. It filed them with the July 1978 merchants' newsletter, and the Boulevard form records the community's petition against a Burger King in the theatre lobby. The buildings' architectural character was becoming part of the district's economic strategy thirty-six years before the National Register district was listed. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, 28 scans.

summary: The revitalization program's lending arm is documented on this block: in January 1980 the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, through the Department of Housing and Community Development, lent the Adlers $67,000 against 3220 Greenmount Avenue as a city rehabilitation loan, mid-program. A comparable stack appears one block north in December 1981, where a $75,000 City of Baltimore / DHCD loan combined with a $125,000 SBA loan was expressly 'applied to the rehabilitation of properties known as Nos. 3202-05-07-09 Greenmount Avenue' for the retail tenant The Princess Shops. Together these establish that the Commercial Revitalization Division's public money was rebuilding Greenmount retail blocks, not merely drawing them.

summary: Every HOLC zone at the Waverly four-corners - A1 (Guilford), B16, C9, D6, and the ballpark's own C4 - was appraised by the same man on the same day: Louis Kroner, property review appraiser, H.O.L.C., May 4, 1937. His sheets (verbatim, Mapping Inequality transcriptions) span a sevenfold income gradient across ~150 m: A1 "Executives, Professional men," income "Over $5,000," Negro "No," trend upward, favorable influence "Close to business area on Greenmount Ave."; D6 "Laborers," income "$700-1,000," "Negro: Yes, 35" (35% foreign-born), "Houses in very bad condition. Many alley properties"; remarks "Vandalism in this section" - and, as D6's listed FAVORABLE influence: "Near desirable properties." C4 (the Oriole Park V ground): population "Mixture," income $2,000, favorable "Goucher college located in the section. Desirable location," detrimental "Industrial plants. Continuing obsolescence of old property," trend static. The four-corners was not four judgments that collided; it was one administrative act - executed three weeks after the ballpark's Negro National League opening day (April 10, 1937).

summary: The Waverly study Survey Influence section quantified the survey itself as a market intervention, in the year ending June 1, 1940: HOLC loans repaid in full nearly doubled; borrowers in default dropped by more than half; for-sale signs fell about 50 percent and for-rent signs over 90 percent; HOLC sales of foreclosed Waverly properties jumped from 24 percent (prior three years) to 57 percent in one year - while Maryland overall FELL from 37 to 34 percent. The measurement was the medicine. The same chapter found definite evidence of overzoning on Greenmount Avenue between Thirty-fifth and Forty-second Streets (also Old York Rd 34th-35th and 33rd St), and recorded early Master Plan wins: the old junk yard and unsightly frame tabernacle at the NW corner of Venable Ave and Old York Rd removed and the lot paved; the first of 12 planned interior play areas (block 3903-A) approved by the Park Commission at 1,286.25 dollars - an assessment of 36.75 dollars per property.

summary: On the same page, the Frank-Dunhills advertisement is signed "Ted Frank & Len Frank" and gives the address 3212-14 Greenmount Avenue, phone BE. 5-7575. THEODORE FRANK and Sylvia Lee Frank bought 3224 Greenmount on Aug. 4, 1955 for $41,000 (MLP 9873/248) and the family held it until 2008. Ted is the ordinary diminutive of Theodore; same surname, same block-face, same years. So the 1955 buyer was not an outside investor but a Waverly men's-wear merchant six doors down the same side of the street, buying the storefront the Wyman estate was selling. Corroborating: the 1963 deed (JFC 1619/451) shows the Franks holding four corridor parcels (3224 and 2950 Greenmount, 2737 and 2745 Maryland Ave), and their holding company was named "Fransue Properties, Inc." LIKELY BUT NOT PROVEN: test with the SDAT charter record for Frank-Dunhills.

summary: THE INSTRUMENT THE WHITE PAPER MISCITES. Rev.09 cites this conveyance as MSA CE 168-13931 pp.00020-22, which is a 1978 deed. The real citation is Liber S.C.L. Ludwig and wife to George Quong, etc." and the "etc." was a second named person, GEE QU YING, who has never appeared in any account of this building; the records also spell the first grantee Gee Quong, not George. summary: 3224 and 3222 both begin 181 feet north of Merrymans Lane and run in OPPOSITE directions. The Block Book entries make it explicit: the 1918 Ludwig to Gee Quong deed reads "W 100 x N 16" while the Burnham parcel reads "W 100 x S 16" in 1915, 1916 and 1920. They are adjacent lots sharing a boundary at the 181-foot mark, and the modern index remarks simply dropped the N/S. With 3220 at "165 N Merrymans, S 21 1/2," the block face resolves with no overlap and no gap: 3220 = 143.5-165 ft, 3222 = 165-181 ft, 3224 = 181-197 ft. This confirms the 1116 York Road identification by metes and bounds, independently of the Sanborn plate. The 3222 chain also surfaces here: Eben B. Hunting releases to William D. and Annie Burnham and Virginia Hickman (Aug 1915), and on 3 June 1920 the Burnhams assign to RAYMOND B. and EMMA L. KIBLER (SCL 3596/17) — Kibler's Jewelers is still at 3222 in the 1958 Evening Sun ad. The white paper's Burnham family sources belong to 3222, and the Burnhams owned it as well as lived in it.

summary: "MAURICE WYMAN, SHOE DEALER, DIES." Maurice Wyman, shoe merchant, died 20 October 1927 aged 64 at the Emersonian Apartments, Eutaw Place and Park Drive, after a six-year illness; apoplexy. "Mr. Wyman ... had conducted a store at 19 WEST LEXINGTON STREET since January 1, 1891, and, in addition, for the last few years had operated a branch store at 111 East Baltimore street." Born in Alexandria, Va.; came to Baltimore as a boy; began at Posner's Department Store and became buyer in the shoe department; left late in 1900 to take over the business of J. Pels & Son at the Lexington Street address "now occupied by the Wyman store." Buried Baltimore Hebrew Cemetery. "Mr. Wyman is survived by his widow, MRS. STELLA E. WYMAN; a son, HENRY E. WYMAN, and three brothers, Julius, Simon and Samuel Wyman. Mrs. Wyman was Miss Stella E. Eiseman." THIS CLOSES THE WYMAN QUESTION. 19 West Lexington Street is location 1 in the white paper's own 1941 Wyman Young Moderns advertisement (S103) and the "Wyman LEXINGTON STREET" of the 1950 shoe advertisement (S104). Stella E. Wyman and Henry E. Wyman are the same two people who took one-third interests in 3224 Greenmount in the February 1941 deed (MLP 6129/439). So the family that owned a third of the building IS the family that founded and ran Wyman Shoe Co., the tenant. The paper's ca.1935-1955 tenancy and the 1941-1955 ownership are one family, and both ended in the same month of 1955.

summary: Death notice, verbatim: "FRIEDLAND. On January 10, 1957, BELLE (nee Frank) beloved wife of the late Harry Friedland of 301 Eighty-sixth street, Miami Beach, Fla., mother of Janet Sue Friedland, DAUGHTER OF EVA AND THE LATE EPHRAIM FRANK and SISTER OF THEODORE AND LEONARD FRANK and the late Charles B. Frank. Services at the Jack Lewis Home, 2100-02 Eutaw place, on Sunday precisely at 11 A.M. Interment B'nai Jacob Lodge Cemetery, Herring Run." This closes the Frank identification the same way the Maurice Wyman obituary closed the Wyman one. Ephraim and Eva Frank held 3212-3214 Greenmount from 1923; the Frank-Dunhills advertisement in the Evening Sun of 11 June 1958 is signed "Ted Frank & Len Frank" at 3212-14 Greenmount; and THEODORE FRANK bought 3224 Greenmount on 4 August 1955 for $41,000 (MLP 9873/248). Theodore and Leonard are Ephraim and Eva's sons. So the 1955 purchase of 3224 was a second-generation Waverly merchant family buying the storefront six doors from the store their parents had held for thirty-two years. Four siblings named: Belle (Friedland), Theodore, Leonard, and Charles B. Frank (deceased by 1957). The family buried at B'nai Jacob Lodge Cemetery. Notice ran in the Sun 11, 12 and 13 January and the Evening Sun 11 and 12 January 1957.

summary: "FRANK, Sylvia Lee. On September 3, 2001, SYLVIA LEE FRANK (nee HYMAN), mother of FRANCES F. KATZ of Owings Mills, MD and SUE SCHWARTZ of Silver Spring, MD, mother-in-law of Robert H. Schwartz" and in the 2008 land record as "SCHWARTZ, HARRIET S" - so Harriet Sue Schwartz went by Sue. summary: READ IN FULL. SEB 146/730 (MSA CE 164-146). $5, "there being no actual consideration for this transaction"; transfer tax not required. No. 3611, folio 20, was granted and conveyed by THEODORE FRANK AND WIFE unto the grantor herein, FOR AND DURING HIS NATURAL LIFE, WITH POWERS OF DISPOSITION." SETTLES THE TWO-THEODORES QUESTION: there is ONE Theodore Frank. summary: READ IN FULL. SEB 146/732-735. Lee Klavans conveys to "THEODORE FRANK and MILDRED A. FRANK, HIS WIFE ... joint parties of the second part," for and during their natural lives, with full powers to sell, mortgage, lease or convey the whole fee (except by will). Then the remainder, verbatim: "...then unto and to the use of MILDRED A. FRANK, FOR AND DURING HER NATURAL LIFE OR SO LONG AS SHE SHALL REMAIN UNMARRIED AFTER THE DEATH OF THEODORE FRANK, and immediately after the death or remarriage of the said Mildred A. Frank, then unto FRANCES F. KATZ and HARRIET F. SCHWARTZ, their personal representatives and assigns, IN FEE SIMPLE FOREVER." TWO FINDINGS. (1) DIVORCE, NOT DEATH: Mildred is called Theodore's WIFE in December 1983 while Sylvia Lee Frank was still living (she died 3 September 2001), so Theodore and Sylvia divorced between April 1978 and December 1983. (2) THE DAUGHTERS' REMAINDER WAS NOT EXTINGUISHED, IT WAS RE-CREATED behind a second-wife life estate with the classic until-remarriage limitation. That is why Frances F. Katz and Harriet S. Schwartz are back on title in June 2008 (10788/504): Theodore died, then Mildred died or remarried, and the remainder fell in. The whole Frank arc is one estate plan running fifty-three years: buy 1955, life estate with remainder to the daughters 1978, restructure for the second wife in 1983 with the daughters preserved behind her, daughters take 2008.

summary: Baltimore County Liber J.W.S. No. 167, folio 402 (MSA CE 62-167), read in full. "This Sub-Lease made this first day of February A.D. 1888 by DAVID STEWART of Baltimore City of the first part to SARAH E. SINCLAIR and JAMES E. SINCLAIR her husband, of Baltimore County, of the second part ... does hereby lease unto the said Sarah E. Sinclair ... ALL THOSE FOUR LOTS of ground lying in Baltimore County on the west side of the York Turnpike Road north of Merryman's Lane." The four lots, measured from Merryman's Lane: FIRST 132 ft 8 in, running north 12 ft (about 3218); SECOND 144 ft 8 in, north 20 ft, through the centre of a partition wall (about 3220); THIRD 164 ft 8 in (3222); and FOURTH, verbatim: "Beginning for the fourth thereof at a point on the west side of the York Turnpike Road distant NORTHERLY ONE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY ONE FEET from the intersection of the northeast side of Merryman's Lane ... and along the northern boundary of the lot thirdly above described one hundred feet to an alley three feet wide ... NORTHERLY SIXTEEN FEET ..." THAT IS 3224 GREENMOUNT, word for word the description carried in every deed for this parcel from 1890 to 1978. SO 3224 WAS THE FOURTH LOT IN THE SINCLAIR SUBLEASE. This reverses the Round 0 finding that the Sinclair material is only block context: it is this parcel's own chain of title. What was wrong was the street number, not the connection. The deed also recites that the four lots cover the whole area of the two lots in the 1884 W. Hall Harris to James E. Sinclair lease, that the Sinclairs had assigned them to Stewart on 3 January 1888, and that lots first and second carry an $80 annual rent while lots thirdly and fourthly carry $80.84, payable 11 June and 11 December, redeemable at six per cent from 11 June 1889.

summary: Baltimore Sun, 17 October 1904, p.12, in a year-end list of fatal burn cases: "July 7 - MRS. SALLIE SANDERS, 1116 York road, horribly burned, presumably as the result of filling a lighted stove at the home of her mother, Mrs. Thomas Dowery, 103 Reese street, Waverly; died two days later." 1116 York Road is 3224 Greenmount. The 1904 Polk puts "Sanders Wm A. carp. 1116 York rd" at this address, so Sallie was almost certainly the wife of William A. Sanders, carpenter. She died 9 July 1904. This is the earliest named death connected to the building, and it places a family upstairs in the same year Sing Lee's laundry was working the ground floor. Her mother lived at 103 Reese Street in Waverly.

summary: "GIRL (colored), experienced ironer in laundry. 3224 GREENMOUNT AVENUE." The white paper holds this as a single Evening Sun advertisement of 13 April 1937 (S09). It ran far wider: Evening Sun 13 and 14 April, and Baltimore Sun 14, 15 and 16 April 1937. Five insertions over four days in both city dailies. A campaign of that size for one ironer's position indicates either urgent need or high turnover, and it is much stronger evidence of an operating workforce than a single notice.

summary: Consolidated from the advertisements. The people who worked inside 3224 Greenmount are recoverable, and they were overwhelmingly Black women. Documented hiring rounds: JANUARY 1921, four insertions across both dailies over two days - "COLORED Woman to Wash and Iron. Apply SAM LEE LAUNDRY, 3224 Greenmount ave." phone Madison 6853 (Evening Sun 12 and 13 Jan, Baltimore Sun 12 and 13 Jan). OCTOBER 1926 - "WOMAN to wash and iron for laundry. CHAS. DIER, 3224 Greenmount ave." APRIL 1937, five insertions over four days in both papers - "GIRL (colored), experienced ironer in laundry." JUNE 1937 - "GIRL (colored) to work in laundry." AUGUST 1937 - "GIRL (colored) to work in laundry." That is at least eleven separate insertions across five hiring rounds spanning sixteen years. None of the women is named; Baltimore employers did not name them. But the trade, the race, the sex and the address are all on the record, repeatedly, in the employers' own words. NEGATIVE FINDING WORTH STATING: none of these advertisements appears in the Baltimore Afro-American. Employers placed them in the Sun and the Evening Sun, the white dailies, which is itself a fact about how this labour market was organised.

summary: Baltimore Sun, 11 July 1893, p.3, an advertisement placed from this address: "STORE AND DWELLING, on line of electric road, good opening for a Confectionery and Notion Store; county taxes, city water, &c.; 16x100; g. r. $48. [and a second property at] 203 Clinton, (Canton,) STORE and DWELLING, now occupied by a saloon; 19.2x100 feet; ground rent $28. Address 1116 YORK ROAD, Waverly." THIS IS THE EARLIEST DESCRIPTION OF THE BUILDING'S FORM, and it matches this parcel on every measurable point: 16 by 100 feet, ground rent $48, on the electric streetcar line, at 1116 York Road. FOUR CONSEQUENCES. (1) The building was a STORE WITH A DWELLING ABOVE in 1893 - the second floor was residential from the start, which bears directly on the Upper Front Room and the second-floor occupancy question. (2) It independently confirms the 16x100 lot and the $48 ground rent created by the 1890 Legg-to-Drechsler lease. (3) IT COMPLICATES THE ca. 1910 CONSTRUCTION DATE: a store-and-dwelling of exactly these dimensions with exactly this ground rent stood on this lot in July 1893, and the Drechsler family had been living in it since at least May 1891. That does not prove the current building is the 1891 one, but any construction-date claim must now account for a documented building here eighteen years earlier. (4) Drechsler was trying to let or sell it three years after taking the lease.

White (737:mdlr-jhl48-502-litzinger-white-lease-1866) recites land between the turnpike and the Old York Road that a P. Merryman (the first name reads like 'Olivr', probably Oliver) and wife deeded Litzinger on June 27, 1865 (J.H.L. 46/149). Whether that is the Merryman deed recited here is not shown. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1865 Oliver P. Merryman deed is read (737:mdlr-jhl46-149-oliver-merryman-litzinger-brown-lease-fee-1865): it is a different parcel (the Jesse Brown lease ground, from Charles R. Carroll, 1859), so it is not the deed this 1884 deed recites, but it shows Oliver P. Merryman held Carroll reversions on the turnpike. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Oliver P. Merryman bought the reversion of the whole 11-acre Jesse Brown lease from Charles R. Carroll in 1859 (768:mdlr-ghc27-45-charles-carroll-oliver-merryman-brown-lease-reversion-1859), and the 1801 Brown-to-Wheetley and 1811 Whitely-to-Wilson assignments filed here are parts of that lease: so the 'deed from Oliver P. Merryman' this 1884 deed recites is very probably his conveyance of the reversion of Sinclair's part (inference).

summary: The oldest instrument in this parcel's chain, read in full for the first time. W. Hall Harris — PROVEN to be William Hall Harris (1852-1938), President of the Maryland Historical Society 1920-1935 — and his wife Alice P. (Patterson) Harris lease three lots on the westernmost side of the York turnpike road back to Sinclair the same day she took the fee. 3224 lies in the northern half of the second lot (164 ft 8 in to 197 ft). The descriptions run off party walls, proving houses already stood on this block face in June 1884. Update Oct. 17, 2026 (R.O. 1661, R.O. 1715 and S.C.L. 2610/548 read): the lease had a third lot. R.O. 1715/35 (Jan. 18, 1898; 768:mdlr-ro1715-35-harris-alice-gerry-stewart-third-lot-1898) recites 'the same lot of ground thirdly described in a lease from W. Hall Harris and Alice P. Harris his wife to James E. Sinclair dated June 11, 1884 ... W.M.I. No 141 folio 407', 'creating a redeemable ground rent of one hundred and fifty dollars ($150.) per annum': 60 ft of frontage from 36 ft 1/2 in to 96 ft 1/2 in north of Merryman's Lane, the lot just north of the apex. summary: On July 14, 1922, State's Attorney Robert F. Leach entered a nolle prosequi before Judge Gorter dismissing all charges in what wire coverage called "the Boulevard theatre scandal": conspiracy to bribe City Councilman Wilson J. Carroll (November 12, 1920) by promoter E. J. Wiley (a $250 bribe, January 1921) and Thomas M. Elliot (a $25 bribe, October 5, 1920), plus embezzlement and larceny charges against Alfred G. Buck and treasurer Bernard H. Dundon (of $1,200 and $1,500 respectively) from the American Theatre company's funds; Leach said a divided grand jury (indicting only three of four presented principals — Edwin T. Dickerson, Carroll, Buck and Dundon) had already cut conviction odds by 90 percent.
data: {"url":"https://www.newspapers.com/image/315810538/","page":"4","excerpt":"STOPS ACTION IN BOULEVARD THEATRE CASE. Baltimore, July 15. Proceedings against the principals in the Boulevard theatre scandal were quashed yesterday when State's Attorney Robert F. Leach entered a nolle pros. before Judge Gorter... This action means that the state will not prosecute Edwin T. Dickerson, Wilson J. Carroll, Alfred G. Buck and Bernard H. Dundon.","evidence":"A wire-service report datelined Baltimore, July 15, 1922, naming all indicted principals, the specific bribe amounts and dates, the embezzlement/larceny amounts, and the state's attorney's stated reason for dropping the case.","headline":"\"Boulevard theatre scandal\" charges dropped by State's Attorney","image_id":"315810538","relevance":"Closes out the Boulevard Theatre's founding-era corporate scandal: no one was ultimately convicted, and the theatre continued operating under American Theatres Company management until its 1926 sale to the Durkee organization.","confidence":"documented","publication":"The Evening Leader (Staunton, VA, wire item)","source_document":"The Evening Leader (Staunton, Virginia), 1922-07-15, p.4 — Newspapers.com image 315810538"}

summary: A Baltimore grand jury investigating bribery "in connection with the American Theatres ordinance" heard witnesses including James Kelly and Michael Kelly (the latter said to have told Roy Palmore, of the firm Palmore & Homan, that his own theatre's ordinance could be passed speedily if money were paid), architect Oliver White, Thomas M. Elliott (who said he paid Councilman Wilson J. Carroll $25 for an ordinance permitting a home addition, not a theatre), and lawyer Morris A. Rome; E. J. Wiley, represented by attorney Eugene O'Dunne, was to be examined when the session resumed the following Monday.

Carroll $25 with the understanding that Carroll would have an ordinance passed authorizing him to add an addition to his home.","evidence":"The grand jury's own witness list, naming each person examined and, for several, the substance of their testimony.","headline":"Grand jury hears witnesses in \"American Theatres ordinance\" bribery inquiry","image_id":"1921-12-slush-fund-witnesses","relevance":"Clarifies that Thomas M. J. Wiley and Alfred G. Buck; the Bar Association's grievance committee was separately investigating attorneys Harry W. Nice and Edwin T. Dickerson in connection with the case, with its report due to Bar Association president Edgar Allan Poe's executive committee that same afternoon.

summary: Within weeks of opening, a creditors' committee met over the Boulevard Theatre's finances: the land had cost $15,000 and the building $256,000, for a $271,000 total against an original $250,000 budget; of 600 stockholders, $163,000 had been paid in full plus roughly $20,000 more arriving monthly, with stock redeemable at $110. Promoter E. J. Wiley denied any "tangled financial difficulties," and architect E. G. Blanke declined to discuss the matter, saying "the newspapers can have no interest in it."

summary: George Shinosky died June 22, 1968, vesting sole title in his widow Louise Shinosky by survivorship. Louise Shinosky, by then living in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania, sold the property to Effielinda Eveline McShine for $5 and other valuable consideration by deed dated May 2, 1974. The deed explicitly notes: 'the improvements thereon being now known as No. 3603 Greenmount Avenue, formerly 3615 Greenmount Avenue' -- documenting a house renumbering distinct from the 1919 York Road renaming (this building was itself later readdressed from 3615 to 3603).

summary: By then living at 1909 Aster Road, Ramjankar and Zulphina Mohamed sold 3607 Greenmount to Peggy Hamilton via a seller-financed land installment contract dated February 16, 2000, for $59,900 ($3,000 down, $56,900 financed at 11% over 360 months). summary: Charles C. McColgan, 'Lexington street real estate dealer', buys the old Oriole Park grounds from Charles E. Dickey: 290 feet on Huntingdon Avenue, 258 feet on the York Road, 236 feet on CAMP STREET and 384 feet on Barclay Street, $50,000 (the whole transaction reported at $80,000). The ground had held the Pompeii and Siege of Vera Cruz exhibitions and adjoined Union Park. Camp Street is the dedicated-but-never-accepted street that the Baltimore Belt Line cut later severed, the street at the center of McColgan v. Baltimore Belt Railroad (1897). Three months later McColgan bought the Pratt lots north of here around Oxford Street (27th), the ground beside and behind 2602. Follow-up story May 13 1892 p.6, image 372944911.

summary: Executors' sale, Dec 16 1913, of the estate of Carrie L. Gunby of Crisfield: an unimproved fee-simple lot 50 by 200 feet on the west side of the York Turnpike Road, now Greenmount Avenue, 85 feet north of Lorraine Avenue (26th Street); executors Gordon Tull and Warren C. Gunby, attorneys Pattison & Gahan. So the southern half of the Conklin complex was still VACANT ground in December 1913, sold out of a Crisfield estate; George R. Conklin's 1921 building permit for 2602-4 follows.

summary: Building-permit column: 'George R. Conklin applied for a permit to build a two-story brick structure at 2602-4 Greenmount avenue, to cost $6,000.' This is the birth record of the 2602-04 building. Conklin, a contractor-builder before he was a warehouseman, built it with his own firm (his 1966 obituary: 'both of his warehouses at 2604 Greenmount avenue were built by his construction firm'). The other warehouse, 2606-08, is the earlier one (the business dates from 1910; Herbert Conklin's 1940 draft card gives 2608 as the employer address). Same column: Samuel Tasman, garage at 2733 Greenmount, $2,000.

summary: Deed dated and recorded August 1 1892, 2:20 P.M. (Liber J.B. 1404 folio 446-448): Enoch Pratt and Maria Louisa Pratt, his wife, to Charles C. McColgan, $45,000, fee simple, lots on the Plat of Oxford (Parkhurst v. Frisby): (a) Lots 51 and 52, west side of the York Turnpike from the northeast corner of Lot 50 north 100 feet to OXFORD STREET (27th), 200 feet deep, i.e. the ground of 2610-2616 immediately north of the future Conklin warehouses; (b) Lots 72-74, 114-115 east of the Turnpike north of Oxford, 150 by 400 feet to Frisby Street; (c) Lots 75-81, 107-113 and part of 82 east of the Turnpike south of Oxford, 375 feet down to Edward J. Coll's lot, with the 20-foot Boone Street reservation; (d) Lots 134-135 at Barclay and Oxford; (e) Lots 136 and 137 at the southeast corner of Barclay and Oxford, 200 by 200, running south to Lot 138 and 'binding on Lots 49, 50, 51 and 52', i.e. the REAR of 2602-2616. Lots 49 and 50 (2602-2608) are conspicuously absent: Pratt had already sold them, or they never were his. Recital: Pratt from Whitridge and Dobbin, Trustees, Dec 18 1868, G.R. 60/378. Test Jno. T. Maddox; Jas. Bond, Clerk. Three months earlier McColgan had bought the Old Oriole Park grounds two blocks south; he now held the York Road frontage from Huntingdon Avenue to 27th Street on both sides, minus the two lots that became 2602-2608.

summary: Court of Appeals of Maryland, April 1 1897, Fowler J.: Charles C. McColgan held a $3,543.75 judgment against the Baltimore Belt Railroad Company for damage to his York Road property from the construction of the Belt Line (the B&O's 1890-95 tunnel and open cut through the Camp Street ground he had bought from Dickey in 1892). He levied execution on 24 lots making up the railroad's right-of-way; the railroad obtained an injunction against the sale on the ground that a railroad's right-of-way is not severable property subject to execution; affirmed. The first of two 1897 appeals arising from McColgan's fight with the Belt Line over the ground two blocks south of 2602.

summary: Court of Appeals of Maryland, June 24 1897, Russum J.: McColgan sought to enjoin operation of the Belt Line under the clause of City Ordinance 83 (1890) that let an unpaid judgment holder stop the railroad after sixty days. Held: the ordinance clause applies only to judgments for injuries done under the ordinance (on public streets); McColgan's judgment was for damage at common law to his private rights, because the street the cut severed (Camp Street, on the old Oriole Park ground) had been dedicated on a plat but never accepted by the City, so it was not a public street; injunction refused. The holding entered the Annotated Code of Maryland (1911) under Art. 23 §273 as the standing gloss on the Belt Line ordinance.

summary: Archives of Maryland vol. 372 (Annotated Code of Maryland, 1911), Art. 23 Railroad Companies, §273, p.659, annotation: 'Where a city ordinance assenting to the construction of a tunnel by a railroad company, provided that if any final judgment recovered under this section was not paid within sixty days, the holder thereof should have the right to enjoin the operation of the railroad, such provision was held to have no application to a judgment growing out of an injury to the plaintiff's private rights for which the railroad company was liable at common law and not under the ordinance, and hence the injunction was refused. McColgan v. Baltimore Belt R. R. Co., 86 Md. 326.' The York Road developer's case became black-letter Maryland railroad law, sitting beside O'Brien v. Baltimore, Poole v. Falls Road Ry., Lake Roland Co. v. Webster and Webb v. B. & O.

summary: A 1979 Department of Housing and Community Development file documents the conversion of the gas station at the southwest corner of 33rd and Barclay Streets into Tugboat Anne's, a sub, pizza and carry-out restaurant. Owner John Frank Sr. (6705 Harford Road) brought his own drawing of the proposed restaurant to DHCD staff architect Steve Broache in January 1979. On January 30 Broache sent back two schemes: a standing-seam metal roof and signboard with stucco walls and planters, or the station's existing roof kept with a tugboat graphic on the front wall. He advised against shutters as easily damaged. Permit B06670 (issued March 6, 1979; 345 E 33rd St, Block 3879-B, Lot 49) converted the gas station to a sub-pizza restaurant for an estimated $6,600, with paneling, a drop ceiling and stucco on three sides approved per Broache's drawing. Site plans by A.E. Albiker (March 3, revised April 1979) replaced the pump islands with nine parking spaces, privet and juniper planters and a freestanding sign, approved May 7, 1979. A May 1, 1979 permit by Bonart Contractors added gas heat and rooftop air conditioning for the carry-out, targeting completion by June 30, 1979. A later city plan for extra sidewalk paving at the corner labels the building 'Exist'g Restaurant (Tugboat Anne's)', so the restaurant opened. The plot plan shows two station parcels, the corner lot and a long strip along the alley toward 32nd Street, which are today's Lots 49 and 25. Current city records list Dean W. Frank, also as trustee, as owner of both lots with a May 28, 2026 transfer; a family link to John Frank Sr. is likely but unverified. The drawings spell the name 'Tugboat Ann's'; the city file and letter spell it 'Tugboat Anne's'. City Archives BRG48-43-10-3, 29 scans.

summary: A 1977-78 Department of Housing and Community Development file follows the conversion of the former Waverly Theatre building at 3211 Greenmount Avenue from a variety store into a Shoe World shoe store. In December 1977 Finglass Construction filed for owner Grand Company (5436 Harford Road) to change the use from variety store to shoe store, alter the storefront, rebuild the toilet room and add partitions, an estimated $5,000; DHCD architect Steve Broache approved the work December 14-15. A January 1978 application named the owner as F. H. Durkee Enterprises at the same Harford Road address and the lessee as Shoe World, Inc. of Washington, D.C., for a new glass and aluminum storefront, partitions, an acoustical ceiling, lighting and a packaged heating and air-conditioning unit, an estimated $10,000. Broache approved it February 3, 1978, noting the sign needed its own permit. Shoe World's store plan titles the job 'Waverly Theatre, 3211 Greenmount Ave.' On January 9, 1978, Commercial Revitalization Coordinator Paul Gilbert wrote to Jack Himelfarb of Trout and Fox real estate about 'the status of the former Waverly Theatre building', reminding him that under the urban renewal ordinances the owner, not a lessee, answers to the city for compliance. Phone notes name C. Elmer Nolte Jr. for the owner, contractor Sidney Finglass, a Mr. Gusson of Shoe World, and Roger Garfink of the law firm Weinberg & Green, with Nolte to call back 're: lease'. The permits carry the designation 'R54 Waverly Business Area'. City Archives BRG48-43-10-2, 16 scans.

summary: A city sign drawing specifies a new sign for 3010 Greenmount Avenue reading 'Laura's Budget Shop': an 11'4" by 2' metal panel with brick-red Bookman bold italic lettering on a cream ground, centered on the brick above the storefront. It is undated and was filed among the 1977-78 Shoe World papers of the Department of Housing and Community Development's Waverly revitalization program, which drew signs for individual merchants. summary: The Department of Housing and Community Development's revitalization file 'Gorsuch House and Mr. Nifty' holds five hand-drawn sign studies for the Gorsuch House restaurant at 511 Gorsuch Avenue, all drawn on the same view of its one-story shingled front with porthole windows. The options were a boxed 'GORSUCH HOUSE' panel with or without a projecting blade sign, or script 'Gorsuch House' lettering across the gambrel roof. A second set of four drawings shows a different, unidentified corner with a 'RESTAURANT' canopy proposed over its stair entrance. A 1970s survey photo in the same folder, looking west along Gorsuch toward Greenmount, still shows the 'Gorsuch House Restaurant' hanging sign next to the Mr. Nifty cleaners sign. The folder's title matches the land records, where Garonzik conveyed 511 Gorsuch to Mr. Nifty Cleaners in 1977 (Liber 3457/827). The folder also holds a December 21, 1977 letter from Elizabeth Gabriel of Roberts Manufacturing (430 Merryman's Lane) to Commissioner M. J. Brodie, thanking DHCD for clearing trash from the alley beside her building and asking for an iron gate. Brodie routed it to Paul Gilbert, who on January 27, 1978 asked architect Steve Broache to investigate 'this problem' on his next trip to Waverly. The hanging sign and the roof sign in the 1970s survey photo both still read 'Robinson's Gorsuch House Restaurant'. The drawings are undated. City Archives BRG48-43-10-1.

summary: An envelope marked 'Waverly Streetscapes' in the Department of Housing and Community Development's Gorsuch House folder holds ten black-and-white survey photos of the business district, taken about 1977 judging by the cars. They show Greenmount Avenue at Vinson's Animal Hospital (3015) and Zepp Photo Centers (3040), looking toward the old Waverly Town Hall, then the Northside Bar (3100); the Hack's Shoe Repair corner in the 3400 block; Gorsuch Avenue with the Gorsuch House Restaurant and Mr. Nifty signs, F. W. Woolworth across Greenmount; and Peddler's Village antiques, Nancy Smith's shop at 418 E 31st St. One frame shows the attendant booth of the merchants' free-parking lot, whose board lists the sponsoring stores, among them Adler's, Becker's, Harry's Liquors, The Oriental House, Provident Savings Bank, Thomas Beauty Salon, Boulevard Hardware, the Boulevard Theatre, Kitty's Lounge, Mr. Nifty Cleaners and the White Coffee Pot. A closer reading of the frames adds more names. The parking booth's full sponsor board lists Adler's, Harry Little Carry Out Shop, Harry's Liquors, The Oriental House, Provident Savings Bank, Thomas Beauty Salon, Becker's, Club Continental, Jason Shoes, Radio Center, Boulevard Hardware, Kitty's Lounge, Roeth's Jewelry, the Boulevard Theatre, Mr. Nifty Cleaners and the White Coffee Pot. The L. E. Jefferson & Son frame also shows a '...'s Cleaners & Tailors' window on the corner and, down the side street, a sign for 'The 31st Street Bookstore'. The Peddler's Village frame shows its window lettering, 'Antiques & Furniture - Olde Things Too', with a top-hatted mascot, and on the other side of the parking gap a 'Gorman R. Da... Painting & Decorating' shop (phone 488-6884). The tap room frame reads 'Food - Tap Room - Dancing on Weekends', beside 'Import Motors, Specializing in Repairs, Volkswagen Cars - Repairs, Service, Parts', with a 'Domm Good Roofs' truck at the curb. The dead-end street frame carries an 'E 31st St' sign and a sign reserving parking for animal hospital patrons, so it is the 31st Street stub beside Vinson's. The Greenmount frames add Sunny's Surplus, Travelers, Mia's Wig & Gift, Mother Lode's, Wild Cherry and a self-serve Amoco. A torn campaign sticker reading '...R...N ... PRESIDENT' is not legible enough to date the set. Frames not yet placed: L. E. Jefferson & Son, a food-and-dancing tap room beside Import Motors, a vacant lot posted for towing by Greenwood's Garage, and a dead-end street. City Archives BRG48-43-10-1, pages 14-24.
