summary: The 1977 Maryland Historical Trust survey form for the Waverly Theatre, filed in the city's Waverly Historic Survey folder, gives its common name as 'The Goodwill': the building was a Goodwill store. It describes a two-story front with a Dutch-gable parapet, a black plastic and aluminum second story and a triangular marquee, and gives the history: the Waverly Amusement Company bought the land in 1909 and opened in 1910 with pictures and vaudeville; a roughly $100,000 enlargement in 1920-21 turned the old theatre into the entrance to a new 750-seat auditorium; Durkee Enterprises took it over and reopened it in 1929 and kept it until it closed in spring 1969. The survey photo shows the theatre front still lettered 'WAVERLY' above a triangular marquee, with Rabai's Bakery to the north and a 'Kings Court' store and the Princess Shops to the south. By December 1977 the city was permitting its conversion from a variety store to Shoe World. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, pages 16-18.

summary: The 1977 Maryland Historical Trust survey form for the Boulevard Theatre, filed in the city's Waverly Historic Survey folder, reports that the Durkee organization, owners since buying it at auction in 1926 and reopening it August 1, 1927, planned a Burger King for the Greenmount Avenue lobby, with exterior changes that would make the front unrecognizable, and that the community had petitioned against it. The design-standards team was tracking the same fight: an April 28, 1977 working note lists 'Burger King' compliance with the standards, in the 'style of Annapolis store'. The form also records the theatre's design by Ewald G. Blanke for Alfred E. Eyring and Sons, the private opening on October 8, 1921, the February 1922 auction sale to the Boulevard Theatre Company for $145,000, and the early multi-bulb marquee on 33rd Street. Frank Durkee III sat on the 1976 merchants' steering committee for the Boulevard. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, pages 19-22; BRG48-43-10-5, page 39.

summary: The July 1978 Waverly Merchants Association newsletter reported that Seven-Eleven had contracted to acquire the old Gulf station at 33rd Street and Merryman Lane, across from the library, and would settle within weeks. A convenience store and a lending institution were the Waverly Development Committee's two top business priorities. City revitalization architects were working with Seven-Eleven so the new building would meet the proposed design standards, the franchise was offered to local applicants, and the store was expected to open in fall 1978. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, page 4.

summary: The Baltimore Sun's 'Today' section of Tuesday, July 26, 1988 led with Nora Frenkiel's feature 'Baltimore at the crossroads: Diverse elements mingle at Greenmount and 33rd', photographed at the intersection with the Boulevard's marquee. It portrays the corner as one of the city's most mixed by race, income and way of life, busiest on Orioles game days, and quotes a foot-patrol officer and a local business alliance whose survey found people calling the area dirty and unsafe, a view old-timers and merchants disputed. The city clipped it into its Waverly Historic Survey file a decade after the revitalization program began. City Archives BRG48-43-10-6, pages 25-28.

summary: The Department of Housing and Community Development's 'Waverly Plan (final)' folder holds the Waverly Business Area Urban Renewal Plan with its exhibits dated February 2, 1979. The project area ran along Greenmount from 35th Street south to 29th Street and Exeter Hall Avenue, taking in the side streets between Barclay and Old York Road. Its goal was 'a unique neighborhood retail business district', and it zoned the area Community Business (B-2) along the avenue, Residential behind, and Public for the parking lot. The whole area was designated for rehabilitation to the plan's standards. Any owner who failed to comply within 24 months of written notice could be bought out, by eminent domain if needed, as could any building judged not worth rehabilitating. Only one block was marked for outright acquisition: 3881A, for the public parking lot at 32nd and Barclay. The plan promised relocation help for displaced residents and businesses, was to run at least 20 years, and required every amendment to go first to the Waverly Merchants Association and the Waverly Development Committee for comment. Appendix A lists five non-conforming uses: Vinson's animal hospital at 3015 Greenmount, auto service at 420 Merrymans Lane, auto repair at 3404-16 Brentwood, a barber shop at 3412 Old York Road and an office at 3400 Old York Road. The folder's Exhibit 4 is misfiled: it is the zoning map of the Hamilton Business Area on Harford Road. The plan went to the City Council as Bill No. 2278; this final text already carries the Urban Affairs Committee amendments (the lot 25/26 boundary change and the off-street parking section). City Archives BRG48-43-10-8, 49 scans (two copies of the text).

summary: The Waverly Business Area Urban Renewal Plan went to the City Council as Bill No. 2278. The 'Waverly U.R.P.' folder holds the plan as printed in the bill, followed by a DHCD-drafted sheet of 'Amendments to City Council Bill No. 2278' for the Urban Affairs Committee, in three identical copies, unsigned and undated. Amendment No. 1 added 'lot 25/26, Ward 12 Section 20 Block 3879-B' to the boundary description; Nos. 2-5 fixed a ward number, a lot number and two wording errors; No. 6 inserted a new section, 'Off-Street Parking Requirements', requiring parking to be screened by a four-foot wall, fence or evergreen hedge approved by DHCD, and paved and lit. The 'Waverly Plan (final)' folder, with exhibits dated February 2, 1979, carries every one of these changes, so the two folders bracket the committee's amendment of the bill. Neither folder records the date the ordinance passed. Its passage can be bracketed: the January 25, 1979 minutes plan to send the revised plan to merchants after a February 8 meeting, and on June 20, 1980 Councilwoman Mary Pat Clarke wrote that more than a year of the two-year grace period had passed, so the ordinance took effect between February and June 1979 (BRG48-43-10-11). City Archives BRG48-43-10-9, 29 scans; BRG48-43-10-8.

summary: A hand-lettered invitation under the WAVERLY wordmark reads: 'Mayor William Donald Schaefer, the Waverly Merchants Association and the Waverly Development Committee cordially invite you to celebrate the groundbreaking for commercial revitalization in Waverly at the median, Thirty-Third Street and Greenmount Avenue, Saturday, August 18th, 10:00 A.M.' The invitation gives no year. August 18 fell on a Saturday in 1979 and in no other year of the program (1977-83), and it fits the record: the urban renewal plan's exhibits are dated February 1979, the pylon went out for utility clearance in April 1979, and the public-improvement work on the 33rd Street median, 31st and 32nd Streets and the Shop & Park lot followed. The median itself had been accepted on July 6, 1979, and notice to proceed on the Greenmount sidewalk, tree and bench work was issued by August 24, 1979, so an August 1979 groundbreaking at the median fits the start of the second phase (BRG48-43-10-15, BRG48-43-10-10). This may be the invitation's draft rather than the printed card, so the entry does not prove the event happened as planned. City Archives BRG48-43-10-7, page 6.

summary: Handwritten minutes titled 'Waverly, Summary of mtg. 1/25/79' list the program's next steps as the urban renewal ordinance neared the City Council. Staff were to send letters about street trees; prepare clearer graphics of the 31st and 32nd Street public improvements for a merchants' 'vote'; send notices to merchants and property owners of a February 8 meeting; look into trees at the north end of Greenmount; send the proposed revised urban renewal plan to every merchant and owner after February 8; call Ed Hord about progress on a burned-out store in the 3200 block; revise the parking-lot plan; and meet Harry Little that week about the 32nd Street plan, perhaps with Buck Linder of 3118 Brentwood Avenue. Design-standard revisions softened the sign rules: existing flat signs and existing projecting signs on 31st and 32nd Streets could remain, but new projecting signs could not be lit. Staff noted that presentation drawings should be more three-dimensional for lay audiences and handouts free of ambiguity, and a side note on the yellow-pad draft reads 'positive change rather than restrictions'. summary: On June 20, 1980 Councilwoman Mary Pat Clarke of the Second District wrote to Dave Hunter, Director of Commercial Revitalization, that merchants were asking for inspections to begin so the exterior standards enacted for the Waverly urban renewal area would be enforced, since 'more than a year of the two-year grace period has already passed'. Hunter's July 30 transmittal asked staff to call Watson in building inspection about a schedule. The reply: Watson 'hasn't inspected Waverly yet'; told the notices were needed as soon as possible, he said he would do them that week, and Hunter asked that Clarke be told. It was the merchants, not the city, pushing for the rules to be enforced. City Archives BRG48-43-10-11, pages 35-38.

summary: The DHCD file holds the full 20-page typescript 'Waverly' prepared by Michelle Belco, Planning Assistant at the Commission for Historic and Architectural Preservation, in May 1977 for the City of Baltimore Neighborhood Survey, with footnotes and a bibliography citing Scharf (1881), the 1877 Hopkins atlas, the 1902 Sanborn, Jacob Aull's Old Landmarks and Sun articles from 1893 to 1956. It traces the area from the 1688 grant through the 1866 Gorsuch purchase that laid out the village, the name taken from Scott's novels, annexation in 1888, the rowhouse booms, the Federal Home Loan Bank Board conservation study of 1937-40 and why its plan failed, the Waverly Redevelopment Project (321 units at Mathews and 29th in 1953 and the Waverly Tower Shopping Center in 1957), and the 1975 planning study that fed the revitalization program. It places several buildings on today's corridor: the Aull house and gravel pit at 3116 Greenmount, the first post office behind 'Doc' Barrett's store at the southwest corner of 31st and Greenmount (run by Mrs. Bonsal), the Methodist congregation's first meetings over J. E. Sinclair's store at Merryman's Lane, School No. 115 on the merchants' parking lot and School No. 51 where Adler's stood. It gives the Boulevard Theatre's address as 3320 Greenmount, an error for 3302. City Archives BRG48-43-10-11, pages 11-31.

summary: Michelle Belco's 1977 history for the city's neighborhood survey says the Aull family's shoemaker shop was one of Waverly's earliest businesses, and that Henry Jacob Aull, a Bavarian immigrant, bought a gravel pit 'at, what is now, 3116 Greenmount Avenue' and built there a rambling Virginia Colonial house of bricks brought over as ballast on an English sailing ship. She credits his sons Jacob and Louis with building most of the village's cottages after 1866. This is the only source so far that gives the site a modern house number; 3116 is now part of this parcel. Corridor's other record names the founder Jacob Aull (1804-1876), so 'Henry Jacob' may be Belco's error or a fuller name. City Archives BRG48-43-10-11, pages 14 and 16.

summary: Before the city rebuilt the Waverly Parking Lot, it cleared the block it had acquired. Housing and Community Development's property management section collected rent from the remaining occupants as a relocation account. Margie Fields of 419 Merryman Lane (front), relocation account 180-40, received a vacate notice dated December 31, 1979, and her tenancy ended March 31, 1980, with keys to be surrendered at the Sharp-Leadenhall relocation site office. The existing lot at 3201-3221 Barclay Street had 28 active parking accounts, among them Mary Lambert's. The city kept them going past March 1980 but told every account to stop using the lot on June 1, 1980. Patricia Massey set the schedule on April 2, 1980: bid advertisement April 18, dwelling vacate date May 1, notice to proceed June 1. David Hunter added three small sheds to the demolition, and a May 16 note reports the houses vacant, BG&E coming to cut services and demolition to follow. The 1953 Sanborn map in the folder already labels most of the block 'Park'g', with houses along Merryman Lane; those houses were the ones cleared. A February 7, 1980 memo describes the last occupied building as 'a wood frame duplex residence at the N.E. corner of the proposed lot which has been acquired by the City but is still occupied', due to be vacated by April 15; property management confirmed it would enforce the March 31 vacate date for residents under Relocation Project No. 180 (BRG48-43-10-14). City Archives BRG48-43-10-12, pages 2, 7-9, 14, 23, 64.

summary: Hurst-Rosche Engineers of Timonium designed the lot for DHCD. After a May 16, 1979 review, David F. Paduch put the revised plan at $120,000 and warned that meeting David Hunter's $100,000 target would mean dropping all curbs and laying only an inch of asphalt. Their preliminary plan went out for utility review on July 13, 1979, and the tight budget ruled out $11,400 of conduit for the lighting cable in favor of $2,850 of direct burial. A landscape plan went to Recreation and Parks on October 3, 1979. The first Hurst-Rosche sketch, on May 11, 1979, came in at about $160,000, including $24,000 of lighting and 106 parking meters at $100 each; someone at DHCD wrote 'Too high - too fat!' across the letter. On June 20, 1979 Hunter set the meter posts 64 feet apart on double-loaded aisles of 22-foot stalls and a 20-foot aisle, and sent the plan to Transit and Traffic (BRG48-43-10-13). The Bureau of Highways let Contract 2611, 'Bituminous Concrete Resurfacing of Waverly Parking Lot', with bids due May 7, 1980 in a $100,000 to $250,000 range: 760 tons of asphalt, 1,940 feet of curb, 5,500 square feet of sidewalk, lighting, benches and plantings. R. Marcantoni & Sons of Broening Highway won it, received notice to proceed June 19, 1980 and finished November 22, 1980, with 84 days of authorized shutdown for the planting season. The city accepted the lot at a final inspection on March 3, 1981, with a two-year guarantee on the wood benches. In July 1981 it granted a 13-day extension for delays from a cable relocation and revised grades, and in October 1981 Hunter asked Recreation and Parks to check which trees and shrubs needed replacing. City Archives BRG48-43-10-12.

summary: The median work was the program's first public improvement. City landscape architect Michael Sievers of the Bureau of Operations designed brick paving, benches, trash containers, bollards and plantings for three sections of the 33rd Street median between Barclay Street and Old York Road. The August 23, 1977 estimate came to $56,498 for sod, 53 Loboy pyracantha, 12 Japanese zelkova, 3,300 square feet of brick pavers on a concrete base, and Timberform site furniture (10 trash containers, 27 bollards, 10 benches). On September 6, 1977 coordinator Paul Gilbert told Commissioner M. J. Brodie that final drawings were ready and asked to proceed, hoping to finish by December 1. Transit and Traffic was asked to reset the signal poles at Greenmount so the brick could be laid around their bases. It took two rounds of bidding. The first contract, BP-17378, drew one bid about $20,000 over the city's revised estimate, and on January 9, 1978 Gilbert decided to rebid with clearer rules on when contractors could reach the median (outside rush hours, from Brentwood and Old York Road) and where they could store materials (not within 75 feet of Greenmount). The revised estimate was $69,000. The rebid, BP-32578, went out March 14, 1978 with a pre-bid conference on March 20 and federal equal-opportunity requirements attached; bids were due April 5, 1978. Salco, Inc. bid $125,144. By August 1978 the work was being bid again for a September 6 opening and an October construction start. It was not the first work on the median: city crews had graded, sodded, planted pyracantha and set post and cable on the medians between Barclay and Old York Road in fall 1976 (BRG48-43-10-19). City Archives BRG48-43-10-15.

summary: The median was finally built under Contract No. 11932, 'Site Paving and Landscaping, York Road, McCabe Avenue to Tunbridge Road, 33rd Street Median, Barclay Street to Old York Road', which paired Waverly's median with the York-Woodbourne revitalization area. The contractor was Engineering and Consultants Corporation of Towson, headed by Francis X. Aiello. In May 1979 it could not find pyracantha of the specified size and asked to use smaller plants; the city rejected its offered credit of $347.10 as too small. The Department of Public Works repaired the median curb at 33rd and Greenmount on May 23, 1979 after Commissioner Brodie complained. The city accepted the work at a final inspection on July 6, 1979, subject to a punch list that included replacing 152 pyracantha and re-sodding between Greenmount and Old York Road. An October 5, 1979 site meeting found a dead tree in the median west of Greenmount 'opposite the movie theater', the Boulevard, and thin sod east of York Road. On April 9, 1980 Patricia Massey ordered another zelkova east of Greenmount and noted that pyracantha specified for two triangular beds in the brick paving had never been planted. summary: By 1983 the cast-iron tree grates the city had set into its revitalized shopping streets were breaking. On May 26, 1983 Housing Commissioner M. J. Brodie wrote to Neenah Foundry Company of Wisconsin that at least 17 of its R-8640 48-inch square grates, installed within the past four years, had broken spokes, almost always at the outside corner, and that the city could not keep buying grates that failed in normal use. Neenah tested a stock grate and reported on June 13 that the corner spoke broke only at 1,730 pounds. The city replied in July that it suspected the stakes driven to anchor the young trees' support wires, uneven installation, or planting crews deliberately snapping spokes to fit off-center trees. Neenah's engineer Steven Akkala agreed on July 22 that gray iron resists impact poorly and offered ductile-iron grates, 'nearly vandalproof', or grates with built-in tie-downs; in August David Hunter of the Commercial Revitalization Division was assigned to follow up. The file is filed with the Waverly program, whose 1977-83 capital schedule ends with a 'Tree Grates (1983)' folder, but the problem was citywide: the two photographs of broken grates sent to Neenah are labeled 916 and 918 W. 36th Street in Hampden. It does not say which of the broken grates, if any, were in Waverly. In Waverly itself the Contract 2572 contractor reported in February 1981 that merchants had been removing the bolts that held the new tree grates together, to clear out the trash that collected under them (BRG48-43-10-20). City Archives BRG48-43-10-17.

summary: The 33rd Street median work began two years before the contract, done by the city's own crews. At a meeting on August 18, 1976, recorded by coordinator Paul Gilbert, DHCD and the Highway Maintenance Division agreed to survey the utilities at Greenmount and 33rd, draw a final working plan with the joint-use and light poles, and write specifications for benches, bollards, trash receptacles and pavers. The same memo reports that Gilbert's staff had finished designing three 'Waverly' identification signs and their supports, that Purchasing was buying the signs, that brick piers were to be built by mid-September, and that 'at the point the sign is to be put into place, the Mayor should be on hand.' On November 17, 1976 landscape architect Michael Sievers reported the fall work on the medians between Barclay Street and Old York Road finished on schedule: an 18-inch splash pan, 30-inch post and cable, grading and sodding, and pyracantha planting, $13,416.15 out of $60,000 budgeted for 33rd Street. The 'Waverly' signs were then in storage at the Sisson Street Yard, awaiting brick piers from the Utilities Maintenance Division, and the rest of the median design was expected in spring 1977. These 1976 signs predate the tree-and-letters WAVERLY wordmark of 1977-78; the file does not show what they looked like or whether they went up. City Archives BRG48-43-10-19, pages 59-61.

summary: The heart of the program's public improvements was Bureau of Engineering Contract 2572, 'Commercial Revitalization of Greenmount Avenue' from 30th to 35th Street, with 31st, 32nd and 33rd Streets: new curbs and walks, brick paving, tree grates, zelkova trees on Greenmount and cherries on the side streets, benches, new street lights and a sign pylon. It was advertised May 18, 1979, opened June 6 and awarded July 11 to Mahoney Brothers Company of Erdman Avenue (George P. Mahoney Jr.), with Engineering and Consultants Corporation, Botts Landscaping Service and David Green and Associates as subcontractors; notice to proceed came August 15, 1979. Progress meetings were held at the Waverly branch library at 33rd and Barclay. The merchants shaped the schedule: work on 33rd Street waited until after the Orioles' playoff run, the job shut down completely from December 8, 1979 to New Year's and partly until spring so as not to disrupt Christmas shopping, the merchants asked that Easter shopping be spared too, and their representatives pressed for the new street lights and worried the lighting on 31st and 32nd would not be enough. Association president Nancy Smith polled the merchants on the shutdown dates. In 1980 the limits were extended south to 29th Street and Exeter Hall Avenue, and Councilwoman Mary Pat Clarke asked for the paving to turn the corner onto 29th Street. The work had problems: the brick grouting was rejected and redone, the paving subcontractor was cited for not keeping two lanes open, many winter-planted zelkovas and cherries died, new walks on 31st and 32nd heaved, and property owners complained of damage (see the entries for 2911, 3319 and 3433 Greenmount). It was substantially complete May 7, 1980 and finished June 30, 1980; the bid was $538,182.25, change orders added $160,807.44, and the final construction cost with utility work was $676,653.37. The city accepted it conditionally on December 18, 1980 and finally on June 17, 1981, and the two-year guarantee on the brick, tree grates and benches was closed out on January 25, 1983. On November 1, 1979 DHCD had told every property owner the improvements would cost them nothing. City Archives BRG48-43-10-20, 197 scans.

summary: Sanborn Vol. 7 (1915) sheet 717, block 10, west side of Greenmount between Vineyard Lane and E. 30th St. At the Vineyard Lane corner the plate prints '3020' over '922' on a 2-story frame dwelling with a porch, with a detached 2-story outbuilding and a hatched stable block behind it toward the lane. Mid-frontage it prints '3014' over '920' on a large 2-story frame house with 2-story and 1-story ells, standing about 100 ft back from the street behind an open yard; no dairy sheds are drawn, although the O'Neill dairy was listed there. At the south end it prints '918' on a 1-story store (modern 3008). The long range of one-story 'Green Houses, Glass Roofs' stands behind that 918 store, on the florist lot south of this parcel (modern 3000-3008, where Wm. H. Wolfe, florist, is listed from 1914), not on 3010-3020. Vineyard Lane was Gilmor Lane, the old tollgate road, so the glass houses are probably the nursery ground 'a little below the tollgate' that the 1933 Waverly history gives to Charles Hamilton's hothouses; Hamilton was listed at 908 York Road in 1893, and a florist still traded at 3000 Greenmount in 1922.

summary: Lee McCardell's Evening Sun 'Your Town' feature on Waverly: Henry Jacob Aull, a Bavarian shoemaker, bought a gravel pit on the west side of the York turnpike beyond the Gilmor (now Vineyard) Lane tollgate more than a century earlier and built a clapboard house; other south-German immigrants followed, among them Carl Friederick Gabler, grandfather of the poet Lizette Woodworth Reese. Opposite the tollgate stood an old stone barrack and powder magazine whose stone Episcopalians reused for St. John's Church. Behind the tollgate on Gilmor Lane was Oak Hill, home of Capt. William Kennedy, who founded St. Ann's. The 1866 thirty-acre subdivision was first called Huntington; told there were too many Huntingtons for a post office, the villagers took 'Waverly' on the suggestion of Henry Tyson, superintendent of the York Road Railway. James M. Sinclair still remembered 'Old Man Schofield on duty at the York turnpike tollgate.'

summary: The Sun of July 2, 1913, p. 12: 'FOR SALE-3026 and 3028 GREENMOUNT AVE., in Waverly; 6-room, porch-front; up-to-date, with every convenience, on most accommodating terms. Location unsurpassed. AULL, 210 East Lexington st.' The run code j2-6t means six insertions from July 2; the ad also ran in the Sun of July 3 (p. 14) and July 4 (p. 10) and in the Evening Sun of July 2, 3 and 4 (p. 11). It offers the pair as 'up-to-date' houses; it does not say they are new. The west side of the block had been renumbered before it appeared: Polk 1913, canvassed in the autumn of 1912, already prints Zepp Photo Supply Co. at 3044, the building that had been 3030. So '3026 and 3028' are two of the four brick dwellings Jacob H. Aull put up on the old toll-house lot, for which the permit was issued in April 1912. In December 1912 Aull had leased the four houses for 99 years to Alice M. Chapman and sold only the four ground rents to F. X. Hooper (S.C.L. 2787/374 and /376), so what was for sale here was the houses, held under the lease and subject to the rents; whether Chapman had by then assigned them back to Aull is not shown in the deeds read.

summary: William F. Freitag Sr., 70, a former Baltimore Symphony Orchestra trombonist, died Thursday at Union Memorial Hospital. In recent years he had directed a music school at 3028 Greenmount avenue. He founded the Freitag School of Music in 1945 and ran it until shortly before his death. Before that he taught trombone at the Peabody Conservatory for 25 years and was a soloist with the symphony and the municipal park band. Survivors: wife Belle Hackett Freitag (married 50 years on Feb 20, 1959); daughters Dorothea Freitag and Mrs. Eudrice H. Timmons; sons William F. Freitag Jr., Charles C. Freitag and Orville H. Freitag. Services at the Leonard J. Ruck funeral establishment, 5305 Harford road; burial in Moreland Memorial Park. The obituary gives the middle initial F. and a 1945 founding for the Freitag School of Music, which settles the white paper's William E. / public-web William H. discrepancy in favour of William F.

summary: Rev. summary: Profile of Thomas Lewis, 26, Baltimore artist and painting teacher, who had produced 120 silk-screen 'No More War - Peace' signs and 100 'God Is Love' signs for anti-war marchers at War Memorial Plaza, the Civic Center and Washington. summary: Anti-war leaders reported three acts of vandalism: rocks through the glass front door (Saturday about 4 P.M.) and a ground-floor front window (Sunday evening) of the Peace Action Center, headquarters for Baltimore's peace organizations in the 2500 block of Maryland avenue, and a rear window at the 2700 block St. Paul street home of William O'Connor of the Inter-Faith Peace Mission steering committee. The Peace Action Center became the Baltimore Defense Committee's base, the People's Action Center, where the clinic was planned.

summary: Paul D. Samuel reports that the Baltimore Defense Committee planned demonstrations for November 7-8 around the sentencing of the Catonsville Nine, who were convicted October 10 on three charges. It was writing to out-of-towners who had come during the October 7 trial week, when about 1,500 people gathered. Plans: a reading by Father Daniel Berrigan at Goucher College gym at 8 p.m. Nov 7, a march to the Battle Monument (renamed the 'island of life'), and an all-night vigil. On Nov 8 there would be a 9 a.m. War Memorial Plaza rally and march to the federal courthouse for sentencing by Chief Judge Roszel C. Thomsen, then a 7 p.m. 'political prisoners' rally at St. Ignatius Hall, 700 block N. Calvert Street, which had served as the October headquarters. Spokesman Grenville Whitman expected a smaller turnout and said the committee spent about $1,500 on the trial-week campaign and would be 'surprised if we spend $200 now.'

summary: Sun Magazine feature by Cei Richardson (photos Ellis Malashuk) on the People's Free Medical Clinic. Its logo swaps the caduceus wings for a clenched fist and its letterhead reads 'Medical Care Is a Right, Not a Privilege'; it runs on 130-150 volunteers and donations only. The idea was born at a meeting of the now-defunct Baltimore Defense Committee, which spent nearly a year planning; BDC members included Mary Moylan of the Catonsville Nine. The clinic occupies a green stucco-front former music school in the 3000 block of Greenmount in Waverly; on its opening night in May 1970 only 17 patients came (6-10 PM). Sixteen months later it is open four nights a week (Tuesdays reserved for women), has treated about 3,400 patients in 6,750 visits; only three GPs serve a 115-square-block area of 25,000 residents east of Greenmount and south of 33rd. The magazine counts 17 patients on opening night; Keck remembered 12.

summary: By Sharon Dickman. Baltimore Women's Liberation (BWL) kept a low profile at 3028 Greenmount. Its Women's Center shared 'the crowded household' with the People's Free Medical Clinic and Women: A Journal of Liberation, and had a large second-floor meeting room. Donna Keck, one of about 12 women at the first 1968 meeting, said she and others started Women: A Journal of Liberation in 1969. Office manager Karen Dickinson earned $35 a week and was behind on rent. Kee Hall assigned women to consciousness-raising groups (about 25 in the area, 2 lesbian, 1 co-ed), and more than 500 women got the newsletter. The center planned to move to a rented house, and Waverly Presbyterian Church at Old York Road and 34th Street offered space for a non-sexist day care center expected to open July 1 if $2,000 could be raised. Sidebar: Francine Brown, who ran the office when the center opened two years earlier, recalled the original meetings at the Peace Action Center and painting the Women's Center walls. Waverly Presbyterian at Old York Road and 34th Street (3401 Old York Road) offered space for the movement's day care, likely the Red Wagon Day Care Center later watched by police.

summary: By Jon Franklin. The People's Free Medical Clinic still flew its upraised black fist sign. In January 1974 the national Junior Chamber of Commerce named it one of the country's most outstanding self-help programs. Volunteer Dr. John Ruckdeschel, 28, of Hopkins and the Baltimore Cancer Research Center, said a $1,500 furnace replacement left $300 in the bank against about $2,000 a month in costs. The clinic had about 6,000 patient visits a year, pledges bringing a steady $250 a month, and Medicaid paying about $6 a visit. It already owned a small storefront next to the main clinic at 3028 Greenmount, but paid $375 a month rent on the main building. The lease was about to run out, and buying the main building needed about $10,000 down (about $200 a month in payments). Photos by Carl D. Harris show the storefront sign and Ruckdeschel with patient Kathy Farrell and staffer Leon Bankard. The storefront is 3032: the Rubenstein estate assigned it to the clinic in Oct. 1972, and its sign read "People's Free Medical Clinic / Community Information Center," the name of the drop-in center planned for the aborted 1970 Franklin Square clinic.

summary: Continuation (full page D2 clipped). Pat Cassatt had been director about 3-1/2 years. The center opened in Waverly in 1970 in the first of the three rowhouses it now occupied in the 3000 block of Greenmount. It would mark its 14th year with a 1960s dance, 'Dancin' in the Streets,' at St. John's United Methodist Church, 27th and St. Paul. Bob Cotter, 41, an early patient advocate and later board member, said the founders came mostly from the Baltimore Defense Committee, formed during the Catonsville Nine trial, plus the Baltimore Women's Liberation Movement. summary: By Ellen Hawks. Many patients of the People's Community Health Center at 3028 Greenmount Ave. had no insurance. Health outreach worker Erin N. Grace, a Lutheran Volunteer Corps volunteer from Ohio (Valparaiso University), said the center took the $19 per visit Medicaid paid. The non-profit had a 13-member board and about 20 employees, with Patricia Cassatt as director and Dr. Murray West as medical director. It was partly state-funded for family planning. History as told here: in 1969 the Baltimore Defense Committee and the Black Panthers, who had opened other clinics, joined forces. The Panthers pulled out over safety problems at other clinics, the Coalition of Women's Liberation joined, and the center opened in 1970. When Cassatt took over in 1980 costs rose, some staff were hired, and patients began paying on a sliding scale. Federal designation failed under a funding freeze. Sidebar: nurse Susan Sharp, a Union Memorial nurse who volunteers as patient advocate, and dentist Dr. Harvey (Hank) Landay (UMD Dental 1970), a volunteer of more than 15 years. summary: Deed dated March 6, 1912, read on the page image (a poor bilevel scan of the handwritten record copy; words in brackets are doubtful): The President, Managers and Company of the Baltimore and Yorktown Turnpike Road, a body corporate, to Jacob H. Aull, 'in consideration of the sum of two dollars ($2) and other valuable consideration', in fee simple, 'so much of the following described lot or parcel of ground ... as is outside of both the charter line and the present actual boundary line of the Baltimore and Yorktown Turnpike Road': from the intersection of the west side of the York Turnpike with the north side of Gilmor Lane (38 ft wide), 57 ft north on the turnpike, 100 ft west at a right angle, 51 ft 7 1/2 in south to the lane and 100 ft 1 3/4 in east on the lane. The intersection is tied to a stone [eight] ft to the north marking the beginning of land conveyed to David Mumma in 18[44] (Baltimore County T.K. 354), and the company held the lot by a deed of July 5, 187[-] from David [S.] Wilson [et al.] (Baltimore County E.H.A. liber, number illegible). The deed is recited in later instruments, among them the 1981 mortgage, and later deeds use its north line as the north line of 3032. Its 57 ft of frontage is exactly the four lots Aull leased on Dec. 6, 1912 (15 + 14 + 14 + 14 ft; S.C.L. 2787/374), so the lot took in all of 3026-3032. Thompson's 1889 plat letters the corner lot 'York Rd Turnpike Co.', 41 ft 5 in on the road and 117 ft 6 in deep, with a one-story stone dwelling, brick and frame outbuildings and a stable; the difference from the 1912 figures is not explained. Bromley's plates of 1896 and 1906 show no row there, and the old toll house was to be torn down at the end of July 1907 (Sun, July 28, 1907). A month after the purchase Aull announced four two-story brick porch-front dwellings (Evening Sun, Apr. 6, 1912; architect Jacob F. Gerwig) and took the permit as owner and builder (Sun, Apr. 21, 1912: 'northwest corner York road and Gilmore lane', 15 by 47 ft each). Polk 1913 (canvassed in autumn 1912) has no household at 3026-3032. The houses stood by Dec. 6, 1912, when Aull leased them for 99 years to Alice M. Chapman at $72 and $66 a year, and on Dec. 16 he sold the four ground rents to Frank X. Hooper for $4,500 (S.C.L. 2787/376; Sun, Dec. 17, 1912). Polk 1914 has households at 3028, 3030 and 3032, and Polk 1915 adds 3026. In July 1913 'Aull, 210 East Lexington st.' advertised 3026 and 3028 for sale. Aull (1848-1921, Register of Wills estate 176148) was a Waverly real-estate man from the founding shoemaker family and held at least four lots on Gilmor Lane and Waverly Avenue in 1889. Update Oct. 14, 2026: a fresh copy reads the company's title as E.H.A. 70 folio 92, a deed of July 5, 187[ ] from David S. Wilson et al. (725:research-scl2727-29-second-look-eha70-92). Update Oct. 14, 2026: E.H.A. 70/92 is negative (725:negative-eha70-92-96-not-the-wilson-trustees-deed); the recital's worn liber is probably 76 or 78. Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): the turnpike company's own deed is read (726:mdlr-eha80-97-wilson-trustees-turnpike-first-toll-gate-house-lot-4-1871): Lot 4 of the Wilson estate's Huntingdon plat, 57 by 100 ft at Gilmor's Lane with 'the First Toll gate House', July 5, 1871, $3,000.

summary: By a deed of assignment dated October 12, 1972, Hyman B. Rubenstein, personal representative of an estate, assigned the leasehold of 3032 Greenmount to People's Free Medical Clinic, Inc. (Liber RHB 3152 folio 289, which falls in 1974 in the city's recording sequence, so the existing Aug. 2, 1974 row is probably the recording date). This was the clinic's first property, bought more than two years before it owned 3028. It fits Ken Albright's story of buying the vacant house next door, whose elderly occupant had died, after his summer-1972 bike trip, and the March 1974 Evening Sun report that the clinic "already owns a small storefront next to the main clinic." 3032 had housed a barber shop in 1930-40 (Robinson: the clinic was once "behind an actual barber shop"); by April 1975 it was the clinic's counseling center. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the deed is read (726:mdlr-rhb3152-289-delmond-shields-estate-clinic-3032-1972): the estate is Delmond F. Shields's, who died May 2, 1971 (Register of Wills file A 1328); Alva M. Shields had deeded him 3032 on May 25, 1960 (J.F.C. 873/14). Leasehold at $66; recorded Aug. 2, 1974.

summary: Deed dated Feb. 14, 1975, recorded Feb. 19, 1975, read on the page image: David Siegel to People's Free Medical Clinic Inc., in fee simple, the lot 43 ft north of Vineyard Lane, 14 x 82 ft, running to 'the northernmost outline of the whole lot of ground described in a Deed from President, Manager and Company of the Baltimore and Yorktown Turnpike Road to Jacob H. Aull dated March 6, 1912 ... Liber SCL No. 2727, folio 29': No. 3032. Recitals: the lot is 'fourthly described in a Lease dated December 6, 1912' from Jacob H. Aull and Mary A. J. Aull to Alice M. Chapman (S.C.L. 2787/374), with a $66 rent payable June 1 and Dec. 1; 'THE REVERSION IN FEE together with the annual ground rent was granted and conveyed by a Deed dated November 13, 1964 ... Liber JFC No. 1800, folio 528 from Mercantile-Safe Deposit and Trust Company, Trustee, to David Siegel'; and the leasehold came to the clinic by a deed of assignment of Oct. 12, 1972 from Hyman B. Rubenstein, personal representative (R.H.B. 3152/289). Frank X. Hooper had bought the four rents of the row in 1912 and Mercantile Trust Co. was his trustee in 1945, so the 1964 seller was very probably his trust. Transfer tax not required. The deed merged the 1912 rent with the leasehold the clinic had held since 1972: the 1981 mortgage calls it a deed of merger, and the 2009 and 2014 papers call it a redemption deed. Same day and book as Charles C. Freitag's deed of 3028 and 3030 (folio 657). 3030 kept its separate $90 rent, created in 1951, which later instruments still recite. summary: Deed dated Feb. 14, 1975, recorded Feb. 19, 1975 at 11:03 A.M. (Robert H. Bouse, clerk; Title Guarantee Co. application H-85818), read on the page image: Charles C. Freitag to People's Free Medical Clinic Inc., 'those two lots of ground', for 'the sum of Five Dollars, and other valuable considerations'; transfer tax not required. First lot: on the west side of Greenmount Avenue (formerly York Turnpike Road) 15 ft north of Vineyard Lane (formerly Gilmor Lane), 14 ft front through the partition walls and 82 ft deep to a 4-ft alley, No. 3028, in fee simple. Second lot: 29 ft north of the lane, the same size, No. 3030, 'for all the residue of the term of years yet to come and unexpired therein, with the benefit of renewal forever, subject to the payment of the annual ground rent of $90, payable in equal semi-annual installments on the fifteenth days of March and September'. Recital: the April 1, 1969 deed to Freitag from Deborah C. Zimmerman (R.H.B. 2497/414). The $90 rent, created in 1951, belonged to Belle H. Freitag, who subordinated it at the same closing (R.H.B. 3207/653); the closing also carried a $22,850 first mortgage from The Equitable Trust Company (R.H.B. 3207/659), Freitag's $3,250 purchase-money second mortgage (R.H.B. 3207/664) and David Siegel's deed of the 3032 reversion (R.H.B. 3207/655). The 1981, 2005, 2009 and 2014 instruments all recite this deed. The clinic had rented 3028 from Freitag since 1970 at $375 a month; in March 1974 it needed about $10,000 down to buy. Charles was a son of the music-school founder William F. Freitag Sr. (d. 1959).

summary: On Sept 23, 1927, federal prohibition agents raided a saloon in the 2500 block of Greenmount Ave on a search warrant and arrested eight men. Arrested: Louis Saylor (2500 block Greenmount), John F. Emerick and Edward R. Coggins (2300 block Greenmount), Rignal M. Knott (900 block E 30th), Wilmer A. O'Brien (600 block E 29th), Thomas F. Roddy (2300 block N Calvert), William F. Fitzpatrick (35th St), and George F. Rutherford (no address). Separately, agents seized a 300-gallon still and 4,450 gallons of mash in the 500 block of Mulberry St. The clipping gives only the block, not a house number. The corner at 2500 had been a licensed saloon (Muhl, then the Hamms) until Prohibition, so it is the likeliest place, but that is not proven.

summary: Deed dated Nov. 7, 2016, recorded Nov. 14, 2016 (MB 18621/389), read on the scan: Max Properties, Inc., a Maryland corporation, to 3326 Greenmount Avenue, LLC, a Maryland limited liability company, in fee simple, 'in consideration of the sum of Seven Hundred and Fifty Thousand DOLLARS ($750,000.00)'. Exhibit A describes Lots 16 and 17 of the Wilson plat (citing the 1871 deed to 'John P. Bolgiano'), the 25-ft lot north of them and a rear lot on Brentwood Avenue; the tax accounts listed are 12-18-3884-001, 002, 034, 035 and 036, so the one price covers 3326-3338 Greenmount and 412-414 Venable Avenue together. The deed does not name the members of the buyer company.

summary: Deed, dated 1982-08-25, recorded 1982-09-01 (CWM Jr. 4224/362; MSA CE 168-14544, pp. 362-363, read on the page image). Grantor: Marcus G. Strovel, Personal Representative of the Estate of Bryant C. Vinson, deceased. Grantee: Vinson's Animal Hospital, Inc., a Maryland body corporate. Consideration: $62,500.00. Three lots are described. First, 3015 Greenmount: on the east side of the York Turnpike Road, 175 feet 7 inches south of the two-mile stone in front of the Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church lot (and 252 feet 2 inches south of the north side of Bateman's Alley), running south 15 feet to the northwest corner of the lot Augustus D. Clemens Jr. and wife conveyed to William L. Fink by deed of April 12, 1898 (R.O. 1729/241), east 48 feet 3 inches to the west side of Old York Road, north 15 feet 2 inches, and west 53 feet to the beginning. Second, 3017 Greenmount: beginning 156 feet 5 inches south of the milestone at the southwest corner of a lot Clemens Jr. leased to Jacob H. Aull (R.O. 1728/284), south 19 feet 2 inches 'to the lot conveyed to Charles M. Rahe', east 53 feet to Old York Road, north 20 feet 4 inches and west 58 feet 1 inch. 156 feet 5 inches plus 19 feet 2 inches is 175 feet 7 inches, where the 3015 lot begins, so 'the lot conveyed to Charles M. Rahe' is the 15-foot lot that is 3015; together the two make the 34-foot-2-inch frontage of the present lot. Third, No. 600 East 31st Street, 'in or near the village of Huntingdon', at the corner of Old York Road and an avenue 45 1/2 feet wide 'now known as 31st Street', 108 1/2 feet on Old York Road by 58 feet, part of the land formerly of Jacob Aull (Augustus Bouldin's plat; lease to Martin Kratt, Baltimore County E.H.A. 67/488). summary: Street View captures show the long one-story 3015-3017 building covered in a purple floral mural with a streetcar, a Waverly welcome motif and two women's faces, openings boarded. The mural was there by January 2021, when Jacques Kelly wrote in the Sun that 'the former Vinson animal hospital building has been painted in a playful mural' honoring the No. 8 streetcar and Goetze caramel cremes. A LoopNet table still lists the land use as 'Animal hospital / vet'. The Vinson family held 3015 from 1934 and 3017 from 1943; with 600 E 31st (bought in 1970) the three lots stayed with the family and the Vinson-named corporations (Vinson's Animal Hospital, Inc. from 1982, Vinson's Kennels, Inc. from 1986) until the foreclosure sale of 2004 (FMC 6085/1351). William D. Forester, D.V.M., the hospital corporation's vice president in 1982-84, then held them until he sold them to 3015 Greenmount Avenue, LLC in 2016 (MB 18620/27).

summary: The ordinance chronology DHCD compiled in September 1978, with the City Solicitor's 1977 title inquiry, gives the lot's whole history. Ordinance 567 (Oct. 22, 1956, Mayor D'Alesandro) let the City take 3207-3219 Barclay St for parking; Ordinance 502 (Nov. 25, 1960) sold the 32nd-and-Brentwood parcel, which the merchants leased and then bought (Waverly Merchants Parking Lot, Inc.). In 1972 Ordinances 382/383 and 528 closed and sold a 10-ft alley. In May 1974 Ordinances 1279/1280, 1306 and 1313 closed Brentwood Ave between Merryman's Lane and 32nd and sold its bed to Luck Dome, Inc. for a twelve-story hotel, office and apartment building with a garage and health club; Ordinance 1640 made Brentwood revert if nothing was built in two years. The merchants had sold the lot to Luck Dome (confirmatory deed Liber RHB 3002 f.371) and leased spaces back. Luck Dome mortgaged it to Fidelity Mortgage Investors, went bankrupt, and Fidelity took title by foreclosure on June 10, 1975 (Liber RHB 3239 f.672), with a large deficiency decree (Circuit Court No. 2, Equity 22510-C). Nothing was ever built. City Archives BRG48-43-10-22, pages 0055-0058, 0061-0062, 0109-0110, 0118-0120, 0163, 0174-0175.

summary: A 99-year lease dated March 9, 1973 (recorded March 20, Liber RHB 3002 f.373) from Luck Dome, Inc. (Simantovs Capon, c/o A. D. Gomborov) to Waverpark, Inc., the merchants' new vehicle (officers Alvin Miller and Harry Orman): 100 parking spaces at $5,000 a year, 30 daily and 70 hourly, with tiered free time (four hours for beauty-parlor customers, three for theatre customers, two for everyone else) and signs reading "Reserved for guests of Waverly Merchants." Exhibit 1 describes 3201-3221 Barclay St (25,891 sq ft) plus 415 Merryman's Lane, Block 3881-A. Paragraph 11 bound the site to an office building, motel or hotel and barred competing shops; an October 1973 modification pushed Luck Dome's garage deadline to Dec. 31, 1975. The copy is stamped as a complainant's exhibit, so it came out of the 1975 lawsuits. City Archives BRG48-43-10-22, pages 0141-0151.

summary: With the option unsigned, the Off-Street Parking Commission first raised condemnation on June 19, 1978 (Schaffner's status report); Brodie wrote "Give me details!" Pat Massey's July 14 briefing: the City had been buying from Fidelity at $130,000 since fall 1977, Fidelity went into receivership and Lifetime Communities took possession and sat on the option; improvements were estimated at $70,000; Bernard Klein, who managed the lot outside the merchants' Waverpark lease, proposed a Sambo's fast-food restaurant on part of it and threatened a taxpayer's suit. Brodie: "A wonderful mess, but keep pushing!" Bill Hoffman drafted a condemnation ordinance dated Aug. 4, 1978 for everything bounded by Barclay, Merryman's Lane, Brentwood and E. 32nd, modeled on a 1977 Frankford park-site ordinance; it was introduced in Council by Aug. 10 with hearings in late September, Mary Pat Clarke strongly for it. Terry J. Phillips told Clarke (July 31) that small businesses stored trucks on the lot and Union Memorial employees parked there, yet it hardly filled. On Sept. 25 Massey met Schaffner with a list of open questions (what the City and the developer had paid, lots 16-18, the alley closing, repeal of the hotel ordinance, who owned Brentwood Avenue, whether Fidelity knew about condemnation), and on Oct. 20 Goldfein formally told Lifetime's attorney that a condemnation ordinance was proposed. City Archives BRG48-43-10-22, pages 0033, 0035-0036, 0049-0053, 0060, 0063-0070.

summary: Greater Homewood (Rich Puchalski, Paige Hoswell, Alan Orman) wrote Pat Massey on Sept. 14, 1978 asking whether any funds existed for Waverly, escalated to Commissioner Brodie on Oct. 5 when no answer came, and called an emergency Waverly Development Committee meeting for Nov. 2; Councilwoman Clarke scrawled "Where are we with this?" Massey's candid memo of Oct. 19 put the Waverly estimate at $500,000, cut about $100,000 by dropping brick sidewalks, and proposed phasing: the median now, the parking lot next year, streets and sidewalks in 1980; the Commercial Revitalization account was empty and Clarke suggested raiding Armistead Hotel funds. An undated October memo told Brodie there was no EDA money and Massey would break it to the merchants first. At the Nov. 9 meeting, as the GHCC newsletter reported, Massey said Waverly's bond funds had been spent covering other neighborhoods' cost overruns and the rest liquidated in June at HUD's direction; HCD was applying to the U.S. Economic Development Administration. The community had been promised an ordinance and a construction start on May 1, 1978. City Archives BRG48-43-10-22, pages 0010, 0021, 0023, 0033-0035, 0040-0045.

summary: Purchasing reported on Oct. 17, 1977 that the only bid on BP-17378, the median's brick paving, came from Ralph Marcantoni and Son at about $20,000 over estimate; Gilbert rejected it (Jan. 9, 1978). The fix was a specification letting the contractor use three median sections as a construction compound, not within 75 ft of Greenmount. Requisition G224079 (Jan. 25) priced brick paving, wood benches, trash containers, bollards and landscaping at $69,000; the rebid package went out Feb. 24 with EEO and pre-qualification clauses; the pre-bid meeting was March 20 (bollards and 8x8 pavers deleted from median 3, square trash containers) and bids opened March 29, 1978 as Contract BP-32578, with a 9 percent inspection fee. In August architect David Hunter ordered two new 21'-6" signal poles with 34' mast arms set on brick-paved bases, bids Sept. 6, start Oct. 4. Contract 11932 went to The Engineering & Consultants Corp. of Towson at the Board of Estimates on Nov. 8, 1978, notice to proceed Dec. 6, completion due May 4, 1979; a Dec. 5 change moved paving 7 ft off two elms and added two zelkovas where Parks was removing elms (City Forester Calvin Buikema). Requisition G224079 (Jan. 25) priced brick paving, wood benches, trash containers, bollards and landscaping at $69,000; the rebid package went out Feb. 24 with EEO and pre-qualification clauses; the pre-bid meeting was March 20 (bollards and 8x8 pavers deleted from median 3, square trash containers) and bids opened March 29, 1978 as Contract BP-32578, with a 9 percent inspection fee. In August architect David Hunter ordered two new 21'-6\" signal poles with 34' mast arms set on brick-paved bases, bids Sept. 6, start Oct. 4. Contract 11932 went to The Engineering & Consultants Corp. of Towson at the Board of Estimates on Nov. 8, 1978, notice to proceed Dec. 6, completion due May 4, 1979; a Dec. 5 change moved paving 7 ft off two elms and added two zelkovas where Parks was removing elms (City Forester Calvin Buikema). summary: Gilbert told Highway Engineering on Feb. 17, 1978 that Hurst-Rosche Engineers of Timonium would draw the Waverly public-improvement contract documents; on Feb. 24 William O'Keefe handed over mylars and field books for Greenmount from 31st to 34th and for 31st, 32nd and 33rd Streets east from Barclay to Tinges Lane and Old York Road. The June 30 progress narrative had the Waverly design 30 percent complete, with 31st and 32nd Streets to be narrowed and the Greenmount limits extended to 29th and 31st; preliminary plans were due at the end of July. Gilbert's Feb. 7 memo scheduled construction for fall 1978 alongside three other districts. City Archives BRG48-43-10-22, pages 0083-0089, 0131-0132, 0154.

summary: Gilbert's Sept. 6, 1977 memo to Brodie put the split plainly: the community wanted B-2-3 rezoned to B-2-2 (three stories instead of six) and the merchants wanted the status quo, and he doubted a plan with rezoning would pass. On Jan. 6, 1978 he invited the 2900-3000 blocks of Greenmount into the renewal area with a two-year facade deadline, low-interest loans and the same downzoning. In November 1978 planner Sally Digges sent five neighborhood associations an annotated map, "Proposed Rezoning to be introduced with the Commercial Revitalization Urban Renewal Ordinance": the parking-lot block to B-2-2, two fringes at 34th Street to R-6, the rest staying B-2-3. Oakenshawe's council approved unanimously on Dec. 6 (John Walton: Waverly could be the shopping center for the Hopkins-area apartments, "may not become a Cross Keys"); the Waverly Improvement Association also said yes; Abell could not be reached. City Archives BRG48-43-10-22, pages 0002-0011, 0032, 0171-0172, 0180, 0207.

summary: Dr. Herbert C. Smith, president of the Oakenshawe Improvement Association, wrote Gilbert in early June 1977 about the Shell station closing at Calvin Avenue and rumors that Eddie's Supermarket would close, then wrote Mayor Schaefer ("Dear Don") on June 6: ten resident complaints in a week, "the southern end is dying," asking for a mayoral tour. Gilbert's June 20 reply (copied five times in the file) explained that almost 90 percent of Waverly shoppers arrived on foot or by transit, hence curb ramps, bus shelters and wider sidewalks. The Mayor's Aug. 15 memo demanded an update; Brodie's Sept. 16 reply followed. Gilbert convened the task force at the Waverly library branch on Sept. 6 at 7:30 p.m. with the urban renewal ordinance targeted for November; the sign-in sheet has 33 names and the distribution list 28, among them Tommy Cohen (3104 Greenmount), Stanley Adler (3240), Allen Orman (3113) and Nancy Smith (418 E. 31st). City Archives BRG48-43-10-22, pages 0176-0199, 0207-0213.

Edward F. Costanza, the builder who founded the Costanza Construction Company, had died on December 17, 1960 (Register of Wills estate OLD76913), and the deeds of 2006 to 2020 describe the lot as Lot B of the subdivision plan of the 'Estate of Edward Costanza'. The 1977 entry is therefore his estate, with a bank as its mailing address (the bank was probably a trustee). Michael Costanza is probably his son Michael L., president of the firm in 1960.

summary: The DHCD 'Waverly Property Owners' roster of about 1977 lists 3200 Greenmount: Harry Gorfine, 22 Light Street. City Archives BRG48-43-10-22, page 0113. The listing was out of date. The deed of November 12, 1976 (R.H.B. 3415/175) recites that Harry B. Gorfine took title on June 1, 1966 as surviving trustee under two 1948 deeds of trust from Myles and Betty Katz (J.F.C. 2079/102), that he resigned as trustee on July 5, 1972 (R.H.B. 2927/593), and that his successor, Arthur H. Katz, sold the corner to The Hotspot Family Restaurant, Inc. by that deed. A Harry B. Gorfine died on August 3, 1973 (Baltimore City Register of Wills, estate 138224), very likely the same man. So the roster carried the name of a trustee who had left the title five years before. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Gorfine had resigned as trustee on July 5, 1972, so the 1977 roster entry was stale (752:mdlr-rhb2927-593-gorfine-resigns-arthur-katz-successor-1972).

summary: Herb Smith reported the closing in early June 1977. Gilbert's June 20 reply: the station pumped about 350,000 gallons a year against a break-even of 30,000 gallons a month, so it closed for economic reasons. Gilbert's phone notes with Shell (on the back of Smith's letter): asking $60,000, "low $50's probably," three bays with lifts, no retail gasoline, a garage operator or small contractor the likely buyer; contacts Jim Rounds (Penn Jersey Auto Stores) and Robert Philburn of Shell. Contractors R. J. Hogan and Joseph Ziegler Jr. took the corner in August 1978. The 1977 roster lists Shell Oil Company, Princeton, N.J., as owner of 3400. A confectionery at 2745 was being offered for sale in March 1924, marketed on its proximity to Oriole Park. Oriole Park at 29th St was the selling point. Likely the Burton to Barber handover: Geo. Barber is at 2745 in the Sept 1927 dealer list.

summary: Continuation (from page C22) of coverage of the June 21, 1967 tavern-integration march up Greenmount Avenue. The demonstration began at Dickler's Cafe, Greenmount and North avenues, about 6:45 P.M. (photo caption: 'ANOTHER ROUND - Drawn by loudspeakers mounted on a car, a crowd again forms outside Dickler's Cafe'). At 7:35 the marchers entered the Blue Front Lounge, whose owner Richard McFarland read the trespass act four times and shut off the air conditioning; he closed at 9:55 P.M. to cheers. At 8:30 they found the Lewis Inn locked with white customers inside. After an incident with a National States Rights Party car, shortly after 9 P.M. the march moved north to the 2800 block Greenmount avenue, where 10-15 demonstrators entered the Bear's Den tavern and were served, the only incident being a bartender asking a sandaled demonstrator to get shoes. The crowd grew from 45 to 300-400. Green leaflets read: 'We will not allow the white man to come into our neighborhood, get rich off of package liquor trade and then insult us by refusing us the right to sit in their bar. We will integrate Dickler's, Mickey Griffin's and the Blue Front or we will put them out of business.' Leaders urged support for the 'open tavern' bill, which had missed passing City Council by one vote Monday, and called a meeting at Second Baptist Church, Guilford and Lanvale. Sidebar: 'Tavern Arrest Option Clarified' (Community Relations Commission director David L. Glenn on trespass warrants). The Bear's Den was the northernmost stop and the one bar that served; leaflets promised to integrate Dickler's, Mickey Griffin's and the Blue Front 'or put them out of business', and the 'open tavern' bill had failed in City Council by one vote.

summary: A gunman in a red ski mask and an accomplice with a paper bag robbed the Pixie Pizza and Sub Shop 'in the Waverly Shopping Center' in the 2800 block Greenmount avenue of $288 at 12:10 A.M. on Nov 30, 1972, while seven customers were unaware. summary: David N. Dorsey, 22, a soft-drink bottler of the 300 block E. 25th St., was sentenced to 20 years by Judge Solomon Liss after pleading guilty to attempted holdup and attempted murder. About 9 P.M. June 3, 1973 he entered an ice cream store in the 2800 block Greenmount avenue, demanded money from cashier Pamela Walker, 19, shot her in the stomach when she punched the register key, then shot customer Brenda Mihelich, 21, in the side; he took no money, went home and shot himself in the stomach in a suicide attempt and was found in the same hospital. Brother Tyrone Dorsey, 20, convicted as lookout. Prosecutor H. Gary Bass. Same clip: unrelated 'Fuel Tank Ignites, Burns 4 Campers'.

summary: The Sun's first 'Died' notice for John P. Lacey ran on September 4, 1920, the day after he died: 'JOHN P., beloved husband of Mary E. Lacey (nee Cochran). Funeral from his late residence, 3326 Greenmount avenue, of which due notice will be given.' The Evening Sun ran the identical text the same day (p. 12, image 367973722). The service details (Tuesday September 7, 8.30 from the house, Requiem Mass at 9 at St. Bernard's, burial in St. Mary's Cemetery, Govans) ran in the notices of September 5 and 6 and in the Sun's news obituary of September 4 (p. 7). The 'John P. Lacey, 3326' of the 1927 dealer list and of the Polk listings of 1921-23 is the family firm that kept his name, not a living John P.; the parcel was sold in 1969 by the estate of his widow, Mary E. Lacey.

summary: Editorial. The white Harlem Avenue Christian Church membership is deciding whether to sell its building at Harlem and Fremont avenues to colored Seventh Day Adventists; white churches and residents oppose a colored congregation owning the corner, with the final meeting next Monday. Meanwhile in the Waverly section, where colored people have long lived and built churches, white community associations are asking colored people, by word of mouth and in long letters to neighborhood leaders, to give up their homes and churches and move to the northwest section of Baltimore because more whites are moving to the suburbs. The paper's advice: behave the best we know how and let the neighbors move when they don't like us. The pressure on the Black blocks around Barclay St a generation before the City cleared 3201-3227 Barclay for parking.

summary: William Datcher, 17, of 3205 Barclay Street, drowned Friday after slipping from a rock into the Jones Falls at the old Cedar Avenue bridge, where he had gone swimming with other boys. Patrolman Jack Walter Denley of the Northwestern district, passing on his way to work, dived repeatedly and recovered the body; artificial respiration failed and he was pronounced dead at Union Memorial Hospital. Coroner Ferdinand C. Link of the Northern district heard Charles Sykes (1509 Calhoun St), Andrew Keener (15, 531 McMechen St), William Christian (17, 535 McMechen St), Golbert Davis (18, 1703 Druid Hill Ave) and Lawrence Gross (17, 537 Lanvale St), who had gone with him to the hole adjoining Mt. Vernon Hill, and returned accidental death. Adjacent item: traffic court fines totaled $895.65 on 86 persons this week. The Afro's first account (Friday July 11; Coroner Link; accidental).

summary: Robert Payne, 20, of 3201 Barclay Street, was exonerated Friday by a coroner's jury in Central police court of manslaughter in the death of Pearl Datcher, nine, of 3205 Barclay Street. Coroner Joseph Pokorney found some negligence but not of criminal degree and recommended traffic charges. Payne was driving a truck owned by James K. Carr, white, 3221 St. Paul Street, on Barclay Street near Thirty-second Street on April 4 when the left front wheel passed over the child; she died at Union Memorial Hospital of a fractured skull. Payne had been charged with manslaughter, reckless driving and driving on an instruction card without a licensed operator; the truck owner was accused of permitting an unlicensed driver. The second Datcher child of 3205 to die violently in four years; the driver lived at 3201, the corner lot itself.

summary: Continuation of a human-interest story about the Brown family (seven people, children Vincent 16, Mary 13, Gloria and a little brother) living in a derelict house at 3205 Barclay street for $32 a month on a $143.50 monthly welfare check, with one working coal heater, a leaking toilet, no electricity since summer and shutters nailed shut. Mrs. Brown's written complaint went nowhere until Mr. Brown called the Pine street police station; on Dec 21 Housing Bureau inspectors found 23 code violations and sent the owner a 30-day notice. Mrs. Terry King (Housing Bureau) and Vernon Hoffman (Brotherhood Volunteer Service Unit, 3205 Barclay call) intervened; within a day the family was offered an apartment at Fairfield Homes public housing, with the Brotherhood advancing the first month's rent, the Welfare Department the $10 deposit, the Lutheran Inner Mission $15 for fuel and clothes, and Grace and St. Peter's Church as clearing house. Hoffman moved them on New Year's Eve/Day. Housing Bureau inspectors found 23 violations on Dec 21 and served the owner a 30-day notice; the Brotherhood Volunteer Service Unit moved the family on New Year's Eve.

summary: George W. Biddle, Baltimore's oldest public school teacher, retired on pension after 52 years (37 in Baltimore City schools); honored Thursday at School 118's Community House and Friday by the Principals' Association with a gold watch. Born in South Baltimore 72 years ago, he taught first in Carroll County at age 20, then Kent County, then Baltimore County and Waverly, and entered the city system when Waverly was incorporated into Baltimore. He was the city's first colored principal, when School No. 9 on Carrollton Avenue was turned over to colored people, and has been principal of the Argyle Avenue school for 12 years. Nearly every city principal once served on his faculty; he calls Miss Fannie Barbour the best teacher in the city. The segregated school on this block (School No. 115 in Belco's history) had a teacher of note; the 1938 eulogy repeats it.

Next year marks 50 years since the first colored high school class (nine women, two men) graduated; City Council had made graduates with an 85 average eligible to teach without exam, and a 12-room school was built at Riggs and Carrollton avenues for colored teachers. Seven of the first class qualified; Biddle, then teaching in the Waverly school, was brought into the city system by the 1888 Annexation Act, which also brought Miss Roberta Sheridan, Mrs. Mary J. Camper and Miss Nannie B. Groomes. Biddle became principal of the boys' department at No. 9 and Fannie Barbour of the girls'; school board president John T. Morris called the experiment a success. Adjacent story: Mrs. Violet Hill Whyte, Baltimore's only colored policewoman, completes her first year in the Northwestern district.

summary: Recap of a Baltimore Sun article on 'Lefty' (Clarence) Russell: he began with the Frisby Stars in Baltimore, pitched for a Sunday school team in 1908, and was tipped to Hagerstown by third baseman Eddie Coggins ('that is the way those York road boys take care of each other'); Lefty in turn got manager Will Callahan signed. In spring 1909 Charley Boyer of Hagerstown recommended him to Savannah, but Orioles vice-president Moses N. Frank met him on the street and offered $50 a month over the Savannah contract, so he signed with Baltimore. He pitched three innings against the New York Giants in the 1909 preseason, was loaned to Wilkes-Barre under Mal Kittridge, developed his spitball, wrote a June 15, 1909 letter from Troy, N.Y. to Johnny Frazier of Frederick asking for a job at $150-250 a month (Frederick passed), and went back to Hagerstown, where he became the best pitcher in the 'Wisdom, Hope and Friendship' circuit. The Frederick Post's recap of the Sun feature, with the June 15, 1909 letter from Troy asking Frederick for a job.

summary: Ann LoLordo's account of how the Narcotics Task Force (formed Sept 14, 1981 under Commissioner Frank J. Battaglia) brought down Maurice D. 'Peanut' King's East Baltimore heroin organization using informant Otis Michael Smith ('Colombo'), a stick-up man recruited by Sgt. Gary Childs and Det. Marcellus Ward. King ran the operation from a snowball stand and two corner grocery stores, including one in the 1400 block Holbrook street; the squad spent $45,000 in federal buy money; 11 indicted June 1982; a federal jury convicted King, Thomas 'Joe Dancer' Ricks and six others of a $50 million-a-year ring; King got 50 years on March 18, 1983 and $1 million in property was seized, including a $26,000 DeLorean and a $175,000 Silver Spring house. The companion piece quotes Capt. Joseph P. Newman, State's Attorney Kurt L. Schmoke and U.S. Attorney J. Frederick Motz, and gives the case of street dealer Calvin Roosevelt Young, who bought from a ring run by Cornelia Fryson, 'owner of a Greenmount avenue bar,' managed day to day by Gerald Watkins and supplied by New Yorker Clifford Wright (Fryson and Wright arrested Feb 11, 1982). About 29,000 opiate addicts estimated in the city. The Fryson bar is a second, unlocated corridor address in the 1982 heroin cases (Fryson and supplier Clifford Wright arrested Feb 11, 1982); a liquor-board search for Fryson c. 1981-82 would place it.

summary: Full-column account with block diagram of a fire before 11 A.M. Sunday June 9, 1895 in the block bounded by Monument, Constitution, Front and Forrest streets (East Baltimore, near Greenmount avenue). It started in S. H. Tinley's lumber drying-room behind 557-559 East Monument street, the three-story sawing and planing mill of Storck & Co. (formerly A. Storck & Sons; A. Storck died about two years earlier; sons George J. and Edward J. Storck), also housing Tinley's sash, door and blind factory; ten Storck-owned houses on Monument street and ten on Front street were damaged, as were Henry Niemann's church-organ factory (561-563) and William Silverwood & Son's coal yard (565). Damage estimated at $50,000 (Storck about $33,000, Tinley $15,000), insurance under half; two alarm boxes struck at once misregistered as box 216 half a mile away, delaying engines ten minutes. Many poor tenants lost everything; George J. Storck was at St. Ignatius when notified. The fire briefly halted the York Road line cars of the City and Suburban company on Greenmount avenue until hose tripods let them pass. A. Storck & Sons' East Baltimore mill and twenty Storck-owned houses; the York Road street cars on Greenmount were halted by the hoses. The founder's business before it moved to 2406-2418.

summary: About 2 a.m. on Sunday May 16, 1858 an alarm of fire was raised for St. John's Episcopal church at the first toll-gate on the York road; the church was entirely destroyed except its stone walls, which were still good. Only the Independent fire company went all the way out and it protected the parsonage. A neighbor woke to the smoke and ran to save the sacramental vessels, but they had already been stolen and the door left open. The church was only two or three years old with a large congregation; damage about $2,500, insured for $1,700 with the Baltimore County Mutual Society. No fire had been lit since the previous Thursday, so arson was assumed. Damage about $2,500, insured for $1,700; only the Independent company came out and saved the parsonage.

summary: The Department of Planning's 'Shopping Survey and Parking Analysis: Waverly Business District' (May 1976; W. Anderson, H. Kohn, R. Baltimore, T. Knoche) is the baseline the DHCD program was built on. About 250 interviews in March-April 1976: 56% white, 44% black; 70% from zip 21218; 52% walked in (second only to Hampden), 31% drove, 16% came by bus, 33rd and Greenmount being a transfer point; 54% male, 54% under 30, black shoppers markedly younger. The stores that drew people were the A&P, Eddie's, Read's and Woolworth's and the three shoppers-goods stores, The Red Shed, Princess Shops and Purple Bone; 55% bought clothes in Waverly, the highest share of any district studied. The renovated Pantry Pride at Waverly Towers, Northwood, and a Pantry Pride rising at York-Woodbourne were the threats: 'imperative that investment increase in Waverly.' The parking half counted 693 spaces in 20 blocks (359 curb, 209 metered; 334 off-street, only 15 of them a public metered lot), 442 used at the Friday Feb. 20, 1976 peak; Greenmount's 50 meters held 52 cars with 13 parked illegally, 36% of the area's illegal parking on 14% of its curb. Verdict: no new off-street supply, only signing and management, so 'streetscaping, landscaping and mall development' could proceed even if parking was removed. The cover carries agenda notes for a June 28 meeting: median, kiosks, bus shelters, trees, sidewalk widening paid by merchants, 'get rid of warehouse near post office for park purposes', and '2 merchants groups - smut stores'. The 1976 questionnaire still called the merchants' body the Greenmount Avenue Merchants Association. City Archives BRG48-43-10-21, pages 0006-0041.

summary: Planning's 1976 parking study is the fullest picture of the lot before the City took it. Facility #1041 at Barclay and 32nd, 132 spaces (112 adjusted), was meant to be free with a member merchant's stamp and 50 cents an hour otherwise, but was unattended, enforcement was irregular, and about 15 spaces were leased monthly at $15-$25. At the Friday Feb. 20, 1976 peak it held 55 cars (42%); turnover was 0.8 a day against 4.0-7.6 at the Greenmount meters; Figure 6 shows a block of roughly 40 all-day parkers filling it, and 45 of its 55 peak users were long-term. Drivers on Greenmount could not tell it existed, and from 33rd the only way in was one-way Merrymans Lane heading the wrong way. Recommendations: redesign for access and flow, then signing, cap long-term use at half the lot, add about five meters on Venable between Barclay and Greenmount, pave the Hardware Fair/Baltimore Dictating Machine lot and landscape Eddie's. 'New parking supply as such is not warranted.' Three years later the City condemned the lot to build one anyway. City Archives BRG48-43-10-21, pages 0023-0030, 0037, 0040-0041.

summary: The paper trail of the first attempt to take the block by law. Chief Solicitor William Hoffman sent Mayor Schaefer and Council President Orlinsky the draft on Aug. 4, 1978: its purpose was 'to guarantee issuer that the Waverly Parking Lot will continue to be used as a parking lot,' because an outstanding lease would let the lessor turn it commercial. Introduced Aug. 8 as City Council Bill 1887 (Orlinsky, by request of the Department of Law): acquire by purchase or condemnation, for off-street parking, every interest in the lots bounded by Barclay St, Merryman Lane, Brentwood Ave and E 32nd St, the Off-Street Parking Commission to negotiate and the City Solicitor to condemn under Title XII if no price is agreed. Robert T. Schaffner of the Commission told the Council on Sept. 25 that the bill was introduced at the request of DHCD's Commercial Revitalization office 'to preserve the use of said property for public parking use.' Inside DHCD the report went two ways: R. N. Caasi's Sept. 22 draft, which wrongly said the site 'is not within the boundaries of this Department's community development areas' but urged approval, was struck through, and Pat Massey's rewrite signed by Brodie on Oct. 20 approved the acquisition in principle but recommended the Council withdraw 1887 in favor of the Waverly urban renewal ordinance, due mid-November, which would carry the same power. Two Bureau of Plans & Surveys plats of Block 3881-A came with the file, one marking 'Sites #3 + 3A (3A = lots 1 & 13)', the other outlining the whole triangle and noting the 10-ft alley closed by Ordinance 162 of July 5, 1972. City Archives BRG48-43-10-21, pages 0125-0129, 0141-0157.

summary: The replies to the autumn 1978 alarm (see the 'funds lost' entry). Rich Puchalski's Sept. 14 letter ('no funds available ... after two years of work') and Paige Hoswell and K. Alan Orman's Nov. 2 letter for Greater Homewood, reporting an emergency Waverly Development Committee meeting and recalling that the ordinance and construction had been promised for May 1, 1978, demanded Pat Massey and four deliverables for Nov. 9. Brodie (Nov. 6) said Massey would attend to finalize the ordinance and funding. Massey's Nov. 6 letter to Puchalski conceded bond funds were 'in short supply,' said the City was applying to the U.S. Economic Development Administration, but pointed to two things in hand: a favorable bid on the 33rd St median going to the Board of Estimates Nov. 8, work to start that fall, and an Off-Street Parking Commission allocation for the merchants' lot, to proceed 'as quickly as the property can be acquired.' Real Estate Officer Jerome Goldfein was still asking for the ordinance on Nov. 8 ('we are in process of drafting it,' Massey answered Nov. 13). The Mayor's thank-you letters for the first Waverly Weekend went to Marie Halka and to Alan Orman at 3113 Greenmount the same week. City Archives BRG48-43-10-21, pages 0134-0140.

summary: David Hunter's Nov. 30, 1978 memo to Vito Mangano on Contract 11932 / Job 12-78: keep the brick paving edge at least 7 feet from the centerline of two existing elms, have the contractor notify City Forester Calvin Buikema before excavating there, and add two zelkova serrata because Buikema was removing two elms. Mangano's Dec. 28 letter to Engineering & Consultants Corp. of Towson ordered an itemized proposal for the median west of Greenmount, 'similar to changes already furnished for the eastern median': revised brick shapes, relocated benches, bollards and shrubs. The pencil sketch '33rd St. Median Design Revision, Plan #2, Sheet 6 of 8' (S.B., probably Steve Broache) moves two benches two feet toward the middle and aligns four bollards along the south edge around an existing tree. summary: The two-page lettered summary Pat Massey enclosed to owners in February 1979. Windows not filled, boarded or covered by signs; show windows within 13 feet of grade; security grilles inconspicuous and removable during business hours; only soft retractable awnings; no new Formstone, aluminum siding, wood shakes or pebble-faced plywood, and existing aluminum siding must be removed; rear yards enclosed by a screening wall or used for conditioned parking. Signs: identification only, no manufacturer advertising; flat signs no higher than 13 feet and no larger than three times the frontage; freestanding signs only at gas stations (past or present) to 24 feet; one projecting sign per business, 5-foot projection, 10 to 15 feet up, 12 sq ft a face; no rooftop signs or billboards; 'no marquees on bldgs. other than existing, operating theatres', which protected the Boulevard at 3302. A companion sketch draws the flat and projecting sign envelopes (3-ft projection there, 4 ft in the plan text). City Archives BRG48-43-10-21, pages 0095-0097.

summary: Charles Doble, president of Better Waverly Community Organization (933 Homestead St), wrote Brodie on Feb. 2, 1979 that funds long committed to the Waverly commercial district 'are no longer available,' which 'casts serious doubt on the integrity of the City's financial commitments,' copying the Sun. State Senator John Carroll Byrnes asked for a written status four days later. Brodie's replies (to Byrnes March 9, signed by John A. McCauley; to Doble March 19) fixed the program: the urban renewal ordinance to Council in March; final engineering to Public Works by the end of April; contract advertised May or June; the merchants' lot acquired and improved, new sidewalks, lighting and landscaping on Greenmount, two mini-plazas on 31st and 32nd between Greenmount and Brentwood, and the median under construction; over $1 million from the Commercial Revitalization and Off-Street Parking bond issues. Bernard Berkowitz's March 12 memo from the Mayor's office set Hurst-Rosche's final drawings for the week of April 23-27 and advertisement in mid-May, with every agency's input to Terry Hastings by April 6. City Archives BRG48-43-10-21, pages 0074-0077, 0084-0085.
