summary: The folder holds the working draft of the plan later filed as 'Waverly Plan (final)': title page, contents (Separability moved from page 19 to 18 in pen), 19 text pages and Appendix A, with a reviewer's red marks throughout ('already non-conforming', 'size 3 feet by width', 'what about 2nd floor tenant', a missing 'not' restored in the non-discrimination clause, 'BLOCK 4705' for 4075). Substance: the whole area designated for rehabilitation; DHCD may condemn any property whose owner will not meet the standards within 24 months of notice, after 90 days' warning, for two years; relocation help for displaced businesses 'in or near' the area; Formstone, aluminum siding, simulated shakes and pebble-faced plywood banned, corrugated metal painted duranodic bronze, no sandblasting; flat signs three times the frontage and no higher than 13 feet, one 12-sq-ft projecting sign per store, non-conforming signs gone in two years and billboards over 60 sq ft in five with no lease renewals, every store to show its street number with the Waverly logo; DHCD written approval before any exterior permit and control of demolition permits with a 90-day Board of Estimates acquisition option; twenty-year duration; amendments through the Waverly Merchants' Association and Waverly Development Committee. With it: a hand-drawn 'Waverly Commercial Rezoning Proposal #3' that would have downzoned nearly the whole B-2-3 corridor to B-2-2 (FAR 5 to 2.5), keeping B-2-3 only between 33rd and Venable, and a plain-language zoning explainer; the final plan kept four targeted changes instead. City Archives BRG48-43-10-21, pages 0097-0124.

summary: DHCD (D. Mendelson) formally submitted the Waverly Business Area plan to Planning Director Larry Reich on March 6, 1979 under Ordinance 152 (1968) as amended by Ordinance 325 (1977), with the Summary of Proposals: six privately owned lots to be acquired for public parking (3201/21 and 3223/27 Barclay, 415, 417 and 419 Merrymans Lane, Block 3881A Lot 23, mapped as Disposition Lot No. 1, about 46,830 sq ft), and rezonings of 3336-3413 Old York Road, 501/503 and 500-504 E 34th and 3404-16 Brentwood to R-6 and 3244-3250 Barclay to B-2-2-P. Council President Orlinsky introduced it as Bill 2278 on March 19. The fiscal note (James K. Middleton, DHCD) claimed no departmental impact and 'parking lot revenues'; its capital figures, $200,000 this year and $900,000 total, were whited out, and the typed attachment promised a $500,000 public-improvements contract and $200,000 from the Off-Street Parking Commission (account 9964-577-005) for the lot. The hearing, moved from April 26 to May 8 at Waverly Presbyterian Church, drew about 100 people before Clarence Burns and Mary Pat Clarke: many residents opposed City acquisition of the lot because it would be metered and cost the City upkeep; Philip Kershner of Foster & Kleiser asked that the billboard phase-out be struck; supporters gave six reasons. Amendments adopted on second reading May 14 (Fred Lauer's memo of May 15) added the off-street parking screening section and 3407-3415 Brentwood to the R-6 list; the vote was set for May 21, and Mark Sissman's undated slip to Vidor and Massey reports 'Both ordinances are passed in final form.' Dave Hunter's May 12 note pressed to send the Waverly notices 'A.S.A.P.'; Massey noted Parker was 'working out Felicibus, Hartman, Rose.' City Archives BRG48-43-10-21, pages 0042, 0051-0060, 0065-0067, 0086-0088.

summary: The opposition to the City taking the lot, in its own words. Bernard Klein (Buckingham Arms Apartments, 3706 N. Charles), who operated the lot, gathered a petition of residents, merchants, Union Memorial Hospital nurses and area employees against Bill 1887: meters would be costly, the lot was available now with free validated parking for customers, employees parked cheaply, and the City would lose the parking-license revenue; 'Dan' (Mendelson) forwarded it to Massey with the note that its 572 signatures included 'some of questionable legitimacy.' A yellow handbill called a special meeting for Tuesday, May 8, 1979, 7:30 PM at Waverly Presbyterian, 34th and Old York Road, 'to object to City acquiring parking lot to install meters.' At the CC 2278 hearing that night many speakers made those arguments. DHCD's counter-evidence was a handwritten staff survey: 140-170 spaces, $11 a month, 50 cents the first hour for non-customers, at least half the cars repeaters and many of them Union Memorial employees, three garages (Perry's Auto, Brentwood Auto) storing repair cars, unlicensed cars and trucks, haphazard parking with no lines, a booth staffed 9-5 with lapses, full only on Orioles opening day and Colt games, 'I've never had to turn a shopper away'; conclusion, good for the hospital, secondary for shoppers, 'a physical blight to the neighborhood. Not to mention a speculative property for B. Klein and friends.' City Archives BRG48-43-10-21, pages 0054, 0071-0072, 0089-0091.

summary: John P. Allen, Regional Vice President of Lifetime Communities, Inc. (Toms River, N.J.), wrote Real Estate Officer Jerome Goldfein on July 5, 1979 about '3201-3227 Barclay Street; 415 and 417 Merryman Lane; Lot 23 w/s Brentwood Avenue N.W. corner 32nd St., Block 3881-A, Lots 1/12, 13/15, 16, 17, 18 and 23': the $1.00 option was unacceptable, the $130,000 price 'low and therefore unacceptable,' the 120-day exercise and title periods too long, and the company would convey only the title it had. Fidelity Mortgage Investors had merged into Lifetime; neither was any longer a debtor in possession, the Plan of Arrangement having been confirmed in January 1978 (S.D.N.Y.). 'We are ready, willing and able to sell ... on terms and conditions reasonably acceptable to us.' His cover note to Pat Massey: 'I don't think your friend Goldfein and I are going to get along very well ... what I consider a worthless option.' Massey's note of 7/11: spoke with Goldfein, property to be reappraised in two weeks, final offer to follow, 'if not, will file for condemnation.' Meanwhile Hunter's June 11 note said construction of the lot 'for this year is probably out' and proposed combining its preliminaries with Spaulding Avenue's by Aug. 1, and Massey had asked Hurst-Rosche (April 6) to add a lighting layout, cobra-head fixtures on 30-foot aluminum poles, to their proposal. summary: Vito Mangano told Highway Engineering on May 29, 1979 that the HUD Section 3 clause did not belong in Waverly highway contract #2572 because no federal HUD funds were spent. Hunter's justification for adding storm-water inlets (nine E-combination and one S-type replacing ten old ones, $15,500) carries a large blue 'NO', and a note that Don K. suggested budgeting about $650,000 for the whole job to cover City labor and contingencies. On July 5 Finance's Arthur C. McHugh recommended deferring HCD's proposed $623,974 transfer of City Loan funds meant to fund the contract and a 36th Street change order, since neither was scheduled for award; Brodie penciled 'Let's NOT do this anymore!' and John Q. Parsons answered, 'We did the transfer to supposedly "keep things moving"!!!' The fiscal note had put the streetscape at $500,000; the final construction cost was $676,653. City Archives BRG48-43-10-21, pages 0044, 0048-0049, 0069.

summary: The front of the file. Pre-bid notes of May 25, 1979 (a week after advertisement): crusher run under the walks, four lanes on Greenmount at 33rd in rush hours, 31st one-way west, all-PVC conduit, and, starred, 'Basement entrances hidden!' Vito Mangano confirmed May 16 that only the HUD Section 3 clause belonged in the specs. At the July 24 pre-construction conference (Bill Motley ran it; Mahoney wanted to start Aug. 15 on 31st and 32nd) the contractor took the sign layout for five 8-by-4-foot construction signs, deep blue with the WAVERLY tree logo, 'NEW... SIDEWALKS LANDSCAPING PLAZAS LIGHTS', Mayor Schaefer's name and the HCD seal, and was told 'no dark areas will be permitted' while street lights changed over. Steve Broache found on Aug. 3 that the caulked half-inch cork expansion-joint detail had been left out of the drawings for both Waverly and 36th Street; David Hunter amended the brick-paving mortar spec on Aug. 16 to require a bonding compound; Massey ordered sheet 11 redrawn (Aug. 23) for two wider driveways near Calvin Ave (17 and 20 ft at stations 15+04 and 15+46.5), which Hurst-Rosche red-lined on Sept. 11. Progress Meeting 1 (Sept. 17, at the Waverly library) set the sequence: 31st and 32nd first, then Greenmount south and north from 31st; a second-floor room in the firehouse became the inspector's field office. City Archives BRG48-43-10-20, pages 0175-0193.

summary: Progress Meetings 1 through 6 at the Waverly library (33rd and Barclay), Vernon Fahey presiding for the City, George Mahoney Jr. and J. Amos for the contractor, Steve Broache and later Marsha Rozansky and Bob Quilter for HCD, merchants Nancy Smith (418 E 31st) and Tom Fannin (506 E 32nd) at the table. Sept. 17: finish 33rd Street by Oct. 3 or wait until after the Orioles' playoffs 'and, if necessary (we hope) the World Series' because of Stadium foot traffic; Mahoney agreed but would file a delay claim; BG&E gas services on 31st Street lay 5 1/2, 4 1/2 and 1 inch below the new subgrade at #417, #419 and the bookstore, so test pits were dug. Oct. 8: colored caulk for the brick joints, omitted from the plans, quoted $1.70 (fall) or $1.90 (spring), settled at $1.80 a foot on Oct. 26 (about 2,400 ft, $3,960); the Tugboat Annie's corner and the firehouse driveway added; the 32nd Street sign pylon found two feet off location. Oct. 29: wooden curb forms allowed; a bench on 31st deleted; the Transit and Traffic conduit broken on the south side of 32nd ruled deteriorated and paid time-and-material ($1,251.72 billed Nov. 28, cut to $397.15 in Feb. 1980). Nov. 14, with B. McAllister of Shoe World and G. Gross of Princess Shops present complaining that customers 'can't get in and out of store (sand, mud)' and Shoe World wanting its rug shampooed: work allowed past the Nov. 15 shutdown to Nov. 30, and merchants asked that Easter shopping be spared too. Nov. 26: everything south of 33rd except brick done by Nov. 30; Mahoney's request to keep working the east side of the 3300 block to Dec. 14 referred to Ms. Smith's poll and denied Dec. 10; complete shutdown Dec. 8 to Jan. 1, partial to March 15, 1980; BG&E's new light poles unavailable, merchants doubting the 31st and 32nd Street lighting would be enough. City Archives BRG48-43-10-20, pages 0090-0108, 0150-0153, 0159, 0180-0181, 0194-0197.

summary: The pylon is the contract's one piece of signage: a 20-inch concrete column carrying a 3'-6" triangular galvanized frame with pan-formed aluminum panels, sited on Greenmount at the 32nd Street/Merryman's Lane crossing with its west face parallel to the north-south axis. Broache's Nov. 2, 1979 letter to fabricator Richard Carpenter of Annapolis (David Green's sub) fixed the colors, 2042 Victorian Blue background on all sides of the pan, 2016 Safety Orange letters, 2036 Safety Green trees, 2009 Black and 2029 Citron, and traded the text planned for the concrete for a Thoroglaze or Monocryl anti-graffiti coating, 'an even trade for the sign painting'; sign painter Wilson Pritchett of 1001 E 25th was recommended. The merchants first heard of it on Oct. 24 with 'dismay'. The contractor built the base about two feet off its specified location (Oct. 29) and moved it at his own risk; the coating went on without anyone being told (March 1980); painting it with anti-graffiti paint was still on the Dec. 1980 punch list, and by Feb. 1981 merchants were unbolting the tree grates nearby. summary: The Division of Tests (Lab No. 238-470, Joseph T. Meisel, Nov. 8, 1979) broke three Pine Hall/Pen-Mar pavers for Contract 2572: 8,770, 7,680 and 6,570 psi, average 7,670 against the ASTM C 902-79 Class SX minimum of 8,000 average and 7,000 individual; absorption 7.4% and saturation coefficient 0.76 passed. Hunter's worksheets put the shortfall at 4.2% and 6.2% and the abrasion index at .096 against .11; Pine Hall's Lee Tesh sent a 1978 Pittsburgh Testing report, but for facing brick. The brick was ordered Oct. 29, made Nov. 12 and delivered Nov. 19. In the field the grout failed repeatedly: 'not satisfied w/ grout, he is washing conc. out of it' (March 10, 1980), 'need a foreman to supervise brick laying', a field meeting, corrective work still undone April 21, redone by May 12. Joint sealant: Pecora Urexpan NR 200 substituted for Chem Calk 550 at no change, color #512 Buff (NR-200-341-1148), from Baltimore Sealing Co. By Dec. 1980 the punch list had sunken brick at 3117 and loose brick 'at various locations'; the two-year guarantee closed in Jan. 1983 with one paver replaced. City Archives BRG48-43-10-20, pages 0030, 0037, 0040, 0045, 0050, 0073, 0110-0118.

summary: A Sept. 26, 1979 note priced 'our brick scheme for rest of Waverly (including by church), exclusive of utility work' at $74,000; a take-off for the 2900-3000 blocks came to $71,650 (11,384 sq ft of walk, 1,802 sq ft of brick, 11 trees with grates at $515, one bench). Field markups of the 2900 and 3000 blocks: 328 and 205 ft of curb, 'no bench', 'move tree 2 ft south', a 15-ft driveway, the contact 'Schildwachter 467-4393'. Hurst-Rosche (David F. Paduch) filed sheets 38A-D and a new cross section on Oct. 30. Fahey's Jan. 18, 1980 letter extended the limits to Exeter Hall Avenue at bid prices; Mahoney answered Feb. 4 and 19 that 'the record rate of inflation' since the June 1979 bid required increases: maintenance of traffic $9,500, stakeout $1,500, asphalt $34 to $65 a ton, curb $13 to $15.75 a foot, sidewalk $2.65 to $3.35 a sq ft, tree grates $300 to $350, trees $215 to $270, brick paving $1.50 more a sq ft. Irvin Wyman's street-lighting section asked for care over the duct lines at the Greenmount and 29th corners (March 13). The Board of Estimates passed the negotiated prices April 2, Fahey authorized the work April 14, the original contract was substantially complete May 7 and the extension estimated done June 2, 1980. Councilwoman Clarke's June 2 request to carry the paving around onto 29th Street to the alley behind the lounge was declined by phone on June 10, 'budget considerations ... be diplomatic'. City Archives BRG48-43-10-20, pages 0038, 0059, 0070, 0080-0083, 0087, 0147-0149, 0155, 0162-0164, 0172.

summary: A month of paper over one driveway. Meeting 6's pencil note: 'Steve, call Bank, try to talk them into our scheme. Otherwise, as is, no new work!' Fahey's April 1, 1980 letter deleted the 7-inch concrete pavement at the existing driveway at station 13+11.75 right, serving the Maryland National Bank's drive-in window, for a 2-inch SN overlay; Mahoney quoted $435 the same day to break out and rebuild the concrete-encased structure in the bank's alley with a steel plate so the bank lost no time; Fahey ruled April 17 that the water-meter adjustment fell under bid item #509; on April 21 the area was re-examined and on May 5 the whole thing was dropped, existing driveway left intact. summary: Fahey's Nov. 24, 1980 letter listed the unresolved owner complaints (2911, 3319, 3433, cracked walks and unpainted walls on 31st and 32nd, a roof drain at 411 E 32nd); Mahoney answered Dec. 9. The conditional inspection of Dec. 18 (Fahey, C. Smith, M. Hellman, M. Griffith, Quilter, Mahoney, Amos) produced the Dec. 22 punch list: paint the pylon with anti-graffiti paint; mulch the tree pit at 429 31st; watch the brick patch at 414 31st; observe cracks at Greenmount and 29th, on 31st at the alley and at the NE corner of 33rd; raise the sunken brick at 3117; replace light-base tops at Greenmount and 32nd and on 31st; plug a hole in the walk at 3201; saw-cut and redo the driveway at Greenmount and Calvin; 52 guarantee trees by station. Guarantees ran two years on brick, benches and grates, one growing season on plantings, six months on the rest. On Feb. 17, 1981 Mahoney reported merchants 'removing the nuts and bolts that were holding the tree grates together' to clear trash beneath them. Final inspection June 17, 1981 (with Street Lighting, the City Forester and Sediment Control) accepted the job but extended maintenance on the heaved south-side walks of 31st and 32nd through winter 1981-82 to learn the cause of the 'upheaval'; the guarantee closed Jan. 25, 1983 after one paver was fixed. The Engineer's Certificate (Nov. 11, 1981): bid $538,182.25, as built $495,607.93, change orders 1-12 $160,807.44, utility additions $20,238, construction cost $676,653.37; 160 contract days plus 173 extension (25 complete close-down, 85 partial, 63 for change orders), 321 consumed, 12 days under, no liquidated damages. summary: Alvin Miller, chairman of the Waverly Design Committee, wrote Housing Commissioner Robert C. Embry Jr. on May 19, 1975 on Waverly Merchant's Association letterhead (3240 Greenmount, Adler's) after a May 2 meeting with Embry and Franz Vidor: the merchants had chosen Greenfield, Sommer & Associates of 1372 Broadway, New York, as their designers and asked the City to pay. The firm's May 5 offer: study 'the Waverly area (three to four blocks)' and Highlandtown, capped at $5,000 per district, $35 an hour for a principal. Embry's July 31, 1975 answer created the Neighborhood Commercial Revitalization (Self-Help) Program under coordinator Paul Gilbert: priority for areas with an urban renewal ordinance (East Lombard Street, South Baltimore), a 50-50 match up to $5,000 for others, and for Waverly a full-time City senior architect and, if merchant involvement held up, 'all due consideration in being designated as a priority area.' Gilbert sent the firm a draft contract Oct. 7, 1975; it answered Oct. 17 that the draft asked for more than its offer, and pencil notes on the back work the price down from $10,500 through $8,500 and $7,500 to $5,000 and rank rival firms (Land Design Research, Nelson-Salabes, Smith & Kirwin, Tennenbaum). City Archives BRG48-43-10-23, pages 0235-0244.

summary: Gilbert asked Planning on Jan. 14, 1976 to finish a Waverly parking study by March 31 (the study later published as the May 1976 'Shopping Survey and Parking Analysis'). At a Feb. 2, 1976 kickoff about 20 people heard Gilbert describe $3,000,000 for six commercial districts and call for an advisory committee of six residents and six merchants; Ruth Louie listed the surveys under way and the 33rd Street centerstrip was named a shared project. Grenville Whitman of 3133 Guilford Ave wrote Gilbert on March 2 about choosing the residents' side (Charles Kelly of Charles Village, Tony Marchanti of Waverly Blockbuilders, Philip Marcus of Abell; Ethel Day 'representing herself'), calling the Greater Waverly Community Council 'somewhat a legal fiction' and Waverly a place of 'little fiefdoms with egos to match', and bowed out. The Board of Estimates approved Contract 11088 with Greenfield, Sommer & Associates on March 24, 1976 ($5,000 in two halves, four months; district 29th to 35th Street between Barclay and Greenmount/Old York; storefronts on ten Greenmount block faces from 3000 to 3440 to 'relate and be harmonious'), with notice to proceed March 31. The first steering committee met March 22 at the Waverly Library: members admired the Victorian fronts of the vacant 'Oxford Shop' and Sweeney's, wanted 32nd Street one-way with angle parking, a pedestrian mall on Gorsuch, the 'ugly' merchants' lot's ownership checked, big overhead signs removed, and 'porno stores, too many' looked into. City Archives BRG48-43-10-23, pages 0182-0209, 0213-0214, 0233-0234, 0237.

summary: Arthur Greenfield's June 28, 1976 plan: close Venable Avenue for parking, clear the warehouse on the Old York/Tinges Lane triangle for a park, partial brick sidewalks, low street lighting, 'supergraphics', a sign ordinance, landscaping and signing the merchants' lot, one-way 32nd eastbound and 31st westbound with wider walks, a pedestrian mall on Gorsuch. Alvin Miller asked whether merchants could be made to pay for the brick; Gilbert said probably not legally. The minutes note 'two different groups' of merchants. Ruth Louie's July 2 report: big flashing signs on carry-outs, gas stations and bookstores made the area 'garish'; merchants wanted an all-way pedestrian 'Barnes Dance' at 33rd and Greenmount (Transit and Traffic refused); a 1970s Council bill to downzone parts of Greenmount had stalled. Gilbert convened the city's agency task force for a walking tour July 26; merchants pressed Sanitation (four 20-gallon cans per building), Police (double parking at the 32nd Street newsstand) and Traffic. On Aug. 9 Robert McGee of Off-Street Parking floated a municipal lot at about 5 cents an hour and the group put the money available at about $300,000. Gilbert's Aug. 16 notes on the consultant's draft: no projecting signs ('virtually all' merchants wanted that), no continuous canopy along Greenmount, ten block-face elevations. Greenfield Sommer was paid $5,000 in all (50 hours of Greenfield at $30 on the July invoice). City Archives BRG48-43-10-23, pages 0102-0106, 0113-0114, 0118, 0127-0132, 0137-0165.

summary: Gene Neff's March 23, 1976 memo called removing the utility poles at 33rd and Greenmount the 'first example' of rehabilitating the York Road corridor. On May 19 Embry asked Public Works to enlarge the median plaza at Greenmount and 33rd with kiosks, sculpture, special paving and lighting and drop the pyracantha hedge, offering commercial-district money; Public Works agreed June 3. Mike Sievers put the median at $80,000-85,000 against his $50,000-60,000; his July 27 plan (18-inch splash pan, 900 sq yd of sod, 600 'Lowboy' firethorn by Oct. 31) included two spots for the district signs. Three 'Waverly' identification signs, 6 by 3 feet, white on brown, were designed for brick piers at Old York Road and Barclay (Louie's Sept. 16 letter); by November they sat in the Sisson Street yard. The fall work cost $13,416.15 against $60,000. Gilbert asked the City's International Sculpture Symposium (Shot Tower, Sept.-Oct. 1976) for two pieces; Recreation and Parks said it could not direct the sculptors, and on Jan. 26, 1977 Sievers turned down the metal sculptures and urged ideas developed 'with the community and not for them.' A June 25, 1976 caller from City Hospitals had to be talked out of going to the Mayor, saying Planning had 'screwed it up'. Gilbert ordered the traffic-signal poles at Greenmount and 33rd, with bases adjusted for brick paving, on Aug. 22, 1977. City Archives BRG48-43-10-23, pages 0002, 0064, 0066-0067, 0096-0099, 0107-0112, 0134-0136, 0167-0173, 0212.

summary: Building Permit #687 was filed Aug. 5, 1976 to convert part of the Boulevard Theatre (owner The Grand Co., the Durkee company) into a carry-out restaurant for B.K. of Baltimore, Ltd. (1923 York Road, Timonium), $95,000, the rest to stay a theater. Phil Hoag of BK wrote Aug. 12 that he wanted a Burger King 'at Greenmont and 33rd' using the marquee for the two to two and a half years before the pending sign rules took effect. Paul Gilbert told the Permits office on Aug. 23 that the consultants recommended removing projecting signs and marquees and the merchants agreed, but that he had no legal basis to refuse: 'This type of development is the thrust of our program.' An Aluminum Weather Products sketch of Sept. 14, 1976 shows a renovated canopy and marquee with 4-by-12 aggregate panels. The revised permit (687R) was approved in April 1977 for interior work only, with no Burger King advertising on the marquee ('OK 3/31/77'). summary: Frank H. Durkee III sent a facade sketch in fall 1976; Gilbert rejected its aggregate panels and asked for the stone blocks repaired, the relief sculptures and cornices cleaned, earth tones, dark bronze trim and the billboards removed. The MTA could fit a bus shelter at 33rd and Brentwood only if the Donnelly Advertising billboard on the theater's side came down; Durkee agreed, and Councilwoman Clarke (who on June 30, 1976 had asked for a bench there, a major bus-transfer point) reported Nov. 5 that the shelter would come within two months. In April 1977 the MTA proposed moving the stop to the library side; Clarke and the neighborhood objected, and Gilbert's follow-up says Durkee again agreed to take down billboards so the shelter could stay by the big elm. Durkee's letter of April 27, 1977 backing the shelter says he planned to move the Boulevard's entrance to 33rd Street. City Archives BRG48-43-10-23, pages 0016-0020, 0042, 0077, 0088-0093, 0133.

summary: The March 22, 1976 steering committee asked the City to check the ownership and title of the 'ugly' merchants' lot. On Aug. 9, 1976 Robert McGee of the Off-Street Parking Commission floated a municipal lot at about 5 cents an hour; Alvin Miller urged an investigation of ownership. The Oct. 20, 1976 community leaders' meeting asked the City to take over, repave and meter it. An April 15, 1977 memo says the lot was 'under the cloud of much litigation' from an earlier hotel plan whose developer and mortgage company had reportedly gone bankrupt (Luck Dome and Fidelity); the City put the purchase in its FY 1978 capital budget and Off-Street Parking's lawyer Alan Blumberg was investigating. By April 1977 the plan was to buy, repave and meter it in FY 1979, offering the two houses on it first to their occupants; by June it had been appraised and the Law Department was sorting out its 'muddled' legal status. summary: Councilman Heintz introduced a bill for the Anti-Hotel Committee (3140 Abell Ave) to rezone the B-2-3 district between Southway, 29th Street, Old York Road and Barclay Street to B-2-2, B-2-1, R-5 and R-7: a neighborhood reaction to the twelve-story Luck Dome hotel planned on the parking-lot block. The draft carries no number; it is evidently Bill 1769 of March 17, 1975. On March 16, 1977 the Abell Improvement Association asked for 1769 to be revived, 'utterly opposed to the spector of a mini-downtown on our doorsteps'; Planning Director Larry Reich began a zoning study re-examining it (at Greater Homewood's Martin French's request), and on April 7 Councilwoman Clarke answered that the rezoning belonged in the urban renewal plan and should pass with it. A hand-marked 'Waverly Rezoning Proposal #1' shrinks B-2-3 to the core around 33rd Street. It became the 1977-78 downzoning fight and the four targeted rezonings of 1979. City Archives BRG48-43-10-23, pages 0004, 0046-0051, 0060.

summary: Planning's Oct. 5, 1976 memo questioned the approach: Waverly 'is not Mount Washington or Hampden'; 52% of shoppers walked in; restoring original storefronts was pointless where the originals were ugly (it cited the Red Shed's brash front as right for Greenmount); 'we're not in the area just to paint up.' The Abell Improvement Association (Philip Marcus, Oct. 12) asked to 'make Waverly a new Georgetown, not a new Block', ban flashing signs like Harley's and Polock Johnny's, stop the adult bookstore's open displays and the HIS Shop's loudspeakers. Oakenshawe proposed closing Merryman's Lane as a pedestrian shopping court. The Oct. 20 community leaders' meeting judged the $300,000 budget too small for real change and aimed it at low-cost items, with $2,000,000 named for a second phase; ideas included an outdoor cafe on a closed Gorsuch Avenue and moving the bookstore at Greenmount and 32nd behind the Exxon station. A Nov. 1 meeting with city officials produced the merchants' Christmas clean-up letter. City Archives BRG48-43-10-23, pages 0065-0074, 0084-0087.

summary: A letter in Stanley Adler's name typed in Gilbert's office sent the committee handwritten draft standards on Sept. 10, 1976: Formstone and aluminum siding removed within 24 months or painted, window signs no more than 20% of the glass, no rigid awnings, marquees on theaters only, no rooftop signs or billboards (five years to comply), no flashing signs except barber poles, HCD review of all plans; 'Waverly' in the title is written over correction fluid, so it was adapted from another district's list. The folder holds the model: the 'New Frankford' design guidelines for Frankford Avenue, Philadelphia (Cope Linder Walmsley), annotated by a Baltimore reader who checked continuous sign zones, the ban on projecting and box signs, a required address number on every storefront ('good'), full-facade supergraphics ('good') and keeping cornices. Nick Sheridan's March 15, 1977 memo proposed a paid organizer for the merchants, whose 'participation and trust have been low', and Ruth Louie's April 21 schedule set facade drawings and draft standards for May, a draft ordinance for June and the final ordinance for September 1977. City Archives BRG48-43-10-23, pages 0024-0041, 0052-0053, 0078-0080, 0177-0180.

summary: Nick Sheridan's notes of the April 6, 1977 meeting (Paige Rose of Abell, Charles Kelly of Charles Village, Joan Biegeleisen of upper Waverly, Grady Dorsett of Oakenshawe, and Greater Homewood's Leo Goichochea, Lyn Leight and John Lombardi) list 20 items: the median, tree planting, rezoning the business area to its present use, restoring original facades through a merchant design committee, bicycle-safe grates, and an unexplained 'Burger King'. Ruth Louie turned them into an action list April 20; Paul Gilbert answered point by point on June 7: the lot purchase was in the FY 1979 capital budget and had been appraised; sidewalk cleaning was 'entirely' the merchants' responsibility, so no City sidewalk vacuum; his priorities were the design standards and costing the public improvements; the median belonged to Mike Sievers. George Laurent of Baltimore Neighborhoods, Inc. had written Mayor Schaefer and the Sun on May 17 that 33rd and Greenmount showed new businesses and enlarged stores but was buried in trash; the Mayor's office sent it to Herman Katkow. summary: A 2003 mortgage on 3040 Greenmount describes the lot by pointing back to a deed from Mary S. Ruppersberger and others to George E. Zepp, dated October 15, 1937 and recorded in Liber SCL 5767, folio 252 (the 2003 typist spelled it 'Zapp'). George E. Zepp is the son who ran Geo. E. Zepp & Co., films, beside his father Simon's photo supply business, which had been at this address since about 1913. So this is the family business buying its own building after roughly 24 years there. The Ruppersbergers held 3036-3038 next door until 1975, so they probably owned this whole stretch of the west side. The lot is 56 feet 1 inch on Greenmount and 155 feet 3 inches deep, starting 112 feet 1 inch north of Vineyard Lane (formerly Gilmore Lane), with a half share of the ten-foot alley behind. Its north line is land that Thomas J. Wilson and other trustees leased to B.M. Cook (Liber BHA 67, folio 100). The 1937 deed itself has not been pulled; it is the next document to order.

This is the Baltimore way of selling: the buyers got the buildings, Forrest kept the ground and an income. He had done the same with 3046 three months earlier ($120 a year, December 1984). The buyers borrowed from Golden Prague Building, Loan and Savings Association (mortgage at SEB 465/476, three folios on; released 1993). The lease itself, and so the price, has not been pulled.

summary: Second partial purchase-money mortgage dated January 29, 1991 and recorded February 6, 1991 (Liber SEB 2749, folios 467-473). Darrell K. Carter, then of 726 Reservoir Street, borrowed $48,000 from Regal Savings Bank, F.S.B. of Owings Mills at 14.5 percent, $759.78 a month, due February 1, 2001. It paid for part of 938 North Calvert Street, which he bought the same day from Aaron Wolfson trading as Beowulf Realty, and sat behind a mortgage to Virginia Zeller (SEB 57/764). Cohen, 1989; $120) and 5212 St. Charles Avenue (from Lee Roy Carter, 1990; $65). By 1991 Darrell was a small landlord using the equity in one house to buy the next. Prepared by Dackman, Heyman & Dackman (Gordon B. Heyman); Stewart D. Sachs swore to the disbursement for Regal.

summary: Release of indemnity deed of trust dated May 14, 2019 (Liber MB 21139, folios 99-144). Paul W. and Amy S. Nochumowitz had pledged their Baltimore ground rents to Lexington National Bail Services (Ronald A. Frank, president) as collateral for bail bonds, by an indemnity deed of trust dated December 26, 2008 (Liber 11263, folio 329). Its 44-page Exhibit A lists roughly 1,600 ground rents by address, deed and annual rent. Page 21 lists 3036, 3038 and 3046 Greenmount together, bracketed by the clerk as Block 3856, each at $120 a year and each held under Liber 8354, folio 146, the deed the 3347 Greenmount chain dates to 1999. So Forrest's $240 rent on the combined lot had become two $120 rents, one per house, and the ground under 3036, 3038, 3046 and 3347, all Forrest's, went to the Nochumowitzes in one deed. The 2022-2025 deeds for 3038 still say $120 a year, due March 1 and September 1. Who holds it now is open: the 3046 and 3347 chains show a 2017 bulk deed from the Nochumowitzes to A&P LLC (Liber 19711/506).

summary: Release of indemnity deed of trust dated May 14, 2019 (Liber MB 21139, folios 99-144). Paul W. and Amy S. Nochumowitz had pledged their Baltimore ground rents to Lexington National Bail Services (Ronald A. Frank, president) as collateral for bail bonds, by an indemnity deed of trust dated December 26, 2008 (Liber 11263, folio 329). Its 44-page Exhibit A lists roughly 1,600 ground rents by address, deed and annual rent. Page 21 lists 3036, 3038 and 3046 Greenmount together as Block 3856, each at $120 a year, each held under Liber 8354, folio 146 (1999). Forrest's single $240 rent on 3036-3038 (1985) had been split into one $120 rent per house. The ground rents under 3046 and 3347 Greenmount, also Forrest's, came to the Nochumowitzes in the same deed. Who holds 3036's now is open; the Nochumowitzes sold a block of ground rents to A&P LLC in 2017 (Liber 19711/506).

summary: Deed dated January 13, 1873 and recorded January 15, 1873 (Baltimore County Liber E.H.A. No. 79, folios 37-38). Gustar Ruppersberger and Mary C. Ruppersberger, his wife, both of Baltimore County, conveyed to John Schuman of the same county, for $2,700, a lot in "the Village of Waverly" in Baltimore County: beginning at a post on the west side of the York Turnpike Road at a point North 4 degrees East 57 feet from the corner of the turnpike and Gilmor Lane; thence binding on the turnpike North 4 degrees East 28 feet 3 inches; thence North 85 1/2 degrees West 28 feet 6 inches more or less to a point North 5 1/2 degrees East 50 feet 9 inches from the northern side of Gilmor Lane; thence South 85 degrees East 157 feet 6 inches to the place of beginning. The deed states this is "the Southern half of the lot of ground which was conveyed to said Ruppersberger by David S. Wilms and others, Trustees," by deed dated January 8, 1873, recorded immediately before this one (729:mdlr-eha79-35-wilms-1873) -- Ruppersberger flipped it five days after taking title, for $2,700 against the $1,700 he had just paid for the whole lot. This confirms, with the primary source rather than only a later recital, the hypothesis this row previously carried as "probable": the frontage (57 to 85 feet 3 inches north of Gilmor/Vineyard Lane) matches the parcel the 1990-91 deeds for 3036-3038 except out of their description, and lines up with 3034 next door. Signed Gustar Ruppensberger and Mary C. Ruppensberger (both by seal); witnessed by Frank Lewis; acknowledged January 13, 1873 before Frank Lewis, J.P., Baltimore County; recorded per Edw. H. Ady, Clerk. That fits the Schumans staying on this lot for generations: George A. Schuman's soft-drink stand here in 1920 and George Shuman's restaurant in 1937.

summary: When Brown, Jones and Pettiford, Inc. bought 3036-3038 next door for $42,000 on May 20, 1993 (SEB 3688/480), the clerk's note for returning the deed reads 'Brown Jones & Pettiford, 3042 Greenmount, Balt Md 21218'. Peter and Grace Lee had owned 3040-3044 since September 1992, so the company was their tenant. By about October 1994 the Lees' company owned 3036-3038 as well, and until July 1998 they held every storefront from 3036 to 3044. Monica Ann Brown, who bought 3040-3044 from the Lees in 1998, then lived in Far Rockaway, New York; whether she is connected to the company is untested (its Maryland charter record would name its officers).

summary: Deed dated August 23, 1977 and recorded October 5, 1977 (Liber RHB 3529, folios 425-427). Metropolis Building Association (William B. Sawers, Jr., president) conveyed 3046 Greenmount to Irvin A. Forrest in fee simple for a stated $5. The taxes put the price near $14,000: state transfer tax $70 at half a percent, recordation $61.60 at $2.20 per $500. The deed explains the seller: The Waverly Building Association of Baltimore County became Waverly Savings and Loan Association, which merged into Metropolis Building Association (merger agreement of March 17, 1975, recorded in Harford County, HDC 968/449). So the Waverly thrift's own building of about 67 years was sold two years after the name disappeared. The lot is 16 feet 2 inches on Greenmount, beginning 168 feet 2 inches north of Vineyard Lane (formerly Gilmor's Lane) and running back 64.88 feet along the brick wall of the building to the north. The deed and Forrest's mortgage were both notarized by Anna M. Ozazewski, who witnessed Patapsco Federal's releases in 1984, so the closing was probably held at Patapsco.

summary: Lease dated December 1, 1984 and recorded December 20, 1984 (Liber SEB 387, folios 462-465). Irvin A. Forrest leased the lot to Cherlan Realty Corporation (Jonathan A. Azrael, president) for 99 years, renewable forever for a $1 fine, at $120 a year paid half-yearly from December 1, 1984. Forrest signed on November 21, 1984 before a Florida notary, so he had moved south by then. Cherlan was the lawyers' company (the papers came from Azrael, Gann and Franz, 401 Washington Avenue, Towson) and held the lease for a minute: its assignment to the real buyers was recorded right after. This is how a Baltimore owner turned a building into a ground rent: lease it to a straw, have the straw sell the leasehold, keep the rent. Forrest did the same to 3036-3038 three months later.

summary: Deed dated October 27, 1909 and recorded October 29, 1909 (Liber SCL 2537, folios 193-194), for a nominal $1. Matilda W. Sanger, a widow of New Jersey, conveyed to The Waverly Amusement Company two lots on the east side of 'the York Turnpike Road (now called Greenmount Avenue)' south of Gorsuch Avenue. The first lot begins 102 feet 7 inches south of Gorsuch, runs 78 feet 6 1/2 inches along the turnpike and through to the west side of the Old York Road; every later deed of 3211 starts from this description. The second is a 23-foot lot 201 feet south of Gorsuch. Sanger had put neighbouring lots on ground leases between 1889 and 1895 (to John T. Hickman, John N. C. Deal, William J. Fink and Charles W. Kramer), and those reversions came with the sale. The company gave her a $3,000 purchase-money mortgage the same week. This is the founding purchase of the Waverly Theatre, which opened that year.

summary: Deed and agreement dated July 14, 1927 (Liber SCL 4803, folios 101-104). Leah Schloss, widow, owner of 3207 and 3209 Greenmount, and The Crystal Amusement Company (P. Oletsky, president), owner of 3211, settled two rights between the buildings. It recites that 3211 and its rear to Old York Road were 'used ... as a moving Picture Theatre', with the auditorium on the rear portion behind 3207-3209, and that the theatre had been venting 'permissively' through the northeast corner of 3209. Crystal got the right to keep that ventilator 'so long as' 3211 stayed a movie theatre. Schloss, about to build 'a building that is to be higher than the structures at present existing', got a permanent party-wall right, which dates a rebuild of 3207-3209 to about 1927-28. The Rosenheim estate executors and other mortgagees consented; four mortgages on 3211 are listed. Two of their liber numbers do not fit their dates as typed. It cites Schloss's 1923 deed as SCL 4083/155; the deed itself is recorded at SCL 4082/155-156, so the agreement's copyist was one volume off.

summary: Deed and agreement dated July 14, 1927 (Liber SCL 4803, folios 101-104). Leah Schloss, who had bought 3207 and 3209 from The Crystal Amusement Company in 1923, was about to put up a taller building there. It describes her lot as 34 feet 4 inches on Greenmount beginning 128 feet 11 1/4 inches south of Gorsuch Avenue, 90 feet 7 inches deep, and says the theatre's auditorium ran behind it. So the present 3207-3209 building dates from about 1927-28.

summary: Deed dated May 18, 1993 and recorded June 30, 1993 at 10:39 a.m. (Liber SEB 3755, folios 235-239). Gerald M. Rashbaum and Frances Kessler, as beneficiaries of Samuel Rashbaum's 1976 trust (SEB 1211/555), conveyed both corners to Arkay Properties, Inc., a Maryland corporation: 3100-3104 Greenmount with 422-426 East 31st (tax ID 12-20-3881-010) and 3048 Greenmount with 421-429 East 31st (12-20-3856-013). The stated consideration is zero. An affidavit signed by Ralph Frier says the recordation and transfer taxes were paid on 1.5 times the assessed value, $235,140; the city transfer tax was $3,527.10, 1.5 percent of that. So the $235,140 in the state's sales data is a tax base, not a price. It recites a deed of the same date, recorded just before it, from the two as trustees to themselves as beneficiaries, so the trust had ended, which means Samuel Rashbaum had died, probably by 1987 when the trust was re-recorded. A no-money transfer into a corporation usually means the family's own company; the name Arkay may be the initials R. K. (Frances signed 'Frances R. Kessler'), but the deed does not say who owned it. Witnessed by S. Leonard Sollins, of the firm that drew the 1976 trust; prepared by Lisa D. Eidelberg; returned to Executive Title Group, 8 Reservoir Circle. Folio 240 of the file is an unrelated trustee's deed. Arkay kept 3048 until the city sold it for unpaid taxes in 2009.

summary: Confirmatory deed dated October 30, 1997 and recorded September 30, 1998 (Liber PMB 7723, folios 329-334, nearly a year after signing). Arkay Properties, Inc., by Gerald M. summary: Deed of trust, assignment of rents and security agreement and fixture filing dated March 25, 2022 and recorded July 26, 2022 (Liber MB 24862, folios 392-414). Waverly Arts LLC (Jacob Wittenberg, manager) borrowed $2,000,000 from Standard Insurance Company, an Oregon corporation, secured on Waverly Hall (12-200-3881-010); trustee Old Republic National Title Insurance Company. The refinance affidavit states this loan paid off the March 2021 Reinvestment Fund indemnity deed of trust (MB 22898/346), whose unpaid balance was $1,475,288.67, exactly a year into that loan's term. So the March 2021 guaranty of Waverly Arts II's $1.5 million loan was not simply repaid: Waverly Arts refinanced with its own $2,000,000 loan directly from an institutional lender, more than doubling the debt secured on the building. The note's rate, term and maturity are not given in this instrument. Signed the same day as the refinance affidavit (April 1, 2022, notarized), though the deed of trust itself is dated March 25; recording did not happen until nearly four months later. Prepared by Lawyers Express Title, LLC, Lutherville; the loan is SIC No. C2011903.

summary: Deed dated January 8, 1873 and recorded January 15, 1873 (Baltimore County Liber E.H.A. No. 79, folios 35-37; this was county ground until the 1888 annexation). David S. Wilms, Thomas J. Wilms and Henry R. Wilms, Trustees under the last will and testament of James Wilms, late of Baltimore City, deceased (will dated January 22, 1848, proven and recorded in the Baltimore City Register of Wills), conveyed a lot to Gustar Ruppersberger of Baltimore County. The deed recites that the will gave the trustees full power to sell any of the estate's property; that a chancery bill, William C. Wilms and others v. said trustees and others, was filed in the Circuit Court for Baltimore City over division of the estate; that under a sales plat the trustees filed in that case, they sold "Lot No. 3" at private sale on January 27, 1871 to Ruppersberger for $1,700; and that the court duly ratified and confirmed the sale (with others made at the same time) before the purchase money was paid in full. The lot: situate in Baltimore County in "the Village of Huntingdon or Waverly," beginning at a post on the west side of the York Turnpike Road at a point North 4 degrees East 57 feet from the corner of the turnpike and Gilmor Lane (later Vineyard Lane); thence binding on the turnpike North 4 degrees East 56 feet 6 inches; thence North 85 degrees West, binding on Lot No. 4 of the same plat, 155 feet 3 inches; thence South 5 1/2 degrees West 57 feet to a point 50 feet 9 inches north of Gilmor Lane; thence South 85 degrees East 157 feet 6 inches back to the beginning. Five days later Ruppersberger split the lot and sold the southern half (28 feet 3 inches of the 56 feet 6 inch frontage) to John Schuman for $2,700 -- more than he had just paid for the whole lot, on half the land (729:mdlr-eha79-35-schuman-1873). Signed D. S. Wilms, Thos. J. Wilms and Henry R. Wilms, Trustees, each under seal; acknowledged January 8, 1873 before John I. Maddox, J.P., City of Baltimore; certified by George Robinson, Clerk of the Superior Court of Baltimore City; recorded per Edw. H. Ady, Clerk. Research lead: the trustees' 1871 sales plat evidently numbered at least four lots (No. 3 sold to Ruppersberger, No. 4 adjoining it to the north) along this stretch of the York Turnpike -- worth locating the full chancery case file or plat to see whether Lots 1, 2, 4 and beyond line up with other Corridor parcels on this block. Update Oct. 12, 2026: 'Wilms' here is the clerk's spelling of Wilson. The trustees' deed to John Bolgiano of Jan. 14, 1871 (Baltimore County E.H.A. 70/115-118, scan on file with 3326 Greenmount, mdlandrec-eha70-115) names the same three trustees, David S., Thomas J. and Henry R. Wilson, under the same will of James Wilson dated Jan. 22, 1848 (Register of Wills D.M.P. 24/154), and recites the same Circuit Court for Baltimore City case, William C. Wilson and others against the trustees (decree of Oct. 7, 1869, reports ratified Jan. 7, 1870). Both deeds sell numbered lots on a plat (Lots 16 and 17 there, Lot No. 3 here); neither says whether it is the same plat.

summary: Two same-day instruments, Baltimore County Liber E.H.A. No. 65, folios 405-408 (recorded March 11, 1870): (1) a deed, David S. Wilson, Thomas J. Wilson and Henry R. Wilson, Trustees, to the President, Managers and Company of the Baltimore and Yorktown Turnpike Road, of a lot on the west side of the York Turnpike Road "a short distance north of the present first toll gate"; (2) a $3,000 bond from the Turnpike Company to the Huntingdon Land Company of Waverly, reciting that the Turnpike Company has sold this same lot to Huntingdon Land Co. for $1,500 (due October 1, 1870) and binding itself to convey the fee once paid. The bond describes the lot by the same metes and bounds as the trustees' deed, and adds: "on which piece of ground moreover is now building a public hall erected by the aforesaid Huntingdon Land Company of Waverly." That pushes the start of construction to early 1870 at the latest, earlier than "1872-73," the date this chain had carried until now. David S., Thomas J. and Henry R. -- the same three first names and initials, trustees for an estate settling multiple lots along the York Turnpike in Waverly at almost the same moment -- also sold "Lot No. 3" a few blocks south to Gustar Ruppersberger in 1871-73 (EHA 79/35, property 729), acknowledged and recorded by the same clerk, Edward H. Ady. That deed spells the surname "Wilms"; this one spells it "Wilson." The surname is spelled 'Wilson' in this deed and 'Wilms' in the 1873 deed, and it is now confirmed to be one set of men: the trustees' deed to John Bolgiano of Jan. 14, 1871 (Baltimore County E.H.A. 70/115-118, scan on file with 3326 Greenmount, mdlandrec-eha70-115) names David S., Thomas J. and Henry R. Wilson as trustees under the will of James Wilson dated Jan. 22, 1848, and the 1873 deed (729) recites the same will and the same Circuit Court case. This deed does not itself recite the will, so that these 1870 grantors are those trustees rests on the names, the county and the year, not on a recital.

summary: Assignment dated March 1, 1870, recorded March 11, 1870 (Baltimore County Liber E.H.A. No. 65, folios 408-409). summary: The North Greenmount credit union in the 400 block of E. 31st St. was found insolvent and closed in July 1987. The National Credit Union Administration expected to pay its 800 depositors in full by Aug. 10 (about $1.364 million in deposits). NCUA liquidation director Anthony LaCreta said it had been started eight years earlier (1979) on a federal loan of $100,000 or $200,000 that was never fully repaid, was awash in bad loans with delinquencies approaching 60 percent, and suffered from weak collections and the neighborhood's depressed economy; it was one of several government-created inner-city credit unions, many of which had failed. A 1982 Sun story compared it with the Matanuska Valley credit union in Alaska (Sun June 27, 1982 p.24, image 225707804). Source: The Evening Sun, July 16, 1987, p.58 (also EvSun July 17, 1987 p.51, image 372521086; Carroll County Times July 17, 1987, image 869145845).

summary: Contributing building in the historic district listed December 31, 2013. Originally 2-story town hall built in 1873, ca. 1910 divided into multiple commercial spaces with entrances on E. 31 st St. and Greenmount Avenue, 1-story rear addition built ca. 1920, 1-story addition on north side built ca. 1950, windows infilled and storefront altered ca. 1970. This white Georgian-style brick building with some green trim celebrated its centennial in 1973 by commemoration of the Maryland State Senate. It is known historically as the Waverly Town Hall. This building was historically used as the Waverly Post Office ( 1928) and later Mildred Mae Wonneman' s beauty shop ( 193 7). A portion of this building was historically addressed as 3102 Greenmount Avenue and was apartments and Seward's Drug Store in 1928 and later a plumber's shop, a hat cleaner, and a dentist's office in 1937. In 1936, an addition was made onto the back (west side) of the building that is addressed 422-428 East 31 st Street.

These were replaced with three newer plain windows. The first floor use to feature a center doorway with a large ornate arch with two widows on either side, but those details are now covered by the front additions that are north side Tavern and small store front. This building was historically used as the Waverly Post Office ( 1928) and later Mildred Mae Wonneman' s beauty shop ( 193 7). summary: The correct 1928 Sanborn plate is Baltimore Vol. 7 (odd/east-side volume), sheet 735 (address range 3001-3133 per that volume's own printed street index). It shows the 'Tin Shop' building at 3011/1003 as the southernmost built structure on the block; the stretch below it, from 3009 down through 3001 (encompassing 3005/3007) to Vinyard Lane and E. 30th St, is blank -- no building outline of any kind. The 1915-era upholsterer/hay-and-feed building (see 717:sanborn-1915-sheet711-uphol-hayfeed) was gone by this date, and nothing had replaced it. This directly explains why the parcel's next documented building dates to ca. 1958 (per NPS B-5229 and SDAT): the ground sat vacant for roughly three decades in between.

summary: On the same sheet 735, the 'Tin Shop' building immediately north of the vacant 3001-3009 stretch is printed with two numbers stacked together: '3011' (the modern Greenmount number) over '1003' (an old number). summary: The Sun, April 7, 1912, 'To Face Cutting Charge.': Robert Appleby, 19 years old, of 3340 Greenmount avenue, was released on his own recognizance for a further hearing by Justice Llewellyn of the Northeastern Police Station, on the charge of cutting George Geilfus, 17, of 1826 Aisquith Street, in a fight on Hope Street near North Avenue on a Friday evening. A witness said Appleby had called on Miss Dora Staples on Hope Street and that some young men held him up as he left, which led to the fight. In 1912 the number 3340 was not on the ground of today's 3334-3338. The 1915 Sanborn (Vol. 7 sheet 716) prints '3340 / 1140' on a 2-story frame dwelling on the west side about 27 to 78 ft north of 33rd Street, the lot on which the Boulevard Theatre (3302 Greenmount) was built in 1921, and Polk prints 'Appleby Elsworth, h 3340 Greenmt av' in 1913 and a laborer, 'Apple John', at 'h 3340 York rd' in 1912. So the Applebys of 1912 lived in the 1140 York Road house, south of Venable Avenue (the lot match is measured from the plate, not surveyed).

The one fish dealer the directories put on that block is Eugene L. That the Waverly Fish Market was Carroll's store is possible, not established: his number in 1914 was 3344, not 3336.

O'Keefe said Greenmount would be resurfaced there the next year. New curbs and walks on Greenmount from 29th to 35th, on 33rd from Brentwood to Greenmount and the 33rd Street median were to start by fall 1978; 31st and 32nd would be let with them if time allowed, or else with the rehabilitation of the parking lot at Barclay and 32nd. Surveys was mapping Greenmount from 29th to 31st and would survey the lot once the owner gave permission. Two days later DHCD put $1,000 on work order 127287 for consulting-engineer monitoring of Waverly and West Baltimore Street, and a March 31 phone note from Bill Smith of Hurst-Rosche had sketched the schedule: 2 1/2 to 3 months of design and about six weeks of reviews. summary: After a Jan. 5, 1978 scoping meeting, William K. Smith, P.E., office manager of Hurst-Rosche Engineers (2323 York Road, Timonium), sent DHCD commissioner M. J. Brodie a proposal on Jan. 23 for a cost-plus-fixed-fee design contract of $67,142. Waverly had three items: curb and sidewalk replacement on Greenmount and 33rd ($6,342 of salary), street reconstruction of 31st and 32nd ($5,870) and the parking lot ($4,830), in two sets of contract documents, streets and lot. West Baltimore Street had street reconstruction ($8,452) and a parking lot ($4,116). Salaries of $29,610 were doubled for overhead to $59,220, which is the base figure of Contract 11821, plus a 10 percent fee ($5,922), $800 of principals' time and $1,200 of direct costs. The rates were $13.50 an hour for a project manager, $10.50 for a senior engineer, $7.50 for an engineer, $7.00 for a technician and $5.50 for a senior draftsman. HCD was to supply the tree, paving and lighting details, the city's Survey Division the surveys, and Hurst-Rosche would study extending the work on Greenmount to 29th Street and on the 1300 block of West Baltimore Street. DHCD's pen notes on the file read 'Sept. as earliest date', '5 1/2-6% tops' and 'man hours per sheet 30 max'. The 11-page breakdown survives in two annotated copies. City Archives BRG48-43-10-25, pages 0015-0038.

summary: DHCD's Feb. 1, 1978 notes with Bill Smith of Hurst-Rosche set the Waverly scope (curbs and walks from 35th to Old York Road, 33rd from Greenmount to Brentwood, regrading and wider walks) and a May 1 date for DHCD's preliminary tree and paving plans. At the April 26 design meeting at HCD (Paul Gilbert, David Hunter and Stephen Broache for HCD, David Paduch and William Smith for Hurst-Rosche), the group agreed to meet Transit and Traffic and the Bureau of Engineering about narrowing 31st and 32nd Streets, to survey Greenmount from 29th to 31st and the parking lot at 32nd and Barclay through Joe Melocik of Surveys and Records, and to have Hunter lay out trees and lights once utility prints arrived, with Irv Wyman on lighting. The plan was to advertise in late summer and do only the Greenmount sidewalks in 1978, with 31st and 32nd following in spring 1979, 'so that the commercial area would not be torn up during the holiday season'. The lot would probably be its own contract, and West Baltimore Street might grow to the 1300 to 1500 blocks. Hurst-Rosche took home the 33rd Street median plans to fold into the Greenmount drawings. summary: The July 6, 1978 'Waverly Estimate' put Greenmount and 33rd at $328,488 (say $350,000): stripping, widening, curbs, $198,902 of sidewalk, utility adjustments, 34 trash receptacles, 12 benches and 40 trees with grates at $700 each; the 33rd Street median at an estimated $80,000; and 31st and 32nd Streets at $118,521 (say $140,000). All-concrete walks would have saved $52,290. Quantity takeoffs by plan sheet counted 56,882 square feet of sidewalk and 5,376 feet of curb on Greenmount, 16 trees each on 31st and 32nd, and a separate $51,975 estimate for rebuilding 32nd Street. The revised estimate of Nov. 3, 1978, for the project from Vineyard Lane to 175 feet south of 35th Street, came to $261,090 for 33rd and Greenmount (including $31,000 of traffic signals), $127,521 for 31st and 32nd, and $100,000 for 20 street lights at $3,000, traffic maintenance and stakeout: $488,611, or $537,472 with a 10 percent contingency, plus $49,000 already spent on the median. That $537,472 is within $710 of Mahoney Brothers' winning bid of $538,182.25 the following June. The file also holds Hurst-Rosche's list of 'latest prices', from $2.30 a square foot for 5-inch sidewalk to $11.00 a foot for curb and gutter. summary: The typed special provisions for Contract 2572, dated April 17, 1979 and marked up by hand, name the streetscape's materials. The brick pavers are Watsontown Brick's 'Highlandtown Red', from Saco Supply in Timonium, laid in Flamingo colored mortar. The tree grates are Neenah Foundry R-8640 48-inch cast iron, painted Rust-Oleum flat black (local supplier Budeke's Paints, 418 S. Broadway). The benches are Victor Stanley redwood model CR-18, 'as modified' for the city's Washington Hill park lot. Double-leaf sidewalk cellar doors were to be Inryco steel, and the planting spec called for licorice-root mulch and banned topsoil from the Patapsco River Valley. The provisions were adapted from Highlandtown's commercial-revitalization job: a crossed-out table of cellar doors still lists 500-509 Conkling Street and 3520 Eastern Avenue, and water-meter items are struck through in red. A handwritten clause of the same date let the Engineer stop any phase of work to limit disruption to businesses and required a 4-foot walkway to every storefront; Vernon Fahey was to check its wording. City Archives BRG48-43-10-31, pages 0003-0021.

summary: The WAVERLY sign pylon was sited on the north side of East 32nd Street between Brentwood Avenue and Greenmount, where Merryman's Lane cuts in, as a three-faced steel sign on a 2-foot round concrete column (cast in a 24-inch Sonoco Sonotube) whose shaft was wrapped in repeating 'NEWS' lettering. A 1975 Claude Neon Signs drawing of the 'Jack's Corned Beef Pylon' (drawing 75346) is in the file as a model. On May 1, 1979 Patricia Massey and Steve Broache sent the design to Commissioner M. J. Brodie, who wrote back 'Too high, too fat!'; on May 4 Massey asked whether the sign should be concrete, noting 'we're trying to keep sign at same level as bldgs', and Brodie answered 'Both, try another sketch'. On May 9 the revisions went to Hurst-Rosche: the diameter cut to 1 foot 8 inches and the column lowered from 10 feet to 8, with painted letters. The paint was Tnemec (Hi-Build Epoxoline and Endura-Shield). The Fire Department, Water, Transit and Traffic and BG&E cleared the site in April. Only a color study survives in blue with orange lettering. The 'NEWSNEWS' shaft graphic was later removed on site after merchants objected in October 1979. City Archives BRG48-43-10-31, pages 0002, 0024-0031, 0056, 0066-0077, 0081-0082, 0094-0097.

summary: HCD's red 'Waverly Logo' folder holds about 30 design studies in pencil, marker and ink, none signed or dated. Three families appear. The tree-row wordmark that became the district's mark (WAVERLY in a rounded geometric letter above a row of round-canopy trees) survives as a black master, blue and orange color studies and letter-construction sheets. An 'avenue of trees' version sets a serif WAVERLY under two rows of trees receding to a vanishing point (purple-black and green marker). A slanted 'stadium' version turns the final letter into Memorial Stadium's horseshoe, with trees and a crossroads slash; one quick sketch labels its ends '33rd' and 'Stadium', and another hand-letters GREENMOUNT above WAVERLY. A handwritten brainstorm list of themes (the median, the stadium, the crossroads of York Road and Greenmount, the Boulevard Theatre, 'melting pot', 'old and new') sits with them. The tree-row mark went on the 1978 merchants' newsletter, the Waverly Weekend flyer and the 32nd Street pylon. City Archives BRG48-43-10-26 (the 'Waverly Logo' file), pages 02-03, 05-09, 12-22, 24-40.

Marcantoni & Sons about $125,326, B.A.P.C. $133,639, Salco $147,609, a Robbins and Schweizer (?) firm $148,648, Mahoney Brothers (the streetscape contractor) $150,298, then Flanigan, Benhoff (?), Flintkote, and Potts and Callahan at $194,145. summary: Until 1921 the whole south end of the 2500 block's east side was one tract, the Knobloch family estate. The buyer split it in two and held the northern parcel, where the mansion had stood, until the 1930s. The Food Fair Company, one of the first self-service grocery chains in Baltimore, then bought it and on October 31, 1935 opened a one-story grocery that ran until about 1959. summary: About 1883 Waverly coal merchant and developer Augustus D. Clemens, Sr. (1818-1897) added to the north side of his porticoed frame house a two-story-and-mansard High Victorian frame residence for his daughter Mary and her new husband Jacob H. Aull (1848-1921). After Clemens' death the two houses became one, and the Aulls lived there, despite the Belt Railroad's encroachment to the north in the early 1890s, until 1912, when they moved to Govans. The Sun of May 30, 1912 reported the Baltimore Union Benevolent Association had acquired the Aull home and its acre of grounds as a home for girls. During the First World War the house went to a nursing establishment, 'The Southern Hospital and Home', which added a north wing; the address was renumbered to 2520-2528 in the interim. Its last directory listing, in 1961, was as the 'Silver Cross Home and Hospital'. The nineteenth-century buildings were probably demolished soon after and eventually replaced by the one-story brick church on the site in 2012. Corridor's city-directory rows carry the earlier numbering, 2510-2512.

summary: The Passano-O'Neill card for 3014 Greenmount (citing Aull's Old Land Marks, pages 46-47) describes the site as a rambling frame 'country seat' built around the end of the Civil War by the seedsman Abram G. Mott as a retreat from his business near Belair Market. At his death the property was taken over by the Waverly dairyman Michael F. O'Neill, who gradually covered the grounds with stables that became garages as he moved into auto repair. The house survived into at least the early 1950s and was replaced by the present one-story commercial row. Mott died on October 3, 1895, at his home, 918 York road, aged about 85 (Baltimore Sun, October 4, 1895, p. 10), so he was born about 1810; the card's dates for him (c1820-1897) are wrong at both ends. The O'Neill house was 920 York road from 1899, and which lot Mott's 918 was is contested. The commercial row went up bay by bay, about 1954 to 1958.

summary: There were several sites for the first, or Waverly, tollgate of the Baltimore & York Turnpike Company. The earliest was apparently the northwest corner of Greenmount Avenue and Merryman's Lane; sold derelict to the Huntingdon Company in 1869, it became the site of Waverly Hall. In 1870 the turnpike company apparently bought the building on the northwest corner of Greenmount and Gilmor's Lane (now Vineyard Lane) as its replacement. Hollifield describes that house as built in the 1770s, long and low with a porch across the front and many small rooms, earlier a country store, a recruiting station in the Mexican and Civil Wars, and a hospital for Union soldiers with fevers; it served as the gatekeeper's house until the tollgate was removed in 1894, stood vacant a long time, then was a private residence. Because it extended into the road, residents asked for its removal in 1900 and sent a delegation to the United Railways & Electric Company, which controlled the turnpike; nothing was done until the road was paved northward in 1907 and the house was torn down. The card notes the surviving photograph is hard to square with the description.

summary: Suburban communities of the nineteenth century considered a meeting place central to their identity. In 1869 the Huntingdon Company, early developers of the neighborhood now called Waverly, bought this land for such a hall, which opened in 1872. The two-story brick building held shops on the ground floor, whose rent paid the taxes, and a lofty public hall on the second story for lectures and public meetings; Hampden had a similar hall at 3551-3553 Roland Avenue, since converted to apartments. 'Waverly Hall' last appeared as such in the 1923 city directory, after which the auditorium was apparently divided into apartments. In 2012 the building became a registered Baltimore City historic landmark as 'Waverly Town Hall'.

summary: Waverly, like every Baltimore County community, was on its own for firefighting and protected only by volunteers long after the city organized a paid force in 1859. In time the county helped: a firehouse was built on this site and a 'chemical engine' (the county's fourth) stationed in it; the Sun of May 18, 1882 covered the county fire department's parade celebrating the opening. When the city annexed Waverly in 1888 it inherited the two-story firehouse, the chemical engine and its men, and the Waverly Volunteers, who became the city's Hook & Ladder Company No. 7. In 1901 the chemical engine company was merged into the hook and ladder company and a larger firehouse built for it on the old site. When the city's hook and ladder companies were restyled truck companies in 1908, H&L No. 7 became Truck No. 7, and it kept watch over Waverly until the station was closed for economy.

summary: The lot was still vacant when the Waverly Amusement Company bought it in late 1909 and put up a classic early movie theater: a shallow brick structure entered through a rounded archway with the theater's name in the brickwork over the door. In 1920 it was sold to the Crystal Amusement Company of Benjamin Cluster, who ran several east Baltimore theaters; he turned the original building into the lobby of a much larger 750-seat auditorium built to its east. The Durkee chain acquired the Waverly in 1929, replaced Cluster's square marquee with a triangular one, removed the old vertical sign, and showed movies until 1969. It was then a Goodwill store for about a decade, and since the early 1980s, shorn of its marquee but otherwise in excellent shape, a Shoe City shoe store.

summary: Probably a small grocery serving Waverly at first, the building was absorbed about 1919 into the Knobloch Bros. grocery chain, an east Baltimore operation that seems to have sold out entirely to A&P about 1929; A&P kept a store here until 1937. In 1938 Louis Rabai (died 1957) bought the building, gave it a fresh Art Deco facade and made it Rabai's Bakery. Its spot beside the Waverly Theater must have helped, because Rabai sold it to another baker shortly before his death: from 1956 the directories list Burri's French Bakery, through 1978. The Waverly closed in 1969, but the shop became the Butter Crisp Bakery in 1979 and stayed one through the 1988 directory. Then its luck as a bakery ran out and it became Blackstone Menswear, still there in 2007. Corridor's own rows place Rabai's founding in the 1920s and at 3205 in 1936, before this Art Deco store.

summary: By 1877 Baltimore County had one of its rare public schools on this site for the village of Waverly. When 'The Belt' passed to the city in 1888 the brick schoolhouse became 'Annex School #2', and the Board of Commissioners of Public Schools complained from the outset: four teachers and their classes were housed in the basement of a church two squares away (the 60th annual report, 1889; the card identifies it as Waverly Hall), two teachers shared one room (61st), several classes sat in rented rooms in the neighborhood (62nd). Revived in the mid-1890s, the 67th report chose overcrowding over 'small, badly-lighted, heated and ventilated rooms' for rent, the 68th repeated the 62nd word for word, and the 69th and 70th (the last to consider buildings individually) asked for an enlarged main building at 'Gilmore Lane, near York Road'. Nothing much was done beyond renaming it Public School No. 51 in the 1900 reorganization, until it was demolished about 1911 for the eastward extension of 33rd Street from Charles Street. The school then got a new building at 800 East 34th Street, and the Greenmount site was developed with the stores standing there in 2010.

summary: In 1808 Baltimore County gave the route to York, Pennsylvania to the new Baltimore & York-Town Turnpike Company. In 1860 the General Assembly chartered a 'Baltimore and Towsontown Railroad Company' and let the turnpike host its tracks; lawyers agreed 'railroad' need not mean steam, and in spring 1863 track was laid from City Hall to the Towson courthouse for what was really an interurban horsecar line. Northbound, the Greenmount route met two hills, North Avenue to 29th Street and 35th to 43rd, so fresh teams were supplied at stops just south of each incline, with stables at Greenmount and Lafayette and at Greenmount and 35th for the horses and the 'hill boys' who tended them. The Union Passenger Railway bought the line in 1891, was absorbed in 1892 into the City & Suburban Railway, and on April 2, 1893 the first electric trolley reached Towson. The company sold its horses and its southern hill station and made the Waverly one a storage site for extra cars and equipment, until a major fire destroyed it in January 1906. United Railways & Electric, its successor, built the replacement car barn at 4341-4345 York Road instead, and the Waverly site was sold and quickly covered with the line of two-story pressed-brick rowhouses still there in 2012.

summary: A second set of cards on the same corner follows the transit companies. From 1863 to 1891 the Baltimore & Towsontown Turnpike Railway ran horsecars along Greenmount and York Road between the county courthouse and City Hall, keeping a stable for changing teams at the top of the hill dividing Waverly from Govans and eventually connecting at 31st Street with the Baltimore, Peabody Heights & Waverly Railroad. In 1891 financier Nelson Perrin's Baltimore Union Passenger Railway bought it; in 1892 he combined his lines into the heavily capitalized City & Suburban Railway and decreed total electrification, starting with York Road, choosing to build the new depot and repair shops in Waverly rather than Govans. Perrin merged City & Suburban with the Baltimore Traction Company in June 1897 to form Baltimore Consolidated, and in January 1899 with City Passenger Railway to create the United Railways and Electric Company (he quit as president in 1900). The nearly new Waverly carhouse survived the mergers, but on January 10, 1906 it was the last of a series of carhouse fires: with York Road in poor condition and hydrants frozen, the fire department was slow, and the company lost the building and 56 cars, destroyed or unsalvageable. Land values in Waverly had soared, so United sold the site to developers, who quickly built the rowhouses facing 35th Street and York Road; the new carhouse went up at 4341-4345 York Road.

summary: An advertisement transcribed on the card: 'Dr. Dyck has opened Waverly Hall for the reception of a selected number of persons afflicted with Insanity, Imbecility and Nervous Disorders. Waverly Hall is about four miles from Baltimore on the York Turnpike and has a farm of 100 acres attached affording the means of pleasant recreation in the midst of retirement.' summary: Eighteen cards on the estate that gave Vineyard Lane its name, on the northwest side of the lane between 28th and 29th Streets. In 1802 William Gilmor (1775-1829) bought a two-story brick house and 17 acres from Charles S.P. Wante, who apparently built it. John and Hugh Findlay painted the house onto chair medallions about 1805; Dr. J. Hall Pleasants described that image as a plain two-story hipped-roof house with a two-column portico, and argued it could not be the three-story house with wings and a set-in loggia known in his day as the Holmes-Whiteley house, so there may have been two 'Vineyards'. William B. Marye wrote that the estate stayed with Gilmor's family and was acquired between 1852 and 1857 by William Stevens Whiteley (1826-1910), whose grandson said Whiteley added the third floor, the wings and the greenhouses; Dr. R.R. Beirne believed three generations of Whiteleys grew up there. The card's author suggests the Ross mansion at 325-343 East 30th was an expansion of Gilmor's original house, Gilmor's widow Marian having sold most of the estate to Samuel Brady in the 1840s and her heirs the house to Charles H. Ross. The Holmes-Whiteley 'Vineyard', last of the country seats on Vineyard Lane, stood as 300 East 29th Street until 1958, when it was demolished for the Barclay Elementary School.

summary: A sepia photograph of a two-story frame house with a deep columned porch, rocking chairs, louvered shutters and a lattice fence, posted to the Facebook group The Original Baltimore Past and Present Photos with the caption that it was constructed around 1876 as the country estate of Henry R. Wilson (1819-1905), located north of what is now East University Parkway between North Calvert Street and Greenmount Avenue. This was Oakenshawe, the Wilson family's summer place; Henry R. Wilson sold the land to the Mueller company early in the twentieth century, and by 1916 steam shovels were grading it for more than 350 houses on Calvert Street, University Parkway and the Guilford, Homewood, Oakenshaw and Birkwood terraces and places (Jacques Kelly, Sun, March 14, 2019). The Wilsons are the same family whose place the 1865 auction notice on the Passano-O'Neill York Road card names as adjoining a cottage 'on the west side of the York turnpike, three and a half miles from Baltimore city', and a Wilson house also appears as 'Oak Lawn' on the file's Vineyard Lane card. Filed on the Old Waverly dossier because no Corridor parcel covers the Oakenshawe ground.

summary: A black-and-white photograph, circulated by the Flickering Treasures project, of the Waverly Theatre's front: the original round-arched brick facade with WAVERLY worked into the brick over the entrance, a rectangular marquee lettered WAVERLY, and a tall vertical sign on a steel frame above the roof. Cobbled Greenmount Avenue with streetcar rails runs in the foreground; a shop awning is at left and a parked car at right. The Passano-O'Neill card says Benjamin Cluster's Crystal Amusement Company bought the house in 1920 and made the 1909 theatre the lobby of a 750-seat auditorium behind it, and that the Durkee chain, which took over in 1929, replaced Cluster's square marquee with a triangular one and removed the old vertical sign. Both the square marquee and the vertical sign are here, so the photograph dates between the February 1921 reopening and the Durkee changes of about 1929.

summary: A two-panel composite. Left, a Google Street View of the block about 2017: Shoe City in the old theatre front, with its stepped parapet clad in vertical metal siding, next to the 'Grocery & Dollar Mart' at 3209 and a nail spa beyond. Right, a black-and-white photograph of the same front in the 1970s: the marquee still reads WAVERLY but the attraction board says GOODWILL and 'Goodwill Industries', the sign of a bakery (the frame reads 'Buddi's Bakery', the Burri's French Bakery listed at 3215 from 1956 to 1978) is next door, a 'Kings' sign hangs at right, and a late-1960s sedan is parked out front. The Passano-O'Neill card has the theatre closing in 1969, Goodwill occupying it for about a decade, and Shoe City there since the early 1980s, so the photograph falls in the 1970s. The two panels show the marquee and stepped parapet survived into the Goodwill years and were stripped before the shoe store.

summary: A color photograph, posted by Marvin Welch to Baltimore Past and Present Photos on December 7, 2021 as 'The Old Waverly PS#51 School on 35th street near Memorial Stadium circa unknown'. It shows a three-story buff-brick school with a Spanish-baroque center gable, two copper-domed cupolas, an arched entrance porch and a corner lamp, with Memorial Stadium's light towers at left, a boarded one-story shop with a Diet-Rite Cola sign at right, and cars of about 1980 parked in front. The Passano-O'Neill card for 3226-3232 Greenmount says Public School No. 51 left the Greenmount site when it was demolished about 1911 for the extension of 33rd Street and got this new building at 800 East 34th Street, so the caption's '35th street' is off by a block; the building faced the 801-827 East 34th rowhouses across the street. summary: Jacques Kelly's columns of January 9, 2021, May 22, 2021 and January 1, 2022, and a March 9, 2024 follow-up, read through a summary rather than the full text. The 1870 Waverly Hall at Greenmount and 31st, a long-neglected building last the Northside Bar, once held a public school, a private library, a post office, a drugstore and a cigar factory making a 'Waverly' brand; named tenants include Forney's restaurant, the Northside tavern, Dr. Joseph Jameson's dental practice, and the Kelly brothers' grocery in the 1920s annex. The Central Baltimore Future Fund bought three contiguous vacant properties in 2018 for $414,000 (Corridor's deed shows $414,000 from WABKF LLC in November 2018) and, with State of Maryland support, planned a $1.5 million restoration into seven apartments and five retail spaces, with street-facing shops on Greenmount and 31st. Sarah Keogh, the Fund's executive director, and developers Ted Rouse and Jacob Wittenberg are named; Better Waverly, Abell and Waverly Main Street are credited with the push. When the boarding came off a painted 'Prescriptions' sign from the original drugstore appeared, and inside workers found a second-floor chamber with old-growth timber trusses and an unusually broad staircase. By January 2022 the interior had been gutted and rebuilt as loft apartments with a food operation at street level and tenants due to move in February 1. In March 2024 Kelly wrote that the Thai restaurant, after more than 23 years, was moving to the hall's rear annex on East 31st, the former Guilford Grocery Co. space, with Wittenberg as co-owner. Corridor's deed rows for the hall run from 1943 to 2023 and stop short of this story.
