summary: A Baltimore City Archives photograph: a two-story stuccoed corner building with 'Drugs, Run Right to Read's, Soda' on fascia boards along both faces, display windows lettered 'Perfumes' and 'Prescriptions', a recessed corner entry, an awning, pedestrians in 1940s coats, a barrier reading 'Street Closed' with a pile of dug-up earth and lumber at the curb, and at the right a square brick tower, which the Archives' own 'Then and Now' post of July 22, 2022 identifies as the tower of Engine Station No. 31. The Archives' caption says circa 1948, that William H. Read founded the Read Drug and Chemical Company in the 1890s, that the Nattans family bought the business in 1899 and grew the chain to about forty stores by 1934, that the Waverly store opened sometime in the 1920s, and that the building held a Rite Aid when the caption was written (Corridor's 2021 deed rows show a Walgreens parcel after a sale-leaseback, so the drugstore use has run for about a century). The barrier and rubble show street or utility work in front of the store. Commenters recall Read's as the after-school stop for snacks and ice cream (an Eastern High graduate of 1963), the prescription pads from Read's that got a doctor's patients a free ice-cream cone, a section of 'Miss Nancy' toys advertised on Romper Room, cherry sundaes, and the slogan 'Run Right to Read's'. This gives an address to the Read's that two other threads place 'with the Waverly' and 'on Greenmount and 32nd': 3133, at the corner of 32nd Street, with one storefront between it and the Engine 31 firehouse at 3121-3123, a short walk south of the Waverly Theatre. The Archives' 2022 post adds that Read's hosted Hendler's ice cream stands, that streetcar tracks show in the Belgian block street and the sidewalk on the north side of the store was under construction in the photograph, that a storefront then stood between Read's and the fire station but the two properties have since merged into one larger store, and that the corner held a Rite Aid until recently and is now a Dollar General (Corridor's 2021 deed rows show the sale-leaseback to DG Greenmount LLC).

summary: Facebook posts in the Baltimore Past and Present groups give the chain's history (text apparently from its public encyclopedia entry): Sunny's Surplus began in 1948 selling World War II surplus, taking the name of the first store's manager (another post credits the founder as Sidney Weinman); at its peak it had 29 stores in Maryland, Virginia and Delaware, added camping gear, and in 1990 renamed itself Sunny's The Affordable Outdoor Store. It filed Chapter 11 in 2000 and emerged 13 months later, filed a second time, began liquidation sales in January 2007 and closed its remaining stores on March 16, 2007; three stores briefly reopened that fall and closed again by March 2008. It appeared in Barry Levinson's 'Liberty Heights' and in 'Homicide'. The pictured store is, per a commenter, the Washington location in the former Joy Theatre building, not Waverly. Waverly's branch, which the Passano-O'Neill card puts in the one-story building at 3114-3116 that stood by 1956 and closed in 1995 (later The Red Shed), is remembered in other threads as where 'everybody got their army jackets'; Frank Mikulski, who managed a Sunny's store from 1990 to 1999, says the chain was hurt by expanding too quickly.

summary: Joe Stewart's 2009 photograph of the former home and office of Louis J. Aull, built in 1888 at 414 Waverly Avenue, at 3101 Talbot Street, now East 31st Street and Brentwood: a Queen Anne house in yellow clapboard with red scalloped shingles on the second-floor bay, teal trim, a pointed gable with a Gothic-arched attic window, a storefront-style ground floor of paned windows, a red door with a large red bow, deep snow on the roofs, and in front a big painted fish sculpture lettered 'We all swim...'. He notes that in the 1990s the space became a tea room celebrating old Waverly village and that merchants in this century added the 'Fish out of Water' sculpture. His notes on the family: Henry Jacob Aull, a Bavarian shoemaker, bought a gravel pit on the west side of the York Turnpike in the 1830s, built a house and opened a cobbler shop, 'considered to be the first non-agricultural enterprise' there, where there were said to be a corn-husk depot, a blacksmith and three small stone houses. Jacob Aull (1804-1876) and his wife Christiana Gusema (1812-1880) had five children: a daughter who married and whose name he has not found; two daughters who lived at 3116 Greenmount, Louisa Frederika and Margaret Eva; and two sons, Louis J. at 414 Waverly Avenue and Henry Jacob at Eagle Nest on York Road near 25th Street, both in building and real estate. That matches the Passano-O'Neill cards (the two Aull sisters at 3112-3116, and the 2520-2528 card, where the son is Jacob H. Aull, 1848-1921, and whose house Corridor's Old Land Marks rows call Eagle Nest) and Corridor's own rows on the 1836 cottage, Christiana's death in 1880 and Louis Aull's death at 414 in March 1912. Stewart's text uses 'Henry Jacob' for both the immigrant and the younger son; the cards give the father as Jacob (1805-1876) and the son as Jacob H. (born 1848).

summary: The Baltimore City Fire Department's Engine 31 page (Waverly's firehouse) posted: 'On this date in 2000, Truck 7 was disbanded.' Truck 7 had been housed with Engine 31 except for a short time before its disbandment, when it was moved to Engine 42. When Truck 7 left Waverly, Medic 3 was relocated in from the station it had shared with Engine 33 on Gorsuch Avenue. Medic 3 was itself disbanded in 2016 when the department went to a two-tier EMS system, and Ambulance 3 was placed in service at Engine 31's station. Code 3 Collectibles made a model of Truck 7's 1994 Seagrave tractor-drawn aerial (the post's picture is that model). Comments from firefighters and neighbors add that the house had been the No. 7 truckhouse and a chemical company before Engine 31 was organized there, and before that a Baltimore County volunteer and then career station (which fits the Passano-O'Neill card), that Engine 33's house closed and Engine 33 moved to a 25th Street station, with a firehouse later used for Ladder 49 (the comment does not say which), that Truck 7 later became Truck 5, and one who remembers visiting as a child in the white-and-orange paint days, the sirens 'like background music'. The Passano-O'Neill card leaves the year blank for when the station's truck company ended ('19__'); this post supplies 2000 for Truck 7. Corridor had no row for Engine 33's Gorsuch Avenue station, which is a lead for a parcel near Gorsuch.

summary: The handwritten caption on the print reads 'Aug 9 22, S. side 29th St. W. of York Road.' summary: A black-and-white view (it looks like a glass negative) of a wooden mansion with a tall two-story columned portico, a sweeping gravel drive, a huge shade tree, a picket fence and one boy in a white shirt standing near the porch. summary: The tour's opening history says that in 1688 Lord Baltimore granted estates known as Huntingdon and Merryman, that a settler named Thomas Gorsuch built a house here in 1736 and called it Homestead, and that the York Road followed a wooded rise called 'Britain's Ridge' between the Jones Falls and Herring Run. It says toll gates came off the road in 1894, that horse-drawn double-decker cars gave way to electric cars beginning in 1893, and that in 1886 the Gorsuch heirs subdivided their land into small cottages and country residences, which drove away an estate holder named Tinges (Tinges Lane lasted into the twenty-first century). It gives the street renamings as Jefferson to Homestead, Madison to Montpelier, Brady to 30th, Waverly to 31st and Republic to Frisby, the last to keep the memory of the vanishing Frisby Woods near 25th Street, where villagers picnicked and gathered berries, nuts and holly. It says that when the area was annexed in 1888, Henry Tyson, president of the York Road and City Passenger Railway, chose 'Waverly' for the new post office because Huntington was already taken. It quotes the 1878 Maryland Directory, which called Waverly 'pleasant and picturesque' and listed a postmistress, blacksmith, carriage maker, confectionery, druggists, florists, hotels, saloons and a shoemaker. Corridor already holds the toll gate, the Clemens subdivision of the Quaker lots as Friendship and Oxford, and the post-office history; the street renamings, the Tyson naming and the 1736 date are the parts not otherwise in the record here, and the 1736 Gorsuch date and the Tyson story are worth confirming against a deed or a Sun clipping. summary: Woods' Baltimore directory (no house numbers in Waverly before annexation): 'Lacey Wm, gardener, Waverley' 1878 and 1881; 'Lacey Wm, grocer, Waverley' 1883, 1884, 1886; 'Lacey Thos, clerk, Waverley' 1883-85. Polk (first numbered edition for Waverly, 1887): 'Lacey W, 1202 York rd' (1887 p. 1329); 'Lacey Wm., grocer, 1202 York rd' 1888 p. 671, 1889 p. 689, 1892 p. 724; the Polk business directories of 1890 and 1893-94 list 'Lacey Wm, 1202 York rd'. 'Lacey John, clerk' at 1202 in 1891 (p. 758) and 'Lacey John P., clerk' in 1892 (p. 724) is the son, b. 1873-04-07 (Maryland death record). The Sun supplies the family: William and Eliza Lacey, son Willie (12) dying from 1202 York road in May 1891; Eliza d. 1910-05-28. Why it matters for title: William Lacey is a gardener in Waverley in 1878 and a grocer by 1883, on Lots 16 and 17 of the Wilson plat, which the Wilson trustees sold to John Bolgiano in 1871 (Baltimore County E.H.A. 70/115). The land records name other holders of the leasehold in his years: Bolgiano leased the two lots to Bernard Bertling for 99 years at $200 a year on Sept. 21, 1876 (recited), Bertling assigned the lease to George Miller in 1880 (Baltimore County W.M.I. 119/71), and Miller's widow and executrix Elizabeth Mueller held it from 1888 until she sold it to John P. and Mary E. Lacey in 1904 (J.B. 1206/357; R.O. 2083/495). So William Lacey's grocery was evidently a tenancy under the Bertling and Miller leasehold, and his son's family bought the leasehold in 1904; no lease to William himself has been found. The 100-ft frontage and the 10-ft half-alley on the rear are the Wilson plat's.

summary: The Sun's news obituary of Saturday Sept 4, 1920 (p. 7, 'Obituary' column). John P. Lacey, 47, a grocer in Waverly, died Sept 3 at his home, 3326 Greenmount avenue, after a three-month illness from stomach trouble. Born in Baltimore; his father, the late William Lacey, owned the store on Greenmount avenue that the son had conducted since he was a youth (this ties the Polk line 'Lacey Wm, grocer, 1202 York rd' 1888-93 to this lot and this death). Member of St. Bernard's Catholic Church and of the Baltimore Council of the Elks. Survivors named: widow Mary E.; six sons William, John, Lambert, Charles, Lawrence and Eugene; two daughters Margaret and Josephine; a brother James D. Lacey of Wilmington, Del.; a sister Mrs. James T. Doyle of Hamilton. Funeral from St. Bernard's Tuesday morning, burial St. Mary's Cemetery, Govans. Age 47 puts his birth about 1872-73, so the 'Lacey John, clerk' at 1202 York rd in Polk 1891-92 is him at 18-19. The Polk 1921-23 lines 'Lacey John P (Mary E) grocer 3326' and the 1927 dealer list name him after he was dead: the firm and its listing kept his name (widow and sons; son Wm J. listed as clerk in 1922-23). A James T. Doyle estate exists in the Register of Wills, Baltimore City (174407, d. 1920-10-12), a possible but unproven match for the sister's husband.

summary: Sun, October 4, 1895, p. 10, news obituary: 'Mr. Abram G. Mott, whose age was about eighty-five years, died yesterday at his home, 918 York road, from pneumonia.' He had ridden the electric cars from Waverly to Towson and walked to the Timonium fair, caught a cold in the rain on the way home, and it became pneumonia. A Baltimorean by birth, until two years before he had been in the agricultural implement and seed business on Ensor Street near Belair Market; a Mason and Odd Fellow; his wife, formerly Miss Thompson, survived him; they had no children. So Mott was born about 1810 and died on October 3, 1895. He is the man the Passano-O'Neill card and Old Land Marks name as the first occupant of the frame house later numbered 3014; his own address is 918 York road, and which lot that was is contested.

summary: Woods' Baltimore City Directory lists Townsend S. Bonsall as 'keeper 1st tollgate, York' in every volume from 1871 to 1875 (printed pp. 64, 74, 71, 69 and 73). No house number is printed, because Waverly was Baltimore County ground until 1888, and Woods gives no place beyond 'York'; the Hopkins atlas of 1876 puts the first gate at the mouth of Gilmor's Lane. His listing in the 1876 and 1877 volumes has not been confirmed on the page. The Woods volumes of 1860-1870 name no keeper for this gate. Bonsall (1836-1877 on the St. John's Church interment roll) died in 1877, and his widow, Sarah A. Bonsall, succeeded him as Waverly's postmaster. Old Land Marks (about 1906) names the gate's keepers as David Mumma, William Eaton, T. S. Bonsal and T. Schofield.

summary: The Sunday Sun, July 28, 1907, p. 20. Headline block: 'PASSING OF TOLL GATE / House On York Road Is Soon To Be Demolished. / HAS SERVED MANY PURPOSES / Was Successively Country Store, Postoffice, Recruiting Station, Hospital And Private Residence.' The house at York road and Gilmor lane was to come down 'in a few days' for the paving that 'has gradually extended up the York road from North avenue'; it 'extends several feet over the street line', and the city had 'imperatively ordered' it demolished. The family of Mr. Charles Clarke moved out on Saturday, July 27, and the tearing down was to begin on Monday, July 29. The article says the house was built '130 years ago', according to the late David Mumma, 'who for nearly a decade collected tolls at the old gate'; that it served as the crossroads country store, the post office, a recruiting station for men to serve in the Mexican and Civil wars, and a hospital for fever-stricken soldiers 'sent to Gilmor lane'; and that the keepers held the gate 'until ten years ago, when the United Railways bought the road, ruts and all', after which 'the old place was idle for a long time. Lately it has been inhabited by private families.' It describes 'a long, low structure, lifted from parts of the low ground by piles of stones. It rambles in its one story and far back into a field', with rooms added by an early storekeeper 'of rapidly growing family'. The Baltimore County Union reprinted the article on Aug. 3, 1907, p. 3 ('The Old Waverly Toll-Gate House to Go'), and the Sunday Sun Magazine's 'This was Baltimore 50 years ago' column reprinted its opening in 1957. The article gives no house number and does not say which of the later lots 3026-3032 the house stood on; its '130 years' and 'ten years ago' differ from the Union's 'perhaps 150' years of 1900 and from the 1894 removal of the gate on the Passano-O'Neill card.

summary: The Sun's real-estate transfers of Dec. 17, 1912, p. 12: 'Jacob H. Aull and wife have sold to F. X. Hooper four lots on the west side of Greenmount avenue, near Gilmore lane, for $4,500 in fee. One lot measures 15 by 82 feet, and the other three 14 by 82 feet each.' The item gives no house numbers; the four lots have the shape of the row (15 + 14 + 14 + 14 = 57 ft, each 82 ft deep), 3026 and the three 14-ft bays 3028, 3030 and 3032. The deed behind it (S.C.L. 2787/376, Dec. 16, 1912) settles what was sold: Aull had leased the four new houses for 99 years to Alice M. Chapman on Dec. 6, 1912 at $72 and $66 a year (S.C.L. 2787/374), and Hooper bought the fee subject to that lease, 'particularly the aforesaid rents or reversions'. So '$4,500 in fee' is the price of the four ground rents, $270 a year capitalized at 6 per cent, not of four houses. The houses stayed under the lease, which is how Aull could still advertise 3026 and 3028 in July 1913 and sell houses of the row subject to ground rent in 1917 and 1918 (3026 to Spellman in Feb. 1917; lots to Shields and to Sanner, the families of 3032 and 3028, in Nov. 1918). The buyer, 'Frank X. Hooper of the County of Baltimore' in the deed, is probably the F. X. Hooper of the F. X. Hooper Company, the Glen Arm maker of corrugated-box machinery: the Sun of Feb. 3, 1914 (p. 12) records F. X. Hooper and wife conveying 2 acres at Glenarm, with the 'plant and good will of plant', to the F. X. Hooper Company for $150,000, and a Sun ad of Apr. 12, 1913 has him selling a small hotel at Lewes, Delaware. His testamentary trustee sold the 3028 rent in 1945 (M.L.P. 6799/549). The item spells the lane 'Gilmore' and calls the road 'Greenmount avenue'; the April 1912 notices said 'York road' and 'Gilmor'.

summary: The Sun of Nov. 27, 1920, p. 18: Mrs. Sarah A. Bonsall (nee Huff), 'one of the first woman postmasters', died Nov. 26 at her home, 3120 Greenmount Avenue, one block north of the toll-house lot. She was appointed postmaster of the Waverly post office to succeed her husband, Townsend S. Bonsall, 'who died about 40 years ago' (he kept the first tollgate in Woods' directories of 1871-1875 and died in 1877), and 'remained postmaster for 14 years', so to about 1891; she was the incumbent challenged for the post in April 1890. Survivors: a daughter, Miss Florence V. B. Bonsall, and a brother, Joseph Huff. The Evening Sun's death notice the same day (p. 11) gives the funeral from her home on Sunday at 3.30 p.m. and private interment in St. John's Cemetery, Waverly; the Baltimore City Register of Wills has her estate (174965, filed Feb. 10, 1921), and the St. John's interment roll lists her as Sarah Ann Huff Bonsall, 1849-1920. The item does not mention the toll house. Two accounts place the post office differently. Anna Cole (1933) says it was at the tollgate under T. S. Bonsal and that his widow moved it to rooms in the Hamilton Hotel after his death. Charles T. Leight's Sun Magazine memoir of 1949 says Mrs. T. S. Bonsal ran the toll gate after her husband died and that 'the toll-gate building also contained the post office', with her as postmistress. Both put the post office in the toll house in Townsend's time; they differ on whether it stayed there under her.

summary: The Sun of May 27, 1901, p. 7: 'The funeral of Mr. Tilghman Schofield, who was for 17 years keeper of the toll-gate on the York road at Waverly, took place yesterday [Sunday, May 26] from his home, 405 Montebello avenue.' The Rev. W. G. Herbert of the Caroline Street Methodist Episcopal Church officiated with the Rev. G. W. Feelemyer of the Waverly Church; a delegation came from Wilson Post, G.A.R., of which he was a member, and four men from Waverly Lodge, Knights of Honor, of which he was a charter member. The pallbearers were John Kahl, Charles Carroll, Charles Schofield, William H. Parker, H. Carroll and John Keller. Interment was in the Baltimore Cemetery; Henry C. Wiedefeld had charge. The death notice of May 25, 1901 (p. 4) gives the death: 'On Friday, May 24, at his late residence, No. 405 Montebello avenue, Waverly, TILGHMAN, in the 66th year of his age, beloved husband of Caroline Schofield.' He was a Union army man (the Sun of Oct. 15, 1892 says he was 'crippled in action'; Find a Grave gives Battery A, 1st Maryland Light Artillery). summary: The Baltimore County column of the Sun, Oct. 15, 1892, p. 10 ('The Assault on Toll-Gate Keeper Schofield'; the right edge of each line is cut in the copy). Schofield was beaten about the face with the butt end of a whip on Friday, Oct. 7, and was out again on Oct. 14. James Thompson, 'who lives in upper Baltimore county', was arrested on the charge; the hearing set for Oct. 12 was postponed to the following Wednesday because Schofield could not appear, and Thompson gave $1,000 bail. The men had had words about toll money; Schofield was knocked down, passers-by separated them, and a man named Hart (his title is cut) carried him into the toll-gate house and attended him: his nose was broken and he was cut over the right eye. The Sun adds that he received many complaints about the road, then being regraded, but was 'a general favorite with those who travel the York turnpike', deducted toll for the bad parts of the road, denied using the word thief, and had served in the Federal army and been crippled in action. The same day's front-page county digest says he is out of doors again. The column does not name the gate; it is the Waverly gate, which the directories give Schofield from 1878 to 1892, and the toll-gate house is probably the house the Sun described when it was pulled down in 1907. The details fit the elder Tilghman Schofield (born 1834-35), not his son.

Vinson and Kathryn R. Vinson his wife convey to Ella Thorington, for $5; the recital calls the lot 'now known as 3015 Greenmount Avenue' and recites the 1934 lease from Lillie E. Norris at $120 a year and the Phelps deed, 'under which the leasehold estate and the fee were merged and the said annual rent forever extinguished'. (3) July 11, 1944: Ella Thorington, unmarried, reconveys to Fletcher L. and Kathryn R. Vinson as tenants by the entireties (M.L.P. 6619/479, the deed the 1961 deed cites). Mildred R. De Rusha was witness and notary; all three were recorded July 12, 1944 (M. Luther Pittman, clerk). The same-day round trip through Thorington was a conveyancing step to create the joint tenancy, not a sale.

summary: Read on the scans. Randolph B. Mason assigns the 3017 leasehold to Michael G. Kilchenstein for $5 ($2 U.S. stamps, about $2,000) on April 28, 1921, reciting S.C.L. 2500/73 (S.C.L. 3785/519, recorded Oct. 5, 1921). The same day Kilchenstein mortgages it to the York Road Building Association of Baltimore City for an advance of $2,080 on 16 shares, 'being part purchase money' (S.C.L. 3785/520), and assigns it to the association by a deed of April 28, 1921, witnessed by Catherine Gossman, which was not recorded until Sept. 15, 1942, together with a confirmatory deed of May 11, 1942 (M.L.P. 6366/79 and 6366/80), both reciting the Mason deed and the $54 rent. Kilchenstein, who gave a purchase-money mortgage, was a financed buyer or the association's nominee rather than a bare straw; in 1930 he deeded a lot by Waverly Hall to Lennox B. Clemens (S.C.L. 5163/46). So the association named in the 1923 directory and in the Sunday meeting lists of 1925-26 held 3017 from 1921, under an assignment not recorded until 1942.

summary: Read on the scan (M.L.P. 6413, pp. 491-492). J. Calvin Carney and Harry E. Parkhurst, receivers for the York Road Building Association of Baltimore City under Circuit Court No. 2 of Baltimore City in William A. Kreisel v. The York Road Building Association of Baltimore City (Docket 50A, folio 542), authorized by an order of Oct. 13, 1942 'to sell the leasehold property known as No 3017 Greenmount Avenue', sold it to Fletcher L. Vinson and Kathryn R. Vinson his wife for $5,700; the deed is dated Jan. 6, 1943 (Mary Davie, notary) and was recorded Jan. 12, 1943. 'FOR TITLE see deed from Michael G Kilchenstein to the York Road Building Association ... Liber MLP No 6366 folio 79 also Confirmatory Deed ... Liber MLP No 6366 folio 80 subject to the payment of the annual ground rent of fifty four dollars'. The same day the Vinsons mortgaged it to the Premier Building Association for $2,500 on 20 shares (M.L.P. 6413/492). With 3015 already theirs, the Vinsons now held both buildings. The leasehold of 3017 ran from Clemens Jr. (to 1909) to Randolph B. Mason (1909-21), the York Road Building Association (1921-43) and the Vinsons (from 1943); they bought the fee from Harry R. Sinclair and wife in 1951 (M.L.P. 8666/310, recited in the 1961 deed, not read). Who held the fee before Sinclair is not known. Fisher's Manual of Valuable and Worthless Securities (1946) indexes the association under 'Md. 1944'. Correction/pointer, Oct. 13, 2026: who held the 3017 reversion before the Sinclairs is read in M.L.P. 8666/310 (721:mdlr-mlp8666-310-sinclair-vinson-3017-1951): Leopold Lehman, then his widow Mary C. Lehmann (will W.J.P. 16/78; her son Ernest George died c. Jan. 13, 1924), who sold the Sinclairs on Dec. 21, 1946 (M.L.P. 7060/156); the Sinclairs sold the Vinsons the reversion on Dec. 20, 1951, merging the lease and extinguishing the $54 rent.

summary: Eight volumes (1903, 1904, 1905, 1906, 1907, 1908, 1909, 1912; 1910 and 1911 are not available) print 'Rahe Louis W, shoes, 1007 York rd'; the 1909 entry continues 'h 105 Tinges la', with no '1/2' after 1007 (page image read). Der Deutsche Correspondent's list of Democratic candidates of Sept. 25, 1909 also prints 'Louis W. Rahe, Nr. 1007 York-Road'. The 1915 Sanborn plate puts 1007 on the brick office at 3015 and 1007 1/2 on the frame store at 3017, and the land records show that Charles M. Rahe bought the 15-foot lot that is 3015 in March 1902, the year before Louis W. is first listed at 1007. So the shop of these years was in the 3015 brick building: the directory lines are certain, the building is an inference from the plate and the deed. In 1907 and 1908 Rahe was also agent for a flour line at the same address ('Lewis W Rahe, agt, flour, 1007 York rd', Crescent Milling Co.).

summary: Polk 1913 and 1914 print 'Rahe Louis W, shoes, 1009 York rd, h 105 Tinges la' (1913 page image read). The 1914 volume also prints 'Rahe Louis W, real estate, 3017 Greenmt av, h 105 Tinges la' and lists him at 3017 among real-estate agents; the 1915 volume prints 'Louis W, boots and shoes, 3017 Greenmt av, h 505 e 28th'. The Maryland Manual notary lists print 'Rahe, Louis W., 1007 York Road' for 1913-14 and '3017 Greenmount Ave.' for 1914-15 and 1915-16. 1009 York rd was a shoemakers' stand in these years: Polk lists Samuel Piazzo there in 1909, the shoemaker Louis Stoler in 1912, and the Waverly Electric Shoe Repairing Co. as well as Rahe in 1913; Stoler moved to his own shop at 3208 Greenmount in 1913. Which building 1009 was, 3017 or 3019, is not settled (Polk has the York Road Building Association at 1009 York rd in 1909 and at 3019 from 1912). The probable reading is that the shop left the 3015 brick in 1913, when the O'Mailey Mfg. Co. was already using it, and settled in the larger two-story frame store at 3017.

summary: The Sun of Sept. 16, 1904: 'Bequests of Chas. M. Rahe / Leaves Fair Oak Avenue Dwelling To Widow For Life'. The will, admitted to probate the day before (Sept. 15), gives the widow, Mrs. Mary E. Rahe, the dwelling 2 Fair Oak avenue, Waverly, with its furniture, free of taxes and repairs, for life; the residue is held in trust, the widow to receive $50 a month and the house expenses and the balance to be divided equally among the eight children, named here: Miss Sophia W. Rahe, Lewis [Louis] W. Rahe, Mrs. Eva E. Tilling, John G., Mary G., Eleanor E., Herman W. and Charles M. Rahe Jr.; John G.'s share is held in trust until he is 40; $100 marriage portions; Thomas Mackenzie is executor without bond; the will was executed Dec. 3, 1903, and the testator died Sept. 12. The Court of Appeals quotes the same will in Reilly v. MacKenzie, 151 Md. 216 (1926), and the Circuit Court's opinion below (Mackenzie v. Mackenzie, 4 Balt. C. Rep. 450, Feb. 16, 1926) gives the death date: 'The testator died on September 12th, 1904, leaving a wife, Mary E. Rahe and eight children surviving him.' This is the trust whose trustee sold the 3015 lot in 1926 (S.C.L. 4613/367); the dwelling it left the widow is the house at 600 E 31st, and Herman W. Rahe is the lessor of that lot in 1931. The page number was not captured.

summary: Polk 1913 (page image read, leaf 1444): "O'Mailey Mnfg Co (John A O'Mailey), flavoring extracts, 3015 Greenmt av" and "O'Mailey John A (O'Mailey Mnfg Co), h 426 e 21st n". The firm is not in Polk 1912, which lists John A. O'Mailey only at 2103 E. Madison St., nor in 1914 or 1915. Its newspaper advertisements give 3015 Greenmount from Sept. 22, 1912 (salesmen for extracts) to January 1913 (shoe polish). So the tenancy ran from about September 1912 into 1913, in the 3015 brick after the Rahe shoe shop moved next door, and it is the earliest use found of the number 3015, while Polk still printed the old York road numbers. The O'Mailey family had been leather dealers ('O'Mailey John & Co', 221 S. Sharp St., Polk 1908). No charter or trademark was found for the firm.

summary: The Evening Sun of Wednesday, Feb. 2, 1955, p. 38: Dr. Fletcher L. Vinson, 57, 'widely known veterinarian and dog-show judge', died that morning at Union Memorial Hospital after a heart attack ten days earlier. 'Born in Alabama in 1897, Dr. Vinson was graduated from Alabama Polytechnic Institute in 1918, and came to Baltimore in 1931, establishing an animal hospital.' He was a member of the State Board of Veterinary Medical Examiners, president of the English Setters Association of America and of the Baltimore County Kennel Club, and a member of the American Animal Hospital Association and the AVMA; he lived at Glen Arm, where he raised prize cattle. Survivors: his wife, Mrs. Katherine Robertson Vinson, a daughter, a sister, Ethel Vinson, and 'a brother, Dr. Curtis B. Vinson', who is Dr. Bryant Curtis Vinson with the names reversed. The Sun's longer obituary of Feb. 3, 1955 (p. 17) says his services to pets had 'endeared him to thousands of Baltimoreans for almost 24 years' (that is, from 1931), that 'His hospital in the 3000 block of Greenmount avenue was widely known as a treatment center for small animals, especially cats and dogs', that he helped organize the Baltimore Kennel Club, and that the funeral would be on Saturday, Feb. 5, at Trinity Protestant Episcopal Church in the Long Green Valley, with burial in its churchyard. Find a Grave (memorial 54520050) gives Fletcher Leroy Vinson, Aug. 4, 1897 to Feb. 2, 1955, buried at Trinity Episcopal Church Cemetery, Glen Arm, and links a wife, Margaret Cotton Vinson (1895-1971), probably the Margaret C. Vinson of the 1934 deed. The 1931 date fits the hospital's opening (at 3013, March 1931), not his arrival: the AVMA journal of October 1929 lists him at 426 W. North Ave., Baltimore. The AVMA journal of April 1955 misdates his death to Feb. 3.

summary: The Evening Sun of Friday, June 18, 1982, p. 47: services for Dr. Bryant C. Vinson, 'who operated a veterinary hospital in Waverly for more than 20 years before his retirement in 1975', at the Lassahn funeral establishment, 7401 Belair road. He was 72 and died on Wednesday (June 16) of cancer at his home in the 3300 block of Beverly road. 'He joined two older brothers in practicing at the hospital in the 3000 block Greenmount avenue in 1930 after graduating from the Auburn University veterinary school.' He was president of the Baltimore County Kennel Club for many years, a life member of the American and Maryland State veterinary associations, a native of Loachapoka, Ala., a Mason (Highland Lodge, Scottish Rite, Boumi Temple), and a supporter of animal research at Cornell and at the Auburn veterinary school. Survivors included a sister and a nephew, Dr. Edmund H. James Jr. of Towson, the hospital's long-time associate. Find a Grave (memorial 270514793) gives Bryant Curtis Vinson, Aug. 9, 1909 to June 16, 1982, buried at Dulaney Valley Memorial Gardens, Timonium. His retirement year, 1975, is the year Vinson's Animal Hospital, Inc. was chartered.

summary: Known from the recital in every later description of the 3015 lot (1902, 1982, 2001, 2004, 2016): the 3015 lot begins 175 feet 7 inches south of the two-mile stone in front of the Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church lot and runs 15 feet south 'to the northwest corner of a lot of ground conveyed by Augustus D. Clemens, Jr., and wife, to William L. Fink, by Deed dated April 12, 1898', recorded in Liber R.O. No. 1729, folio 241. The 3013 lot's own description (R.H.B. 3116/428, 1974; F.M.C. 9050, p. 275, 2007) begins exactly there, 190 feet 7 inches south of the same stone, and runs 14 feet south. So the Fink lot is 3013, the lot the 1915 Sanborn plate numbers 1005 York road. The 3015 lot was 'a portion of the ground' Clemens Jr. had bought from a Keller, widower, on Dec. 20, 1897 (R.O. 1710/105, recited in the 1902 deed); the Fink lot very probably came out of the same purchase. The buyer was very probably the William L. Fink whom Polk lists in Waverly from 1889 to 1892: 'fancy gds, 1039 York rd, h 845 do' (1889), then 'dry gds, 1047 York rd, h 845 do' (1890-92). Woods and Polk carry a William L. Fink as a shoemaker and shoe dealer downtown from 1865 to 1888 (East Lombard, East Baltimore and North Eutaw streets), probably the same man. Bertha Fink kept a dry goods store on the lot, at 1005 York road, from 1901 to 1904, with her home at the same 845 York road, so she belonged to his household. A William L. Fink died July 8, 1946 (Baltimore City estate OLD45631); whether he is the grantee is not known. The deed itself has not been read. Correction/pointer, Oct. 13, 2026: the deed is read (720:mdlr-ro1729-241-clemens-fink-1898, R.O. 1729/241): it is dated April 18, 1898 and recorded April 20 (not April 12); the price is $500, fee simple; and the parent ground came from Shepard G. Miller, widower, by a deed of Dec. 20, 1897 at R.O. 1710/153, not from 'a Keller' at 1710/105.

By Polk 1903 the Rahe shop is at 1007 York rd, the 3015 brick, on a lot Charles M. Rahe bought in March 1902. Woods directories of 1871 to 1886 list Charles Rahe, shoemaker, at Waverly from 1871 and Louis W. from 1881, without house numbers.

summary: Recited in the 1970, 1982 and 2016 deeds: the lot is part of the land 'formerly belonging to said Jacob Aull as designated on a plot of said property heretofore prepared for said Jacob Aull by Augustus Bouldin surveyor and since filed with a lease to Martin Kratt', recorded in Baltimore County Liber E.H.A. No. 67, folio 488, in or near 'the village of Huntingdon' (Waverly's old name), at the corner of Old York Road and an avenue 45 1/2 feet wide now 31st Street. The description is fixed from a lot sold to John Litzinger by Henry N. Bowerman, Walter T. Allender, Jacob Hoke and Henry Hammond and their wives (date not given). E.H.A. is the Baltimore County series of the clerk Edward H. Ady: Liber 65 was recorded in March 1870 and Liber 70 in January 1871, so No. 67 dates from 1870. The ground was in Baltimore County until the 1888 annexation. Neither the lease nor the plat has been read.

summary: The Baltimore Sun of Sept. 12, 1996 reports the death of Edward P. Rahe Sr., a retired Bethlehem Steel Corp. shipbuilding executive, of cancer at St. Joseph Medical Center; the Towson resident was 81. He was technical superintendent and assistant plant manager at the Key Highway shipyard from 1938 to 1977, was 'born and raised in Govans', graduated from Polytechnic in 1932 and from the University of Maryland in electrical engineering in 1935 (the Terrapin of 1935 lists 'Edward Preston Rahe, Baltimore, Md., Engineering'), and was a 45-year member of Towson United Methodist Church. His wife of 58 years was the former Bettie Cake (Bettie Cake Rahe died in 2011). The match to Edward Preston Rahe and Bettie C. Rahe, who sold 600 E 31st to Bryant C. Vinson in 1970, rests on his full name and his wife's. The obituary names no parents; the 1970 deed recites that he received the lot under the will of Eleanore L. Cooksey, a Rahe by birth, so he was a relation of the shoemaker family, though how is not shown.

summary: Lease dated Feb. 7, 1887, Baltimore County land records (Waverly was county ground until the 1888 annexation took effect): Augustus D. Clemens Junior and Mary Clemens, his wife, of Baltimore County, to William H. Oliver of the same county, two lots on the west side of the York Turnpike Road. The first is 17 x 120 ft beginning 100 ft south of Calvin Avenue (today 3360 Greenmount) at $51 a year; the second is 16 x 120 ft at 117 ft south of Calvin Avenue (the next lot south) at $48 a year; each from May 1, 1887, payable May 1 and Nov. 1, for 99 years renewable, each lot liable only for its own rent, with re-entry after 60 days' arrears. The lots are parts of lots 4 and 3 on a plat filed with William H. Brune Jr.'s 1886 lease to Clemens (J.W.S. 153/55); Clemens held the fee by deed of May 1, 1886 from Thomas J. Wilson and Henry R. Wilson, trustees (J.W.S. 153/52, as the 1887 Fuller deed, J.W.S. 162/110, and the 1886 Henry deed, J.W.S. 157/35, both cite it; J.W.S. 152/527, given here before, is a farm deed, read October 14). The lot is identified by its own description and by four later instruments that recite this lease (S.C.L. 2440/335, S.C.L. 2427/497, J.W.S. 164/231, and R.O. 2164/97 onward to the deeds that say 'known as 3360'). The $51 rent created here ran until Greenmount Avenue LLC redeemed it from Middlebury College in 2016. Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): Clemens sold this lot's fee and $51 rent to Charlotte B. Fuller on June 20, 1887 for $886.95 (785:mdlr-jws162-110-clemens-fuller-51-rent-reversion-1887); the lot was not in his 1886 sale and lease-back to Brune (785:mdlr-jws153-60-brune-clemens-lease-end-sale-leaseback-1886). Update Oct. 14, 2026 (later): Clemens's fee is read (785:mdlr-jws153-52-wilson-trustees-clemens-lots-18-28-1886): Lots 18 to 28 of the June 20, 1871 Wilson equity plat, $16,000, May 1, 1886.

summary: Assignment dated Sept. 3, 1887, Baltimore County land records: William H. Oliver of Baltimore County to Laura A. Phillips, wife of Solomon Phillips, for $1,200, the lot on the west side of the York Turnpike Road 100 ft south of Calvin Avenue, subject to the $51 rent under Clemens Jr.'s lease of Feb. 7, 1887 (J.W.S. 158/447), 'Together with the buildings thereupon'. A price of $1,200 for a leasehold that still owed the full $51 rent implies improvements on the lot by September 1887 (inference, probable); 'together with the buildings thereupon' is standard wording and proves nothing by itself. Laura A. Phillips held the leasehold 18 years, to 1905: she owned the building while the Boehm grocery (1890-93), a grocery offered for sale in 1896 and Tom Lee's laundry (1901-04) were listed at 1214 York road (the tie of the 1890s number 1214 to this lot is probable).

summary: Assignment dated Dec. 14, 1907, recorded Dec. 16 (Stephen C. Little, clerk): Francesco Zito to Grafton Lloyd Rogers of Baltimore, for $5 and other valuable considerations, the leasehold of the lot on the west side of the York Turnpike Road 100 ft south of Calvin Avenue, subject to the $51 ground rent. Recital: Zito had it from Michael J. Fitzpatrick (R.O. 2308/167, Feb. 8, 1907). Rogers was a lawyer and real-estate man (Polk 1905; office at 611 Equitable Building 1907-1914) who advertised the store himself in 1909 and 1914. He held the building until his death on Jan. 16, 1955; his executors conveyed it to his sons in 1961 and the sons sold it to the Robinsons in 1967. So the tenants from the 1908 Cornett eating house to the 1950s Appliance Center probably all rented from the Rogers family (no lease is recorded).

summary: Deed dated May 25, 1908 (the July 30, 1908 deed to George W. Kimball (will dated Oct. 29, 1901, Baltimore County wills H.B. 13/324), to herself, with Edward Norris Kimball and Charlotte Stuart Kimball joining. The trust's real estate was the reversions in 28 Baltimore City lots and their ground rents. Lot 27 (p. 501) is the $51 rent on the lot on the west side of the York Road 100 ft south of Calvin Avenue, under Clemens Jr.'s 1887 lease to William H. Oliver. The deed also cites ('See also') a deed from Clemens to Charlotte B. Fuller of June 20, 1887 (Baltimore County J.W.S. 162/110), probably his sale of the newly created rent; that deed has not been examined. Kimball's title came through the Fuller family: the wills of Richard Fuller (J.H.B. 43/143), Charlotte B. Fuller (R.T.B. 59/91) and Florence Fuller (T.W.M. 77/51), a deed Florence Fuller to Richard F. Kimball of July 16, 1890 (J.B. 1302/143) and a partition of June 9, 1891 (J.B. 1347/150). Two months later Jane McNeale Kimball sold the 3360 rent to George W. Walther (S.C.L. 2440/335). Update Oct. 14, 2026 (late): three of the cited instruments are pulled: the Fuller deed (785:mdlr-jws162-110-clemens-fuller-51-rent-reversion-1887, $886.95, this lot only); Florence Fuller's 1890 deed to Kimball, a blanket assignment of her share under her father Richard Fuller's will that names no lot (785:mdlr-jb1302-143-florence-fuller-kimball-assignment-1890); and J.B. 1347/150, which holds no partition (785:negative-jb1347-150-no-fuller-kimball-partition).

summary: Lease dated Dec. 6, 1912, acknowledged that day before a Baltimore County notary and recorded Dec. 16, 1912 (Stephen C. Little, clerk), read on the page image of the handwritten record copy: Jacob H. Aull and Mary A. J. Aull, his wife, of Baltimore County, to Alice M. Chapman of Baltimore City, 'all those four lots of ground' on the west side of Greenmount Avenue (formerly the York Turnpike Road) at Vineyard Lane (formerly Gilmor Lane). The first lot is the corner, 15 ft on the avenue and 82 ft deep to a 4-ft alley (3026); the second, third and fourth are 14 x 82 ft lots beginning 15, 29 and 43 ft north of the lane (3028, 3030, 3032), the fourth running to the northernmost outline of the lot the Baltimore and Yorktown Turnpike Road company deeded to Aull on March 6, 1912 (S.C.L. 2727/29). Each lot is bounded through the partition wall between 'the house erected on the lot now being described' and its neighbour, so the four houses stood by Dec. 6, 1912. Term 99 years from Dec. 1, 1912, renewable forever on a $1 fine; rent $72 a year on the corner lot and $66 on each of the other three, half-yearly on June 1 and Dec. 1. Ten days later, on the day this lease was recorded, Aull sold the four rents to Frank X. Hooper (S.C.L. 2787/376), whose deed says the lease was 'recorded prior to the execution hereof'. The lease does not say that Chapman was a nominee, but the pattern, a lease to an individual followed by the sale of the rents while Aull himself advertised and sold the houses from 1913, is the usual one for a Baltimore builder creating ground rents. The date: the lease's own date line and Aull's deed to Hooper say Dec. 6, as does a 1975 recital (R.H.B. 3207/655); the 1945 deed of the 3028 rent recites the lease as 'December 12th 1912' (M.L.P. 6799/549). Lot one, 3026, is the separate parcel next door. Update Oct. 16, 2026 (1929 and 1935 read): S.C.L. 5517/92 (MSA CE 168-5525, read; 726:mdlr-scl5517-92-hooper-trustees-waverly-bldg-redemption-3030-1935) is the deed of Feb. 18, 1935 by which Mercantile Trust Company of Baltimore and William Jenkins, trustees under Francis X. Hooper's will, on the Waverly Building Association's statutory notice to redeem, conveyed it the 1912 $66 reversion on 3030 for $1,100, 'to the end and intent that the leasehold estate created by the lease aforesaid shall be merged with the fee'. So the trustees of the 1935 recitals are Hooper's, and the 1912 lease and rent on 3030 merged in the Association by that deed, not by inference. S.C.L. 5076/70 and /71 (MSA CE 168-5084, read) show how the leasehold reached the McCoys: Jacob H. Aull's executors deeded it to his widow Mary A. J. Recital: 'Being the same parcel of ground which by deed dated the 1st day of October A.D. 1880 and recorded among the Land Records of Baltimore County in Liber W.M.I. No. 119 fol. 71 &c. was granted to said George Muller from Bernard Bertling and wife.' The recital calls the 1880 buyer 'George Muller' and cites the 1880 deed, in which he is 'George Miller of the City of Baltimore' (W.M.I. 119/71), so the George Miller of 1880 and the John George Mueller of 1888 are one man. The parcel had come into the city with the annexation of 1888.

summary: Confirmatory deed dated March 6, 2015, recorded March 27, 2015 ('NO TITLE SEARCH / No CONSIDERATION'), read on its first page (folio 76; pages 77-81 not read). The volume is L.G.A. 17028. The directors-trustees of The Miller Realty Corporation, as grantor, quitclaim to Max Properties, Inc., for 'Zero Dollars ($0.00)', Ward 12, Section 18, Block 3884, Lot 036, described in the recital as 'a 25' x 60' lot on the east side of Brentwood Avenue 110 feet north of Venable Avenue'. summary: Handwritten indenture dated Feb. 29, 1848, acknowledged that day in Baltimore City and received for record March 30, 1848 (Baltimore County Court land records; A. W. Bradford, clerk), read on the page image. The volume is a Baltimore County one (MSA CE 66-444): Waverly was county ground until 1888. John D. Nicoll of Baltimore County to Lorentz Leicht of the same county, 'in consideration of the sum of Two hundred Dollars current money', assigns the lot beginning 'at a stone planted in the ground at the corner of the York Turnpike Road and the Lane leading to Mr. Gilmor's', running 36 ft south on the road, 76 ft 4 in west, 38 ft north and 76 ft 6 in east, 'Being a part of a tract of land conveyed by a certain David Mumma to the said John D. Nicoll by his certain deed of Lease' dated Jan. 21, 1846 (A.W.B. 372/234, opened on Oct. 12, 2026: it holds no Mumma lease, see 719:negative-awb-372-234-mumma-nicoll-lease), for the rest of that renewable term, subject to 'the yearly rent of Nine Dollars current money' to Nicoll from Feb. 1, 1848. Witnesses Wm. Stansbury and Edw. J. Peters. The dimensions are exactly those of the 3020 corner lot in the deeds of 1953, 1954 and 1956, which still bound the 3010 lot on 'the sub-lease from John D. Nicholl to Lorenz Leight', so Lorentz Leicht is the cabinetmaker Lawrence Leight (1809-1892) of the lane corner. Old Land Marks dates his house there to 1845, before both this sub-lease and Mumma's 1846 lease to Nicoll; either the family occupied the corner before the leases were written or the tradition's year is early. David Mumma is the first of the toll-gate keepers Old Land Marks names, and the turnpike company's 1912 deed ties the north corner of the lane to a stone marking the beginning of land conveyed to him in 184[4]: Mumma's ground probably lay on both sides of Gilmor Lane. Update Oct. 13, 2026: the $9 rent of this sub-lease is traced: Abraham G. Mott 'bought out' the original (Mumma) rent on the whole lot (Balt. Co. J.B. 96/352, not read), so the $9 became an original rent; Mott sold it with the rest to Dodson and Griffith in 1892 (J.B. 1422/568); they sold it to Mary Clemens on May 7, 1896 (719:mdlr-ro1619-244-dodson-griffith-mary-clemens-9-dollar-rent-1896); and she merged it into the Leights' leasehold on June 9, 1924 (719:mdlr-scl4210-380-mary-clemens-leight-3020-merger-1924). Update Oct. 14, 2026: the parent lease of 1846 was at $32 a year (719:mdlr-jb96-352-mumma-heirs-mott-1876); Abraham G. Mott held Nicoll's leasehold from Samuel Hamilton Caughy by an assignment of Oct. 4, 1860 (Balt. Co. G.H.C. 30/473) and bought the fee in 1876, after which this $9 sub-rent was his to collect. Update Oct. 14, 2026: Nicoll made a second sub-lease out of the same Mumma lot a year before this one: to Franklin Wilson, Feb. 7, 1847, at $7 a year (A.W.B. 378/206, recited in 719:mdlr-ghc30-473-caughy-mott-1860), which Caughy bought back in 1855. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the head lease this sub-lease rests on is read (719:mdlr-awb372-23-mumma-nicoll-lease-1846, A.W.B. 372/23, Jan. 21, 1846), and so is Nicoll's earlier sub-lease to Franklin Wilson, dated Feb. 27, 1847 (not Feb. 7 as the 1860 deed recites) (719:mdlr-awb378-206-nicoll-franklin-wilson-sublease-1847).

summary: Deed made March 2, 1953, read on the page image (The Maryland Title Guarantee Company; Maryland stamps cancelled March 3, 1953): Charles T. Leight, widower, of Baltimore City, to Jacob Rashbaum and Rheba Rashbaum, his wife, as tenants by the entireties, for $5 and other considerations, 'those three lots': (1) the corner of the west side of Greenmount Avenue (formerly York Turnpike Road) and the south side of Vineyard Lane, 36 ft by 76 ft 4 in, No. 3020; (2) from 36 ft south of the corner, 67 ft 11 2/5 in on the avenue to the southern outline of the land formerly of Mary Clemens, 215 ft deep, wrapping around the lot of 'the Sub-Lease from John D. Nicholl to Lorenz Leight' (A.W.B. 394/156), No. 3010; (3) a lot on the southeast side of Vineyard Lane beside the lot Mary Clemens leased to Allen K. Wood in 1901 (R.O. 1928/77). Federal documentary stamps $20 + $10 + $5 + $2 + $1 + 50 cents = $38.50, seventy units of $500 at 55 cents: a price of about $35,000. Recitals: 3020 from William H. Flayhart, Jr. and wife to Charles T. and Ella B. Leight, Oct. 5, 1932 (S.C.L. 5328/111); 3010 by assignment from Lula Smith to Charles T. and Ella B. Leight, Oct. 31, 1931 (S.C.L. 5263/428), 'The said Ella B. Leight having since died thereby vesting full interest' in Charles T. Leight, with further deeds from William H. Wolfe and wife of June 21, 1948 (M.L.P. 7491/449) and Oct. 24, 1950 (M.L.P. 8259/53); the lane lot from William H. Wolfe and wife, Feb. 4, 1953. The 1932 grantor was the husband of Leight's daughter Catherine, so the corner stayed in the family. Leight, 'formerly of 3020 Greenmount avenue' in his death notice, died five months after the sale, on Aug. 12, 1953. The sale ended more than a century of the Leight family at the corner (the sub-lease of 1848, A.W.B. 394/156). Update Oct. 12, 2026: the Leights' title to these lots is now read: 3020 was bought as a leasehold in 1919 and its reversion in 1924 (S.C.L. 5328/110 recites both); 3010's $180 leasehold was bought in 1927, put in the Wolfe and Leight entireties in 1931 (S.C.L. 5263/428), and merged into the fee by the Wolfes' deed to Charles T. Leight on Oct. 24, 1950 (M.L.P. 8259/53, 719:mdlr-mlp8259-53-wolfe-leight-reversion-3010-1950). Update Oct. 13, 2026: the Vineyard Lane lot's deed is read (719:mdlr-mlp9085-398-wolfe-leight-vineyard-lane-lot-1953): William H. and Carrie Wolfe to Charles T. Leight, Feb. 4, 1953, M.L.P. 9085/398, recorded Mar. 3, 1953 at 1 p.m.; and the Rashbaums gave Leight a mortgage on the three lots recorded the same day (M.L.P. 9085/395), released in September 1953 by Catherine B. Flayhart as executrix of his will.

summary: Deed made Sept. 22, 1954, acknowledged that day, read on the page image (The Title Guarantee Company, application H-9852): Jacob Rashbaum and Rheba Rashbaum, his wife, of Baltimore City, to Costanza Construction Company, Inc., a Maryland corporation, for $5 and other valuable considerations, in fee simple, the same three lots (3020 at the corner; 3010 around the Nicholl-to-Leight sub-lease lot of A.W.B. 394/156; the Vineyard Lane lot). Stamps: federal $30 + $30 + about 50 cents, about $60.50, or 110 units of $500 at 55 cents; Maryland $22 + $22 + $11 and a partly legible fourth: a price of about $55,000. Recital: the March 2, 1953 deed from Charles T. Leight, widower (M.L.P. 9085/400). The Rashbaums held the ground about 18 months and sold for about $20,000 more than the stamps show they paid. The 3010 bay was already trading as a self-service laundry by May 1954, four months before this deed, so it went up while the Rashbaums held the ground (who built it is not recorded), and the Sun's March 21, 1954 offer of the '105x286' lot at 3010-3020, which names no seller, was probably theirs. Under Costanza ownership the rest of the row followed, 3012 by late 1955, 3020 in 1956, 3014 in 1957 and 3016 in 1958; Edward Costanza is named as builder at 3014 and 3016.

summary: Deed made March 13, 1956, read on the page image: Costanza Construction Company, Inc. to Edward Costanza of Baltimore City, for $5 and other good and valuable considerations, in fee simple, four lots: (1) the corner lot at the south side of Vineyard Lane (formerly Gilmore Lane), 36 ft on Greenmount, 'No. 3020 Greenmount Avenue'; (2) 67 ft 11 2/5 in on the avenue 'to a boundary stone and the southernmost outline of the whole land formerly belonging to Mary Clemens', 215 ft west, around the lot of 'the sub-lease from John D. Nicholl to Lorenz Leight' (A.W.B. 394/156), 'No. 3010 Greenmount Avenue'; (3) the lot on the southeast side of Vineyard Lane beside Allen K. Wood's 1901 lease (R.O. 1928/77); (4) 105 Witherspoon Road, Lot 63, Block 5, Plat of Homeland, which the company had from Chester C. Jennings, trustee, in 1949 (M.L.P. 7792/242). Federal documentary stamps $10 + $5 + $1 + 40 cents + 20 cents + ten of $10 = $116.60, about $106,000 at 55 cents per $500, but for all four lots, so they do not price the Greenmount ground. Recital: 'The first 3 lots being the same lots or parcels of ground which by deed dated September 22, 1954 ... Liber M.L.P. 9590, folio 2, were granted and conveyed by Jacob Rashbaum and Rheba Rashbaum, his wife, unto the party of the first part'. 105 Witherspoon Road was the home of Edward F. Costanza, the builder who founded the company, at his death on Dec. 17, 1960, which ties the grantee to him. The deed came in the middle of the build-out (3012 by late 1955, 3020 in 1956, 3014 in 1957, 3016 in 1958); the 1985 trustee's deed calls the Greenmount ground 'part of the first two lots' of this deed.

summary: Deed made April 16, 1985, received for record April 29, 1985, read on the page image: The First National Bank of Maryland, surviving trustee under the will of Edward Costanza, to Warren Komins and Jack I. Needle, as tenants in common, for 'the sum of One Hundred Ten Thousand Dollars ($110,000.00)', in fee simple, 'Lot B as shown on plat entitled "Subdivision Plan, Property of Estate of Edward Costanza", which Plat has been recorded among the Land Records of Baltimore City in Plat Pocket Folder No. 2989. The improvements thereon to be known as Nos. 3010, 3012, 3014, and 3016-3020 Greenmount Avenue.' Recitals: Edward Costanza, owner of the lot, died on or about Dec. 17, 1960; his will (Register of Wills L.C.S. 281/43) named First National Bank of Baltimore (now First National Bank of Maryland) and Paul Berman trustees of the residue of his estate, which included the lot, and Berman has since died. Title: 'part of the first two lots' of the March 13, 1956 deed from Costanza Construction Company, Inc. to Edward Costanza (M.L.P. 10063/7). The bank's acknowledgment is dated 'the 1st day of April, 1985', fifteen days before the date the deed bears; the record copy does not explain the difference. The row stayed in the builder's testamentary trust for 24 years (the city's owner roster of about 1977 lists 3010-3016 under Edward Costanza in care of the bank), and Plat Pocket Folder 2989 was on record by April 1985.

summary: The Sun's real-estate transfers of Sunday, Feb. 18, 1917, p. 15, print two lines about the row that Jacob H. Aull built on the old toll-house lot in 1912: 'Jacob H. Aull to John T. Spellman, Jr., and wife, n.w.c. Greenmount ave. and Vineyard lane, g.r. $72.' and 'Alice M. Chapman to Jacob H. Aull, 4 lots.' The northwest corner of Greenmount Avenue and Vineyard Lane is 3026, and $72 is the yearly rent that the lease of Dec. 6, 1912 put on the corner lot (the other three lots paid $66 each; S.C.L. 2787/374). Read together, the lines show the four leaseholds that Aull had put in Alice M. Chapman's name in 1912 most probably coming back to him, and the Spellmans buying the 3026 house subject to the ground rent, which Frank X. Hooper had owned since Dec. 16, 1912 (S.C.L. 2787/376). The column gives no price and no liber. It is the earliest record of the Spellman family as owners of 3026; Polk's 1917 directory lists John T. Spellman Jr., plumber, living in the house ('h 3026 Greenmt av'), so he may have been there as a tenant before the purchase. The family held the house until Dec. 8, 2006 (FMC 8778/605, recited in FMC 9256/107). The directories of 1912 and 1913 have him a few doors north ('Leight L Wm, 1144 York rd'). The lot, scaled from the plate, falls within today's 3302 Greenmount (block 3883 lot 002), the ground on which the Boulevard Theatre was built in 1921, which must have replaced the house and shop. Earlier lines at '3340 York rd' (John M. Foster, carpenter, 1908; Benjamin F. Lusby Jr. and William W. Lusby, decorator, 1909) may be this house or a number farther out the York Road and are not placed.

summary: Known from recitals only; the 1910 deed itself has not been read. The 1969 executor's deed (R.H.B. 2529/79), the 1989 confirmatory deed (S.E.B. 2000/313) and the 2016 deed (MB 18621/389) all describe a second lot beginning on the west side of the York Turnpike Road 100 ft north of Wilson Street (Venable Avenue), 25 ft on the turnpike and 120 ft deep to a 10-ft alley, and the 1969 deed recites it as 'the same lot of ground which by Deed dated November 15, 1910 and recorded among the Land Records of Baltimore City in Liber S.C.L. No. 2620, folio 254 was granted and conveyed by James D. Lacey, unmarried, to John P. Lacey ... and Mary E. Lacey, his wife, in fee simple.' It is the north 25 ft of today's lot 002 (about where 3336 and 3338 stand), held in fee while the 100 ft to the south was a leasehold under the $200 rent. On the 1889 ward plat the same 25 ft is William Gutman's, with a one-story brick store; how it passed from Gutman to James D. Lacey is not known. James D. Lacey was a clerk and then a salesman living at 186 Old York Road (Polk 1905-1909: 'Lacey Jas P, clk' and 'Lacey Jas D, salesman'), the house from which Eliza Lacey, John P. Lacey's mother, was buried in May 1910, and was with the Southern Thread Co. in 1912-13; he was evidently John P.'s brother, which no record read here states. The deed came six months after Eliza Lacey's death. summary: Known only from a recital in the 1989 confirmatory deed (S.E.B. 2000/313, Exhibit A, Parcel 3), read on the scan; the 1972 deed itself has not been read: 'BEING also the same lots of ground which by Deed of Reversion dated January 17, 1972, by and between Mercantile-Safe Deposit and Trust Company, as Trustee under a Deed of Trust from Mary Mildred Hazen and Joseph T. Hazen, dated December 28, 1935, and Mercantile-Safe Deposit and Trust Company as Trustee under a Deed of Trust from Jane Collison Weiss and Frederick A. Weiss, and The Miller Realty Corporation ... which Deed was recorded on January 18, 1972 among the Land Records of Baltimore City, Maryland, in Liber R.H.B. No. 2876, folio 259.' A deed of reversion from the owner of a ground rent to the leaseholder is the usual way a rent is bought in, so this was evidently Miller Realty's purchase of the $200 rent that John Bolgiano reserved when he leased Lots 16 and 17 to Bernard Bertling in 1876, and that the 1969 sale ad called irredeemable; the recital gives no price and does not say in terms that the rent was extinguished. If so, the Hazen and Weiss trusts held the rent by 1972; how it reached them from Bolgiano is not known. The rent lay on the south 100 ft of the corner: all of 3326-3332 and the south 30 ft of the 3334-3338 lot.

summary: Thompson's plats of the 21st and 22nd Wards (1889), Section 3, 7th Precinct (Maryland State Archives frame 0553), west side of the York Road from Wilson Street (Venable Avenue) north: 'Mrs. E. Miller', 82 ft by 155, '2 S. B. Store & D., 1 1/2 S. F. Stab., 2 S. F. B. S. Shop, 2-1 S. F. Sheds' (a 2-story brick store and dwelling, a 1 1/2-story frame stable, a 2-story frame shop, evidently a blacksmith shop, and two one-story frame sheds; the plat does not say where on the 82 ft each stood); 'J. B. Henry', 18 ft, 'Vacant'; 'Wm. Gutman', 25 ft, '1 S. B. Store'; then A. D. Clemens 16 ft ('1 S. B. Store'), Mrs. W. Gards 16 ft, S. Phillips 17 ft and a last lot of 16 ft. Miller's 82 ft plus Henry's 18 ft are the 100 ft of Lots 16 and 17 of the deeds, and Gutman's 25 ft is the lot James D. Lacey deeded in 1910; so today's lot 002 (70 to 125 ft from Venable) was the north 12 ft of Miller's lot, all of Henry's and all of Gutman's. 'Mrs. E. Miller' is Elizabeth Mueller, widow and executrix of John George Mueller, who had bought the leasehold of the 100 ft in 1880 as George Miller and whose executrix assigned it to herself in 1888 (J.B. 1206/357); she sold it to the Laceys in 1904. Henry is John B. Henry of J. B. Henry & Sons, blacksmiths at 1204 York Road in the directories of these years, so the shop on Miller's lot was probably his firm's. Gutman was a butcher and provisions dealer ('Gutman Wm, prov, 1210 York rd', Polk 1889).

summary: Polk lines at 1206 York Road: 'Irwin John, tinner, 1206 York rd' (1890 p. 626; 1892 p. 628, home Woodberry); 'Jones Wm H, blksmith, 1206 York rd' (1901 p. 794); 'Franklin Morris, blksmith, 1206 York rd' (1905 p. 609; 1907 p. 700; 1908 p. 757; 1909 p. 762; 'carriage bldr' in 1906); 'Rainey Robt, plumber, 1206 York rd, h 1015' (1906 p. 1646, a branch of the plumber of 1015 York Road); 'Brooks Wm A, carp, 1206 York rd, h 3109' (1908 p. 395). The 1915 and 1928 Sanborn plates print '1206', with no newer number, on the south part of today's lot 002, where the 1915 plate shows a 1 1/2-story frame building marked 'VACANT (OLD)'; that these directory lines belong to that building assumes the number stayed on the same lot from 1890 to 1915, which is probable for the Franklin years and less sure for 1890. Whether the building was the '2 S. F. B. S. Shop' of the 1889 ward plat is not established: that shop stood somewhere on Mrs. Miller's 82 ft, the plat calls it two stories, and the ground the 1915 plate marks 1206 was mostly J. B. Henry's lot, vacant in 1889. A smith's and wagon-builder's shop in 1901 and 1905-1909, it stood empty in 1915, was an open shed in 1928 and was gone by May 1950. Morris Franklin later appears at 1045 York Road (1909), 1204 York Road (1912) and 3337 Greenmount (1914-1918), a junk dealer by 1918.

summary: Polk 1888: 'Gutman Wm, butcher, Waverly'. Polk 1889: 'Gutman Wm, prov, 1210 York rd, h 430 Calvin av'. Polk 1891 and 1892: 'Gutman Wm, butcher, 170 Old York rd'. The 1889 ward plat names 'Wm. Gutman' as owner of a 25-ft lot with a one-story brick store, 100 to 125 ft north of Wilson Street: the lot that is now the north part of 3334-3338. That his provisions store of 1889 was the brick store on his own lot is probable, not proved: the 1915 Sanborn prints 1210 on a one-story brick store two lots farther north, and shows only a frame bicycle shop on this lot, so either the numbers shifted between 1889 and 1915 or his store stood on the neighbouring ground. No Baltimore City estate for a William Gutman is indexed, and how the lot passed to James D. Lacey by 1910 is not known. Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1910 Lacey deed names no Gutman (778:mdlr-scl2620-254-james-d-lacey-john-p-mary-e-lacey-two-lots-1910); the Laceys had their two lots from Henry W. Fox, trustee (Oct. 25, 1898, R.O. 1758/40) and Wilhelmina McLaughlin (1904). A trustee's sale in 1898 is the likelier route from Gutman (inference). Update Oct. 14, 2026: the 1898 trustee's deed (778:mdlr-ro1758-40-fox-trustee-lacey-25ft-lot-waverly-building-assn-henry-1898) names no Gutman: the lot was John B. Henry's, mortgaged in 1895 and sold under a 1898 decree, and lies in the 1886 Brune-to-Clemens lease plat (Lot 1 and part of Lot 2). Update Oct. 14, 2026: the Henrys owned the lot in fee from 1886 (778:mdlr-jb1546-108-henry-waverly-building-assn-mortgage-1895), so William Gutman, on the 1889 plat, was probably their tenant (inference).

summary: Sun, Sunday, May 4, 1969, p. 87, Auction Sales (Sam W. Pattison & Co., auctioneers): 'EXECUTOR'S SALE. VALUABLE FEE SIMPLE AND LEASEHOLD COMMERCIAL AND RESIDENTIAL PROPERTIES 3326-28-30-32-34-36 & 38 GREENMOUNT AVE. AND 412 AND 414 VENABLE AVE.', offered under the will of Mary E. Lacey on the premises on Monday, May 5, 1969, at 2 p.m. For this lot: '3334 Improved by a one-story brick building with store front. Central air conditioning. 3336 and 38: Each improved by a one-story brick building with store fronts.' The Venable Avenue houses and 3326 had monthly tenants; 'The other properties are under leases.' 'The northern 25 ft. of this parcel is in fee simple. The southern portion (100 ft.) is subject to an irredeemable ground rent of $200.00.' Total yearly income about $17,000; offered as an entirety; William John Lacey, executor. The sale became the deed of June 17, 1969 to The Miller Realty Corporation. The Democratic Association of the First Precinct of the above District will meet at Sinclair's Hall, Waverley, on Wednesday evening, July 5th, at 8 o'clock', signed John Erdman, Jr., Chairman. summary: The Sun of April 13, 1888, under 'For Annexation. Enthusiastic Belt Meetings. Mayor Latrobe Takes the Stump': 'A rousing annexation meeting was what the Waverly Annexation Club held last night at Sinclair's Hall, corner of York road and Merryman's lane. Not only was the seating capacity of the hall occupied, but an interested and enthusiastic crowd stood in the aisles and at the rear of the hall. Mr. Geo. W. Hyde presided, and F. N. Hoen was secretary.' Mayor Latrobe then spoke for extending the city over the Belt. The club's notice of April 10 had called it the 'first mass-meeting under the auspices of the Waverly Annexation Club, Sinclair's Hall, Thursday, April 12, 8 P.M.', with Winfield J. Taylor, John V. L. Findlay and C. Bohn Slingluff to speak and Gen. F. C. Latrobe to attend. That spring the hall served both sides: annexationists 'crowded Sinclair's Hall, at Waverly, almost to suffocation' on May 4 (Sun, May 5), and 'the anti-annexationists held a meeting in Sinclair Hall, Waverly' (Sun, May 15). On July 18 a meeting 'of those in favor of opening Jefferson street' was held there (Sun, July 19). Placement on this parcel is an inference. The notices say only the corner; James E. Sinclair had lots on both sides of the lane; and Polk's 1888 directory lists the tinner Wallace W. Sinclair and the Waverly Cornet Band at 1102 York road, the apex building, which makes its upper floor the probable hall. The corner south of the lane, where the Sinclair tinshop stood by 1900, is not excluded.

summary: The Sun of November 24, 1888, 'Protest Against Election Arrests': 'About a hundred citizens of the twenty-second ward met at Sinclair's Hall, York road and Merryman's lane, last night and protested against the arrest of three colored men of the ward, John Payne, Horace Holmes and Louis Cheeseman, on the night of November 5. They were charged with registering illegally, and, after being held for five days, were dismissed by the grand jury.' Louis P. Hennighausen said that 'part of the evidence against these citizens was part of a scheme and conspiracy to defraud the people of Baltimore in the election'. Charles C. Cox said: 'When we came into the city I did not expect that the twenty-second ward would be so suddenly plunged into the contamination to which the other wards in the city had been schooled.' Addresses were also made by E. A. McAllister, Henry Lingenfelder (the print is worn), James E. Hooker, F. Albert Kurtz, A. Pillsbury, A. A. Reinhardt 'and James Robson, colored'. The meeting resolved that 'the arrests were instigated and made with the intention of depriving the men of their votes at the presidential election' and 'that the instigators and perpetrators be brought to justice'. The call, printed the day before, was for an 'indignation meeting' at 'Sinclair's Hall, York road and Merryman's lane, to take action about the unlawful arrest of citizens of the ward on the evening of November 5', signed E. J. Guyton, Secretary. November 5, 1888 was the eve of the presidential election. The hall is placed on this parcel by inference, not by any notice: see the entry for the annexation meeting of April 1888.

summary: These reports are about the chain whose restaurant stood on this corner, not about this restaurant by name. Afro-American, December 22, 1956: an interracial group of 45 staged a sit-in at the White Coffee Pot in a northwest Baltimore shopping center, and Jerome and Myles Katz, owners of the chain, are reported as saying that 'fear of loss in revenue was their reason for keeping the restaurants for white only'. March 30, 1957: a citizens' committee had been trying for six months to make the chain change its practice; the centre of the dispute was the Mondawmin restaurant, with pickets also at the Monroe and Edmondson, Howard and Baltimore, and Park Heights and Belvedere restaurants. September 20, 1958: Myles Katz reported to police that a Black customer had sat down at a counter where, in the paper's words, 'colored persons are only allowed to obtain "carry-out" orders'. October 8, 1960: the actress Diana Sands told the paper that she and Lonnie Elder went to the White Coffee Pot near the theatre and were told 'Only carry out'. Against these, the Sun's obituary of Alan R. Katz (January 24, 2020) quotes a family member: 'The restaurants were integrated in the 1950s before it became federal law.' The two accounts disagree. The contemporary reports show the carry-out-only rule in force at named restaurants as late as October 1960. None of the four names the restaurant at 32nd and Greenmount, and when it first seated Black customers is not documented here.

summary: Thompson's 1889 plats of the 21st and 22nd Wards (6th Precinct, Sec. 2, p. 132) draw the wedge between the York Road and Old York Road. The southernmost lot is marked '88.' along the York Road and '8.' across its cut-off point. The name 'Miss Tredway / Jno. T. Ensor Guardian' is lettered across it and the two lots north of it, which are 62 ft and 63 ft on the York Road (the '60.' and '34' printed on Old York Road belong to those two lots, not to the tip). The improvements printed on the tip lot are '2 S. B. B., 2 S. B. B. B., 1 1/2 S. F. B. B., 1 S. F. Shop'. Read against the plat's other entries ('2 S. F. D.' for a two-story frame dwelling, '2 S. F. B. B.' for a frame back building), that is a two-story brick building, a two-story brick back building, a story-and-a-half frame back building and a one-story frame shop. The plat does not show where on the 88 ft they stood. The later deeds give 3011 and 3013 together 72 ft 4 in from an 8 ft 6 in point, and 87 ft 4 in with the 15-ft lot of 3015. So the 1889 tip lot either took in the 3015 ground as well, or was measured from a point further south before the east line of Greenmount Avenue was fixed in 1898; the plat alone does not settle which. Either way it covers the ground of 3011 and 3013. The directories of 1888 and 1889 put a shoe store at 1001 York road and the justice of the peace at 1003, the two old numbers the 1915 Sanborn plate prints on the two-story brick shop at the tip, and Bromley's 1896 atlas draws a brick building at the tip with open ground north of it. The brick building of the plat was therefore probably at the tip, on the site of 3011, and the frame shop may be the 1005 York road store (3013) where Joseph J. Willis, carpenter, was listed from 1887 to 1889. Neither placement is printed on the plat.

summary: Polk's bank pages of 1889 and 1890, read on the page images, list the North Baltimore Savings Bank with a main office on West North Avenue (No. 2 in 1889, No. 4 in 1890) and 'Branches, 1003 York rd, open Saturday, from 5 to 8 P M, 15 North, open from 10 A M to 2 P M'. The officers are J. M. Littig, president, and F. D. Morrison, treasurer, in 1889; F. D. Morrison, president, and Townsend Scott, treasurer, in 1890. The alphabetical entries repeat the branch: 'branches, 15 w North av, 1003 York rd' (1890) and 'branches 15 w North av and 1003 York rd' (1891). No entry for the bank was found in the text of the 1892 volume. The bank was two years old. The Baltimore County Union of May 21, 1887 (p. 3, 'A Belt Savings Bank') reports that 'the citizens of the Belt and North Baltimore held a meeting on Monday night, for the purpose of organizing a savings bank to be located in the Belt', F. D. Morrison presiding, with directors Robertson Taylor, Calvin T. Davidson, John H. Wight, John M. Littig, John S. Ditch, Fred. D. Morrison, John W. Mittendorf, John H. Grimes, Ernest Hoen, Wm. H. Moffit Jr., James H. Smith and Ogden A. Kirkland; 'The bank will be known as the North Baltimore Savings Bank of Baltimore County.' The issue of June 11, 1887 notes its articles of incorporation filed with the County Clerk. The Belt was the county strip annexed to the city in 1888. (The 1887 items were read in the Library of Congress text of the pages, not on the images.) 1003 York road is the north block of today's 3011 Greenmount, the same address as the justice of the peace's office in these years.

summary: Polk lists 'Wright Wm D, justice of the peace, 1003 York rd' from 1888 to 1892; from 1901 to 1908 he is 'real estate, 1003 York rd', living at 650 York road (1901-04) and 2642 York road (1905-08). The business directories of 1890 and 1893 also list him at 1003; the residential volumes of 1893 to 1900 and 1902 are not available. Constables shared the address: 'Mahool Thos, constable, 1003 York rd' in 1888, and George Wise in the business lists of 1890 ('Wise Geo W', a misprinted initial) and 1893 ('Wise Geo Y'); the residential volumes have 'Wise Geo Y, constable' at Gutman Avenue (1890) and at 55 Mount Street, Waverly (1891-92). Wright was the village magistrate before the annexation of 1888: Woods prints 'Wright Wm. D. clerk, Waverley' in 1882 and 'Wright Wm. D. magistrate, Waverley' in 1884, 1885 and 1886, and a William D. Wright at Peabody Heights near Waverly from 1872. The 2013 National Register inventory says of 3011 that 'it was the office of local magistrate W.D. Wright'. A Thomas Mahool appears in Woods as a partner in Sears & Mahool (1879-80) and Mahool & Probest (1881-82), commission merchants, 'Waverley'. Whether the constable was that man, and whether either was related to Mayor J. Barry Mahool (1907-11), is not established. In 1909 the number is Winfield S. Brannock's, carpenter. 1003 York road is the north block of today's 3011: the 1928 Sanborn plate prints '3011 / 1003' on the building. The lines of 1889 to 1908 were checked on the page images; the 1888 line and the Woods entries are from the directory text.

summary: Two Polk publications of 1905, both read on the page images, disagree by one digit. Polk's Baltimore business directory for 1905-06 lists under Undertakers 'Brooks Robt & Son, 1204 w Balto, 17 s Calhoun and 1001 York rd'. The Baltimore city directory for 1905 prints the firm's own entry as 'BROOKS ROBERT & SON (Robert and Robert L Brooks), Undertakers, 1204-1206 w Balto, 3101 York rd and 17 s Calhoun', and its classified list as '17 s Calhoun and 3101 York rd'. 1001 York road is the tip block of today's 3011, between the Rahe shoe store (there to 1901) and James M. Sinclair's tin shop (from 1907). 3101 York road was also a real address in these years, in the block above 31st Street: the 1904 directory has a confectioner there and the 1905 a laborer, and other 3100-block numbers were already in use beside the old 1000 numbers. Which printing is the misprint has not been settled, so the branch cannot be placed at 3011 with confidence. Neither the 1904 nor the 1906 and 1907 directories list a York road branch for the firm.

summary: Polk lists 'Fink Bertha, dry gds, 1005 York rd, h 845 do' in 1901, 1903 and 1904. 1005 York road is the 14-ft lot conveyed to William L. Fink in April 1898, and 845 York road was his home when he kept a dry goods store at 1047 York road in 1890-92, so Bertha Fink was of his household and the family ran its store on its own lot. From 1905 the store is Rosa Vicary's: 'Vicary Rosa, dry gds, 1005 York rd, h 1429 Patterson av' (1905), then 'h 1837 Pa av' (1906-08), and 'Vicary Rosa, milliner, 1005 York rd, h 1837 Pa av' in 1909. She had been a dressmaker at 805 South Sharp Street (1888-90) and a partner in Ankrim & Vicary, 4 South Broadway (1892). By 1913 the store is Harry Peiser's tailor shop, under the new number 3013. The lines were checked on the page images; the homes and earlier careers are from the directory text. summary: Banner investigation of vacancy in the Waverly Main Street Historic District (Greenmount Ave, 29th to 35th St): more than 1 in 4 buildings appear empty. Community leaders blame landlord Matt Herman, whose LLCs own 11 Greenmount Ave properties, most with empty storefronts and about $123,000 in unpaid water bills; his spokesperson says he is in talks to sell most of the portfolio. Herman-owned buildings named: 3028 (Barrus Real Estate Group office), 3030 (yoga contest space, vacant notice), 3026 (proposed cafe, collapsing porch, vacant notice), 3326 (former Mayflower Chinese, empty 5+ years), 3313 (former Zehbras Fitness). Also profiles Red Emma's at 3128 (bought and renovated buildings Herman had acquired for under $400,000 in 2016, $1.6M total) and Jinji's Chocolate at 3100 (opened Oct 2023). Quotes Kate Khatib (Red Emma's) and Jeff Jetton (Toki Underground).

summary: Baltimore Small Business Coalition pushes City Council for a Small Business Bill of Rights (90 days' notice before rent increases or evictions, landlord duty to maintain structure and utilities). Lead example: Jeanelle Spencer of Zehbras CrossFit, now at 3302 Greenmount Ave (opened 2024). Her first attempt, in early 2023 at a long-vacant Greenmount building owned by 3313 Greenmount Avenue LLC, stalled after the landlord never supplied gas or running water and the roof leaked; when she asked for proof of work the landlord terminated the lease. She sued, and a judge ruled in 2026 that the landlord breached the contract and owes her $75,000 in buildout costs; the landlord has appealed and she has not been paid.

summary: Roberta Sheridan, colored, was appointed a teacher at the Waverly colored public school. The Sun called it the first appointment of a colored teacher in Baltimore, made under an ordinance passed before annexation that colored teachers be appointed to all colored schools coming into the city's possession. She was born in Baltimore and graduated from the colored high and grammar school and the colored normal school. The item adds that another colored teacher would be appointed to the Waverly school the following week, and notes the growth of the Belt schools since annexation.

summary: A front-page Afro-American story said Baltimore was paying tribute to George W. Biddle, 'oldest public school-teacher,' retired on pension the previous week by the School Board after his years of service, 37 of them in the city schools. Born in South Baltimore 72 years earlier and privately schooled, he was given his first school in Carroll County at 20, then transferred to Kent County, 'and later to Baltimore County and Waverly. He became a part of the City System when Waverly was incorporated with Baltimore.' He was the first colored principal in the city when School No. 9 on Carrollton avenue was turned over to colored people, taught in seven schools, and for the past 12 years was principal of the Argyle avenue school. School 118's faculty gave him a reception at the Community House and the Principals' Association presented a gold watch. He quoted Dr. J. H. N. summary: The Afro-American's front-page obituary called George W. Biddle the first colored principal of a Baltimore public school and, until his retirement in 1926, the oldest teacher in the system. He was 84 and had been a teacher and public figure for fifty-two years; the board retired him in 1926 at 72. Educated in private schools, he first taught in Carroll County at 20, and also taught in Kent and Baltimore counties 'and in Waverly.' The paper wrote: 'It was while teaching at the Waverly school he became a part of the Baltimore system by the incorporation of that section as a part of the city.' When School No. 9 on Carrollton Avenue was turned over to colored people he became its principal, the first colored principal to head a school in the city; he taught in seven schools and spent his last twelve active years as principal of the Argyle Avenue School.
